descs.en: She saw through the guard nobody else noticed. He has spent ten years making people disappear, and now he wants to disappear with her.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
At a government reception on Battery Hill, sixty guards watch the guests. One of them watches a single man for forty-one minutes, and the only person who notices is Serafina Song, there on a staff pass to inspect a red rally car, in her sister’s dress and her own boots.

She walks across the ballroom and tells him he isn’t a guard. She’s right. Qin Haozhen has spent ten years making people disappear for a state that doesn’t put its name on doors, and nobody has ever looked at him before.

She asks him for a race, not a date. A man who sleeps four hours a night in any bed in any country falls asleep in her passenger seat at three in the morning, and keeps coming back.

Spy and racing driver · She sees him first · Morally grey hero · Complete in four volumes, plus side stories

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
In Terms, Serafina turned up at her sister’s wedding in Milan after two years’ silence, with oil on her boots, and drove the bride away from her own reception. I always wanted to know who could keep up with her.

The answer was the most forgettable man in the room. Haozhen isn’t a good man when this book begins, and it doesn’t pretend he is. It’s about a man finding out he’s allowed to want something, starting with an egg sandwich, and a woman who decides every morning whether she can live with the truth about him.

The racing is as real as I could make it. The spy work stays at story level. And yes, the car really can do two hundred miles an hour. He did the brakes.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers.

A fast, funny book, with some hard moments:

• A state operative’s work, including abductions and killings, mostly remembered

• A man taken from his family in front of his young son

• Trauma, depression and silence after a mission

• A cruel parent and a family’s money troubles

• Threats and surveillance

• A car chase, gunfire and a gunshot wound, stitched without a doctor

• A serious racing crash and a long recovery

• Illegal street racing

• Love scenes on the page

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Nonna — Serafina’s red 1992 Italian rally hatchback, named after their grandmother.
Gilded — Team AURELIA’s matte black race car, number 7, with AURELIA in gold on the bonnet.
Nobody — The getaway car: a grey 2006 estate with wooden-bead seat covers and an engine it should never have had.
Two Hundred — A burnt-out 1991 endurance prototype, bought for scrap.
The garage — Under the railway bridge in the industrial district. Trains every eleven minutes.
Granny Shum’s — The Saturday street races by the paint works: the long straight, the S-bends, the lamp posts round the gas works.
The Needle — The hairpin at the end of the back straight at the circuit in the north.
The Eleventh — The Bureau Haozhen worked for, in a building with no name on it.
Brake on the marker — Braking exactly at the board, to the metre.
Telemetry — The car’s data: speed, throttle, brake and steering, a thousand times a second.

chapters.title: The Guard Nobody Else Noticed
chapters.desc: Serafina is on Battery Hill to check a car for a forged plate, and she spots a guard who isn’t guarding anyone. So she walks over and tells him.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re the only one looking at the right person.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Serafina Song noticed about the man was that he wasn’t looking at anyone.

It was an odd quality in a security guard. The Autumn Reception filled the old Residence on Battery Hill on the twenty-second of October: white columns, a lawn lit gold, a string quartet under the stone arches, four hundred guests checked twice at the gate. Waiters went round with silver trays, and everybody in the building was looking at somebody.

Except him.

He stood by the east service door in a black suit, white shirt, earpiece. Relaxed, almost careless, hands loose in front of him. He wasn’t sweeping the crowd. He wasn’t watching the door. Every so often his eyes went to the long dark windows, where the whole room hung reflected, and then came back. Serafina, who had come in by the kitchens on a pass that said VEHICLE SPECIALIST, LOT 9, stopped with a glass of sparkling water halfway to her mouth.

Interesting.

She had spent the last forty minutes on her back on the floor of the glass pavilion at the end of the east terrace, in her sister’s dress, with a torch in her teeth. Lot 9 was a red Italian rally car from 1974, short as a sneeze and low as a cat, the kind that had won the world championship three years running and still looked like something a boy drew in the back of a maths lesson. Signor Bassi wanted it. He was eighty-one, he lived on Lake Como with eleven cars and a parrot, he had known Nonna in Milan, and he had said on the phone that morning, “Your grandmother would have looked and found nothing, cara, and called me an idiot for wanting it. So I pay you, and you tell me the truth.”

The truth was on the chassis plate. Right shape, right number, wrong rivets: too clean, too round, nothing a Turin factory had put on a car in 1974. Somebody had swapped it and aged the paint round it with what she was almost certain was cold tea. She had taken four photographs, sent them to Signor Bassi, and brushed the dust off Aurelia’s dress, which was too short on her by a hand, like everything of Aurelia’s, and stopped two fingers above her boots. There were limits to what a person did for a car. Borrowing shoes had been one of them.

Which left her with time, and a guard who was doing a remarkably poor job of looking like one.

There were sixty guards in the building. She had counted them on the way in, a habit she had caught off her sister and never managed to give back. Fifty-nine of them did the same thing: a slow, bored sweep of the room, and a long loving look at the prawns. The sixtieth was watching one man. Tall, fair, grey suit, under the third chandelier, with a glass of champagne he hadn’t touched. The guard looked at the door, the windows, and back at the fair man, every time. A compass needle that kept finding north.

She went over. She knew it was stupid halfway across the floor, the way she always knew a gap was too small about one second after she’d gone for it. She went anyway.

“You’re not a guard.”

He turned his head. Dark eyes, calm, unusually still. A face you could stand next to in a lift and never describe to the police afterwards, except for a tiny notch through the end of the left eyebrow, like a pen that had skipped.

“Am I not?”

“No.”

“That’s unfortunate,” he said. His voice was low and level and entirely without embarrassment.

“You’re standing at an entrance, and you haven’t looked at it in four minutes. You haven’t checked anybody coming through, and two waiters have passed you twice without you noticing them.”

“Perhaps I’m a very trusting person.”

“With an earpiece?”

“Fashion.”

She laughed. Not loudly, but it moved the corner of his mouth. Barely. She noticed.

“Your shoes are wrong, too. Everyone else working tonight has been up and down between the service yard and the lawn. Their shoes are wet. Yours are dry, and they’ve been resoled with something thin and grippy. Who expects to run on marble?” She took a sip of water. “I work with expensive cars. People lie about their condition all the time. Sometimes they even forge their identities.”

Something in his face went still. Not much. A fractional quiet at the corners of his eyes.

“You’ve been watching the fair man for forty-one minutes,” she said. “Third chandelier, a glass he isn’t drinking. Everyone in this room is looking at somebody. The consul’s wife is looking at the consul’s assistant. The guards are looking at the prawns. You’re the only one looking at the right person.” She tilted her head. “You’re not here to protect anyone. You’re here to make sure someone gets out.”

He looked at her then. Two seconds. Three. It went all the way in, like a torch into an engine bay, and she had the strangest feeling he had just read the old burn on the back of her right hand, the oil on her thumb, the boots and her pulse, and filed the lot in order.

“Miss,” he said, “you should be enjoying your evening.”

“That sounds suspiciously like advice.”

“It is.”

“Are you always this friendly?”

“Only when people ask questions they shouldn’t.”

“Then I’ll stop.”

“Will you?”

“No.”

This time he almost smiled. Then he reached out and took the torch out of her hand. She had forgotten she was holding it. It was still switched on, making a bright small circle on his lapel. He clicked it off with his thumb, put it back in her palm, and folded her fingers round it with his own. Warm. Dry. Far too close for a staff door.

“So is that,” he said, for her only.

Over his shoulder, the fair man had put down his glass and was kissing a consulate woman on both cheeks. The guard turned to go, and his jacket swung open, and for one second, upside down on the card clipped inside it, she read QIN H. before the cloth fell back.

“Good evening, Miss Song,” he said.

She blinked. “Oh. You know my name.”

He didn’t answer. He walked away across the room without hurrying, and people shifted out of his path without knowing they’d done it. He spoke three words to the fair man. They went out through the east door together.

To anyone watching, it was a guest and his security. Serafina watched until the glass doors closed behind them, and then she frowned.

✦ ✦ ✦

His name was Qin Haozhen. At least, that was the name on the card inside his jacket.

He had been in the building for forty-three minutes, and the assignment was simple. Keep eyes on Lucien Marchal, a Belgian logistics consultant who had been careless with other people’s money and other people’s governments. Walk him out of the east door and hand him on. Nobody was supposed to remember the man who did it. That was the point. He had mapped the exits and every vehicle in the yard. He had marked the woman in the boots as a complication the moment she came in through the kitchens. She had an irritating habit of looking straight at the things other people preferred not to see. And she had looked at him.

The grey estate was waiting at the far end of the staff car park under the one dead lamp, engine running, lights off: a taxi-firm car, big and plain, sitting a little too low on its springs for an empty estate. Marchal got into the back without being told. His face had gone the colour of paper. Haozhen shut the door without a sound, went round to the driver’s side, and stopped.

She was standing between two catering vans forty metres away, with her phone in her hand. She had followed them out.

She should have been frightened. She had just watched something she wasn’t meant to see, and he knew it, and she knew he knew. She didn’t look frightened. She looked interested.

He nodded at her, once, as if she had held a door for him. Then the grey car rolled out of the gate with its lights off, and they came on at the bottom of the hill.

Twenty minutes later, past a shut petrol station on the old ring road, he turned into a service lane under a broken streetlight. A dark van was waiting. Marchal looked up from his phone. “This isn’t the airport.”

“No.”

“Then what is it?”

“Your departure,” said Haozhen.

Two men got out of the van. He opened the rear door and took a black cotton hood out of the footwell. For the first time that evening, Marchal’s composure cracked. “Wait. You can’t—” The hood went over his head. The van door slid shut. One of the men came back and stood by the grey car’s window.

“Anything unusual?”

“No.”

“Witnesses?”

He thought of a voice far too loud for a staff entrance, that didn’t care who heard it. A hand under his for one second, with a torch in it. Boots worn down on the outside of the heels, the way a driver’s wear from working the pedals.

“No,” he said.

The van went. His phone buzzed. Complete. Maintain discretion. Await instructions. He read it once and deleted it.

He didn’t think about the man in the hood. He had stopped doing that at eighteen. There was a room in his head where they went, and he kept its door shut, and it was quiet in there. Ten years of doors. Fourteen countries. He was good at it because eyes slid off him like rain off glass, and Director Duan called him the best she had, in the voice she kept for a good knife. Nobody, in ten years, had ever crossed a room to tell him what he was.

By the time he reached the city lights he had decided not to look her up. By the time he parked, he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The paper came with her coffee on Sunday morning. She was sitting cross-legged on the workbench in the garage under the railway bridge, in an old shirt, eating cold fried rice out of the pan, when she found it on page nine of the business section. One paragraph. Belgian consultant Lucien Marchal, who attended Saturday’s Autumn Reception on Battery Hill, left the city on an early flight to Brussels. His office declined to comment.

She read it twice. An early flight. Sure. She had watched a grey estate leave by the staff gate with its lights off and turn the wrong way for the airport.

She slid off the bench and went to the whiteboard, which was already covered with photographs and chassis numbers and three increasingly aggressive question marks about Lot 9. She uncapped the red marker. Under the forged plate she wrote 22 OCT, AUTUMN RECEPTION, and the grey car’s number plate, which her eyes had grabbed in the car park without asking her. Under that, in her worst capitals, QIN H.

Overhead a train went over, as one did every eleven minutes, and the shelves rattled and a spanner dropped into the bucket.

“What’s that?” Big Wu ducked in under the shutter with the doughnuts.

“A car that’s too heavy for its springs.”

“Whose car?”

“Nobody’s. Yet.”

He looked at the red letters, and then at her face. “That’s not a car face,” said Big Wu. “That’s a man face.”

Her phone lit up on the bench. A number she didn’t know.

Unknown: You should be more careful about walking up to strangers.

She looked at it. Then, slowly, she smiled.

Serafina: You should be more careful about pretending to be a security guard.

Three dots. Gone. Back again.

Unknown: I wasn’t pretending.

Serafina: So you’re just genuinely bad at your job?

A longer pause.

Unknown: You noticed the wrong things last night.

Serafina: I noticed the right things. That’s why you’re texting me.

Unknown: Don’t write my name down again.

She looked up from the phone at the whiteboard, where QIN H. sat in red under the number plate, and then round the garage, at the shutter and the loft stairs and the dark corners under the bridge, and the back of her neck prickled, and she grinned.

Serafina: Too late.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in a parked car on the far side of the harbour when he read it. He should have dropped the phone in the water. He should have reported the exchange and gone back to waiting for instructions. Instead he sat with the screen lit in his hand, and then he typed one more line.

Unknown: Stay away from Lot 9.

He sent it. Then, for the first time in ten years, Qin Haozhen did something that had nothing to do with his orders. He saved her number.

chapters.title: She Finds Out His Name
chapters.desc: Three weeks, one bribed caterer and a note about his terrible brakes. Then the guard turns up in her garage in the middle of the night to ask her to stop.
chapters.epigraph: “A car tells you everything about the man who drives it. His just told me to mind my own business.”
chapters.content:
Three weeks. That was how long it took Serafina Song to establish that the man from the Autumn Reception was either good at his job or extremely annoying. Possibly both.

By Tuesday the fifteenth of November, at twenty-five to midnight, her findings were on the whiteboard over the workbench in red, and they went as follows. One: the grey estate she had watched roll out of the staff gate belonged to a leasing company called Silver Line Fleet Solutions, whose office was on the fourth floor of a block by the old ferry piers that had been knocked down in 2019. Two: the company was registered to a man who had died eleven months before it was formed. Three: in a column of sixty scrawls on the service-door sign-in sheet, one line stood apart, in small square letters each one separate from the next, like type. Qin H. East service. 19:02. Four: the man in question had excellent shoulders.

She considered the fourth finding important, though she wasn’t sure it would stand up in court.

The sign-in sheet had cost her two bottles of good wine and an afternoon under the bonnet of a catering van. Auntie Chu had fed every government party in the city for twenty years, and had refused bribes from consuls, and had three refrigerated vans whose brakes made a noise like somebody sitting on a cat. “I remember him,” she’d said, handing over the photocopy. “The only one who didn’t eat. The delegation ate my prawns with their hands. He stood at that door all night and didn’t touch one.” She had sniffed. “A man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

Serafina had written DOESN’T EAT PRAWNS on the board under the number plate.

“Mouse.”

At the far end of the bench, behind three screens, Mouse didn’t look up. She was twenty-two, had a ring through the side of her nose and a hoodie she’d been wearing since roughly 2019, and could find out anything about anyone if you asked her nicely and stayed out of her eyeline. “What?”

“Tell me something.”

“Is it going to get me arrested?”

“Probably not.”

“Then no.”

She pushed a photograph across the bench. The grey estate in the Residence car park, enlarged until the plate was mush.

“The suspiciously handsome man who pretended to be a guard.”

“He didn’t pretend. He was just terrible at it.”

Mouse looked at the photograph, and sighed, and pulled it under her keyboard. “Give me a day.”

She gave the answer on Thursday, without turning round. “No fines. No parking tickets. No speed cameras. Four years. Not one.” She did turn then, and she looked worried. “Nobody has no parking tickets, Sera.”

“He does.” She wrote it on the board. No parking tickets.

From under Gilded, the team’s matte black race car with AURELIA in gold across the bonnet, a pair of enormous legs spoke. “You’re writing about a man on the wall now,” said Big Wu. “That’s how it starts. My cousin did that. Now she’s married to a dentist.”

“Is that bad?”

“Have you met a dentist?”

“Leave it,” said Mr. Kwok, from the camping stove, frying garlic in a wok you could have bathed a toddler in. He was seventy-one, had driven a taxi in this city for forty years, and was annoyingly right about most things. “A man who comes in with the delegation and leaves with a foreigner in his back seat? You don’t write that man on a wall. You forget you saw him.”

“I can’t forget him.”

“Try harder,” said Mr. Kwok, and threw in a fistful of chilli, and smoke went everywhere.

She didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the car on Saturday afternoon, on the fourth level of the multi-storey by the ferry pier, after eight nights of driving Nonna round every car park on the harbour side between midnight and dawn. Nonna was a red 1992 rally hatchback with three hundred thousand kilometres on her and a gearbox rebuilt four times, named after their grandmother: old, Italian, and never once in her life did what she was told. A car like the grey estate lived near the water, if its owner might need to leave in a hurry. And Serafina didn’t sleep much anyway.

It was parked nose out in a corner bay, between a black four-by-four and an entirely forgettable silver saloon. The camera above it had been turned to face the wall. “A car tells you everything about the man who drives it,” she told the empty level. “His just told me to mind my own business.”

She stood in front of it. “Hello, handsome,” she said. The car didn’t answer.

She crouched by the back wheel with her torch and looked through the spokes, and then she sat back on her heels and laughed out loud in the empty concrete. The left rear disc had gone blue with heat and grown a lip at the edge. The pads were worn at an angle. And it sat low on its springs, carrying something heavy the factory had never meant it to carry.

She wrote on the back of a parts receipt, using the roof of Nonna as a desk.

Your rear brakes are cooked. Your left rear caliper is sticking, your pads are worn on a slant, and your discs are blue. You’re carrying a few hundred kilos in this car it was never built for. First long hill with someone behind you, you’ll lose them. You should really take better care of your things.

She considered it, and added a line.

Especially if you’re planning to keep disappearing people.

That was probably unnecessary. She drew a small smiling face underneath anyway, and the address of the garage under the railway bridge, and tucked it under his wiper, and said “You’re welcome” to the car, and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven minutes past two on Sunday morning she was halfway through an argument with a seized wheel bearing when someone knocked on the shutter. Three knocks. Evenly spaced.

She looked at the clock. “Absolutely not.”

Three more.

“Unless you’re here to pay me, go away.”

“Open the door, Miss Song.”

She went quite still, with the wrench in her hand. Then she wiped her fingers on the rag at her waist and took her time walking over and pulled the shutter up.

He was standing in the street light. No suit. A black jacket, dark trousers, no earpiece. His hair was slightly untidy and there was a shadow along his jaw, and he looked as if he had either been awake for a day and a night or spent the evening doing something a lot less legal than dinner. His eyes went over her: the oil on her cheek, the oversized grey sweatshirt, the shorts, the wrench. Then past her, to the garage. Shutter, side door, loft stairs, window, extinguisher. Then, the whiteboard.

“You’re working,” he said.

“Put that down.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to talk to you.”

“Then talk.”

“Inside.”

She raised an eyebrow. “That’s a very confident request from someone on my pavement.”

His eyes came back to hers, and stayed, and neither of them moved. Then he said, “Please.”

That was unexpected. She stepped aside. He came in, and she pulled the shutter down behind him, and he went straight to the whiteboard and stood in front of it with his hands in his pockets. The number plate. No parking tickets. Delegation’s own man. QIN H. And, in her worst capitals, DOESN’T EAT PRAWNS.

The corner of his mouth moved. Not a smile.

“Doesn’t eat prawns.”

“Auntie Chu says a man who won’t eat a prawn is hiding something.”

“I’m allergic.”

“Are you?”

“No.”

She snorted before she could stop it. A train began; she felt it first in the concrete, and so did he; his weight shifted, slightly, towards the side door. Then the whole garage shook and a spanner dropped into the bucket and he didn’t move at all.

“Coffee?” she said. “Tea? Poison?”

“Serafina.”

It was the first time he’d said her name. She smiled. He didn’t.

“Stop looking into me.”

“That’s an interesting way to introduce yourself.”

“I mean it. How did you find the car?”

“Trade secret, Mr. Guard.”

He let out a slow, controlled breath. She watched him do it with open delight. “You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Trying very hard not to look annoyed. You’re terrible at it.” She folded her arms. “You came here to tell me I’m in danger.”

He didn’t answer.

“Because of you? Or because of the people you work for?”

Nothing. She studied him for a while, and something in her voice came down a notch. “What’s your name? I know Qin H. I’d like to know what the H is.”

The look again. All the way in. Two seconds, three. She looked straight back, and had the oddest feeling that far behind his face a light was coming on in a house she’d thought was empty.

“Qin Haozhen.”

She’d expected a lie, a good one. She’d been looking forward to it. But she could tell a real plate from a forged one, and this one was real.

“Why tell me?”

“You’d have found it. I’d rather you heard it from me than from someone who wanted to know why you were asking.”

“Haozhen,” she said, trying it, and he looked away. She held out her hand, looked at it, black to the wrist, wiped it on her sweatshirt, which did nothing, and held it out again. “Serafina Song.”

“I know. I read your pass.”

“That was three weeks ago.”

“Yes,” he said, and shook it. He let go a beat late, and then looked down at the oil on his palm as if he didn’t know where to put it.

“Right,” said Serafina. “Your brakes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“They’re fine.”

She turned round on her heels by his car, which he had, on her instruction and with visible reluctance, fetched from round the corner and backed under the shutter in one move with a hand’s width either side. The look she gave him was nearly offensive.

“Do you want me to lie to you?”

“No.”

“Then don’t say ridiculous things. Get the jack.”

He looked at her for a second as though nobody had told him to get anything in several years. Then he got the jack.

She had the rear wheel off in four minutes. The disc was worse close up: heat spots on the friction surface, the lip at the outer edge, pads worn at an angle. She turned the hub and watched the caliper. It didn’t let go cleanly.

“Your left rear caliper’s sticking.”

“I know.”

She went still. “You know?”

“Yes.”

“And you went on driving it?”

“I had no choice.”

“There’s always a choice. You could have taken a different car.”

“This was the car I needed.”

“Well, congratulations. You nearly turned it into a very expensive paperweight. Whoever looks after this is either lazy or wants you dead.”

“The motor pool.”

“Then the motor pool wants you dead!”

“Possibly,” he said.

She laughed. Then she looked at him, because he wasn’t joking, and he looked back at her with no expression whatsoever, so she laughed again, harder.

She freed the slide pins and cleaned them and greased them, and fitted pads off her own shelf, and wrote down a matched pair of discs on the parts list for the week. He stood by the bench and watched her hands, never her face. When she reached for the sixteen-millimetre socket it was already in her palm.

“I didn’t ask for that.”

“You were going to.”

“Are you reading my mind?”

“You looked at it. Four minutes ago. You always look at the next thing before you need it.”

She sat back on her heels. “Have you had mechanical training?”

“No.”

“Military?”

Silence.

“Government?”

Silence.

“Secret underground organisation?”

“Serafina.”

“Fine. Keep your secrets.” She went back to the caliper. “But stop it. Noticing things about me. That’s my job.”

“Then we have a problem,” said Haozhen.

At ten past three she found the scrape across his knuckles, the skin taken off in a neat line, and took his wrist before he could put the hand in his pocket. He went still; she felt the muscles under her fingers draw tight. She loosened her grip. “Relax. I’m not going to amputate it.”

“I know.”

“When did you do this?”

“It doesn’t matter.”

“Everything matters when you work with your hands.” She cleaned it with an antiseptic wipe. He let her. “You’re very co-operative when you’re injured.”

“I’m always co-operative.”

She looked up at him and burst out laughing. “You’ve refused to answer every question I’ve asked you for an hour.”

And then, without any warning at all, he smiled. Small, reluctant, as if it had got out before he could stop it. Her laughter went soft. That was unfair. He had a nice smile. She looked at it a second too long.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“I’m watching.”

“That’s what staring is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to four she was explaining brake bias with a pad in one hand and the other hand in the air, “and if you keep loading the rear that hard on a cold surface the back end’s going to want to come round, because the tyres aren’t warm enough to—”

“Serafina.”

“—hold it, and then you’ll wonder why—”

“Hold still.”

“What?”

He had the rag off her waistband. He wiped the corner of her mouth with it, where she’d had oil for two hours, once, and then again, slower, and his thumb stayed there.

She stopped talking. It was an extraordinarily rare event.

“Most people,” she said eventually, “just tell you you’ve got something on your face.”

“I said hold still.”

“I was holding still.”

“You weren’t,” said Haozhen, and kissed her in the middle of the next word.

It wasn’t gentle at first. There was something almost impatient in it, something that had been held back longer than either of them had any business admitting. His hand came to her jaw, knuckles under it, thumb where the oil had been. Her fingers found the front of his jacket and closed. For a few seconds he forgot the car, the shutter, the reasons he’d come, and kissed her as if he had made a decision and had no intention of going back over it.

Then he lifted his head an inch. She blinked at him. Once. Twice.

“You’re quiet,” he said.

“That,” said Serafina, “was incredibly rude. You interrupted me.”

He laughed. A real laugh, low and short and unmistakable, and her face lit up like a dashboard.

“Oh. You can laugh.”

“Apparently.”

She looked at his mouth. He saw her look. “Are you going to do that again?”

He didn’t answer. He did it again. This time she thought she was ready for it, and found out that she wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past four he stood in the street under the bridge, fastening his watch. The grey estate stayed on her lift; the discs wouldn’t come till Wednesday and she had flatly refused to let him drive it out on one good side. He had agreed. That was perhaps the most alarming thing that had happened all night.

“When are you coming back?” She was in the gap under the shutter with her arms folded.

“When the parts come.”

“Fine. I’ll see you when your brakes stop being embarrassing.” She tilted her head. “Night, Guard.”

Something happened at the corners of his eyes. Then it went. “Don’t look into the people at the reception.”

“Why?”

“Because I asked you not to.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s the only one I can give you.”

“You’re worried about me.”

“I’m telling you to be careful.”

“That’s not what I said.”

He held her eyes, and she thought he might actually answer. Instead he said, “Lock your garage,” and walked away down the street of shut workshops, and at the corner a dark car she hadn’t heard arrive opened its back door for him and took him away.

She looked down at the rag in her hand. It smelled of his soap. She pulled the shutter down and locked it, twice, and said to the empty garage, “Well. That was unexpected.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nineteen minutes past four, in a room with no name on its door, a screen was playing. A garage under a bridge. A woman in an oversized sweatshirt. A grey car on a lift. A man standing beside her, who leaned down and kissed her.

Haozhen watched himself do it and said nothing. The duty officer beside him glanced up. “The mechanic. You went yourself. You told her your name.”

“Yes.”

“You’re getting careless.”

On the screen she was laughing at something he had said. He remembered the sound. He remembered her face after the first kiss, offended and delighted at once, and her fingers holding his wrist while she cleaned a scrape he hadn’t noticed. Small things he shouldn’t have remembered.

“Have the footage taken down. All of it.”

“You think that’ll stop her looking?”

“No.”

“Then why bother?”

He looked away from the screen at last. “Because I don’t want anyone else watching her.”

The room went quiet. The officer closed the file. “You’re making this difficult.”

“Then don’t make it more difficult,” said Haozhen, and walked out.

Behind him the screen went black. But the footage had already been copied. And in the roof of a garage under a railway bridge, a camera smaller than a fingernail that Serafina had never once noticed went on recording. Qin Haozhen had found her first. He had only let her believe otherwise.

chapters.title: A Race, Not a Date
chapters.desc: She makes him race her at Granny Shum’s, his grey taxi of a car against her red rally hatchback. He loses on purpose, and she’s furious about it.
chapters.epigraph: “A circuit is a circuit and a road is a road, and I’m not giving up the road for anybody.”
chapters.content:
Qin Haozhen had developed a habit. An irritating one, according to Serafina. He turned up at the garage without warning, stood about looking unnecessarily handsome, and behaved as if he had every right to occupy her personal space. He also brought coffee, which made it difficult to complain.

“You’re late,” she said, on Thursday the twenty-fourth, from inside Nonna’s engine bay.

He looked at his watch. “It’s sixteen minutes past eight.”

“Exactly.”

“You said eight.”

“I said around eight.”

“Then I’m early,” said Haozhen, and put two paper cups on the bench. “One without sugar.”

She looked at the cup, and then at him. “You remembered?”

“You complained about the last one. You said it tasted like someone had dissolved a tyre in it.”

“That was constructive criticism.”

He nodded as if this were reasonable. She took the coffee and tried not to smile, and failed, and pointed at the bonnet. “Hold this.” It was the inspection lamp. He looked at it. “That’s what I’m here for?” “Among other things.” He took it.

The new discs had come on Wednesday with the wrong brackets, of course, so the grey estate was still on the lift and Nonna was getting her timing belt while they waited. For twenty minutes he stood at her shoulder and held the light exactly where she needed it. When she moved round to the other side, the beam was already there.

She reached for a socket and he put it in her hand, and she looked at him, and he looked back. Then she saw that he had taken a small black notebook out of his inside pocket and was writing something in it, in small square letters, each one separate.

“What are you writing?”

“Nothing.”

She abandoned the engine and went for it. He lifted it out of reach without appearing to move. “Haozhen.”

“Serafina.”

“What are you writing?”

“Your language.” He turned it round. Porca miseria. Bloody hell. For God’s sake. You absolute bastard. And under those: Whoever designed this bracket should be shot.

She stared at it. “You’re taking notes?”

“Your vocabulary is extensive. Am I pronouncing them correctly?”

“Don’t you dare.”

“Bloody hell,” said Haozhen, with a perfectly straight face, and she put both hands over her eyes and laughed until the shelves rattled, or perhaps that was a train. For a man who spent his days being deliberately forgettable, he had a surprisingly good sense of humour. He just didn’t seem to know what to do with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes to midnight the discs were on and the grey car was down off the lift and he was sitting on the end of the bench turning a bolt over and over in his fingers. He had been quiet for ten minutes.

“What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re thinking.”

“Is that a problem?”

“Usually.” She wiped her hands. “You’re allowed to talk, you know.”

He watched her for a while. “Why do you keep looking for me?”

“Because you’re interesting.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s a perfectly good reason.” She sighed, theatrically. “Fine. Because you turned up at a government reception and walked a very important man into a car, and the newspaper said he’d flown to Brussels, and I watched you drive him the other way. And because you’re apparently incapable of maintaining a vehicle.”

“That too.”

“You’re curious about things that don’t concern you,” he said, to the bolt. “That gets people hurt.”

She put the rag down. “Haozhen. You’re allowed to want something, you know.”

His face changed. Only slightly.

“You’re allowed to have coffee with someone. You’re allowed to stand in a garage at midnight and hold a lamp. You’re allowed to laugh at terrible jokes.”

“I don’t have time.”

“Everyone has time.”

“Not everyone.”

She looked at him, and then her smile came back, softer. “Well. You’re here now.”

He didn’t have an answer to that.

Near dawn she took the grey estate round the industrial district twice with him in the passenger seat, braking hard on the empty road by the gas works until the new pads bedded in, and parked it back under the shutter and slapped the bonnet. “Done. Now you owe me.”

“How much?”

“Not money. A race.” He looked at her. “Not a date. I don’t do dates. Dates are two people sitting still being polite at each other over soup. A race. Saturday night, Granny Shum’s. You in this, me in Nonna.”

“Street racing carries three years now.”

“I know. My mother posted me a copy of the law.” She leaned on his bonnet. “I’ve got a national licence. A team. My sister’s name in gold on my race car. And I still go to Granny Shum’s on Saturdays. A circuit is a circuit and a road is a road, and I’m not giving up the road for anybody.”

“There’ll be phones.”

“Wear a hat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly six when he finally went, and she walked him out to the street in his spare jacket, which she’d complained about the cold until he gave it to her without a word. He stood by the driver’s door.

“Two good nights,” she said.

“What?”

“Last night you brought coffee. Tonight you held the lamp and entertained me with your excellent grasp of profanity. I think you’ve earned a reward.”

His face didn’t move. “What reward?”

“Use your imagination.”

He looked at her. Then he took one step, and her back met the cold door of his car, and he put one hand flat on the roof beside her head.

“You’re standing very close,” she said.

“I know.” His eyes went to her mouth, and came back. “Is this the reward?”

“Depends. Are you asking?”

He didn’t ask. He kissed her. She made a small surprised noise against his mouth and then took two fistfuls of his jacket and pulled him in, and it was slow, and almost careful, his hand at her waist, hers finding the back of his neck. When he drew back she followed him an inch without meaning to. He noticed. Of course he noticed. His mouth curved.

“Again?”

“Don’t look so pleased with yourself.”

“You’re the one holding on.”

She looked down. Both hands were still locked in his jacket. She let go at once. “I was checking the material. Very poor quality.”

“Terrible,” he agreed, and kissed her again, and this time she didn’t bother pretending to inspect anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum’s wasn’t a place. It was a person, and a junction.

She ran the Saturday meet from a folding chair at the crossroads by the paint works, with a thermos of chrysanthemum tea, a blanket over her knees, and a police scanner on a string round her neck like a crucifix. She was eighty, or said she was. Her husband had raced these roads in the seventies in a car with no doors and died of something boring in bed in 2005, and she had kept the Saturdays going ever since. She called it respect. Everybody else called it spite. On the lamp post beside her chair hung a sign painted on hardboard: NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING.

Serafina had been coming since she was nineteen, the week she walked out of the house on the Peak. On the first night Granny Shum had looked her up and down and said, “Rich girl. You’ll crash by Christmas.” On Christmas Eve Serafina won four runs in a row in a car she’d built out of two dead ones, and Granny Shum handed her a clementine and never mentioned rich girls again.

At twenty to eleven on Saturday the twenty-sixth, the floodlight off the paint works lit forty people and eleven cars: modified coupés with wings like dining tables and one expensive thing nobody was allowed to touch. Mouse was leaning on her own little hatchback with a can of something fluorescent.

“You’re late.”

“Everyone keeps saying that to me.”

Mouse looked past her and her face did something. “Oh.”

The grey estate had come down from the gas works with its lights off and parked at the end of the line behind a purple coupé with a kid on its roof filming himself. Every single person turned and stared at it. Somebody laughed. Then everybody did. It looked like something a middle-aged accountant drove to the supermarket.

“That’s him?” said Mouse. “That’s his car?”

“Unfortunately.”

He got out. Dark jacket, black cap pulled low, hands in his pockets, head down. When the kid on the roof panned his phone along the line, he got a cap and a shoulder and nothing else.

“Who’s the taxi?” said Granny Shum.

“A friend.”

“Not a friend.” Granny Shum sipped her tea. “Friends don’t stand like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like they know which way the police will come,” said Granny Shum, and turned her scanner up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four kilometres and twenty metres. Serafina could have driven it asleep, and in 2018 nearly had. Off the line at the paint works. The long straight past the container yard, where cars with big engines and nothing else always got ahead. Left at the fish-ball factory. The S-bends between the warehouses, blind and tight, where cars with big engines and nothing else went into the wall. Then the long right round the gas works, with a lamp post every fifty metres. Sensible people braked at the third lamp post. Serafina braked at the fourth.

Granny Shum’s granddaughter stood between the two cars with the white scarf. Sixteen, purple nails, bored. “One run. No contact. Scanner goes, you go home. You know the rules.”

“He doesn’t,” said Serafina.

The granddaughter peered in at him. He’d taken the cap off. Hands on the wheel at a quarter to three, which nobody did. “No contact,” she told him.

“No contact.”

Then he got out again. Three steps to Nonna, out of the floodlight. Her leather jacket was hanging open over her vest, the way she always raced. He didn’t say a word. He reached in through the open window and took hold of the zip and drew it up, slowly, to her chin. His knuckles brushed her throat at the top.

“It’s cold.”

“I can do up my own jacket.”

“I know. You weren’t.”

He went back. She sat with her mouth open and her jacket zipped up like a schoolgirl’s, and from the folding chair Granny Shum said, “Friend,” in a voice like a door shutting.

“Watch your braking point,” he called, across the gap.

“Watch your mirrors.”

The scarf went up. She held Nonna at five thousand revs and the whole car shook like a dog on a lead. She looked left once. Through two windows and a metre of cold air, he looked back. The scarf came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nonna went off the line like a gunshot, all four wheels biting, the turbo coming in at the top of second with the long rising whistle that always made the back of her neck go hot. Half a car up at the paint works. A whole car by the container yard. She checked the mirror for the estate dropping back, because heavy cars always dropped back on the straight. It stayed exactly one length behind her. Exactly one, as if it had been painted on the glass, all the way down the straight, at a speed no family estate with a few hundred kilos in its doors had any business doing.

“What the hell have you got in there?”

Left at the fish-ball factory. She braked late and turned in hard and felt the tail go light and caught it, and came out sideways on purpose with her foot flat. In the mirror the grey car took the same corner on rails, no slide, no fuss, and came out one length behind her. The S-bends: left, right, left, warehouse walls a hand from her mirrors. She went through them faster than she ever had, and when she burst out onto the gas-works straight he was closer. Half a length. She could see his face by the glow of his dashboard. He looked like a man doing his taxes.

She started laughing. Flat to the floor, hands loose, the gasholders black against the orange sky, cackling like an idiot. Nobody had ever sat on her bumper through the S-bends as if it were nothing.

First lamp post. Second. And at the second, a whole lamp post before anyone sane would brake, his brake lights came on. Clean. Perfectly timed. Fifty metres early.

She went to the fourth, like always, and turned in with the tyres screaming. By the service road he was three lengths back, and he stayed there, politely, all the way to the line.

The crowd went mad. People hammered on Nonna’s roof. She got out and walked straight down the line to the grey car.

“You lifted.”

He didn’t answer that.

“Your brake lights came on at the second lamp post! Nobody brakes at the second lamp post. Mr. Kwok brakes at the third, and he’s seventy-one and drives a transporter. You sat on my bumper through the S-bends in a car that weighs as much as a bus, and then you braked at the second lamp post?”

He looked at her from under the cap. In the floodlight his face was all shadow, and calm. “You won.”

“That’s not the point!”

“You were having fun. I could see you in your mirror. If I’d gone past you at the gas works, you’d have stopped.”

She stared at him. A man in a black cap had just told her he’d lost on purpose so that she’d go on laughing. Three languages, and not one word in any of them.

“That is the most insulting thing a man has ever done to me.”

“I’m sorry.”

He clearly wasn’t. She narrowed her eyes. “And people were filming. If you’d won, they’d have the man who beat Serafina Song in a taxi. That’s it, isn’t it? You can’t be filmed winning.”

“That too.”

Over his shoulder somebody had a phone up, pointed their way. His face changed. “Come here,” he said, and before she could argue he had opened the driver’s door and drawn her round it, into the dark gap between the door and the warehouse wall, out of the floodlight. Nobody could see. She worked out later that he had made sure; even then, even with her, some part of him had found the one place on that road where no phone was pointing.

“Are you still angry?”

“Yes.”

“All right.”

“That’s all?”

“What do you want me to say?”

“That you won’t do it again.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

“Yes.”

A pause. “Would you have won?”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

“Haozhen.”

He laughed, and kissed her, hard, his cap knocked back, his hand spread on her spine under the leather, the edge of the door cold between her shoulder blades and the whole industrial district yelling forty metres away. She bit his lip. Mostly not on purpose. He made a sound in his chest that she felt more than heard, and pulled her closer, and oh, she thought, so this was what he did when he wasn’t lifting.

Then the scanner on Granny Shum’s chest said something short and official, and Granny Shum stood up out of her chair and blew the whistle she kept for exactly this, and forty people and eleven cars began to vanish into the industrial district like water into sand.

He let her go and put his cap straight. His hand wasn’t quite steady. “The circuit in the north has a track day on the tenth. I’ll book it.”

“How do you even know that?”

“I checked,” he said. “On Thursday.” And the grey car slid away towards the gas works with its lights off, and was gone before the first blue light came round the paint factory.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a folded paper under Nonna’s wiper. Her own note, the parts receipt from the ferry car park. Your rear brakes are cooked. He had kept it a week and brought it to a street race and put it back while she was marching down the line to shout at him. Folded inside it was a small amount of money. On the back, in small square letters, a phone number. A different one from the unknown number that had texted her in October. This one is mine. For the brakes. And under that, one more line.

You brake at the fourth lamp post because you like the noise the tyres make. It’s a beautiful noise. It costs you a tenth.

She read it four times sitting in the dark in Nonna with the engine ticking. Then she saved the number as GUARD. Then she deleted that and typed GUARD (LIFTS). Then she sat there furious, because he was right about the tenth.

Serafina: I’m not taking your money.

Haozhen: Keep it for the next time you fix my car.

Serafina: Your car is terrible. There will definitely be a next time.

Serafina: And I still think it’s ugly.

Haozhen: I’ll remember that.

Serafina: I won. Say it properly.

The answer took a while.

Haozhen: You won, Miss Song.

She laughed out loud, alone in the car. She had no idea that the man who had just given her his real number already knew the route to her garage by heart, and every way out of it, and the plate of every car that had been parked outside it in three weeks. Nor that he had lost a race on purpose because, for once, he had wanted to see somebody else happy more than he wanted to win. For Qin Haozhen that was a great deal more dangerous than losing. He was beginning to enjoy having something to lose.

chapters.title: Rematch
chapters.desc: A track day in the north, one car, two drivers and Mouse on the stopwatch. This time he drives like himself, and she kisses him in the empty paddock.
chapters.epigraph: “Five laps each, same car, Mouse on the clock. Then we both know.”
chapters.content:
Serafina Song had a problem, and his name was Qin Haozhen, and at fourteen minutes past eight on the second Saturday in December he was standing beside her car in the paddock of the circuit in the north with a coffee in his hand, looking entirely too pleased with himself.

It wasn’t the coffee. The coffee was excellent. Nor was it that he had arrived twenty minutes before anyone else. What got to her was his face: that quiet, maddening composure of a man who knows something you don’t.

“You’re smiling,” she said.

“Am I?”

“You’re enjoying this.”

“Enjoying what?”

“Whatever you’re thinking.”

He drank some coffee. “Nothing.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

“I’ve been told.”

“Don’t use my words against me.”

Mouse, perched on an upturned crate with a laptop and a transponder the size of a matchbox, looked from one of them to the other. “Are you two going to drive, or should I go home?”

“Mind your business.”

“It became my business when you asked me to give up my Saturday.”

“You’re being paid.”

“Not enough.”

Haozhen turned. “How much?”

“Don’t you dare,” said Serafina, but he had already taken a folded note out of his jacket and handed it over, and Mouse looked at it and sat up straight.

“Actually, this is a very worthwhile event.”

“Traitor.”

“I’m easily bought.”

She threw a cleaning cloth at her. Haozhen caught it before it got there, looked at it, and then at her. “You’re wasting equipment.”

“Oh, you think you’re funny now?”

“A little,” said Haozhen, and she knew she was going to have a difficult day.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu was rolling Nonna off the transporter, and Mr. Kwok was setting up his camping stove under the awning, and the morning was so cold her breath smoked. She had thought about it all week. Two cars wouldn’t work. Two cars meant his armour against her turbo and an argument at the end about whose car had done it. So: one car. Five flying laps each, timed to the hundredth by Mouse, who couldn’t be bribed, at least not by her.

She patted Nonna’s red roof. “Five laps each, same car, Mouse on the clock. Then we both know.”

He looked the car over. Thirty years old, the paint going pink at the edges of the roof, arches wider than any factory had made them because Serafina had made them wider, a dent in the driver’s door from 2020 that she had never fixed. “She’s very old.”

“So’s the Pope. Get in.”

She was checking the front tyres when he crouched beside her. “Your left front is slightly low.”

She checked it. It was. “How did you know?”

“The sidewall.”

She hated that he was right. “Fine. You may look. Don’t get comfortable.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it.” He watched her. “You’re nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“Your hands are moving faster. And that’s the third time you’ve checked that tyre.”

She turned her head slowly. “Do you want to live?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop talking.”

He stood up and went away. Mouse leaned over from her crate. “He’s good.”

“At what?”

“Being your boyfriend.”

She nearly dropped the gauge. “He’s not my boyfriend.”

Mouse looked at her, and then at Haozhen, and then back. “Right.”

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“Your face did.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the drivers’ briefing he sat beside her in a borrowed race suit with the sleeves tied round his waist and his helmet on his knees, and he looked like a different man. Not the one who held a lamp at her bench. His whole attention was on the instructor, and the questions he asked were precise and few: the braking zones, the track temperature, the overtaking rules. When the instructor got to the map he leaned towards her.

“Turn four. Don’t carry too much into the entry. The surface is uneven. The car will move under braking. Don’t fight it.”

She turned all the way round in her chair. “Are you giving me driving advice?”

“Yes.”

“Darling,” said Serafina, “I rebuilt your brakes.”

“That’s true.”

“And I beat you.”

“Also true.”

“Then concentrate on your own driving.”

“All right,” he said, and then as she turned back, satisfied, “Try not to miss me when I’m ahead.”

“Haozhen.”

He was smiling. Actually smiling.

She went first, to show him the circuit, and also, fine, to show off. She talked him round it on the radio she’d wired into his headset at the pit wall. “Turn one. Long right. Brake at the hundred board; it feels too early, it isn’t. The esses. Don’t use the kerb on the second one. Back straight, nine hundred metres. You’ll see two hundred on the clock if you’re brave. And at the end—”

“The Needle.”

“You have to thread it. First time, everyone brakes too late and goes into the gravel. Second time, too early, and looks stupid. Third time—” She braked on the marker, two gears down, heel and toe, and Nonna swung round her own middle like a dancer on one foot and came out with her tail wagging. “Third time you thread it!”

Her best of five was one fifty-eight forty-one. For a thirty-year-old car on road tyres that wasn’t good, it was great, and she rolled into the pit lane with her heart going and pulled her helmet off with her hair standing up in spikes.

“Well?”

“You lift a fraction at the top of the esses,” he said. “Second lap and fourth. Not the third. I think it’s when the sun gets in your eyes.”

She stared at him. It was absolutely the sun.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took off his watch first. She saw him do it: steel strap undone, laid face down on the camping table beside Mr. Kwok’s wok, carefully, like something he meant to come back for. Then her spare helmet. Seat forward two notches, both mirrors. Then he sat for ten seconds with his hands on the wheel at a quarter to three and his eyes shut.

“Is he praying?” said Big Wu.

“He’s reading the circuit,” said Mouse, without looking up. Big Wu turned, and slowly shut his mouth.

Haozhen was different behind a wheel. There was nothing extra in it. Every driver she had ever watched put something into a car that it didn’t need, a twitch, a stab, a little flick out of a corner to feel the back go; she did it herself. He didn’t. He turned the wheel exactly as far as it had to turn and braked exactly as hard as the tyres would take, and came off the brakes in one long smooth line as the car turned in, so that the weight poured across it like water from one cup to another. On his third lap Mouse’s speed trap at the end of the back straight said two hundred and three.

“Madonna,” said Serafina.

On his fifth lap he crossed the line, and Mouse looked at the laptop, and looked again, and turned it round. Two columns, five laps each, a best lap in red at the bottom of each. 1:58.41. 1:58.41.

“To the hundredth,” said Mouse. “Same.”

She looked at the screen, and at Haozhen climbing out with his hair flattened on one side and colour in his face, which was new. “You did that on purpose.”

“I couldn’t do that if I tried. Nobody could. Ask Mouse.”

Mouse shook her head once, which from Mouse was a speech. Serafina started to laugh, and had to sit down on the transporter ramp. Mr. Kwok said, from the wok, that it was the cold, it went to people’s heads, he’d seen it at the New Year market in 1983.

“Good lap,” said Haozhen, standing over her.

“Don’t be nice to me.”

He moved a strand of hair off her face with one finger. “You’re very competitive.”

“Unfortunately,” she said, “so are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch a dentist came over.

He had a silver sports car and a padded gilet and the face of a man who had been passed on the back straight by a thirty-year-old hatchback and hadn’t waved it by. He marched under the awning to where Serafina was eating Mr. Kwok’s noodles standing up.

“You. Red car. You came past me without a wave. That’s a black flag. I’ve been coming here six years—”

“You did wave.” Serafina slurped a noodle. “With one finger.”

“I’ll be reporting you to the organisers. Name?”

She didn’t get to answer. Haozhen had put his water down and come round the camping table, and stopped between them. Not close, not touching anyone. He stood there with his hands loose at his sides, and the dentist found that he was looking at a stranger instead of a woman with a bowl of noodles.

“Dr. Cheuk.”

The dentist blinked. “How do you—”

“Your car is in bay eleven. Your number is on the entry list. You live on the hill road, in the building with the green awning.” His voice didn’t change at all. Polite. Bored, nearly. “Your daughter has piano on Saturday afternoons. You’ll want to leave soon, if you’re collecting her.”

The dentist went a different colour. “Is that a threat?”

“It’s traffic advice.”

Dr. Cheuk went back to his silver car and drove it out of the paddock gate an hour before his session ended. He didn’t wave.

Serafina had stopped chewing. “How do you know where he lives?”

“I read the entry list on the way in. Then I looked.”

“You looked up forty dentists?”

“Thirty-one. Nine were surgeons.”

She ought to have been horrified. She stood there with her noodles going cold, waiting to be horrified, and it didn’t come. What came instead was a hot mean little thrill all the way down her back, and she knew that was probably bad, and she put it away to look at later.

Big Wu, who had done two stretches inside and never talked about either, watched the silver car go. He wiped his hands on a rag and came and stood beside Haozhen, looking at the gate. “I know men who talk like that,” he said. “Most of them I wouldn’t let into my mother’s kitchen.” He folded the rag. “She likes chilli. Sera. On everything but breakfast.”

“I know.”

Big Wu gave him a long, unfriendly look sideways. Then he grunted and went back to the wheels. And Mr. Kwok, without a word, put a second bowl of noodles into Haozhen’s hands with extra chilli on top.

Later, on the pit wall, Mouse said, low, “He’s not an ordinary security guy, Sera. I’ve seen people who’ve done proper track work. He doesn’t drive like somebody who learned it for fun.”

“I know.”

“Does he tell you anything?”

“No.”

“And you’re fine with that?”

She considered. “He’s handsome.”

“God help me,” said Mouse.

Her phone buzzed.

Haozhen: Eat properly.

She looked up. He was twenty metres away talking to a marshal, not looking at her.

Serafina: Stop watching me.

Haozhen: You’ve eaten half a bowl.

Serafina: It’s a big bowl.

Haozhen: It isn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon was cold and bright and the wind got up. She was in a thin vest under her race suit and he took his jacket off and put it round her shoulders and did up the buttons himself, one and then the next, his fingers brushing her collarbone, his eyes on the buttons.

“I can dress myself.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

“Because you’re cold,” he said, and fastened the top one under her chin, and then, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world, bent and kissed her forehead. She went completely still. He stepped away. “Your turn.”

They drove until the light went, turn and turn about. The dentists went home one by one, and then it was just them and Mr. Kwok and a bored marshal in an orange coat at the Needle. He showed her the sun thing at the top of the esses. She showed him how much kerb he could take at the long right. They traded tenths and then hundredths, and Mouse started to giggle without making a sound. He beat her by six hundredths. She came back with the cleanest lap she had ever driven, and the laptop said one fifty-eight twenty-six, and she beat him by two.

“Two hundredths,” she said, climbing out.

“Good,” he said. “Very good.”

“That’s it? You could at least pretend to be devastated.”

“I’m not devastated. You’re fast.” He let that sit. “Still not as fast as me.”

“Haozhen!”

He laughed, and she decided on the spot that next time she was going to beat him by a tenth.

The marshal waved the chequered flag at them with enormous weariness. They rolled in for the last time with the brakes glowing and the engine ticking and the tyres smelling of burnt sugar. Big Wu crouched at the front left with the probe. “Ninety-four,” he said, and stood up. “I’m going to get the van.” He went fast, and took Mr. Kwok with him, and took Mouse by the sleeve, and Mouse let herself be taken.

✦ ✦ ✦

The paddock was empty. Cold blue light under the awning, her race suit unzipped and tied round her middle, steam coming off her shoulders, so happy she didn’t know what to do with her hands. He came round the bonnet still wearing her spare helmet with the visor down, the rest of him buttoned up the way he always was. She could see his eyes through the plastic.

She stepped in and took the chin of the helmet in both hands and kissed the visor. Loudly. A great smacking kiss right on the plastic. He went completely still.

“That’s for the six hundredths,” she said. “Good job. You’re the best driver I’ve ever sat next to. And you haven’t been happy in about ten years, have you?”

He didn’t answer. It was in his eyes anyway, for a second, through the visor: something old and tired and surprised.

She undid the strap and pulled the helmet off him and put it on Nonna’s roof. “Come here.”

He bent his head, and she kissed him properly, late and hard, the way she took corners. For one second he didn’t move at all, as if he had been passed on the inside where he hadn’t left a gap. Then his hands came up, one at her jaw with the thumb under her ear, one flat at the small of her back where the race suit was knotted, and he took it over. Every other time some part of him had been watching a clock. Not now. He walked her back a step, two, until she met the side of the car, and the metal was still warm from the engine, and she made a noise she would deny until her grave. He heard it. She felt him smile against her mouth, a real one, and her knees went.

When she could, she said, “You’re doing that thing again.”

“What thing?”

“Where you make me want to kiss you instead of argue.”

“Is that a problem?”

“Potentially.”

“Then don’t argue,” he said, and kissed her again. Then he rested his forehead on hers, and she could feel him shaking, slightly. He wasn’t a man who shook.

“You took your watch off,” she said. “Why?”

His thumb moved once along her jaw, as if checking it was still there. “I didn’t want to know what time it was.”

Round the end of the paddock came the transporter with its headlights on and Big Wu leaning on the horn, two long and a short, for no reason at all, and Mr. Kwok in the passenger seat with his hands over his eyes. “YOU’VE GOT FOUR MINUTES!” Big Wu bellowed, and then heard himself. “Five! Five minutes. Never four.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home in the grey car, because Nonna’s brakes had worked hard all day and needed the transporter, he said, and she told him he could have just said he wanted her in his car. “Would that have worked?” he said, opening the passenger door, and she thought about it and said maybe.

There was a bottle of water in the cup holder and a folded blanket on the back seat. “Why do you have a blanket?”

“For emergencies.”

“What kind?”

“Cold ones,” he said.

She looked at the blanket, and at him, and something in her face went soft. Halfway down the valley she put her hand over his on the gear lever. He looked down at it. Then he turned his hand over under hers and laced their fingers together, and drove the rest of the way one-handed, and for once he didn’t let go until they were home.

chapters.title: 3 A.M., Passenger Seat
chapters.desc: He hasn’t slept properly in ten years. Then he falls asleep in her passenger seat, and she drives round the harbour till dawn so he won’t wake up.
chapters.epigraph: “In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.”
chapters.content:
“Big Wu says you’re a vampire.”

“Big Wu has never seen me.”

“That’s his point.”

He came at strange hours after the track day. Never in daylight. One in the morning. Half past four. Once just before six, with the sky going grey over the railway bridge. The garage felt different with him in it. Fuller, as if somebody had shut a window she hadn’t known was open.

And he had a mug. This was becoming a problem. A plain white mug with a chip by the handle. He used it on his second visit. He used it on his third. By the fifth, Serafina had written HAOZHEN on the bottom in permanent marker, and at twenty-two minutes to midnight on the Thursday before Christmas he picked it up, read his own name, and turned it round on the bench so the writing faced the wall.

“Did you just turn my mug round?”

“It was facing the wrong way.”

“There’s a wrong way to face a mug?”

“People would see it.”

“It’s a mug, Guard.”

“Fine. It’s yours. Your mug, your coffee, your little corner of my workbench. Would you like a sign? A small memorial?”

He put the mug down, reached for her waist, and pulled her in between his knees where he sat on the stool. She laughed and put both hands on his shoulders.

“You’re very affectionate tonight.”

“Is that a problem?”

She pretended to think. “Not yet.”

He kissed her. It was becoming familiar, this thing he did: twenty minutes of saying almost nothing, and then reaching for her as if he had been thinking about it the whole time. Once, on the bonnet of Gilded, until she was so dizzy she put a socket wrench in the fridge.

When he drew back she ran her thumb along his jaw. “You look tired.”

“I’m fine.”

“How long have you been awake?”

“Since yesterday morning.”

“Haozhen.”

She took the mug out of his hand. “You’re not a machine.”

“I have things to do,” he said, and smiled, a smile, and somehow that made her feel worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past twelve she was closing up and found him on the old leather sofa by the office door. He hadn’t moved in ten minutes. Head back, eyes shut, one hand on his thigh. She crouched in front of him and said his name, and then said it again, and his eyes opened at once. Too quickly. His whole body was awake before his face had worked out where he was. She held still until his shoulders came down.

“Sorry.”

“Don’t be.” She sat beside him. “Do you actually sleep?”

He looked at the ceiling.

“Four hours a night. Sometimes three. Since I was eighteen.”

“That’s ten years.”

“You get used to it.”

“You don’t get used to that. You just forget what not being tired feels like.”

A whole train went over. She thought she had pushed too far. Then, when she had given up, he spoke to the ceiling.

“In hotels I sleep in the chair by the door. In my flat I sleep on top of the covers, dressed. I don’t sleep on planes. In ten years I’ve never sat in a car I wasn’t driving or guarding.”

She didn’t ask why. She took his hand instead. His fingers were cold. “You’re staying here tonight.”

“I should go.”

“I’m not negotiating.”

“You’re bossy.”

“Yes.”

A pause. “All right,” he said, and Qin Haozhen agreed to something without asking about the conditions, the risks or the way out. She put a blanket over him. In the morning the blanket was folded and he was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Christmas Eve she raced at Granny Shum’s, because Granny Shum’s on Christmas Eve was where she had become herself at nineteen, and because he had told her not to, in the kind of voice that meant he knew she would.

“You’re not going to tell me not to?” She was by Nonna under the paint-works floodlight, pulling her gloves on.

“You’ll do it anyway.”

“See? You understand me.”

“I understand that you’re stubborn.”

“Practically the same thing.”

He took the zip of her jacket and drew it up to her chin. She laughed. “Again?”

“It’s cold.”

“Maybe I like being cold.”

“Why?”

“So you’ll give me your jacket,” she said, and he looked at her for a second and took it off and put it round her shoulders and settled the collar.

“Happy?”

“Very.”

Then, quietly: “Brake at the fifth lamp post.”

“What?”

“The council resurfaced the gas-works bend on Tuesday. New tarmac to the fifth lamp post, the old stuff after it. Brake at the fifth and you’ll have grip. Past it you won’t.”

She stared at him. He was entirely serious. He had been out to look at the road. She touched his cheek, and then put her helmet on, and kissed his cheek through the gap under the visor, and said, “Don’t worry,” and he said, “I’m not,” and she said, “Terrible liar,” and got in.

She raced three times. The third was a woman in an old black coupé who was good, properly good, who got past her in the S-bends and held her off round the gas works and lost by half a car only because Serafina went to the fifth lamp post, which nobody in the history of Granny Shum’s had ever done, and the new tarmac held her like a hand.

“Fifth.” Granny Shum held a clementine out through Nonna’s window. “That was stupid.”

“It worked!”

“Stupid things work until they don’t,” said Granny Shum, and looked past her at the man standing at the edge of the light with his hands in his pockets, and said nothing else at all.

He was waiting by the car when she climbed out. “Won,” she said. “You don’t look impressed.”

He took the helmet from her and put it on the roof. “You’re safe,” he said.

Her face changed. “Oh.” She stepped in and put her arms round his waist and her face against his chest, and he put one hand on the back of her head, and after a while she felt his mouth against her hair. “Well done,” he said, and that was better.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Tuesday after Christmas, at twelve minutes past one in the morning, he fell asleep in her passenger seat.

She was driving the grey estate round the harbour because hers was on the lift, and he had been looking out at the water, and then his head tipped towards the window and his eyes closed and he was gone. She looked at him. She looked at the road. She looked at him again. Oh.

She slowed down. The harbour lights lay in long gold stripes on the black water. His breathing was slow. His hands lay loose in his lap. He looked younger. Not much. Enough. Without the watchfulness in his eyes and the careful set of his shoulders, he looked as if he had finally put something down.

She turned the heater up a notch and moved the vent off his face. She thought about waking him, and didn’t. She drove the way Mr. Kwok drove: no hard braking, no sudden turns, the engine never above a murmur. Along the harbour road past the container cranes. Over the old bridge. Through the tunnel and out round the long empty loop of the coast road, black sea on one side, the city lit up on the other. And round again. On the coast road his head slid off the window and landed on her shoulder. Oh, no. She kept both hands on the wheel and didn’t move that shoulder a millimetre for twenty minutes, not on the bends, not at the lights. It was harder than the fifth lamp post. Halfway round the third loop she peeled Granny Shum’s clementine one-handed against the wheel, ate half, and left the other half on the dashboard for him.

At twenty-five past three, parked on the harbour wall with the engine ticking, he woke. Not all at once, for the first time since she’d known him. Slowly. His brow creased. His eyes opened without that animal alertness in them, and for several seconds he looked confused. Then he turned his head and saw her watching him.

“Morning,” she said.

“What time is it?”

“Three twenty-five.”

“How long?”

She made a show of considering. “Two hours and eleven minutes. I timed it.”

He went still. “I don’t sleep in cars.”

“You do in mine. Well. Yours. With me driving.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“You looked comfortable. You’re welcome.”

He rubbed a hand over his face. “I shouldn’t have—”

“Don’t.”

He stopped. He sat back, and looked at the harbour, and for the first time since she had known him, he looked disoriented by something that wasn’t dangerous. She found it unbearably endearing.

“Why does it work?” he said. “In this seat.”

She thought about it. “Because you know how I drive. You’ve been behind me through the S-bends. You know I won’t crash. Not with you in the car. You trust my driving, that’s all.”

He turned his head and looked at her: the side of her face in the light off the water, her hand on the wheel with the old burn on the back of it, the shoulder she still hadn’t moved.

“That isn’t all it is,” he said, and ate the clementine, every piece of it.

At home, in the cold flat above a laundry on the far side of the market, he sat in the chair by the door with his coat on and listed what might have happened while he was asleep in that car. A car pulling alongside at the lights. Someone in the lay-by. A phone pointed through the glass. A woman driving the same loop three times in a night, where anyone at all could time her. He got to eleven. He ought to have been frightened by all of them. He was only frightened by number eleven.

Serafina: home??

Haozhen: Yes.

Serafina: you slept 2h11m in your own car and NOW you’re awake

Haozhen: Yes.

Serafina: that’s insulting to my driving

Haozhen: Your driving is fine.

Serafina: you owe me petrol

Haozhen: How much.

Serafina: one (1) more nap. thursday. 3am. corner of your street. don’t be late guard

He read it four times. Then he did something he had never once done on any phone in ten years. He saved her number under a name. He typed SONG S., looked at it, deleted it, and typed Sera.

✦ ✦ ✦

After that she picked him up. Nobody decided it. Two or three nights a week, a text, or no text, and she would be there on the corner of whichever street he named, and he would get in, and she would drive the long loop, bridge, tunnel, coast road, until the sky went grey. He slept against the window, or on her shoulder. He learned the shape of the route. He learned the way she drove when she was trying to make him sleep.

“You’re losing sleep,” he said on Thursday, at ten to three, with his eyes half shut.

“I’m a mechanic. My hours are already terrible. Go to sleep.”

He reached across and took her hand on the gear lever, and his thumb moved across her knuckles, and a few minutes later his eyes closed.

On Friday he took the grey car away from her garage and got as far as the corner at the end of the street, and she heard him stop. Then reverse, all the way back, and get out under the shutter.

“What did you do?”

“Your dampers were finished. The bushes were worn out, the alignment was off and the back end was doing something I didn’t like. It was falling over. It doesn’t fall over now.”

He looked at the car. “You didn’t ask.”

“You’d have said no.”

“Yes.”

“So I didn’t ask. Obviously.” She wiped her hands. “You drive like you’re being chased. And you keep turning up in a car that needs work, and I want you to keep turning up.” She straightened his collar. “In one piece, preferably.”

“How much do I owe you?”

“Don’t you dare.”

He looked at her as if nobody had ever touched his car without a form, and then he bent and kissed her forehead, and then, when she lifted her face, her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

On New Year’s Eve she drove, because she insisted, and he objected, and she ignored him. Mouse’s cousin had a farmhouse in the hills behind the reservoir with a view straight down over the whole harbour, and at twenty to midnight they were on the last narrow lane up to it, in the grey estate, with the city spread out below like something spilled.

“Are you awake?”

“Yes.”

“Good. I think you’re getting addicted to my driving.”

“Perhaps.”

“That’s practically a confession.”

He turned his head. “I like being here,” he said. “In your car.”

Her face went soft, and she was about to say something when the back of the estate stepped out on a patch of loose gravel, and she caught it, and the lane narrowed, and the nearside wheels dropped off the edge of the tarmac with a heavy thump, and the car came to rest at a ridiculous angle in a shallow ditch with its headlights pointing at a hedge.

Silence. “Well,” said Serafina.

“Are you hurt? Your head? Your shoulder?”

“I’m fine.” She stared through the windscreen. Then she turned slowly towards him. “Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

“Two wheels in a ditch,” said Haozhen, “is still parked.”

“Your car is in a ditch, Haozhen.”

“Our car,” he said.

She laughed so hard she had to hold on to the wheel. He reached over and touched her cheek, checking, once more, and then he undid his seat belt, and hers, and made sure she wasn’t caught on the wheel, and drew her over the console into his lap, sideways, her back against the door, her knees over his. Her hands found his shoulders. He kissed her. He took his time, and whatever was in it made her forget the ditch entirely. She took a fistful of his sweater. His hand spread at the small of her back under her coat and pulled her closer, and his mouth went to her jaw, and under it, slow, to the place where her pulse was, and stayed there as if he were counting it.

Below them the whole harbour went up at once. Gold and red and white, slow enormous flowers of fire opening over the water, the bang coming a second late and rolling up the hill.

She watched the fireworks. He watched her. She could feel him doing it.

“You’re supposed to look at the fireworks.”

“I’ve seen fireworks. Nine countries. From roofs, mostly.” The gold came down over the water and lit his face. “I was always watching somebody else. Somebody I’d been told to watch.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m not told.”

“Happy New Year,” she said.

“Happy New Year.”

She kissed his cheek. “Resolutions?”

He was quiet so long she thought he wouldn’t answer. “I don’t know how to want things,” he said at last. No self-pity in it. A plain fact, like the motor pool. “They tell you where to stand. What to eat, when. Which chair to sleep in. For ten years I’ve wanted the job done and the car to start.”

She sat back on his knees and poked him in the chest. “Then start small. Want a sandwich. A good one. With egg, from the stall under the flyover. That’s this year. Once you get the hang of it you can want something bigger.”

His mouth moved. The real smile.

“I want to sleep,” he said. “I want to work less. I want to stop driving everywhere on my own. I want the passenger seat. In your car, in mine, it doesn’t matter. With you driving.”

“That’s your resolution?”

“Part of it.”

“What’s the rest?”

His hand flattened on her back and gripped, hard, as though somebody might try to lift her off him. “Mostly you.”

She had to look at the water before she could speak. Then she held his face in both hands and kissed him, and didn’t make a joke about it, and when she drew back she said, “That’s a very good resolution, Haozhen.”

“Then I’ll keep it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The tow truck brought the grey car down to the garage at a quarter past two. A scraped bumper, a cracked undertray; the suspension had held. She slid out from under it on the creeper and found him standing over her.

“You’re tired,” she said.

“Yes.”

She blinked. Usually he would deny it. Tonight he just said yes. She took him to the sofa and got the blanket, and he sat, and without being asked he moved over to make room for her, and when she sat down he put his head on her shoulder and found her hand.

“Wake me in the morning,” he said, already quieter. “Don’t let me sleep all day.” A pause. “Unless you want to.”

She kissed his temple. “Go to sleep.”
