And he did. Not because his body had made him. He slept because he was warm, and somebody was holding his hand, and the room was quiet, and for once he didn’t feel that he had to stay awake to keep himself alive.

His mug stood on the bench with its name turned to the wall. She noticed it after a while, and reached over with her free hand, and turned it round to face the room.

chapters.title: What He Does for Work
chapters.desc: Mouse finds the missing Belgian in a newspaper and a camera in the garage roof. Serafina lays out everything she knows on the workbench, and he doesn’t tell her she’s wrong.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”
chapters.content:
Mouse came in at sixteen minutes past ten on the second Saturday in January with two coffees, a paper bag of pastries, and the face of a woman who had found something she very much wished she hadn’t.

Serafina looked up from the gearbox on the bench. “That’s a terrible face.”

“Good morning to you too.” Mouse put the coffees down. She didn’t take her coat off. “Remember the Belgian?”

Serafina’s hand stopped. There were a great many Belgians in the world. Only one had been walked out of a government reception by a man who wasn’t a guard and put into the back of a car that sat too low on its springs.

“Marchal.”

“I found him.” Mouse took a folded printout out of her bag. “Not where. In a newspaper.”

It was a Brussels paper, in French. A photograph of a tall fair man in a grey suit, smiling at what looked like a wedding: Lucien Marchal (46). Under it, smaller, a woman on a doorstep in Antwerp with her hand over her mouth, and two teenage boys behind her. A family appeal, a week old. He had been last seen at a reception on Battery Hill in October. The police here said he had left the city. The police there said he had never arrived.

“His ticket home was used on the twenty-third,” said Mouse, flat. “He wasn’t on the plane.”

Serafina read it twice. She remembered the fair man’s face going the colour of paper. She remembered him walking anyway, with a hand at his elbow, not gripping.

Mouse leaned on the bench. “There’s something else. I swept the place last night. After you told me about the brakes, and the knocks at two in the morning, I thought I’d look.” She put a small thing down on the steel between them. A lens on a sliver of circuit board, no bigger than a fingernail, with a hair of wire trailing off it. “It was in the roof. Over the lift. Pointing at the bench. Pointing at you.”

Serafina looked at it. Then she picked up her coffee, and found that her hand wasn’t steady, and put it down again.

“Have you asked him?” said Mouse.

The answer was no. She had thought about it every night since October. But now there was a mug with his name on the bottom. His coffee in her cupboard. His spare jacket on the hook behind the office door. And a newspaper from Brussels.

“I’ll ask him,” she said. “When he comes. He always comes.” It sounded less like confidence than like something she had got used to leaning on. Mouse pushed one of the coffees closer and said, “Drink it before it goes cold,” and went to sit behind her screens without putting her headphones on, which she never did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu came in at noon with a crate of oil, put it down gently, and came and leaned on the bench next to her, not looking at what she’d laid out on it. Looking at his own hands.

“You going to tell him to go?”

“I don’t know.”

“Two stretches, me. You know that. You never asked what for. Week I got out, you gave me a key. Said the kettle’s there, the toilet’s out the back, don’t touch Gilded’s gearbox.” He rubbed his thumb over an old scar on his knuckle. “Nobody else gave me a key.”

“That’s different. You didn’t take anyone’s dad, Wu.”

Big Wu was quiet for a while. “No,” he said. “I didn’t.” He pushed off the bench. “I’m only saying. You’re the one with the keys. You decide who gets one. Always have.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Haozhen came at eight forty-two. She heard the grey car in the alley, the brakes biting clean at the corner, her brakes, and then the side door. He came in, and stopped.

There was no coffee waiting for him. She had laid it all out on the bench under the work lamp the way she laid out the symptoms of a car nobody else could fix, in a row, until they stopped being separate things and turned into one. A photograph of the grey estate. The Autumn Reception guest list. A strip of black cotton, frayed at one end, which she had found caught in the runner of his back seat in December and kept without knowing why. A photograph of a dark van, taken by a delivery camera in the lane on the old ring road. The photocopy from Auntie Chu: Qin H. East service. 19:02. The camera from the roof. And in the middle, the woman on the doorstep in Antwerp.

He took his gloves off, slowly. “What’s all this?”

“Your hobbies.”

He looked at her. She didn’t smile.

His face didn’t change when he saw the newspaper. That was the first thing she noticed. No surprise. No irritation. He read the headline.

“His family?”

“Antwerp. A wife and two sons. Nobody’s heard from him since October.”

He put his gloves down beside the paper. “That’s unfortunate.”

She laughed, once, in disbelief. “Unfortunate?”

“Serafina—”

“Don’t.” She held up the photograph of the van between two fingers. “This is what he went into. Registered to a company with a director who died six years ago. Same trick as your car. This is your car. You changed the plates after the reception, but the scrape on the back left corner is the same scrape.” She put it down. “I found the brakes. I found the company. I found the sign-in sheet. I found your name. I watched you take a man out of a building and put him in a car. And now his children are in the newspaper.” She looked at him. “Tell me I’ve got it wrong.”

He didn’t. The silence weighed more than any denial.

“Who are you?”

He looked tired. He looked as if he had come round to spend the evening with his girlfriend. “I move people,” he said at last.

Her fingers closed on the edge of the bench. “Move them where?”

“Where they’re supposed to go.”

“Police? Military? The government?”

He neither confirmed nor denied any of it.

“Was Marchal a criminal?”

“I can’t tell you that.”

“Was he alive when you handed him over?”

“Yes.” It came at once. “He was conscious. He was breathing. He could walk, though he’d rather not have. Two men in a van, under a broken streetlight on the old ring road. I don’t know what happened after. I’m not told. Mostly I’m not told.”

“And you don’t ask?”

“I was eighteen. They’d told me since I was sixteen that asking was somebody else’s job.” He looked at the paper. “Once you’ve done it without asking, it’s very hard to start.”

“His wife is looking for him. His sons.”

His jaw moved, slightly. “I know.”

“Then how do you sleep?”

For the first time, he looked away. Not for long. Long enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had imagined this a dozen ways. In one he laughed and told her she’d misunderstood. In another he explained that Marchal was a danger to a great many people and there were reasons she couldn’t see. She hadn’t imagined this: him standing in her garage looking at a photograph of a man’s family as if it were a piece of information he had already accounted for.

She came round the end of the bench, so there was more space between them, and made herself ask it. “Do you kill people?”

He didn’t move. The question seemed to take something out of the air.

“Sometimes,” he said.

She felt the word land before she understood it. She looked at his hands. She knew those hands. She knew them on a steering wheel, at a quarter to three. She knew how they passed her a socket before she asked for it, and how carefully they had wiped oil off the corner of her mouth. She had never once let herself think about what else they had done.

“Was Marchal one of them?”

“No.”

“Would you have?”

He considered it, which was the worst thing he could have done. “If I’d been told to.”

She took a step back. “That’s a horrible thing to say.”

“I know.”

“You’re telling me the parts of the truth you can afford.”

He held her eyes. “I don’t lie to you. I’ve never lied to you. I just haven’t told you most of it.”

“I’d rather you were someone else,” she said, and it was out before she could stop it, and she saw it reach him. He didn’t flinch. He took it, and that was how she knew it had gone in. “I’m sorry,” she said.

“Don’t be.”

“Have you done it since you met me? Taken someone? And then come here and drunk coffee out of that mug?”

A long pause. “Yes.”

“When?”

“The Tuesday before Christmas.”

She shut her eyes. The Tuesday before Christmas he had come in after midnight and sat on the sofa while she fought a seized bolt, and reached over without a word and loosened it for her, and later she had fallen asleep against his shoulder, and he had held her till it was light. She had thought it was an ordinary night. Perhaps, to him, it had been. Perhaps that was what frightened her most.

She picked the camera off the bench and held it up between them. “And this? Is this why there was a camera in my roof pointing at my bench?”

His face tightened. “I had the footage taken down.”

“You had the camera put up.”

“Yes.”

“You watched me.”

“I watched the building.”

“No, Haozhen. Don’t make it sound different from what it was.”

Something moved under his face then. Not the composure. Something beneath it. “I don’t want you in this.”

“I’m already in it.”

“You don’t get to keep me beside you when you want me and keep half of yourself locked in a room I’m not allowed into.”

“Serafina—”

“Do you know the number? How many?”

He went still. “Yes. Every one. Names. Dates. Where. What they were wearing. I don’t let myself forget them.”

“Then I don’t want it,” she said. “Not tonight. Not the names, not the stories. Not a number you’d give me and expect me to know what to do with.”

“If you ever want it, ask me, and I’ll tell you all of it. Not standing up, with that photograph on your bench.”

“Then leave,” she said.

He looked at her. “Do you want me to leave?”

“Yes.” He didn’t move. She swallowed. “Yes. I do.”

He nodded once, as if she had told him the time. “All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He put his coat on without hurrying. He didn’t argue, and that made her angrier than anything else he could have done. At the door he stopped with his hand on the frame and his back to her.

“If you tell anyone about this—”

She went cold all over. “Then what?”

He turned his head. “Then nothing. I’d make sure nobody touched you for it. That’s all I was going to say.” His knuckles had gone white on the frame. It was the only part of him that moved. “Lock this door after me. And the shutter. You leave the shutter up at night. You shouldn’t.”

Then he came back across the garage. Not fast. Past the bench and the row of evidence and the camera. He stopped in front of her, close enough that she could feel the cold of the alley still on his coat, and his hands stayed at his sides where she could see them, the way they had on the first night.

“May I?”

She should have said no. She stood still. His fingers came to her jaw, gently enough to make her throat ache, and he kissed her once. Quiet, and restrained, and unbearably familiar, as if he were learning her face well enough to keep it.

She kissed him back. Furious with him, with herself, with a doorstep in Antwerp. She took his coat in both fists and pulled him in and kissed him as though she could make him answer for every word he’d refused to say, and her face was wet, and she didn’t know when that had started. She was the one who stopped. She put her hand flat on his chest and pushed. Not hard. He went back one step and no further.

“Don’t do that,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“Go.”

He went. The side door closed. A moment later she heard the grey car start in the alley, and the brakes at the corner, clean, and then nothing.

His mug was on the shelf, name to the wall. She took it down. She put it upside down on the bench, and walked away from it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past eleven she drove the loop alone. Bridge, tunnel, coast road. No music. Her body had learned it his way: no hard braking, the engine murmuring in third. On the coast road, at the bend where his head always slid onto her shoulder, she dropped her right shoulder a fraction to catch it. There was nobody there.

She put her foot down then. For a few seconds there was nothing but speed, and then she lifted, and turned into the lay-by above the harbour, and killed the engine. The silence came in like water.

A wife in Antwerp. Two boys. A man who had been alive when he was handed over. Sometimes.

She put her forehead on the wheel. “Fuck,” she said, and her voice sounded small in the car.

Then she cried. Not the quiet kind she could wipe off. Her shoulders shook and her nose ran and she made an ugly helpless noise. She thought of him asleep in the passenger seat. Two hours and eleven minutes. She thought of him saying Sometimes. She hit the wheel with the heel of her hand. “Goddamn you,” she said, and it came apart in the middle.

She got out into the cold and let the sound out, a raw furious howl that put a bird up out of the dark somewhere below, and bent over with her hands on her knees and cried until her throat hurt. Nobody came.

When she got back in, she looked at the empty passenger seat. For the first time since December she didn’t want to drive anybody home. She drove herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was parked on the old service road below the lay-by with his lights off. He had followed her from the end of her street, two cars back. He knew where she would go.

He watched her car rock a little on its springs when she hit the wheel. He heard her, when she got out. The sound came down the hill and across the road, and he heard her voice break, and he sat with his hands on his own wheel and did nothing. She had told him to go. He had gone. He only made sure nobody else stopped in that lay-by. A van slowed, once. He flashed his lights at it, and it thought better of it.

His breathing was wrong. Too fast. His phone lit up on the passenger seat. Transfer confirmation pending. Call when available. He looked at it, and turned the phone off. Then he turned it back on, typed Are you under her name, deleted it, and put the phone face down on the empty seat.

He followed her home, and watched her go up the iron stairs to the flat above the garage. He stood under the overhang of the print works at the end of the alley. He knew which window was hers. At a quarter past two her light went out. At four it began to rain. At half past five the first delivery van came through and its headlights slid over the wet stones. He didn’t sleep. He hadn’t expected to.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down the iron stairs at twelve minutes past six with her hair up and her face washed in cold water until the red had nearly gone, and the first thing she saw was the grey estate at the end of the alley. The second was him, beside it, his coat dark with rain, his hands in his pockets.

She stopped on the bottom step.

“You followed me. To the harbour.”

“Yes.”

“Did you watch me?”

“I stayed across the road.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

A pause. “Yes.”

“I told you to leave, and you don’t get to decide you can stand outside my house all night instead.”

“Then what were you doing here?”

“Making sure nobody followed you.”

“You think that makes it better?”

“No.”

He could have told her about the people who had been asking about him since the reception. About the copies of the footage he hadn’t been able to have taken down. He had no right to give her more only when he wanted to keep her close. So he said nothing.

She unlocked the garage and pushed the side door open. “Go, Haozhen.”

He didn’t move. “Are you safe?”

Her face changed. Not softer. Worse. “Don’t ask me that.”

He swallowed. “All right.”

He walked away up the alley with his shoulders straight and his hands still in his pockets, and didn’t look back. At the corner he paused for one second.

Inside, the garage was cold. His mug was still upside down on the bench. She looked at it. Then she turned the lights on, and picked up her wrench, and went back to work, and for the first time she didn’t leave a space for him beside her.

chapters.title: She Should Run
chapters.desc: She knows exactly how to run. Instead she turns up outside his flat at six in the morning with two egg sandwiches and four rules.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to run. I’m the one people run with.”
chapters.content:
Serafina knew exactly how to run.

She knew which roads out of the city missed the busiest cameras, and which petrol stations along the coast still took cash without looking up. She knew how to change cars without anyone noticing, how to rent a room by the week, and how to leave a place without leaving anything behind that someone could use to find her. Since she was nineteen she had driven people away from the industrial district at two in the morning, once a woman with a suitcase and a split lip all the way to the border road.

And she had learned some of it, she realised on the Sunday he left her standing by the side door, from him. She had watched him long enough. The reflection checked before a room. The car remembered if it passed twice. Never his back to a door.

She spent the rest of Sunday with a map. On Monday morning she found a listing for a workshop lease outside Turin, with a flat above it and a yard for two cars, and she read it four times. At one she closed it. At two she rang Mouse and asked whether she knew anyone who wanted to buy a red 1992 rally hatchback with three hundred thousand kilometres on her.

Mouse went quiet. “Nobody asks about selling Nonna unless somebody’s died.” A pause. “Leaving the garage?”

“Maybe.”

“Leaving him?”

Serafina shut her eyes. “Especially him.”

“Then I’ve got nothing useful. Don’t sell Nonna,” said Mouse, and rang off, and Serafina looked at the little blue line she had drawn out of the city on the map, and found it perfectly reasonable, and hated it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-five to five on Monday she was at Granny Shum’s yard, the lean-to behind the paint works where the Saturday crowd kept their stove and their spare tyres and argued on the nights there was no meet. Mr. Kwok was examining a stack of tyres that didn’t need examining.

“You’re late.”

“It’s four thirty-five.”

“Exactly.”

She helped him shift the wheels. For a while they worked without speaking. Then he said, to a tyre, “Where’s your man?”

She nearly dropped one on her foot. “He’s not my man.”

“Then why do you look like somebody stole him?”

“Mm. Where’s he taking you?”

“Nowhere.”

“Good. I don’t like men who take women places without telling them where.”

“He’s not taking me anywhere.”

“Then why do you look at the road every time a car comes in?”

She stopped.

“I don’t know,” she said.

Mr. Kwok didn’t ask her to explain. He put the tyre down. “Forty years I drove a taxi. You know what a good driver knows? When to leave the race.”

“You drove a taxi into the fish market.”

“Once.” He considered it. “Still. I knew when to leave.”

“I’m not in a race.”

“No? Then why are you so frightened of losing?”

She didn’t answer. A few minutes later he asked if she wanted tea, and she said yes, and neither of them said his name again.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten to midnight on Tuesday, in the flat above the laundry, Qin Haozhen wasn’t sleeping, which wasn’t unusual. What was unusual was that he had stopped trying.

The flat was clean and nearly empty: a narrow bed he didn’t use, two shirts, a saucer for keys, and the hard chair by the door. Below him the machines ran until one and the window shook on the spin. The laundry woman’s cat, a fat tortoiseshell who belonged to nobody in particular, slept on a heated pad under the counter and despised him.

On his laptop was a file he had read twice. SONG, SERAFINA. The Bureau had asked for a follow-up on the Autumn Reception. The operation was marked complete, but there were loose ends: the copied footage, questions about the car, the attention a Brussels paper was giving Marchal. And a line in an internal note. Possible civilian witness. Not a subject. Not yet.

He rang the duty number. It answered on the second ring.

“Qin.”

“She isn’t involved,” he said.

“Who?”

“Serafina Song. She was at the reception. She works in the motor trade. She noticed a car. That’s all.”

“She’s been asking questions. About Marchal.”

“She doesn’t have access to anything operational.”

“Does she?”

“No.”

It wasn’t a careless lie, or an instinctive one. He knew exactly what she had seen. He knew what she had found, and that she had enough to identify him and more than enough sense to know the story he’d told her was incomplete. He lied anyway, slowly, with his eyes on the photograph of her in the file.

“Are you certain?”

“Yes.”

“Then keep it that way.”

It was the first time in ten years he had knowingly given the Bureau false information about a civilian. He didn’t feel guilty. He felt something colder, and he opened a blank page and began a list. The camera in her roof: gone, because Mouse had found it before he could. No new equipment near her. The copied footage, to be traced. Anyone with access to her file, to be named. Any future question about her, to come through him.

He stopped at the last line. He was planning to protect her. He was also planning to do it without telling her. He looked at that for a while, and didn’t change it.

He typed Are you all right? and deleted it. He typed I owe you an explanation and deleted that too. He put the phone face down. He wouldn’t go to her. Not unless she asked. He had promised himself that much, and it was the only promise he had left that he hadn’t broken.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four minutes to six on Wednesday morning he came down the stairs with a laundry bag and stopped on the last step.

She was sitting on the bonnet of his grey estate, in a dark wool coat and trainers, with her hair tied back and her cheeks pink with cold and a paper bag beside her. She was eating.

“Morning,” she said.

He looked at his watch. “It’s nearly six.”

“Excellent observation.”

“Why are you here?”

“Breakfast.” She held up the second half of something. “Egg. Too much sesame. The stall under the flyover. You said you’d want one.”

“Is that for me?”

“No. I brought two to eat in front of you.” She took a bite. “I haven’t decided if you’re allowed one.”

He put the bag down. He genuinely didn’t seem to know what to do with his hands. Then he put his keys on the roof.

“Why didn’t you come up?”

“You haven’t invited me. You should have thought about that before you got mysterious and emotionally unavailable.”

“Is that what I am?”

“Among other things.” She held out the sandwich. Their fingers brushed. Neither of them said anything about it. He leaned on the car next to her and ate.

“You’ve been thinking about leaving,” he said.

She turned her head. “How do you know that?”

“You asked Mouse about selling Nonna. Mr. Kwok rang me. He wanted to know where I was taking you.” He looked at his sandwich. “He also said I should stay away from you.”

“What did you say?”

“That he was probably right.”

Something went across her face.

“I don’t want you to leave,” he said.

“That’s unfortunate. Because I thought about it for four days. I could have been gone by Thursday.” She brushed crumbs off her coat. “But I’ve watched people run since I was nineteen. I’ve driven them. I know what I am.”

“And what’s that?”

“I’m not going to run. I’m the one people run with.” She folded the paper bag into a square. “So. I have rules. Four.”

“I’m listening.”

“One. No lies. Not about work, not about where you are, not about what you’ve done. If you can’t tell me something, you say you can’t tell me. Don’t make something up to keep me comfortable.”

“Agreed.”

“Two. Nothing in the garage. No weapons. No files. No cameras. Nobody you’re hiding. Nobody coming in the side door because you need somewhere to do business. And you don’t use my tools or my cars for work.”

“Agreed.”

“Three. If you’re going to disappear, you tell me. If you can’t say where, say you’re going. If you can’t say when you’ll be back, say that too.”

“I can’t always give you notice.”

“Then tell me when you can.”

“Agreed.”

She looked at the paper square in her hands. “Four. If I say I want out, you let me go. No questions. No following me. No watching the garage. No sending somebody to check on me. No standing outside my house all night because you think I’m having a bad one.” She looked up. “And if you ever want out, of all of it, you say it to me first. Before anyone. Before you’ve even said it properly to yourself. You come to the garage and you say Sera, I want out, and I’ll have the car outside.”

He went still.

“Is that what you want now?” he said. “Out?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“Because I need to know I can.”

He lowered his eyes. It reached him further than she’d meant it to; she saw it go in. “All right,” he said.

“Just like that?”

“Would you rather I negotiated?” He looked at her. “If you stay, I want you to stay because you chose it.”

She slid off the bonnet. They were close enough that he could have kissed her, and he didn’t, and she noticed that he didn’t. “Your laundry bag is leaking,” she said, and it was, a thin line of water across the step, and he looked down at it and sighed, and she laughed at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, at half past six, he made tea. She looked round his flat, and there was nothing to look at.

“Do you own anything that isn’t black, grey or white?”

He opened a cupboard. On the top shelf sat one red bowl.

She stared at it. “That’s a cry for help.”

He put a mug in front of her and sat down opposite, and she wrapped both hands round it and asked the thing she had come up the stairs to ask.

“What was the first job?”

He looked at the tea for a while. “I was eighteen. There was a teacher. I was told he was dangerous.”

“Was he?”

“I don’t know. They gave me a photograph and an address. I was to find him and confirm where he went every day. Then I was told to help move him.”

“Where?”

“I wasn’t told.”

“Did you ask?”

“No. I wanted the job.” He said it without asking for anything, the way he’d say the road was wet. “Two years at an academy first, from sixteen. Then a woman came to watch us on the range and chose three of us. I was the one who never asked.”

“What happened to the teacher?”

“I don’t know. By the time I thought to ask, I had another job. And then another.” He looked up at her. “I didn’t find out because I was afraid of the answer.”

“You were a child.”

“I didn’t feel like one.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

He didn’t answer that. She understood something then about the man across the table. Not enough to forgive him. Enough to see the boy who’d been handed an address.

“Do you remember his name?”

“Yes. I’m not going to tell you.”

“Okay.”

He looked surprised. “You’re not going to push?”

“I asked. You said no. I’m allowed to be annoyed about it without pretending you didn’t answer.” She drank her tea. He reached across the table and turned her mug so the handle faced her hand. She noticed. Neither of them said anything.

At four minutes past seven, beside the grey estate, with the sky gone pale and colourless over the laundry, he asked if he could come to the garage later.

“For what?”

“To see you.”

“After six. Don’t bring work. Or coffee. I have coffee.”

“Your coffee is terrible.”

She gasped, and he smiled. It was the first one she’d had from him in days, and before she could think better of it she reached up and took a sesame seed off the corner of his mouth.

“You missed one.”

“Did I?”

She leaned in and kissed the place where it had been. A small kiss. Almost nothing. She was already turning away when his hand came to her waist.

“That’s not fair,” he said.

“What isn’t?”

“You can’t do that and leave.”

“I can. I have four rules.”

He drew her back in, and she laughed, startled, as he lifted her onto the bonnet of the car, and the laugh went into his mouth. It was warm and deliberate and full of everything he’d held back since she told him to go, and she took two handfuls of his coat and pulled him in between her knees and held on. When he lifted his head their foreheads stayed together.

“Is this allowed?”

“Barely.”

“Which rule does it break?”

“None. You’re just annoying.” She put her palm on his cheek. “Don’t make me regret staying.”

“I won’t take it for granted.”

She slid down. “After six,” she said, pointing at him, and walked to Nonna, and when she looked back he was still standing by the estate with his hands in his pockets, and she gave him a small wave, and he gave one back. It was an ordinary thing. It felt enormous.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday, Lunar New Year’s Eve, he arrived at Granny Shum’s yard at eighteen minutes past five with two bottles of red wine and a box of oranges. He had been told to bring neither.

“Who told you to bring gifts?”

“No one. It’s New Year’s Eve. People bring things.”

“People bring things when they know what they’re doing.” She took the box off him. “You’re hopeless.”

Inside, somebody had hung red paper over the door and pushed three tables together under the lean-to, and they were covered: dumplings, white-cut chicken, a great dish of braised duck with mushrooms, greens, and a whole steamed fish under a scatter of ginger and spring onion. Auntie Chu came out of the kitchen with a plate, looked Haozhen up and down, said, “Have you eaten?” and when he said not yet, said, “Good. Sit,” and pointed. He sat.

Big Wu’s mother came late. She was small and silver-haired and wore a red scarf and the authority of a woman who had spent sixty years making sure everybody ate enough, and she stopped at the head of the table with a bag of her own dumplings and said, “Who’s this?”

“Sera’s friend,” said Big Wu.

His mother looked at Haozhen. At Serafina. At Haozhen. “Boyfriend?”

Serafina choked on her tea. “Ma!”

“I’m asking.”

“Friend,” said Haozhen, to his tea.

“Friend is not a proper answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

She studied him. Then she put her bag down and took his hand in both of hers. “You’re too thin. Look at your face, it’s all corners. Do you eat?”

“What do you eat?”

He thought about it. “Food.”

She turned to her son. “Why are all the young men stupid?” and the whole table went up, and Serafina covered her mouth, and Haozhen bowed his head. Big Wu’s mother sat down in the chair next to him as though it had always been hers.

“Your family coming?”

He hesitated. “No.”

“Then you come here. New Year, you eat with us. You don’t sit on your own.” She patted his hand. “Now you have another family. Eat.” And she put a piece of chicken in his bowl, and another, and a dumpling, and he ate them.

When the fish came she took the spoon. “Fish for everyone. Good fortune.” She served Serafina, then Big Wu, and when she reached for his bowl he turned it gently towards her.

“Give it to her,” he said. “She likes the belly.”

Serafina looked up. She hadn’t told him. He had watched her pick the same piece off every fish since November and kept it somewhere in that impossible head of his. Big Wu’s mother smiled the smile of a woman who has been proved right. “A man should know what his girl likes.”

He didn’t correct her that time. He moved a piece from his own plate to Serafina’s. “Careful. Bones.”

“I know how to eat a fish.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you telling me?”

“Habit.” She ate it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine, out by the estate, under the red lanterns, with the leftovers on the back seat and firecrackers going off three streets away, Serafina leaned on the passenger door.

“They’ll expect you tomorrow.”

“I know.” A pause. “I don’t mind.”

“Don’t mind what?”

“Being expected.”

For a man who’d spent ten years being available to people who only called when they wanted something done, a chair at a table was a different thing. No assignment. Nobody waiting for him to deliver anyone. A bowl, and somebody who would notice if he didn’t come. She took his hand.

“Happy New Year.”

“It isn’t midnight.”

“Don’t ruin it.” She kissed him, brief and warm, and he put his forehead against hers.

“Oranges tomorrow?”

“Absolutely not.”

She got in. He closed her door and walked round, and for once he didn’t look at his phone before he started the engine. There was a box of fish on the back seat, an orange rolling on the floor, and her hand lying on the console between them. He started the car. She took his hand. And he drove her home.

chapters.title: The First Time He Bleeds in Her Garage
chapters.desc: He’s late for Valentine’s dinner because of a knife in a stairwell. He comes in bleeding with cold dumplings, and won’t go near the Bureau doctor.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule two doesn’t cover blood. Sit down before you fall on my car.”
chapters.content:
“You’re late.”

He looked at his watch. “It’s seven forty-two.”

“Exactly.”

“You said eight.”

“I said dumplings at eight. I didn’t say you could turn up whenever you liked.”

He stood under the half-raised shutter on the fourteenth of February with a paper bag in his hand, and behind her the garage had been made unrecognisable. The bench was cleared. The tools hung in order along the wall. Two bowls sat on the little table by the office, with a bottle of wine and a plate of sliced oranges and a candle that she had clearly bought for the sole purpose of making fun of him.

“What’s the candle for?”

“Atmosphere.”

“It’s a garage.”

“Exactly. We need all the help we can get.”

“Is this a date?”

“No. It’s dinner.”

“On Valentine’s Day.”

“An unfortunate coincidence.”

He nodded gravely. She took the bag and looked inside. “Chive and egg?”

“And prawn.”

She looked up. “You remembered.”

“You like both.”

“That’s suspiciously thoughtful.”

“I’ll try to be less considerate next time.”

She was wearing a dark green knitted vest over a white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow, and there was a streak of grease along her cheekbone she hadn’t found. He rubbed it off with his thumb.

“Distracting,” he said.

“Then stop looking at me.”

“I’ve tried.”

That got him the small, pleased smile she gave when she’d won an argument without having to finish it. He took his coat off. His phone buzzed. He looked at the screen, and nothing about him changed, and everything did: his shoulders stayed easy and his face stayed calm and his attention went somewhere beyond the candle and the bowls and the garage walls.

“Work?” she said.

“Yes.”

“Tonight?”

“I’ll be back.”

“You said that last time.” She picked up the wine and put it down again. “Are you going to be in danger?”

“I don’t expect to be.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“There’s a situation I need to deal with.”

“That’s a very polished way of saying yes.”

“I’m not going to lie to you.”

“Good.” She caught the front of his sweater as he leaned in to kiss her forehead. “Half past eight.”

“I’ll try.”

“Nine.”

“Serafina.”

“Ten, and you’re buying me dessert.”

“Agreed.” At the door he looked back. “Happy Valentine’s Day.”

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you mean it.”

“I do.”

“Disgusting.” He went. She looked at the candle for a while. “Not a date,” she told it, and blew it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

At thirteen minutes past nine, in a housing block on the far side of the harbour, he had checked two of the building’s three entrances. The third was a service door behind the bins that didn’t shut unless somebody pulled it.

He saw the man before the man saw him. Thirty metres down, at the bottom of the stairwell. Dark jacket. No bag. One hand in a pocket. Then the man looked up, and neither of them spoke, and there was the particular kind of quiet that comes before violence, when nothing is louder but everything becomes deliberate.

The man moved first. The knife came out low in his right hand, already turning, aimed under the ribs. Haozhen turned with it and caught the wrist before the blade reached him, and they went into the wall together hard enough that the crack of it rang up four flights. The man twisted. The blade came round and opened Haozhen’s left forearm from just below the elbow almost to the wrist, a hot clean line, and he felt it and didn’t look at it. He drove his shoulder into the man’s chest, pinned the wrist against the concrete and bent it back until the fingers had to choose between the knife and the joint. The knife hit the step. The man came round with his other hand.

Haozhen caught that one too. A short, economical movement. Something gave under his grip with a sound like a stick in a fire, and the man screamed and went down on his knees on the landing, holding a hand that no longer pointed the right way.

Blood ran down Haozhen’s arm and collected at his wrist and dripped off his fingers onto the step. He kicked the knife down the stairwell. He checked the other hand, the pockets, the ankles. Nothing. He crouched long enough to make sure the man understood he wasn’t going anywhere near the blade, and the man looked up at him, grey with pain.

“Who sent you?”

Haozhen didn’t answer. His phone rang.

“Qin.”

“Status?”

“Contained.”

“Complications?”

He looked at the blood on the step. “No.”

“Are you injured?”

He pressed his thumb along the cut. “Nothing significant.”

“Medical team’s on standby. Report to the usual place.”

“I’ll deal with it.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“I’ll deal with it,” he said, and ended the call. The man on the landing was breathing in sobs. Haozhen looked at him once more and went down the stairs and out through the door behind the bins. He had promised dumplings at eight. It was twenty past nine.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes to one the side door opened. Serafina looked up from her phone on the sofa.

“You’re—”

He was standing in the doorway with his coat buttoned and his face composed and his hair damp from the rain. There was blood on his left hand. A dark stain had spread out from under the sleeve and down the coat.

She stood up so fast the sofa scraped. “What happened?”

“I’m late.”

“Haozhen.”

“I brought the dumplings.” He held up the paper bag in his right hand. There was a red smear on the bottom of it.

“Put that down.”

“Serafina—”

“Put it down.” He did. She crossed the garage and took his good arm and walked him to the stool by the kettle, and he let her, and that frightened her more than the blood. “Rule two doesn’t cover blood. Sit down before you fall on my car.”

She cut the sleeve. The cut ran down the outside of his forearm, long and clean, gaping in the middle where it went deepest, the edges already crusted. Her face went white, and then it went furious.

“What the fuck?”

“It’s not as bad as it looks.”

“Do you think I’m stupid?”

“No.”

“Then stop talking to me like I am.” She pressed a clean towel over it. “Hold that. Harder. Where’s your phone? Ring whoever you ring.”

“The Bureau has a doctor. No.”

It was the first time he’d said the word to her, and he said it as though it were the name of a dentist. She stared at him. “Your arm is bleeding through your clothes.”

“I noticed.”

“Congratulations. You have working eyes.” She reached for her own phone. He caught her wrist, gently.

“I don’t want them asking questions.”

“Then answer them.”

“I can’t.”

“Can’t or won’t?”

“Both.” He looked tired. Not the ordinary tired she’d learned in the passenger seat. Something sharper, the exhaustion of holding himself together round a wound for three hours. She swallowed.

“Fine. You’re not going to your Bureau doctor. You’re not going to bleed on my floor either.” She rang Mouse.

“Somebody had better be dead,” said Mouse, half asleep.

“Have you still got the big kit? Can you bring it? It’s Haozhen.”

A pause. “I’m coming.”

At seven minutes past one Mouse came in with the kit, two bottles of water and an expression that would have frightened a less injured man. She took one look. “Oh, for God’s sake.”

“Hello, Mouse.”

“Don’t hello me. That’s a knife.”

She cleaned it while Serafina held the lamp. Haozhen didn’t flinch. Serafina did, every time the gauze went in, as though it were being done to her. “That needs closing properly,” Mouse said, “and somebody needs to check there’s nothing cut underneath. I’m not stitching a man’s arm on a workbench, and neither are you.” She pointed at Serafina. “Promise me.”

“I promise I’ll get him seen.”

Mouse drove. The all-night clinic by the ferry pier had a doctor who had sewn up worse at worse hours and asked nothing that the word bicycle didn’t answer. Fourteen stitches. No tendon. Come back in ten days. Serafina listened to every word. Haozhen listened to about half.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to two, on the sofa in the garage office with his shirt off and a fresh dressing on his arm, he watched her lay the spare dressings out on a clean tray.

“Don’t move.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t be brave.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“Don’t tell me it doesn’t hurt.”

“Serafina.”

“What?”

“Breathe.”

“I am breathing.”

“Not very convincingly.”

The bruising round the cut had started to darken. In the lamplight she could see the rest of him properly for the first time, and she looked. Old scars, some thin and pale, some wide and puckered and unmistakably surgical. One near the collarbone. Two along the ribs. A small round one under the right shoulder that she didn’t let herself name. A long one across his side that disappeared under the waistband. She had seen some of them before. She had never counted them. Tonight she did.

“How many?”

“I don’t know.”

“That’s a lie.”

“Then more than I remember.”

“I’m furious,” she said, taping the edge of the dressing down.

“At me?”

“At the whole situation.”

“That’s broad.”

“I have a lot of anger.” He smiled, and she pointed at him. “Don’t.”

He caught the front of her vest with his good hand. “Come here.”

“Your arm.”

“I’m using the other one.”

He pulled, and she came, bracing her hand on the sofa back, and he brought her down sideways across his lap, careful of the arm, and kissed her. It was warm and familiar and she could feel what was under it, the tightness he’d carried in through the door. His hand spread on her back through the wool. She kissed him harder, and slid her palm down over his chest, over the old scar on his ribs, and he made a low sound into her mouth, and she broke away.

“Stop. You’re bleeding.”

A thin red line had come through the edge of the new dressing.

“Oh, you have got to be joking.”

“It’s minor.”

“Don’t say that word to me.” She pressed fresh gauze on it. “I’m charging you labour.”

“I’ll pay.”

“Double.”

“Fine.”

“You’re shaking,” he said.

She looked at her hands. They were. She put the gauze down and breathed. “You scared me.”

“I know.”

“No, you don’t. You walked in here with blood on your hand like you were late for a meeting. You brought me dumplings. You stood there looking at me as if nothing had happened.”

“I didn’t know how to come in,” he said. “I knew you’d be angry.”

“I am angry.”

“And frightened.”

“And now I’m going to be angry and frightened every time your phone rings.”

His jaw tightened. “I don’t want that for you.”

“Neither do I.” He reached for her hand. This time he didn’t pull. He only held it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past two she went to put his coat in the office and found his keys in the pocket, and went out to bring the grey estate in under the shutter before it rained again, and stopped by the driver’s door. Low on the panel, just above the sill, a neat round hole. The paint around it had cracked inwards. The metal round it was dished.

“Haozhen.”

He came to the doorway. She pointed.

“Damage,” he said.

“I’m going to need you to try harder.”

“It’s a bullet hole.”

“When?”

“Ten days ago.”

“Ten days.” Her voice went flat. “You’ve driven this car into my garage every night for ten days. I’ve driven it round the harbour with you asleep in it.”

“I had it checked.”

“Oh, wonderful.”

“It’s armoured. The cabin wasn’t touched.”

She stared at him, and then at the car that had always sat too low on its springs, that had needed new dampers in December and had made her wonder what on earth he kept in the boot. “I knew it was heavy,” she said. “I thought you carried bricks.”

“Was anyone else in the car?”

“No.”

“Were you?”

“Yes.”

Her mouth opened and shut. “Were you hit?”

“No.”

“Was anyone else hurt?”

“Not seriously.”

“Not seriously. I’m standing here looking at a bullet hole in your car and you’re talking about it like a shopping trolley.”

“I didn’t want you to worry.”

She laughed, a small exhausted sound. “You really have to find another excuse.”

“I know.”

She took his good hand. “Come inside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past three she made him sleep in Nonna. He objected once, looked at her face, and stopped. She pushed the passenger seat as far back as it would go and laid a folded blanket over it.

“I can sleep on the sofa.”

“The sofa’s for people who haven’t been stabbed.”

“That’s a strange rule.”

“It’s my garage. Down.”

He lay down. Nonna smelled of old upholstery and the orange cleaner she used on the dashboard. Serafina pulled a stool up to the open door with a notebook on her knee.

“What are you doing?”

“Making a list of things you’re not allowed to do.”

“That’ll be long.”

“It’s already longer than your patience.” She lifted the edge of the dressing. “First check.”

He opened one eye. “You’re counting?”

“I want to know how many times I have to do this before I believe you’re not bleeding.”

She checked at half past three. At four. At twenty-seven minutes past four he opened his eyes and said, “That’s four,” and she said, “Five, I’m counting the first one,” and he looked at her with enormous patience.

“Does it hurt?”

“It’s manageable.”

She looked at him.

“Yes,” he said. “It hurts.”

“Thank you.” She checked it at five, and at twenty to six, and at twelve minutes past six he said, “Are you going to do this until sunrise?”

“Possibly.”

“It won’t heal faster.”

“I’m aware.” She tucked the blanket round his legs. “I wasn’t there. When it happened. I was sitting here waiting for dumplings.”

“You couldn’t have known.”

“I know.”

“You can sleep.”

“I don’t want to.”

He turned his hand under hers and threaded their fingers together. “Then stay.”

She put her forehead against the edge of the seat. “I am.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter past seven the first light was coming through the high windows, and he was asleep. Properly asleep, his breathing slow, his hand loose round hers, his face turned towards the glass. She had checked the dressing eleven times. The twelfth could wait.

The cold dumplings were still on the bench. The candle had never been lit again. His coat lay folded over a chair, stiff down one sleeve, and the keys to an armoured car sat on top of her notebook. She thought about the stairwell she’d never see and the man with the knife and the call he hadn’t wanted to make, and about him coming through her door with blood on one hand and dinner in the other, and about the prawn ones, which he had remembered even then.

She wanted to be angry with him. She was angry with him. And under it was the thing she had been trying not to name since the first night he slept in her passenger seat.

She wanted him alive. Not good at getting out of rooms, not a man who could hold a towel on a wound and finish his evening. Just alive, and here.

She moved a strand of hair off his forehead. He didn’t wake.

“Idiot,” she whispered, and kissed him, and sat back, and stayed.

chapters.title: Twelve Days and a Postcard
chapters.desc: He’s gone for twelve days with no phone. She nearly puts Gilded into the tyre wall, Aurelia notices, and then a postcard comes with nothing written on it.
chapters.epigraph: “When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house.”
chapters.content:
“Hold still.”

“I am holding still.”

“Your hand’s moving.”

“My hand is moving. My arm isn’t.”

“Your entire arm is attached to your hand, Haozhen.”

He looked at the small scissors in her fingers. “That’s anatomically accurate.”

“Do you want these out or do you want to keep them as jewellery?”

It was Friday the twenty-fourth of February, a quarter past six, and he was sitting on the edge of the bench with his left forearm on a clean towel. The clinic by the ferry pier had said ten days. It was nine. She had made him go back that morning and get it looked at and bring her the doctor’s note, and then she had read the note twice because she didn’t trust his translation of healing satisfactorily. The angry red had gone. What was left was a long uneven line, pink at the edges, with fourteen black knots in it.

She snipped the first one. He watched her.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

She lifted the next knot with the tweezers and slid it out. One by one. When the last came free she cleaned the line and pressed a fresh dressing over it, and he flexed his fingers.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t. You still owe me for the dumplings.”

“I paid for those.”

“You brought them cold.”

“I was delayed.”

“You were stabbed.”

“Cut.”

She looked up slowly. He smiled. She threw the used gauze at him and he caught it with his right hand, which was worse. The grey estate was outside with a new door skin. His mug was on the shelf with its name turned to the room, where she had left it.

“Are you working tomorrow?” she said.

“Yes.”

“Here?”

“No.” It was an ordinary answer, and his voice wasn’t. “Abroad. Sunday. About two weeks.”

“About?”

“I can’t give you a date. I don’t have one.”

“Is this one of those jobs?”

“Yes.”

“Dangerous?”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to tell me anything else?”

“No.”

She gave him a tired smile. “At least you’re keeping to the rules.”

“I’m trying.”

“Don’t let anyone cut the other one.”

“I’ll do my best.”

“Two weeks.” She looked at the calendar on the wall. “Don’t say about. It’s an ugly word. Say something reassuring.”

He was quiet. “I’ll come back.”

He couldn’t promise her anything about the job, or guarantee anything at all. It was the most honest thing he had, and he gave it to her, and she nodded and let him take her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes to six on Sunday morning his car was packed in the alley. One small black bag. A coat over the passenger seat. A folder she was careful not to look at.

“Passport?”

“Yes.”

“Phone?”

“I’m not taking it.”

“I know. I was testing you.” She put her hands in her coat pockets. “So. Twelve days.”

“Two weeks.”

“I’m choosing twelve. It’s a better number.”

He considered it. “Then twelve.”

There were things she wanted to ask. Where. Who. What kind of work took a man away for two weeks without a phone, and whether it would be a city with clean streets and good coffee or a hotel that smelled of smoke with an exit he’d already learned. Whether he’d be hurt. Whether he’d think about her. She didn’t ask any of them.

“I’ll be busy,” she said. “The pre-season test is Saturday. Mouse is threatening to reorganise my parts shelves, which is a criminal offence.”

“Stop her.”

“I’m considering it. Don’t go quiet on me.”

“You won’t hear from me. You’ll know when I’m back.”

“How?”

“I’ll find a way.”

She lifted her chin. “Don’t get hurt.”

“I’ll be careful.”

“That’s not the same thing. Don’t be stupid. And don’t—”

He kissed her. His hand came to her waist and he moved her back against the brick of the doorframe, not roughly, but with enough certainty that she felt the cold stone behind her and all the warmth of him in front, and she took two fistfuls of his coat and kept him there. It went on longer than either of them meant. When he lifted his head his forehead stayed on hers.

“Wait for me,” he said.

Her fingers tightened. “I’m not waiting in a cupboard.”

“I didn’t ask you to.”

“I have a life. I have races. If you come back and expect me to have spent twelve days staring at the door—”

“I wouldn’t.”

She touched his cheek. “Come back.”

“I will.” He kissed her again, softer, and got in, and sat with one hand on the wheel looking at her through the open window. She lifted her fingers. He lifted his. Then the grey estate went down the alley, and she stood there until the tail-lights had gone round the corner, and only then went inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel room in Antwerp had two exits, and he had checked both. The air conditioning was too loud and the desk lamp flickered when he moved the chair. At half past eleven on Monday night he sat at the desk with a small paper bag beside his hand.

He had walked past the shop that afternoon, one of a hundred narrow windows in the old diamond streets behind the station, and gone on for two hundred metres, and turned round. In the window, on grey velvet, a ruby in a narrow band of warm gold. Not large, not delicate. A deep red, dark at the heart and bright where the light came through the edges. The woman behind the counter asked if it was for an anniversary. No. A birthday? No. “Then someone special,” she said, and he didn’t answer, and asked to see it, and didn’t ask the price until she’d already put it in a box.

He opened the box again. He could hear exactly what she’d say. That it was too expensive and he had no taste, that a mechanic couldn’t wear a raised stone, that the setting would catch on everything. Then she’d turn it under a lamp and look at the claws. You bought me jewellery? What happened to you?

His phone was sealed in an envelope in the hotel safe with the rest of his own life. He put the box in the inside pocket of his bag, zipped it, and opened the file. There was a man to find.

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past two on Tuesday morning, in the back of a dark van parked under a motorway bridge outside Ghent, the man had stopped asking questions. His hands were cable-tied in front of him. His lip was split and his right eye had closed. He had been asked three times, by other people, before Haozhen climbed in.

Haozhen sat on the bench opposite with a small torch. “Where is it?”

“I don’t know.”

“You do.”

The man spat blood on the floor. Haozhen didn’t react to that. He’d been doing this for too long to mistake anger for courage, or silence for resistance. He leaned forward, took the man’s bound hands in his own, quite gently, and found the knuckle on the right hand that had already been broken, and put his thumb on it.

“I’m going to ask you once more,” he said, in the same voice. “And then I’m going to stop asking.”

The man looked at the thumb. Then at his face. Whatever he saw there made him start talking, fast, in Flemish and then in English: a lock-up in Lokeren, a number, the name of the man who had the key. Haozhen listened to all of it. He didn’t take his thumb away until it was finished. Then he let go of the hand and made a call, and the van moved off into the dark, and the streetlights went past the rear window in long slow intervals.

After a while, the man began to cry. Haozhen looked at the window. He thought of a garage under a railway bridge. A white mug with his name on the bottom. A woman who swore in three languages when she was frightened. He wondered whether she’d eaten.

Then he put the thought away, carefully, the way you put away something you’ll need again, and didn’t look at the man for the rest of the drive.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday the fourth of March, at five past nine, at the circuit in the north, Gilded was fast. Serafina knew it was fast because she’d spent three weeks making it faster: new front geometry, a different pad compound, too many evenings with the steering rack until it told her exactly what the front tyres were doing. It was the first proper test of the year. She was excited. She was also tired and distracted and increasingly annoyed with herself for looking at the paddock gate every time something grey went past.

“Pressures?” Aurelia stood by the car with a clipboard, in a camel coat and pearls, as though the pit lane were a fitting room.

“Fine.”

“That’s not a number.”

“Thirty-one fronts. Thirty rears.”

Aurelia wrote it down. “You’ve been staring at the entrance.”

“I’m checking the traffic.”

“There isn’t any traffic.”

“Then I’m checking the lack of it.”

“Your visor,” said Aurelia, and Serafina put her hand up and found it already shut.

The first lap was easy. The second quicker. By the third Gilded had settled into the rhythm she knew, brakes honest, steering exact, the rears coming up to temperature under her. Then the Needle: the tight right at the end of the back straight that punished anyone who treated it casually. She knew the board. She knew the distance. She knew exactly when to brake.

And for a fraction of a second she was in the alley. His hand at her waist. The brick at her back. Wait for me.

She braked late. The front washed wide. She came off the brake, caught the rear as it went light, got the car turned with the outside wheels over the kerb and the splitter grinding on the concrete, and the tyre wall came at her and stopped coming, less than a metre off the nose, with Gilded sideways and shuddering and the engine still running.

She sat completely still with her hands on the wheel.

“Sera? Are you all right?”

“I’m fine.”

“Come in.”

“I can carry on.”

“Come in,” said Aurelia, in the voice their mother used, and Serafina said, “Copy,” and drove back slowly with the splitter scraping.

In the pit lane Aurelia was already waiting. She looked at the splitter, cracked across the corner, and then at her sister. “Helmet off.” Then she took her by the elbow away from the car, past the trolleys, to a stack of tyres at the quiet end of the paddock, and waited.

“He’s gone,” said Serafina eventually. “Two weeks. No phone. He told me to wait.”

“Are you?”

“I don’t know.”

“You went off at the Needle. You never go off at the Needle. You told me it was the only corner on earth you trusted.” Aurelia leaned on the tyres beside her. “I’m not going to ask who he is.”

Serafina turned her head.

“Oh, please. You think I don’t know what this looks like? I’m married to a man who leaves at three in the morning and comes home at six smelling of the docks and says it’s handled.” Her voice was dry. “I know the phone. I know the face. I’m not going to ask. When you can tell me, tell me. That’s how it works in my house. We say I can’t tell you that yet, and the other one waits.”

“And if I never can?”

Aurelia was quiet. “Then I’ll pay for the splitter. And wait anyway.”

Serafina put her head on her sister’s shoulder. Aurelia smelled of polishing rouge and expensive soap.

“Ten minutes,” said Aurelia. “Water. Then telemetry. And then you stop driving as if your mind’s in another country.”

She was good at waiting for things, Serafina thought, when Aurelia had gone. A car to cool. A part to arrive. A seized bolt to give. A man to come home, apparently. But she was beginning to understand that waiting wasn’t the same as doing nothing. She had a car. She went back to it. In the afternoon she was four tenths quicker than she’d ever been, and she didn’t look at the gate once.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday evening Mouse came in with a bag of something with rice, put it on the bench, and looked at the shelf. “His mug’s upside down.”

“I know.”

“Do you want to talk?”

“No.”

“Good. Neither do I. Eat.” They ate in silence for a while. “Aurelia rang me,” said Mouse. “She said you nearly gave everyone a heart attack. She also said you drove beautifully afterwards.”

“She’s kind.”

“She’s observant.” Mouse bumped her shoulder. “You’ll be all right.”

Serafina didn’t answer, and Mouse didn’t make her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the tenth of March, at eighteen minutes to twelve, the post came, and she almost put it with the invoices. Then she saw her name on the envelope in small, square, careful capitals, and knew the hand before she’d finished reading it.

“What is it?” said Mouse, from the other end of the bench.

Inside was a postcard. The old banking at Monza, the great concrete curve rising under a pale sky, empty, almost peaceful. The stamp was Italian. The postmark said Milano. She turned it over.

Nothing. No hello. No I’m fine. No home soon. Not even a date. Only, small in the bottom corner, his name. Qin Haozhen.

She ran her thumb over it. The same square strokes as the note under his wiper in November. The same little pressure at the end of each line.

“Is that from him?” said Mouse. “Where is it?”

“Monza.” She laughed. “Unbelievable.”

“Are you happy?”

Her eyes had already gone bright. “Yes.” She put it on the bench by his mug, and then picked it up again, because she didn’t want it near the grease.

That night she stayed late. She told herself Gilded’s gearbox couldn’t wait. At half past ten she gave up and went upstairs, and at eleven came down again for her phone, and at twenty past eleven she was sitting on the garage floor with her back against the bench and the postcard in her hands, feeling ridiculous. A picture of a racetrack. No words. No promise.

“Idiot,” she said to it.

The side door clicked. Somebody came in and shut it behind them, and in the dark by the shelf a hand reached up towards the mug.

She was on her feet. “Haozhen?”

He turned. Dark coat, hair longer than when he’d left, his face drawn with tiredness and his eyes exactly the same. “Hello.”

She crossed the garage so fast she nearly went over a toolbox, and he barely had time to open his arms before she reached him and hit him in the chest with both hands. Not hard. Hard enough to make him take a step back.

“You absolute bastard.”

He caught her. “I know.”

“Twelve days. You sent me a postcard. With nothing written on it.”

“I didn’t know what to write.”

“Then why send it?”

“Because I wanted you to know I was thinking about you.”

Her mouth trembled, and she hated that, and she put her face against his chest, and his arms closed round her and held on. When she pulled back it was to look at him properly. “Are you hurt? Don’t lie.”

“I’m not.”

“Your arm?”

“Fine.”

“Your head?”

“Still attached.”

“Don’t be funny.” She put her palms on his face. His cheeks were cold. His coat smelled of rain and of streets she didn’t know. She wanted to ask where he’d been, and what he’d done, and who, and whether. But he was here, and she had spent twelve days learning how long a night could be, so she kissed him instead, hard, both hands in his hair, and he answered at once and lifted her onto her toes.

“I’m back,” he said, against her mouth.

“Good.”

“I missed you.”

She couldn’t say anything. “I missed you too.”

He looked past her at the shelf. “Your mug is upside down.”

She laughed, real and a little broken. He reached up and turned it over, and turned it again, so that the name on the bottom faced the room.

“Monza?” she said.

“Work finished in Milan. I went on the last afternoon.” He looked at the card in her hand. “You told me once it was the only circuit you’d ever cried at. Your grandmother took you when you were nine.”

She held the postcard flat against his chest. “You could have written something.”

“I wrote my name.”

She stared at him, and then she laughed again and pushed him. “You’re impossible. Coat off. Shoes. Sit.” She brought him a glass of water and inspected his face and his hands like a car back from a long race, and he let her. “Are you staying?”

“Yes.”

“Tonight?”

“Yes.”

“Tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

She took his mug off the shelf. “Tea?”

“Yes, please.”

She filled the kettle. Behind her she heard him get up, and his arms came round her waist from behind and his chin settled on her shoulder.

“You’re meant to be resting.”

“I am.”

“Then why are you standing up?”

“Because you’re here.”

She shut her eyes, and leaned back into him, and the kettle began to hum. “Next time,” she said, “write something.”

“I will.”

“More than your name.”

“I’ll try.”

The kettle clicked off, and for the first time in twelve days she had somebody to make tea for.

chapters.title: The Ring Was in the Glovebox
chapters.desc: She goes into his glovebox for the tyre gauge and finds a ring. He had a speech in four parts, and she says yes before he gets to part two.
chapters.epigraph: “I had a plan. It had four parts. You were supposed to let me finish.”
chapters.content:
“You’re staring.”

“I’m checking.”

“Checking what?”

“Whether you’re real.”

He looked at her over the rim of the mug. It was two minutes to midnight. “And?”

“Still investigating.”

She was sitting on the bench swinging one leg, in a clean shirt with a smear of grease she’d missed along the inside of her wrist, and she hadn’t stopped touching him since he came through the door. A hand on his shoulder when she passed. Fingers through his hair. Her knuckles against his cheek, once, as if to make sure he hadn’t gone again. He hadn’t said anything about it. He liked it.

“Come here,” he said.

She slid off the bench and stood between his knees, and took his left arm and turned it over. The scar was a long pink line now, the stitch marks fading either side of it like a railway on a map. She traced it with one finger without pressing. Then she bent and kissed it, just above the wrist, and he went still. She kissed it again further up, and turned his hand over and put her mouth in the middle of his palm, and his fingers closed round her face.

“Serafina.”

“Hmm?”

“I missed you.”

“You’ve said that.”

“I’ll keep saying it if necessary.”

“It isn’t.” She kissed him, and there was no hurry in it this time, no attempt to fit twelve days into one breath. Only his mouth, and his hands at her waist, and the plain certainty that he was here. “Are you tired?”

“Yes.”

“Then sleep. Not the sofa.” She took the mug off him. “Nonna. You sleep better in the passenger seat.”

“That isn’t a compliment.”

“It’s a very expensive passenger seat. You should be grateful.”

She’d already made it up: the seat back, a folded blanket, a cushion. He looked at it and then at her. “You’ve thought about this.”

“Don’t sound so surprised. I’m a very competent woman. Comfortable? Too much light? Need anything?”

“You.”

He said it, without smiling. She stopped. Then she bent and kissed his forehead. “I’m right here.”

He took her hand before she could move away, and she sat down on the floor by the open door with her back against the sill and let him keep it. Within minutes his breathing slowed. She watched his face come undone in sleep. Four hours and six minutes. She knew because she looked at her phone when his eyes closed, and again at half past four, when his fingers moved in hers and he opened his eyes and looked confused, and then saw her.

“Morning,” she whispered.

“It’s not morning.”

“It’s morning somewhere.” She stretched and winced.

“Your back.”

“Don’t start. You’ve just slept four hours and six minutes. You’re not allowed to supervise me.” He looked at her and then kissed her knuckles, and she smiled at him in the dark. “Welcome home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At sixteen minutes past ten on Saturday morning, bright and cold, she was crouched by his front wheel with his coffee in his hand, because she’d told him he could help by holding it.

“Front left’s low.”

“How low?”

“Low enough to annoy me. Thirty. Should be thirty-two.” She held her hand up without looking. “Gauge.”

“Glovebox.”

She went round to the passenger door. “You keep one in here. I saw it in November.” The glovebox held a torch, a map that looked as though it had been through a war, a parking receipt from last year, tissues, a cheap black petrol-station gauge. And, pushed in behind the handbook, a small square box in dark red velvet gone pale at the corners.

Her hand stopped on the gauge.

Behind her, he’d gone completely still. The east-service-door kind.

“That’s not,” he said. A breath. “I was going to.”

She took the box out. She held it in her oily palm and looked at it and then at him, and he had shut his eyes.

“I had a plan. It had four parts.” His voice was level. Too level. That was how she knew. “Part one was the coast road. The lay-by. Three in the morning, because that’s where you asked me what I wanted, at New Year. Part two was what I was going to say. I’ve had eleven days to write it, and it still isn’t—”

She opened the box. The ruby caught the morning. Deep red, held in a narrow band of warm gold, small and plain and exactly right.

“You bought me a ring.”

“In Antwerp.”

“And you put it in your glovebox.”

“I didn’t want to lose it.”

“Next to the tissues. And a map that’s been in a war.”

He paused. “When you say it like that it sounds less romantic.”

She laughed, and it came out breathless, and she put the box down on the roof of the car carefully and took his face in both hands and kissed him hard enough to put him back against the door. He caught her round the waist and held on, too tight, almost, as if somebody might lift her off him.

“Haozhen.” He loosened his arms at once. “Yes,” she said.

He stared at her.

“Yes, you idiot.”

“I haven’t asked.”

“Then ask.”

He looked at the box on the roof. “Can I have a moment?”

“Of course.”

He took one breath, and stepped back, and knelt on the garage floor, in a patch of oil by the front wheel, among the cardboard from a box of filters. She put both hands over her mouth.

“The first part is why,” he said. “Because when I come back from somewhere, you’re the person I want to find. Because I sleep when you drive. Because I know where you keep your sockets and which coffee you’ll drink and what you sound like when you’re trying not to laugh at me. Because you’ve never asked me to be someone else. You asked me to be honest. And you gave me a place where I can be tired without being frightened of what happens if I close my eyes. The second part—”

“I’m saying yes.”

He stopped.

“Now. You don’t have to do all four. Qin Haozhen, I’ve been waiting twelve days for you to come home, you bought me a ruby in Antwerp and you’re kneeling in my oil. What do you think?”

Something in his face came loose. Then he smiled, not the small held one but the real one, and opened the box. “Serafina Song, will you marry me?”

“Yes.”

He took her left hand, and the ring, and paused. “Your little finger.”

“What?”

“I wasn’t sure of the size. I measured the silver one on your dressing table.”

“That’s too big for my ring finger.”

“I know. It fits your little finger.”

He slid it on, and it fitted perfectly, and they both looked at it. “You’re very lucky,” she said.

“I am.” He came up off his knees to meet her, and she bent and kissed him halfway. “You can finish later,” she said against his mouth. “Save the third part for the wedding.”

“And the fourth?”

“Especially the fourth.”

“I had a plan,” he said. “It had four parts. You were supposed to let me finish.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven minutes past eleven, in the office, she had been looking at her hand for forty minutes. He was at the desk with a work tablet out of his bag.

“Does it fit?” he said, without looking up.

“Yes.”

“Too tight?”

“Are you asking whether my engagement ring is comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“It’s perfect.” She turned it so the stone caught the light. “Do you have to tell anyone?”

He stopped typing. “The Bureau. The engagement has to be declared.”

“Declared. Like a change of address.”

“There’s a form for a change in personal circumstances.”

“Is there a box for engaged?”

“There’s a field for intended marriage.”

She laughed so hard she had to cover her face. “Does it want to know you proposed in a puddle of oil? That I said yes before you’d finished?”

“That might be relevant.” He waited until she’d stopped. “There may be a review. Next of kin. A conflict-of-interest assessment. Possibly a security review.”

“Because you’re marrying me?”

“Because you’re now someone who could be used to put pressure on me.”

The laughter went out of the room. He didn’t look away.

“I won’t let them involve you,” he said.

“You don’t get to decide that on your own. Rule one. No lies, and no deciding about my life in a back room.” She reached across the desk for his hand. “So we deal with the form when it comes. We answer what we can. We decide together what they get.”

“Together,” he said.

“Still can’t believe there’s a form.”

“Neither can I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nineteen minutes to three they were meant to be going for lunch, and got as far as the end of the alley before she told him to stop. The estate sat with the engine off and the noise of the street coming through the glass.

“You were quiet,” he said.

“I was thinking about the second part.”

“I didn’t get to it.”

“Exactly.” She turned in her seat. “Were you nervous?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you could have said no.”

“I wasn’t going to.” She looked at her hand in his. “I thought you’d leave one day. Not because you didn’t love me. Because you’re so used to leaving. Because every time something happens you think you have to deal with it alone. I don’t want to marry a man who disappears whenever it gets hard.”

“I don’t want to be that man. I can’t promise there won’t be work. I can promise I won’t make you guess whether I’m coming back.”

“Good.” She unclipped her belt, climbed over the console, and settled in his lap with a knee either side of him. He caught her hips without thinking. “I’m going to kiss you,” she said.

“You already have.”

“I’m going to do it again.”

“I won’t object.”

She did, and set the pace, and he let her. His hands stayed at her waist and didn’t pull her closer until she moved against him, and when she drew back he followed only as far as she let him.

“You’re letting me win.”

“This isn’t a race.”

“Everything’s a race.”

“Not this.”

“Then don’t try to win it.” She bent until her lips were on his. He didn’t. For once in his life he let himself be led without working out where it would end. When she finally settled against his chest he held her, carefully, and said, “Lunch?”

“Later.”

“Your stomach is not as patient as you are.”

“Are you arguing with your fiancée?”

The word caught him somewhere he wasn’t expecting. “No,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The loft was small. A bed under the slope of the roof, a narrow wardrobe, a table and two chairs, a window onto the alley where the wet stones shone. Every eleven minutes a train went over the bridge and the whole building hummed with it, and she had lived there long enough to stop hearing it.

At sixteen minutes past eight he was standing at the window in a clean dark shirt with his hair still damp, and she came out of the shower in an old T-shirt and stopped when she saw his face.

“What?”

“I like seeing you here.”

“It’s my loft. I’m allowing you to visit.”

“Very generous.”

“I’m a generous woman.” She came to him. He kissed her slowly, without the hurry of the alley or the car, and she drew him in by the front of his shirt. When he lifted his head he looked at her.

“Are you sure?”

“I’m sure. If I change my mind I’ll tell you. And you?”

“I’ll tell you.”

“Good.” She undid his top button. And the next, watching his face, and the next, until she could push the shirt back off his shoulders and let it drop. She put her palm flat on the scar by his collarbone and then her mouth, and felt his breath go. He stood still and let her. He let her walk him backwards to the bed and push him down onto the edge of it, and when she pulled the T-shirt over her head and dropped it on the floor he looked at her as if he had been told he would have to give her back.

“Hands,” she said, and he held them open on his knees, and she took one and put it on her hip. “There. You can move when I say.”

“Yes.”

She climbed onto him and kissed him until he made a low sound and his fingers tightened on her, and she said, “Not yet,” and he stopped, shaking slightly, and waited. She liked that more than she had known she would: a man who had spent ten years deciding what happened in every room he walked into, holding perfectly still under her because she’d asked. She learned him slowly. The long scar on his side and the hollow of his throat and the place under his ear that made him shut his eyes. When she lay back and drew him down with her and said, “Now,” he came, and his hands went everywhere she’d been wanting them, unhurried, careful of nothing, his mouth at her breast and her ribs and the inside of her knee until she had her fingers in his hair and her heels hooked round him and was saying his name like an order.

He was gentle and then he wasn’t, because she told him not to be. She held his face and watched him the whole time, the way his jaw went tight, the way his eyes didn’t leave hers, and somewhere in it a train came over the bridge and the bed hummed under them and she laughed into his mouth and didn’t stop moving. When it broke over her she was still looking at him, and she felt him follow her a moment later with his face in her neck and her name in his mouth and his whole weight shaking.

Afterwards the room was dark except for a line of streetlight under the curtain. She lay with her head on his chest and listened to his heart come down.

The building hummed.

“One,” she said.

“What?”

“Trains. We’re counting them.”

“Why?”

“Because I can’t sleep.”

“You were nearly asleep.”

“I was thinking.” He laughed into her hair. Eleven minutes later the hum came again. “Two,” she whispered.

“Two.”

“Do you think the form wants a wedding date?”

“Possibly. I haven’t got one.”

“Good. I haven’t chosen a dress. I’m going to be very difficult. Very demanding.”

“I know.”

“Possibly unreasonable.”

“Frequently.” She pinched him and he caught her hand and kissed it. “Three,” he said, when the bridge went again.

“Are we counting all night?”

“You can sleep. I’ll count.” She traced his jaw with one finger. “Thank you for asking me. I know you’d thought about it. But you still asked.”

“I wanted you to choose it.”

“I did.”

And when the next train came over, he was still awake. “Four,” she whispered, and he smiled in the dark, because Big Wu would have hated that.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past ten on Sunday, at the long table in Granny Shum’s yard, Big Wu looked at Haozhen and at Serafina and at Haozhen again. “Engaged?”

“Yes,” said Haozhen.

Big Wu looked at her hand. “That’s a strange finger for a ring.”

“It’s the one it fits.”

He nodded as though that were a sound mechanical explanation. “On your knees?”

“Yes. In the garage.”

“Good. At least you didn’t do it somewhere stupid.” He pointed. “And you owe me. The bottle from New Year.”

“You said I could have a glass.”

“I gave you the bottle because I thought you’d die before you got married. You didn’t. So replace it.”

Serafina choked on her tea. Mr. Kwok put his down and said, “Congratulations,” and meant it, and told Big Wu to let them breathe, and Big Wu ignored him and said they needed a date and a place and food and somebody to stop Haozhen standing in a corner like a security camera.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding list began at twenty to three that afternoon, on the back of an old parts invoice, in his small square hand. Date. Venue. Guests. Food. Documents. Big Wu’s whisky. She took the pen and added Dress. Flowers. Music. Photographs. Cake.

“Big or small?”

“Not too big. People we care about. Somewhere you can see the cars.”

“Now you’re thinking.” She wrote Bureau paperwork under Documents. Then she looked up. “Will your mother come?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“Does she know about me?”

“Not yet.”

“Haozhen.”

“I’ll tell her.” He looked at the list. “She doesn’t leave the town. She hasn’t for years. But I’ll tell her.”

She didn’t push. She leaned over the bench and kissed him instead, and when she drew back he was smiling at the paper. “I like the list.”

“It’s very incomplete.”

“We have time.”

She looked at the ring on her little finger and the man beside her, and for once the future didn’t look like something she’d have to chase down a road. It was here, on the back of an invoice, smelling of oil and coffee. She wrote Speech at the bottom, and under it, smaller: Four parts. No interruptions.

“You’re going to let me finish?”

“Don’t push your luck, fiancé,” she said, and he took her hand and turned the ruby to the light.

chapters.title: He Has Never Planned a Party
