chapters.desc: He has stood at the door of eleven weddings and never been inside one, so he makes a list. Then he puts the engagement on a Bureau form, she buys a burnt-out race car, and he forgets his own toast.
chapters.epigraph: “Depends how many people love you. Start counting.”
chapters.content:
Qin Haozhen had stood at the door of eleven weddings.

He knew because he had counted. Eleven venues, eleven evenings standing by an entrance watching the guests, identifying anyone who didn’t belong, making sure the people inside could celebrate without ever knowing he was there. He knew where the exits were. He knew the groom’s family always came late, that photographers always blocked the one useful corridor, and that drunk uncles were harder to manage than most actual threats. He had never once eaten the food or heard the speeches or stayed long enough to see anyone cry over the third bottle.

He didn’t know how to plan a wedding. At eighteen minutes past four on the Sunday after the glovebox, this was becoming a problem.

He sat at her bench with a new notebook. At the top he had written WEDDING and underlined it, twice, and after some thought a third time. Under that, in order: 1. Date. 2. Venue. 3. Guests. 4. Food. 5. Documents. 6. Security.

Serafina came in with two coffees and looked over his shoulder. “Security?”

“It’s a wedding. People will attend.”

“That’s generally how weddings work.”

“Some of them may be unfamiliar.”

“Are you planning to do threat assessments on our guests?”

“Not individually.”

She took his pen and crossed out Security. “I refuse to have my uncle’s table decided by his threat level.”

“And Big Wu?”

“He’s a threat to the whisky supply. That’s different.” He considered it, took the pen back, and wrote Whisky underneath the crossed-out line. “You’re impossible,” she said, and kissed his cheek. “Come on. Mr. Kwok wants to talk to us about food.”

He closed the notebook. He looked more worried than he had about security.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mr. Kwok was at the back table in Granny Shum’s yard with a cup of tea and a notebook of his own, which was a bad sign.

“Wedding,” he said.

“Yes,” said Serafina.

“Banquet. First, a cold platter. Second, soup. A proper one, not that thin stuff restaurants do now. Third, steamed fish.” He pointed his pen at her. “You like the belly. So the fish must be big enough. Don’t let them give you the tail.”

Haozhen was writing it down with the attention he gave an operational briefing.

“Fourth, roast duck. Fifth, prawns, garlic, not too much chilli, your girl complains. Sixth, braised abalone. Seventh, vegetables. Proper ones, not leaves arranged on a plate. Eighth, noodles, long. Long life. Nobody cuts them. Ninth, red bean soup, and little peach buns for the old people.” He tapped the table. “Round tables. Ten to a table. Never square. Then you go round every table with her and drink. Every one. You don’t sit down till you’ve done them all.”

“How many tables?” said Haozhen.

Mr. Kwok gave him a long hard look over the cup. “Depends how many people love you. Start counting.”

Haozhen wrote that down too, word for word. Serafina laughed so hard Mr. Kwok had to wait for her to finish.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday the sixteenth, at nineteen minutes to six, she was driving the grey estate along the coast road, because she’d insisted and he hadn’t argued, which she counted as progress. The sea came and went through gaps in the low stone wall. The windows were open a crack. He sat beside her with his shoulders loose, looking at the water.

“You’re thinking,” she said.

“Partly about the wedding. Partly about work.”

“Can you stop thinking about work for ten minutes?”

“I can try.”

She pulled into the little lay-by above the water and turned the engine off, and it ticked as it cooled. For a while they just watched the sea. “I don’t want to choose a date yet,” she said. “Not until it’s safe. Properly safe. Not just a day when nobody’s shooting at you. I want to know what happens when they find out. Whether they review you. Whether they decide I’m a problem.”

“They may review my position.”

“And if they tell you to end it?”

“I won’t.” It came so fast her chest tightened.

“You don’t know what they’ll say.”

“I know what I want.” He took her hand across the console. “I’ve spent ten years letting other people decide what I’m allowed to have. I won’t blame you for wanting a future.”

She looked at him. “Can I call you something?”

“You already do.”

“Something else.” It was one syllable. It felt more intimate than she’d expected. “Hao.”

He went still.

“Too familiar?”

“No.”

“Too short?”

“No.” He turned his palm up under hers. “Say it again.”

“Hao.”

“Again.”

“Don’t get greedy,” she said, and he lifted her hand and kissed the ruby.

“Too late.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight minutes past eleven that night he sat in a windowless room on the fourth floor of the Bureau’s building by the river with a document called a Personal Circumstances Declaration, and disliked it on sight.

Nature of change: Engaged. Name of intended spouse: Serafina Song. Date of engagement: 11 March 2023.

Does the intended spouse have any known involvement in activities that may present a security concern or create a conflict of interest?

He read it twice. He thought of her at the circuit, studying a corner before she drove it. Of Gilded and Nonna, and of the crossroads by the paint works at two in the morning with Granny Shum’s police scanner hissing on its string. He picked up the pen and wrote None known, and signed it, and sent it. He didn’t feel guilty. He felt irritated, which was close to it. He had told them she existed. He hadn’t given them a list of her Saturdays. There was a difference between reporting her and making her interesting. He wanted her to stay a person. Not a file.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it the next evening, by accident, looking for a pen. The black folder in his bag under the desk looked like the wedding paperwork, so she opened it, and read the heading, and his name, and hers, and turned the pages until she got to the question and the answer.

“Serafina?” He was in the office doorway with two cups of tea. His eyes went from her face to the page, and he put the cups down.

“None known?”

“Yes.”

“I’m a racing driver. I own cars that have been to street meets. I’ve been stopped by the police more times than I can count. I nearly put Gilded into a tyre wall two weeks ago.”

“I know.”

“Then why does it say none known?”

“Because I didn’t report your racing.”

“You lied.”

“Yes.” The honesty came at once, and it didn’t make anything better.

“Why?”

“Because reporting it would make you interesting to them. They’d ask who you know, where you go, which events, whether you’ve ever stood near anyone connected to my work.”

“Then you should have told me. You could have said, I’m putting this down and I’m not telling them about your racing. You could have asked me. We said together. That was Saturday.”

“Yes.”

He didn’t defend himself, which was almost worse.

“Do you understand why I’m angry?”

“Because I decided something about you without you. And I signed something that wasn’t true.”

“I don’t want to be a secret. I’m not asking you to hand them my whole life. I’m asking you not to decide which parts of it are fit to be seen.” She handed the form back to him. “Next time there’s a question about me on anything, you show me before you send it.”

“Yes.”

“And next time you’re going to lie for me, tell me first.”

“That’s a strange request.”

“I’m a strange woman.”

“I’ve noticed.” He touched her hand. “I’m sorry.”

“I know.” She kissed his cheek, not quite. “Drink your tea. We’re engaged. We’re not invincible.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday the twenty-seventh of March, at twenty-six minutes past eight, the car was ugly and she loved it on sight.

It sat at the far end of a salvage yard on the east side of the docks, half hidden behind a stack of crumpled panels. The paint had once been dark blue and was now mostly blistered or gone. The rear bodywork had burned. The front clam was missing altogether, one headlight hung loose on its wires, the wheels didn’t match, and someone had apparently tried to take the diffuser off with a crowbar.

“That’s the one?” said Mouse.

“Yes.”

“It’s dead.”

“It’s burnt. That’s different.”

“It’s missing half its body.”

“Weight reduction.” Serafina crouched by the front wheel and looked at the uprights, the lower wishbone mounts, the tub. Dirty, scorched, and straight where it mattered. At the back, under the heat-blistered engine cover, the shape of the engine was still there. She rubbed the grime off a small plate on the bulkhead and read it, and smiled.

“Oh no,” said Mouse. “That face. The one you do before you spend money on something that ought to be buried.”

“It’s a 1991 endurance prototype.”

“It’s a burnt 1991 endurance prototype.”

Serafina was already seeing it with the bodywork made and the suspension rebuilt and the engine running, the long nose and the low cockpit and the wide rear haunches, and the sound it would make at the end of a straight with the revs climbing and the world narrowed to a strip of tarmac. She asked the yard man about the paperwork and which parts were original and whether the engine came with it, and Mouse listened with growing disbelief.

“You’re actually buying it.”

“I want to build something fast.”

“You’ve got Gilded. You’ve got Nonna.”

“And I’ve got a garage,” said Serafina, “with a space at the back.”

At a quarter to two Haozhen sat at the bench with the sale papers and the yard’s photograph and turned the pages slowly.

“That’s a burnt-out prototype.”

“Yes.”

“It’s from 1991. It’s missing its front bodywork. It’s classed as salvage.”

“Technically.”

“Serafina.”

“Hao.”

He stopped at that, as she’d known he would. “What have you bought?”

“A 1991 endurance prototype. Because it’s beautiful.”

“It’s burnt. It hasn’t got a headlight.”

“I’m not driving it home tonight.”

“How much?”

She told him. He looked at her, and then at the photograph, and rubbed the bridge of his nose. “Where’s it going?”

“That’s what I hoped you’d help me with.” She leaned on the bench. “You’re very good at organising things.”

“I organise security operations.”

“Same principle. Moving people and objects about without anyone getting hurt.”

He laughed, quiet and helpless. “What’s the target?”

“Two hundred miles an hour.”

The laugh went into something more thoughtful. “On a rebuilt 1991 prototype.”

“That’s the idea.”

“Engine, gearbox, cooling, brakes, suspension. The tub needs crack-testing before you even think about running it. You need a proper test programme.”

“I know. I’ve already planned it.”

He turned to a clean page in his notebook under the wedding list and wrote 1991 PROTOTYPE, and under it Chassis. Engine. Bodywork. Cooling. Brakes. Suspension. Tyres. Test programme. At the bottom he wrote Target: 200 mph, and underlined it.

“My organised fiancé,” she said.

“Your expensive fiancé.” Outside, a flatbed reversed into the alley with a burnt blue car chained on its back. Qin Haozhen, who had spent ten years making sure people disappeared without leaving a trace, looked round her garage for the space he’d have to make for a loud, damaged thing that would take months to bring back to life. She was already reaching for her tools.

“Show me what you bought, Hao’s girl.”

She turned round, and her grin was immediate. “Gladly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The engagement drinks on Saturday the eighth of April hadn’t been planned by Haozhen. This was obvious from the lack of seating plan, security assessment or printed list, and from the fact that nobody had tried to control how much whisky Big Wu brought.

There were three tables of food. Auntie Chu brought a tray of dumplings. Mr. Kwok brought wine and a handwritten banquet plan that had somehow grown from nine courses to eleven. Mouse brought a camera. Big Wu brought the replacement bottle he’d demanded and drank a good third of it himself. Granny Shum brought a bowl of clementines, and Aurelia, who had come straight from lunch at Da Gianni with Chen Si’s assistant Qian at her shoulder, brought her own glass because she didn’t trust anybody else’s.

Haozhen stood by the bench with a whisky he wasn’t drinking and watched Serafina laugh in the middle of all of it. Granny Shum came and put a clementine in his hand.

“Eat.”

“Thank you.”

“You look nervous.”

“I’m not.”

“Don’t lie to an old woman.”

He looked at Serafina. “I’m not used to this. Parties.”

“It’s not a party. It’s just people who like you.” She patted his arm. “Eat your clementine. Good boy.” He didn’t know what to say to that, and she didn’t wait for him to.

Serafina appeared at his side and took a segment. “She’s adopted you. It’s official.” She looked round the room. “You have to say something.”

“What?”

“A toast. It’s your engagement. Your fiancée’s standing right here.”

He looked at the garage. Big Wu arguing with Mr. Kwok about whether eleven courses was the minimum. Mouse trying to photograph Auntie Chu, who was refusing. Aurelia watching him over her glass. Everybody, somehow, waiting. He raised his glass, and the room quietened, and he opened his mouth and discovered that every sentence he had written in the notebook upstairs had gone.

“I’d like to thank everyone for coming. I’m grateful for your support.” A pause. He looked at the glass. “And I—”

Nothing.

“Is that it?” said Big Wu, much too loud.

“I had more.”

“Where is it?”

“I forgot.”

The room went up. Serafina laughed hardest, trying to look sympathetic and failing completely. He looked at her for a second, and then he put his glass down, stepped in, took her face in both hands and kissed her. In front of everyone. Not the quick polite kind he allowed himself when there were people watching. Properly. Her hands went flat on his chest and then into his shirt, and the garage erupted, and somebody cheered, and Mouse’s camera went, and Big Wu shouted that there was a loft upstairs for that.

He didn’t stop. Neither did she.

Mouse would later swear it had lasted exactly twenty-six seconds, because she’d timed it, which Serafina said made her a terrible friend, and Haozhen asked her for the photograph. But right then there was only the warmth of his hands on her face and whisky on his mouth and the noise of people who had somehow become his.

“You forgot your speech,” she said, when he let her go.

“Yes.”

“Do you want to try again?”

“No.” He bent and said in her ear, “I can think of something better to do,” and she went pink and pushed his chest.

“Behave.”

“I am.”

“Barely.” He picked up his glass again, and didn’t try to speak, and only raised it to her. She raised hers back.

chapters.title: Her Sister Finds Out Who Pays for the Racing Team
chapters.desc: Aurelia does the team’s books and finds sixty thousand she didn’t pay. At Da Gianni the whole restaurant hears whose salary bought Sera’s gearbox.
chapters.epigraph: “He overpaid by a third. I like him.”
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen was good at numbers, and better at noticing when numbers were lying.

It started with a gearbox. On the first Friday of April, at sixteen minutes past nine, in the workroom over her shop on Harbour Road with the quarter’s team accounts open beside a tray of unset stones, she found the invoice for Gilded’s replacement gearbox, fitted two days before the test in March. It was marked paid. She hadn’t paid it.

She checked the bank statement, and the supplier’s receipt, and the reference. The money had come from a company called Northgate Services. She went back through the quarter, and the one before. Tyres. Transport to the circuit in the north. Track fees. A replacement splitter in March. Engine parts in December. Every few weeks since November somebody had been paying Team AURELIA’s bills. She filtered the column and looked at the total at the bottom.

Sixty thousand.

She checked the sum twice. Then she rang Qian.

Qian Yu had worked for her husband for eleven years and could find anything that had been written down anywhere, and some things that hadn’t. He rang back at twenty to twelve. “Northgate’s held through two holding companies. Both registered at a corporate services address. Nominee directors. But all the money comes out of one account.”

“Whose?”

A pause. “An account in the name of Qin Haozhen.”

“Which Qin Haozhen?”

“The one your sister is engaged to.” Another pause. “It looks like a salary account. Regular deposits, every month, for about ten years. Not much ever taken out of it. Until November.”

Aurelia sat still. She thought of him at the drinks they were having tomorrow night, in a garage, with a glass he wasn’t drinking. Of a man who had never once mentioned money in her hearing. Of the gearbox, and the splitter, and the tyres.

“Does Sera know?”

“I doubt it.”

She closed the laptop. “Then we’re going to lunch.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Da Gianni at half past twelve on Saturday was full: dark wood, white cloths, a waiter who knew every regular by name, garlic and warm bread and coffee. Serafina was already at the corner table beside Haozhen, with the ruby on her little finger catching the light every time she moved her hand. Aurelia kissed her cheek. “Hello, trouble.”

“I’m entirely innocent.”

“That’s what worries me.” Qian sat down, glanced at the ring, and said, “Congratulations,” in the voice of a man noting a change to a file.

For ten minutes it was ordinary. Serafina complained about the state the prototype had arrived in. Qian asked whether the tub had been crack-tested. Haozhen listened. Then Aurelia put her phone face up on the tablecloth.

“Qin Haozhen. Did you pay sixty thousand of Team AURELIA’s expenses?”

Serafina stopped talking.

He took a moment. “Yes.”

Serafina turned in her chair. “What?”

“I paid some of the team’s bills.”

“Some,” said Aurelia. “Sixty thousand.”

“Sixty thousand.” Serafina stared at him. “You paid for our team? Why?”

“It needed the money. It was a practical solution.”

“It’s also an undeclared contribution from a company with no connection to motor racing,” said Aurelia. “Through two shells with nominee directors.”

“From your salary?” said Serafina.

“From my savings.”

“How much of your savings?”

He didn’t answer. “I didn’t expect you to find it,” he said to Aurelia.

“I do the books.”

“I know.”

“Then you should have expected it.”

Serafina was looking down at the figures on the phone. Every line. The gearbox two days before the test. The tyres she’d thought Aurelia had got cheap from a new supplier. The splitter. “I thought you’d found a discount,” she said. “I thought we’d finally got the accounts under control.” She looked up at him. “You don’t know what it’s like to have someone pay for something and then spend every day wondering what they expect for it.”

“I don’t expect anything.”

“That’s not the point.”

“I know.”

“You did exactly the same thing,” said Serafina to her sister. “For three years. Before it had your name on it.”

Aurelia didn’t flinch. “Yes. That’s how I knew what I was looking at.” She held out her hand. “Now give me that ring.”

From her bag she took a jeweller’s loupe, and Serafina, after one glance at Haozhen, held out her little finger. Aurelia turned her hand under the window light and looked: the stone, the claws, the band.

“Well?” said Serafina.

“It’s a very good stone that he overpaid for by about a third. To a man who saw him coming.” She lowered the loupe. Her face had gone soft. “He didn’t haggle. He had no idea what it was worth.”

“He said it was the colour of my car.”

Aurelia looked at her. Then she put down the loupe and laughed out loud, the real one, the bark, in front of the whole room. She had to wipe her eyes with her napkin. “He overpaid by a third. I like him.” She pressed the napkin to her mouth. “Oh God. I like him.”

“You’ve known him an hour!”

“That was plenty.” She gave the hand back. “The band’s too wide for your little finger and too big for the right one. I can make it fit. You’ve still got the little gold horn badge off Nonna’s steering wheel?”

“In a jam jar.”

“Nonna had it made in Milan the year she bought the car. It’s eighteen carat. She never did anything halfway.” Aurelia closed Serafina’s fingers over the ring. “I’ll make you a new band with it.”

Serafina looked at Haozhen. “Would you mind?”

“It’s yours,” he said.

“Next time,” said Aurelia to him, “tell us before you spend sixty thousand.”

“Preferably before the end of the quarter,” said Qian.

“You’re all talking about him like a badly behaved sponsor,” said Serafina.

“He is one,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

The food came. Nobody ate much. Aurelia was explaining to Qian how she’d reclassify the payments when Serafina’s phone buzzed against her glass.

Hao: You’re going to shout at me when we leave.

He was sitting directly opposite her.

Sera: I’m already considering it.

Hao: There’s more. You’ll shout louder.

She looked up. He had put his phone face down beside his plate and was looking at her with the expression he wore before he told her something she wouldn’t like.

“What?” she said out loud.

“The splitter.”

“What about it?”

“I paid for it after the Needle.” He said it to her but the table had gone quiet round him. “I watched the test. The circuit runs a feed for the teams. I was in a hotel in Antwerp with it on a laptop and the team radio in one ear.”

Serafina felt cold. “You watched me nearly hit the wall.”

“I watched you lose the car and bring it back.”

“Live.”

“Yes.”

“From another country. Without a phone, because you weren’t allowed one, but with a laptop and my radio.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“I didn’t want to distract you.”

Aurelia had stopped talking. Qian had stopped writing. Serafina put her fork down and pushed her chair back.

“Haozhen. Outside.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The pavement outside was busy. A delivery cyclist swerved round a van and a bus sounded its horn down by the harbour. She stopped by the restaurant wall and hit him in the chest. Once. Then again. Not hard enough to hurt. Hard enough to make him understand.

He caught her wrists, gently. She pulled free. “Don’t.”

He let go.

“You don’t get to do this. You don’t get to sit in a hotel room and decide what I need. You don’t get to buy a part because I nearly crashed. You don’t get to pay my team’s bills because you think I need help.”

“I didn’t think you needed help.”

“Then why?”

“Because I wanted to.”

“That’s not enough.” She pointed at him. “You cannot buy gearboxes in case I die.”

His face changed. “Serafina—”

“No. Listen. You can’t pay for my car and my team and my tyres and my repairs and tell yourself it’s practical. You can’t make yourself responsible for keeping everything round me running because you’re frightened I’ll get hurt. I’m a racing driver. I know the risks. I choose them. And if I crash, you don’t get to pay the damage away.”

He looked at her.

“I watched you brake,” he said. “I watched the car go towards the wall. I watched you bring it back.” His voice was even and his jaw was tight. “For about two seconds I didn’t know whether you were going to get out. I couldn’t reach you. I couldn’t ring. I couldn’t do anything at all.”

The anger went unsteady in her. “So you bought a splitter.”

“It was something I could do.”

“You don’t have to do something every time you’re frightened.”

“I don’t know how not to.”

It was so quiet she felt it more than heard it. She reached for his coat and stopped with her hand in the air. “You have to learn. You have to let me be a person, not a problem you solve. And you have to tell me when you’re scared.”

That seemed harder for him than anything else she’d said. She waited.

“I was scared,” he said.

She hit his chest once more, lightly. “Idiot.” Then she took his coat in both fists and pulled him down and kissed him, furious, with everything she hadn’t been able to put into words, and he met her at once. Then he slowed it. His hand came up to her jaw, his thumb under her ear, and he let the anger run out of the kiss without trying to make it go away, until it wasn’t angry any more and only a little sad, and a little relieved, and entirely hers.

“I won’t do it again without telling you,” he said, with his forehead on hers. “I won’t make payments for you without asking. I’ll give Aurelia the documents.”

“Good.”

“I’m sorry.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside, Aurelia looked up. “Are we all right?”

“We’re discussing it,” said Serafina, and sat.

Qian pushed the bread basket towards them. Haozhen said he’d stop the transfers and send everything to Aurelia on Monday, and Aurelia said if the team ever took his money again it would be through a proper sponsorship with a contract and his name on it, and Serafina said, “Not today,” and Haozhen said, “Understood.”

The tiramisu came. Serafina took a spoonful and then put the spoon down. “The worst part is you bought the splitter before I’d even decided to replace it. I was going to repair it.”

“I know. I saw the damage on the feed.”

“Hao.”

“I’m sorry.”

She sighed and pushed the plate across to him. “Have some.”

He did. Aurelia leaned towards Qian and murmured, “They’re going to be exhausting.”

“They already are,” said Qian.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes to six, back in the garage, Aurelia sat at the bench with her loupe and a jam jar with a small gold horn badge in it, turning the ruby under the lamp. Through the open shutter, Haozhen was standing beside the burnt prototype at the back with Qian, one hand on its scorched flank, listening to something Qian was telling him with the air of a man who’d been waiting all day to say it.

“It’ll be a narrow band,” said Aurelia. “Her gold worked into it. Not a perfect match. It’ll be warmer than the rest. But it’ll be yours.”

“I like that.”

Aurelia put the ring in its box. “Are you happy?”

Serafina looked out through the shutter. He glanced up from the car, as though he’d felt it, and found her, and smiled.

“Yes.”

“Good,” said Aurelia. “Then let’s make it fit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-six minutes to midnight, when the drinks were over and the last of Big Wu’s whisky had gone home in Big Wu, she found him at the prototype again, with a torch, looking at the front suspension mounts.

“Give me your hand.”

“Why?”

“Give it to me.” She took his left wrist and turned it over, uncapped a marker with her teeth, and wrote on the inside of it, in her worst capitals: QIN H.

He looked down. “What’s this?”

“Identification. In case you get lost.”

“You’re writing my name on me.”

“You’re worse than a child. You disappear.”

“It’s not very legible.”

“It’s temporary.” She capped the pen. “Now you can go.”

He caught her hand before she could step away and looked at the letters on his wrist. “Thank you.”

“For writing your name?”

“For finding me.”

She kissed his cheek. “Don’t make me do it too often.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday at seventeen minutes past nine, she climbed into Gilded to check the wiring and found that the car had acquired a taxi. A tiny toy one, no bigger than her thumb, the same dull grey as his estate, with a little white light on the roof, stuck with a dab of glue to the corner of the dashboard where she couldn’t help seeing it. Under it, folded small, a note in his square hand.

For when you need someone to take you home.

She found him in the office with his coffee. “Hao. What’s this?”

“A taxi.”

“I can see that. You stuck it to my dashboard.”

“You drive too fast.”

“That’s your solution?”

“It’s a reminder. That someone’s waiting for you.”

She looked at the little grey taxi in her palm and then at him, and sat down on the edge of his desk. “You’re ridiculous.”

“I’ve been told.”

She bent and kissed him, and he put his mug aside and his hand on her waist. “I’m keeping it,” she said. “If it falls off I’m blaming you. If it distracts me at the Needle you’re buying me another dashboard.”

“I’ll consider it.”

Outside, the burnt car from 1991 waited to be brought back to life. Inside, she went back to Gilded and glued the taxi on again, more firmly, so that it would still be there at two hundred and something with the world gone narrow, to remind her that the road went both ways and somebody was waiting at the end of it.

chapters.title: Two Professionals at One Table
chapters.desc: Dinner on the forty-fourth floor. Two men go for the same chair, the ruby moves to the right finger, and Chen Si takes Haozhen out on the balcony.
chapters.epigraph: “Mr. Qin. Welcome. You don’t exist.”
chapters.content:
The lift to the forty-fourth floor had no buttons, only a brass plate and a small black eye in the corner of the ceiling. Serafina looked at the eye and then at the man beside her in the mirrored wall.

He was wearing a suit. Not his work clothes, not the grey jacket he wore when he wanted to be forgotten. A properly cut dark suit, a white shirt open at the neck, his hair combed. It was a quarter to eight on the twenty-first of April, and he looked, she thought, offensively handsome.

“You look like you’re about to buy the building.”

“I thought you liked this suit.”

“I do. That’s the problem.” She watched the numbers climb. “Do you know him?”

“I’ve read about him.” He said it to the numbers. “There’s a file on everybody who matters in this city. His is very thick and says very little. That’s how you know someone’s good.”

“And yours?”

“Mine’s thin. And says nothing at all.”

The doors opened on a short corridor with one door at the end, and in it, holding it open, stood a small tired man in glasses with a packet of antacids in his top pocket. Qian looked at Haozhen for three full seconds without blinking.

“Mr. Qin. Welcome. You don’t exist.”

“Thank you,” said Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The apartment took up the whole floor. Glass on three sides and the harbour lit up behind it, low lamps, a long table laid for five, and from the kitchen the faint unhappy whine of a dishwasher that nobody in the household had ever managed to fix. Aurelia came out of the kitchen with her sleeves pushed up and kissed her sister on both cheeks.

Chen Si came behind her, drying his hands. He wasn’t tall. He was still, with neat black hair and a white shirt and hands that didn’t move when they didn’t need to, and Serafina had known him for four years and still didn’t think she’d ever seen him surprised.

“Chen Si,” said Serafina. “This is Haozhen.”

“Qin Haozhen.”

“Chen Si.”

They shook hands. The handshake went on a fraction longer than handshakes do, and neither man seemed to want to be the first to let go. Aurelia watched them, and then looked at her sister. “Oh, this is going to be interesting.”

At the table, there was one chair that could see the lift door and the kitchen door and the dark glass of the terrace at once, and both men put a hand on its back at the same moment. They stopped. Chen Si’s eyes went to the lift. Haozhen’s did the same. Then Chen Si looked back at him.

“You take it.”

It was his own chair, in his own house. Haozhen held his eyes for a second. “Thank you.”

Serafina leaned to her sister. “Did they just fight over a chair?”

“Not exactly,” said Aurelia, unfolding her napkin. “Professional courtesy.”

“That’s a ridiculous name for it.”

“It’s better than the alternative,” said Qian, sitting down. “Two men refusing to admit they’re doing the same thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia had cooked, which in that household meant she had made the sauce and the risotto and let her husband do the fish, because he did fish the way his mother had. It was grouper, steamed with ginger and a little wine, and when it came to the table Chen Si served Serafina first, and gave her the belly without being asked. “I’m told you like it,” he said, and she looked at her sister, who looked innocent. He had rolled his sleeves to cook. On the inside of his left forearm was an old burn, a ridged pale band like the mark a grate would leave, and Haozhen looked at it for exactly one second and then away, and Chen Si saw him do it and rolled the sleeve down. “The road,” he said, to nobody in particular, and nobody asked which road.

Over it they talked about the prototype. The tub had been crack-tested and was clean, said Serafina, the engine was a horror, and Chen Si asked whether she meant to keep the original layout, and she was halfway through explaining why that would be a crime when Haozhen moved her water glass back from the edge of the table without looking at it. She noticed. He didn’t, or pretended not to. Aurelia noticed both of them.

“You’re very attentive.”

“Habit,” said Haozhen.

“An expensive one,” said Chen Si.

“Sometimes.”

“Are you two going to talk normally tonight?”

“Yes,” they said, at the same time, and Aurelia took a sip of wine and said, “Let them.”

When the plates were gone she put a small velvet box by her sister’s hand. “Finished.”

Inside lay the ruby in a new band, slimmer, with a thread of different gold worked through it, a shade warmer than the rest. The horn badge off Nonna’s steering wheel, made in Milan in 1992 because Nonna never did anything halfway. It looked understated. It looked like something that had always been Serafina’s.

“Aurelia.”

“I told you I would.”

Serafina slid it onto her little finger, and it sat beautifully, and she held her hand up. “Look.”

Aurelia looked at Haozhen instead. “You should put it on the right finger.”

Serafina went pink. “Oh.”

He was already holding out his hand. “May I?”

She gave him the ring and her left hand. He took the ring off her little finger and held it between his fingers, and then put it on the fourth one, and it fitted. He didn’t let go of her hand afterwards. He ran his thumb along the band once.

“Better,” he said.

“Much better.”

Qian raised his glass. Chen Si didn’t. Chen Si was watching Haozhen. Not the ring. Him.

✦ ✦ ✦

“May I ask you something?” said Chen Si, at half past eight.

“Of course.”

“How long have you known her?”

“Since October,” said Serafina.

“The twenty-second,” said Haozhen.

“You remember the date?”

“Yes.”

“And when did you first notice her?”

Haozhen looked at Serafina, then back. “Twenty-two minutes past nine.”

The table went quiet.

“You remember the time?” said Serafina. “Why?”

“You were standing beside Lot 9. You looked at the entrance before you looked at the car. Then at the reflections in the pavilion glass. Then you saw I wasn’t watching the guests.”

“You were pretending to be a guard.”

“I was working.”

“You were pretending to be a guard while working.”

“That’s not inaccurate.” She laughed. Chen Si didn’t.

“Did you approach her that evening?”

“No. I wasn’t there for her.”

“But you noticed her. And afterwards?”

“I kept an eye on her.”

Serafina’s smile went.

“For how long?” said Chen Si.

“Until I understood who she was.”

“That’s not what I asked,” said Serafina, and turned to look at him properly. “How long?”

He was silent. “I watched you for several weeks.”

The words landed hard. Aurelia looked down at her plate. Qian stopped turning his glass.

“You told me about the camera,” said Serafina. “You told me you watched me in the car park by the ferry pier. You didn’t tell me you’d been watching me before that.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because I didn’t know how to say it without making it sound worse.”

“It does sound worse.”

“I know. I noticed you because you saw me. I kept watching because I wanted to understand why. That was my decision, and it wasn’t fair to you.”

“Did you keep anything? Photographs? Recordings?”

“No. The footage was taken down. I did it.”

She held his eyes, and nodded. Not forgiveness, exactly, but an answer she could work with.

“Interesting,” said Chen Si. “You remember the minute you noticed her. You didn’t remember to tell her the truth.”

Haozhen took it without flinching. “No.”

“You’ll need to improve that.”

“I know.”

“I’m sitting right here,” said Serafina. “Stop interviewing my fiancé.”

“I’m not interviewing him. I’m getting to know him.”

“Wonderful,” said Serafina. “Two professionals at one table.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past nine, while Serafina was in the kitchen arguing with the dishwasher, Chen Si stood up. “Qin. Come outside.”

It wasn’t a request. The terrace ran round the glass in the dark, forty-four floors up, with the city below in lines of light and the black water beyond. Chen Si leaned on the rail. Haozhen stood a few feet from him.

“The Eleventh,” said Chen Si.

“You’ve heard the name.”

“Not many people have.” He turned his head. “Ten years. Transfers. Recoveries. People who leave rooms and aren’t seen again. Different countries, different names. I’ve read what there is to read. And some things that weren’t written down for people like me.”

“I’ve read yours,” said Haozhen.

Chen Si’s face didn’t move. “Which one?”

“Block C. January 2010.”

A short silence. Then Chen Si laughed once, without anything in it. “That’s unfortunate.”

“There are three versions of that January in it. Two of them are wrong.”

“And the third?”

“The third’s the true one.”

“And you’ve read it.”

“Once.”

“Then you know what I’m capable of.”

“Yes,” said Haozhen. “That’s why I’m glad you’re on her side.”

Chen Si pushed off the rail. “Let me be clear. I don’t care what you did for ten years or what they called you or how many doors you can open without being seen. I care about her. If she’s ever harmed because of your work, or someone you know, or a decision you make, I will find you. And there won’t be three versions of what happens.”

“I understand.”

“I don’t think you do.” He took a card from his breast pocket. A number on it in ink. No name, no address. “If you ever need to reach me without going through the usual channels, use that. It connects to a door.”

“What door?”

“The one you knock on when there’s nowhere else.”

Haozhen put it inside his jacket. “And the threat?”

“Still stands.”

“Fair.”

“Don’t mistake it for trust.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t make her regret choosing you.” Chen Si turned for the glass, and stopped. “She’s stubborn. She’ll try to fix things that aren’t hers to fix. She’ll tell you she’s fine when she isn’t.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t make her do it alone.”

Haozhen thought of the coast road and the passenger seat and her hand on his wrist with a marker pen, writing his name there so he wouldn’t go missing. “I won’t,” he said, and they went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did you talk about?” said Serafina, at the door.

“Nothing important,” said Chen Si.

“That means something important.”

“Work,” said Haozhen.

“Yours or his?”

“Both.”

“Wonderful.”

This time the handshake was an ordinary length. Aurelia kissed her sister and held her a moment longer than usual, and said, low, “He’ll do,” and let her go.

The lift doors closed. They were alone with the mirror and the small black eye in the ceiling. She leaned back against the glass. “Well?”

“He gave me a number. In case I need help.”

“Chen Si offered you help.”

“Yes.”

“That’s either very nice or very threatening.”

“Both.” She laughed, and looked down at her hand. The ruby on the fourth finger, the warmer gold in the band.

“Do you like it there?” he said.

“I love it. It’s strange, seeing it there.”

He took her hand and turned it and pressed it gently flat against the mirror beside her head, and stood looking at the ring against the glass and then at her.

“Qin Haozhen,” she said. “Are you about to kiss me?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

He kept her hand there, his fingers over hers on the cold glass, and put his other hand at her waist, and kissed her slowly, as though he had all night and the building were his. Not the hurried kind from the garage, not the angry one outside Da Gianni. She turned into him and took his jacket in her free hand, and when he drew back she went after him.

“Again?” he said.

“Are you asking?”

“I’m being polite.”

She pulled him down by the collar. “Don’t be.” He laughed against her mouth, and she felt his hand come off the mirror and into her hair, and the lift slid down the building in the dark with the two of them pressed into the corner under the eye.

It chimed at the lobby. The doors opened on a marble hall and a concierge behind a desk, who looked up, and looked down again at once.

Haozhen stepped back, perfectly composed, and straightened his cuff. “Good evening,” he said to the concierge. Then he looked up at the camera in the lift ceiling as the doors closed on it. “He’ll have that by morning.”

“Let him,” said Serafina, and started laughing, and didn’t stop until they were outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes to ten, by the grey estate in the cool, she held out her hand under the streetlamp and looked at the ring again.

“Do you know what I like most about it? That Aurelia used Nonna.”

“She did well.”

“When you first noticed me, I was standing next to a car with a forged chassis plate.”

“Yes.”

“And you were dressed as a guard.”

“I wasn’t pretending.”

“You were dressed as one.” He opened the passenger door for her. Before she got in, she caught his sleeve. “Hao. I’m glad you noticed me.”

His face went quiet. “I’m glad you looked back.”

She kissed him once and got in. He closed her door and walked round, and checked his mirrors before he pulled out, and in the passenger seat she turned the ruby on her finger in the passing lights. Two professionals had sat at one table that evening. One had read the other’s file. One had threatened the other. And somewhere between them she’d been given a number for a door that might one day matter. But for now there was a ring on the right finger, a man at the wheel, and a long road home.

chapters.title: The Director Sends Congratulations
chapters.desc: His director has read the form. She brings congratulations, a silver pen with a 7 on it, and a folder for Lisbon. Serafina uses the pen to enter a hill climb.
chapters.epigraph: “We look after our families. It’s in the training.”
chapters.content:
The summons came at ten past nine on Monday the eighth of May, with a line under it that he read twice. Bring your fiancée’s preferred coffee.

He had been in the Bureau long enough to know a trap when it came dressed as hospitality. He bought a flat white with an extra shot from the stall under the flyover, because that was what she drank when she’d been up all night with a gearbox, and carried it up to the corner office on the top floor of the building by the river.

Director Duan Qiuyan was knitting. She sat by the window in a grey cardigan with a long red ribbed scarf coming off her needles into her lap, and she didn’t stop when he came in. She was fifty-five and looked like somebody’s aunt on a ferry. The office had two doors, a view of the river and no photographs, and the desk was so clean it looked unused. On it lay a folder, a small white box, and nothing else.

“Qin. Sit.” She held out her hand without looking up, and he put the coffee in it, and she drank some and made a face. “Strong. Of course it is.” The needles clicked. “Congratulations. I’m told that’s customary when a subordinate gets engaged.”

“Thank you.”

“Serafina Song. Remarkable young woman. Mechanically gifted. Competitive. Unusually observant. A little reckless.”

“She’d disagree with the last one.”

“I imagine she would.” Click. “Sixty thousand through a company called Northgate into the accounts of Team AURELIA. A gearbox. Tyres. Transport. A splitter in March.”

“Yes.”

“And Granny Shum’s.” She turned the scarf on her knee. “You spent ten years making sure nobody knew where you were. Now you spend your evenings in a garage where half the district knows your name, eating noodles with retired mechanics.”

“It’s quieter than here.”

“Is it? And the dinner on the forty-fourth floor. I know Chen Si was there, and his assistant. I know your fiancée wore a ruby you brought back from Antwerp, and that her sister reset it with gold off an old car.” She looked at him over her glasses for the first time. “You’ve become very interesting, Qin.”

“My duties haven’t changed.”

“No. Your priorities have.” She said it without accusation, and that made it worse. Then, mildly, as if reading off a list: “Her sister is married to a man who sits on the docks like a spider. Her parents are about to lose everything they own. And she races against the law on Saturday nights.” Over the glasses again. “None known.”

He didn’t answer.

“She’s a lovely girl,” said Duan. “I’ve seen the photographs. Such a loud laugh.” She put the knitting down. It was the first time she had stopped since he came in. Her hands went still in her lap. “I’m not threatening her, Haozhen. I want to be clear. I don’t threaten people. You know that.” Gentle as milk. “We look after our families. It’s in the training.”

He looked back at her with the east-service-door face, polite and empty. Behind it he was thinking clearly.

She slid the white box across the desk. “A wedding present. Open it.”

Inside, on velvet, a slim silver pen, heavier than it looked, with a single number engraved near the clip. 7.

“Her car number, I believe.”

“Yes.”

“I thought it suitable.”

“I wasn’t aware the Bureau had a budget for wedding presents.”

“It doesn’t.”

“Then I’m curious about the expense code.”

She laughed, a short real laugh. “Still difficult. Give it to her. Tell her it’s from me.” Then she picked up the needles again and nodded at the folder. “Now. Lisbon. June. A financial network moving money through three shell companies. Four ledgers, the originals, still intact. A man who took them when he left. We want both. Mo Tianyi goes with you.”

He opened it. Photographs, a street plan, names, a man’s face. Recovery of documents and subject.

“Alive?”

“Alive. Second week of June. You’ll have the legal framework before you fly.”

“Extraction?”

“Yours.” She watched him read. “You haven’t asked about the man.”

“His name’s in the file.”

“And if he won’t come?”

“Then I’ll find out why.”

“That’s a very careful answer.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

“I need you in Lisbon, Qin. Not distracted. Not fitting your availability round a domestic schedule.”

“My availability hasn’t changed.”

“Good.” At the door she said, without looking up, “Don’t let happiness make you careless.”

“I won’t.”

When the door had closed, Duan Qiuyan finished the row she was on. Then she picked up the telephone. “Send me the revised Lisbon list. And the fiancée. No, not the public profile. The whole thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past eleven, in a records room two floors down, he did the second thing that morning that he had no intention of telling Serafina, and opened a personnel file he had no business opening.

Duan Qiuyan. A flat on the ninth floor of a building by the north station. The early train on weekdays. A sister, younger, a schoolteacher, with a husband and a flat of her own. A posting abroad in her thirties. Two friends.

There was nothing in it that suggested Duan meant Serafina any harm. She had been direct, almost amused. She’d sent a gift. But she knew about the gearbox and Granny Shum’s and the dinner and the ring, and she had said we look after our families in that voice, and Serafina had become a thing people talked about inside this building. He copied what he’d read into the back of his black notebook, in his own shorthand, and he didn’t write leverage at the top of the page. He wrote contingency. It was an old habit. It was an ugly one. Ten years had taught him that knowing where somebody lived could be the difference between arriving in time and arriving too late.

He closed the file and sat looking at the pen in its box. The seven caught the strip light. For the first time that morning he wondered what she would say if she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes to eight that evening only her boots were sticking out from under Nonna.

“Don’t step there.”

He stopped. “Where?”

“Anywhere. It’s a garage. Everything’s dangerous.” A hand came out. “Ten-millimetre.”

He put it in her palm before she’d finished the word. There was a pause, and then her face appeared upside down under the sill. “Hello.”

“Hello.”

“You’re early.”

“It’s nearly eight.”

“Early for you.” He held out his hand and pulled her out on the creeper, and she sat up wiping her cheek with her wrist and looked at the folder on the bench and the little white box beside it. “Is that a present? Should I be worried?”

“Probably not.”

“That’s not convincing.” She opened it, and went straight to the number. “Seven.” She turned the pen over in her fingers. “Who’s this from?”

“Director Duan. She said it was a wedding present.”

Serafina stared at it, and started to laugh, and stopped. “She knows my number. She knows about the car. The team. How much does she know?”

“Quite a lot.”

“Was she threatening you?”

“No.”

“Me?”

“No.”

“Was she being friendly?”

“Possibly.”

“That sounds worse.” She put the pen back in its box carefully. “What else?”

“Lisbon. June. Ledgers and the man who took them. Tianyi’s coming.”

“How long?”

“I don’t know yet. I’ll tell you before I go. I’ll tell you when I’m back, if I can.” He took his jacket off and hung it on the chair, and didn’t sit. “And I want to tell you everything she said. Not just the parts about Lisbon.”

So he told her. The coffee. The knitting. The money, the dinner, the ring. None known, read back to him over a pair of glasses. Such a loud laugh. The warning about happiness. And then, without being asked, the records room. The ninth floor by the north station. The early train. The sister who taught school. The page at the back of his notebook.

When he finished the garage was quiet. She was sitting on the edge of the bench with her hands flat beside her.

“You wrote down her home address.”

“Yes.”

“And her sister’s.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because she knows about you.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s a contingency.”

“For what?”

“If she becomes a threat.”

“Has she?”

“No.”

“Has she threatened me?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

He didn’t soften it. “I wanted to know what I could use, if I ever needed to stop her.”

Her lips parted. “Use.”

“Yes.”

“Her sister. A schoolteacher. Because your boss knows I’m engaged to you.”

“Because she knows enough to make you matter to the Bureau.”

She slid off the bench and walked away from him, three steps, and came back. “You told me everything she said. You didn’t hide Lisbon. You told me about the file. And you still went and did it.”

“Yes.”

“Do you hear yourself?”

“Yes.”

“Why, Hao?”

“Because I don’t know how to stop getting ready for the worst. I know what happens when somebody has information and I don’t. I know what it costs when I’m late. I know how quickly a person turns into a point of pressure.”

“And collecting her sister makes you safer?”

“No.”

“Then what does it make you?”

“Prepared.”

“That’s what you always call it.” She came close and looked up at him. “I’m not asking you to stop being careful. I’m asking you to understand that not everybody who knows my name is an enemy. Don’t turn people into files because you’re frightened.”

“All right.”

“And you don’t use her sister. You don’t go near her family. Ever.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise me.”

“I promise.”

She looked at him, and then she put her hand on the inside of his wrist, where she’d written his name in April. “Thank you for telling me.”

“I nearly didn’t.”

“I know. You told me anyway.” She rubbed her thumb over the pulse there. It wasn’t a clean ending. Neither of them pretended it was. But he had brought the ugly thing into the light instead of keeping it, and for tonight that was what mattered.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday at seventeen minutes past two, the entry form for the Baizhang Pass hill climb lay on the bench, and she had been looking at it for twenty minutes.

Baizhang was a mountain road above the reservoir, closed to traffic one weekend a year: twelve kilometres of narrow tarmac, blind crests, and stone walls on the outside of the bends where a mistake didn’t end in gravel. It wasn’t a casual event. It wasn’t a place to take a car still being developed. She’d been thinking about it all winter. The deadline was Friday. The car number box was empty. She reached for the silver pen.

“Are you really entering?” said Mouse, from a stool. “In what?”

“Gilded.”

“That’s ambitious.”

“Thank you.”

“It’s not a compliment. The surface changes. There are blind bits. The top hairpins are about as wide as a sofa.”

“That’s why I’m entering a hill climb and not a sightseeing tour.” She clicked the pen.

“Where did you get that?”

“Director Duan. Wedding present.”

Mouse looked at the pen, and at her, and at the pen. “That’s either very thoughtful or deeply sinister.”

“Apparently both are possible.” She wrote. Driver: Serafina Song. Vehicle: Gilded. Number: 7. She signed it at the bottom, and photographed it, and sent it.

Sera: Entered.

Hao: Baizhang?

Sera: You know another hill climb with a seven on it?

Three dots appeared, and went, and came back.

Hao: I’ll look at the course.

Sera: Don’t look at it like you’re going to fight it.

Hao: I’m looking at it like I want you to finish it.

She read that, and put the phone down. “Romantic?” said Mouse.

“Annoying.”

“Same thing, with him.” Serafina threw a rag at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain had stopped by fourteen minutes to midnight. The yard outside the garage was still wet, the security light lying on it in pale yellow patches. She was locking the side door when he came up behind her. He’d been quiet all evening. Not distant. Thoughtful.

“Did you look at the course?”

“Yes. It’s difficult.”

“That’s generally the point.”

“Two of the upper corners brake shorter than they look. The surface goes bad after the second hairpin. There’s a wall on the outside of the fourth.”

“Hao. I know there’s a wall.”

He reached past her and turned the key once more, to be sure it had caught. “You’re entering.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

“Good?”

“I’d rather you entered because you want to than because you think you have to prove something.”

“And if I want to prove something?”

“Then make sure it’s worth proving.”

“That’s very diplomatic.”

“I’m trying.” He took her hand and found the smear of ink on her thumb from marking up the course map, and rubbed at it, and it didn’t come off. She lifted her left hand into the light. The ruby glowed.

“I like wearing it.”

“I like seeing it there.” He looked at her. “I’m worried about Lisbon. About the job. And more than partly about leaving you.”

“You’ll come back.”

“I’ll do everything I can to come back.”

“Good. Then you’ll help me with the top hairpins.”

“That’s my reward?”

“It’s a privilege.” She was about to say something else when he stepped in and put his hand at her waist, and looked at her as though he were deciding something, and said, “Come here.”

“I’m here.”

He drew her in, and then down, and she gave a startled laugh as he lowered her with him onto the wet concrete by the door, one arm behind her shoulders, his other hand braced on the ground. “Hao—”

“Careful.”

“I’m sitting on wet concrete. That’s not careful.”

“I’ll take responsibility,” he said, and kissed her. This one was deep and urgent, nothing like his usual, as if a wind had got up and he was holding onto something that might be carried off, and she took his jacket in both fists and pulled him down onto her and felt all of it, everything he’d kept under his face all evening, the folder and the pen and the knitting and the page at the back of his notebook. She kissed him back as hard. His hand went into her hair and her knee came up against his hip and the cold came through her shirt and she didn’t care.

When they came apart she put her forehead against his. “What was that for?”

“Nothing.”

“Liar.”

“I wanted to kiss you.”

“You could have done it standing up. Why are we on the floor?”

He looked at the concrete. “Bad planning.”

She laughed, and he kissed the corner of her mouth and her cheek and her forehead, and she caught his face. “Lisbon’s in June. Baizhang’s before that. So we’ve got cars to fix and corners to argue about, and you’re going to help me win.”

“I thought you didn’t want me to let you win.”

“I don’t.”

“Then I’ll drive properly.”

And Qin Haozhen, who had spent ten years learning to leave without anybody noticing, stayed on the cold wet concrete with her in his arms until she was the one who said they should go inside.

chapters.title: Five A.M., Departures
chapters.desc: The last night before Lisbon, then the airport at five in the morning. She gives him her grandmother’s tyre gauge, and he says it through the car window.
chapters.epigraph: “You have to bring it back. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.”
chapters.content:
“The suitcase is too small.”

She had said this three times. He had disagreed three times. At twenty to nine on Sunday the eleventh of June she stood over it on the loft floor holding up a fourth shirt, while he sat on the edge of the bed and watched her with the patience of a man who’d survived worse interrogations.

“You need another one.”

“I have four.”

“For two weeks.”

“Possibly.”

“Four shirts for two weeks is ridiculous.”

“I can wash them.”

“You have a very strange relationship with laundry.”

“I have a normal relationship with laundry.”

“You have a relationship with one shirt at a time.” She put the shirt in. Took it out. Folded it again. “Passport?”

“Yes.”

“Documents?”

“Yes.”

“Phone?”

“No.”

She stopped dead. He looked at her. “I’m joking.”

She threw the shirt at him. He caught it, and held it a moment, smiling, and then folded it properly, sleeves behind, in three, and laid it in the case.

“Show-off.”

“It’s a shirt.”

“It’s an attitude.” He got up and came to her and put his hands at her waist, and she let him pull her in and put her cheek against his chest, and the suitcase stayed open behind them, and neither of them made any further effort to finish it.

✦ ✦ ✦

By a quarter past ten it was raining again. It tapped on the skylight in a steady rhythm, and somewhere below them the old garage fridge hummed. She lay on her side tracing the seam of his shirt with one finger. He was looking at the ceiling.

“You said trains help you sleep. Why?”

He was quiet for a while. Then he turned on his side to face her. “I grew up in a mining town. In the north. Most of the work was the mine. My mother worked in the canteen. I went to school and came home and listened to the winding gear.”

“The what?”

“The winding gear. It ran the cage that took the men down the shaft and brought them up. A great wheel on a frame above the pithead, and the engine under it. You could hear it in every street when the wind was right.” He spoke slowly, as if he hadn’t put it into words for years. “It had a rhythm. The cable taking up. The motor. The whole frame humming. A clank when it changed direction. When I was small I couldn’t sleep if it stopped. The town was too quiet without it.”

She understood something then, not all at once, but in the small pieces she’d collected without knowing what they were for: the way he slept in the passenger seat, the way he went loose on long roads, the way the trains over the bridge could pass at three in the morning without waking him.

“The trains,” she said.

“Not the same. But the rhythm’s familiar. Something heavy going along a track.”

“So a train sounds like home.”

“Perhaps.”

“Was it a nice place?”

“It was ordinary.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No. I don’t remember much of the town. I remember the sound. The canteen. The road to school. Coal dust in the gutters when it rained.”

“Do you miss it?”

“Sometimes. Not enough to go back.” He brushed his thumb over her cheek. “My mother’s still there. She won’t leave.”

“Next time you can’t sleep, tell me about it.”

“There’s not much to tell.”

“Then tell me the same thing twice.” She settled against him, and after a while he said, low, “It’s because they sound like something that knows where it’s going. And when I’m with you, I don’t need to know where it goes.”

She smiled into his chest. “That was almost poetic.”

“Almost?”

“You need to practise.” He laughed, and she lifted her face and kissed him, and that time neither of them stopped after one.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Slow,” she whispered, at seven minutes to midnight.

He went still. His hand lay on her hip under the duvet. “Slow?”

“Tonight. No rushing. No clock. No tomorrow.”

“All right.”

He kissed her, and didn’t hurry it, and let her have the pace. When she pushed his shirt up he sat up and pulled it off over his head and dropped it, and lay back down beside her, and she spread her hand on his chest over the old scar and felt his heart under it, steady, then not quite. She took her time with him. Her mouth on his collarbone, his ribs, the long pale line on his side, and he lay under it with his eyes shut and one hand in her hair and didn’t once try to hurry her. When she came back up he was looking at her as if she’d done something he didn’t have a word for.

“See?” she said against his mouth. “You can do it.”

“Do what?”

“Be patient.”

“I’ve been patient for ten years.”

“That’s a terrible thing to say to your fiancée.”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“No.” She laughed, and he kissed the laugh off her, and then he took the hem of her T-shirt and lifted it, and she raised her arms and let him, and he looked at her in the light from the street with his face serious. He put his mouth to the hollow of her throat. To her breast, unhurried, until she arched under him and said his name in a voice she didn’t recognise. Lower. She had asked for slow and he gave her slow, ruthlessly, the way he did everything, until she had both hands knotted in the sheet and was laughing and swearing at him in two languages at once.

“You asked for this,” he said, somewhere around her hip.

“I take it back.”

“Too late.”

She hauled him up by the shoulders, and kissed him hard, and rolled him onto his back and sat astride him with her hair coming down, and for a while she had him exactly where she wanted, watching his face come apart under her, his hands on her thighs, his jaw tight. Then his arm came round her back and he turned them both in one movement, careful and absolute, and she was under him on her front with his weight along her and his mouth at the back of her neck and his hand flat on her stomach holding her to him.

“Still slow?” he said into her ear.

She couldn’t answer. She pushed back against him and he made a sound she’d never heard from him before, and after that it wasn’t slow at all, and she didn’t want it to be. The rain went on over their heads. The duvet slid off the end of the bed. She came apart with her face in the pillow and his name in her mouth and his fingers laced through hers on the sheet, and she felt him follow her, shaking, holding on as if she were the only fixed thing in the building.

Afterwards he reached for the lamp. She caught his wrist. “Don’t. Leave it.” The room stayed dim. She turned and put her face in the hollow under his chin. “Tomorrow you’ll be in Lisbon.”

“Yes.”

“And I’ll be here. And you’ll miss me.”

He kissed her hair. “Already do.”

She was nearly asleep when she felt him kiss her forehead again. “Hao?”

“Yes?”

“Come back.”

His hand moved slowly over her back. “I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes past four the alarm hadn’t gone off, and he was already sitting on the edge of the bed doing up his watch.

“What time is it?”

“Four twelve.”

“That’s not a time. That’s a crime.” She pushed her hair out of her face. “I’m taking you.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

Downstairs the garage was cold, the strip lights coming on one row at a time over the covered cars. She went to Nonna first, opened the driver’s door and felt under the dash in the little compartment there, and came out with something in her fist.

A tyre gauge. Not the cheap black one from his glovebox. Brass, round, the size of a pocket watch, with a scratched glass and a needle that had been bent once and straightened. On the back, two sets of initials scratched with a nail: S.S., and under it, older and smaller, A.C.

“It was Nonna’s. For her old coupé.” She swallowed. “She gave it to me when I was twelve. She said never trust a tyre gauge from a petrol station. You have to tap it twice before you read it. And the rubber on the hose is cracked, so don’t leave it loose in a bag.”

He turned it over in his fingers. “Sera. I can’t take this.”

“You have to bring it back. That’s the point. It’s the only one that reads true. I’ll need it for the hill climb.” She glanced at him. “So bring it back. Before the eighteenth if you can. After if you can’t. But you bring it back.”

“Anything else?”

“Don’t lend it to Tianyi. He’ll lose it.”

“I’ll keep it.”

“And if it stops working, don’t throw it away.”

“I won’t.” He closed his hand round it. He didn’t say anything. Then he put it in the inside pocket of his jacket, over his heart, and said, “Thank you.”

“It’s only a tyre gauge.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.” She looked away before he could see her face.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-one minutes to five the grey estate was running in the alley. He checked the boot one more time. Case. Folder. Passport. The brass weight in his jacket.

“You’re taking the armoured car to the airport.”

“It’s a grey car.”

“It’s an armoured grey car.”

“Still grey.” He held the keys out to her. “You drive. Then keep it. It’s better than the bus while Nonna’s in bits.”

Through the open side door his mug was visible on the bench, chip by the handle, his name on the bottom against the wood where nobody could see it. She looked at it, and got in.

She drove. The city was hardly awake: lights changing for empty roads, the first buses, a delivery van crawling through the industrial streets. He sat with his hand near the gear lever and didn’t sleep.

“You could,” she said.

“I’m comfortable.”

“Better.” At a red light she reached across and he took her hand. “Send me the course map,” he said. “And the build schedule. And don’t run the prototype without checking the brake temperatures.”

“Are you giving me mechanical advice before sunrise? From a man who drove round for a month on cooked rear pads?”

“That was different.”

“Everything’s different when it’s you.” The light went green. She drove on.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four minutes past five the drop-off lane was already busy, doors and boots and people hurrying with the faces of travellers who hadn’t slept. She pulled in. He undid his belt and leaned across and kissed her, and she held his jaw.

“Text me when you can. Even a dot.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t disappear without warning.”

“I won’t.” He touched the ruby on her finger. Then he got out, and took his case, and shut the door, and came round the back of the car and stopped at her window. She wound it down.

“Your jacket,” she said. “It’s cold.”

“You always say that.”

“Because you never dress properly.”

He stood there a moment longer, with the case beside him and the glass doors of the terminal behind. “I love you,” he said.

No warning. Three words through a car window in the middle of a crowded drop-off lane at five in the morning, the first time he had ever said them, said as if they had been ready for months and he’d only now found the door.

She shoved her door open. He looked startled. “Serafina—”

She got out. “Qin Haozhen!”

He stopped. Several people turned round. She didn’t care.

“I LOVE YOU!”

A man with a suitcase stared. A woman by the doors smiled. And Haozhen stood in the lane and laughed, out loud, a proper laugh she’d never once had from him, and she pointed at him across the roof of the car.

“You heard me!”

“I heard you.”

“Good!”

He came back round the car and she took the front of his jacket and kissed him, and he held her face in both hands, and when they parted he put his forehead on hers. “I’ll come back.”

“You’d better.”

Then he picked up his case, and this time she let him go. At the doors he turned. She lifted her hand, and the ruby caught the early light, and he lifted his, and went inside. She got back in, and only when the door was shut did she find she was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Song.”

She looked up. It was twenty past five, and Mr. Kwok was standing by the estate’s bonnet in the short-stay bay with a paper bag in one hand and a thermos in the other.

“Mr. Kwok? Why are you here?”

“Because you’re here. Eat.” Inside the bag was an egg sandwich, still warm. “Before it gets cold.”

“Did Hao ask you to come?”

“Someone has to make sure you eat.”

“I’m not a child.”

“No. Children are easier.” He looked at the terminal. “He gone?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” He nodded as though that settled something, and looked at the car. “Your tyres come today.”

“What tyres? I didn’t order any.”

He took a folded delivery note out of his pocket. At the bottom, in a square hand: QIN H. And beside it, typed, the name of the team’s sponsorship account, the one Aurelia had drawn up a contract for in April, with his name on it where everyone could see.

She shut her eyes. “I’m going to kill him.”

“Don’t. He’s in Portugal.” Mr. Kwok drank from his thermos. “Eat first. Then kill him.” He stood by the bonnet until she’d eaten half of it. “Go home. Don’t drive fast.”

“Me?”

“Especially you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes past six she parked the grey estate in his space in the garage and left the lights on. His mug was on the bench. She turned it over and ran her thumb across the writing on the bottom. HAOZHEN, in her own marker.

Her phone buzzed.

Hao: Through security.

Sera: Good.

Hao: I have the gauge.

Sera: Don’t lose it.

Hao: I won’t.

Sera: The tyres are coming, apparently.

Three dots.

Hao: Mr. Kwok was supposed to give you the sandwich first.

She laughed out loud in the empty garage.

Sera: You arranged the sandwich too?

Hao: I asked him to make sure you ate. I love you.

She looked at that.

Sera: I love you too. Bring my grandmother’s gauge home.

Outside, the first van of the morning came into the alley, and a man unloaded four new tyres and stacked them by Gilded. On the delivery sheet, under the specification, someone had written PAID IN FULL — SPONSOR, and drawn a small square box round it, neatly, the way only one person she knew drew boxes.

“Welcome to the team, Mr. Qin,” she said, and picked up the silver pen with the seven on it, and wrote the date on the build sheet.

chapters.title: Baizhang Pass
chapters.desc: She races up a mountain without her gauge. On the other side of the world, a man and a night porter watch the stream at four in the morning.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a waste of good tyres. His tyres.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Serafina noticed at Baizhang Pass on Saturday morning was that her tyre gauge was missing. The second was that she had known it would be, and had reached for it anyway.

It was twenty past six. Mist lay low over the service paddock in the village at the foot of the climb, between the transporters and the tea sheds and the noodle stalls not yet open, and she stood beside Gilded with her hand in the empty corner of the tool bag where the brass gauge had lived for fourteen years.

“Looking for something?” said Mouse, across the bonnet.

“No.”

“Your hand says otherwise.”

“My gauge.”

“The one you gave Haozhen.”

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.” Mouse drank her coffee. “You could have brought another one.”

“I did.” On the bench by the compressor lay a digital gauge borrowed from the event’s technical crew. Recently calibrated. Perfectly accurate. She disliked it on sight. It was too light. The brass one had weight, and a casing worn smooth by two women’s thumbs, and a needle that stuck unless you tapped it twice. Her grandmother had taught her to read it by feel, by the small give of the valve when the fitting seated properly. And now it was somewhere in Lisbon, in the jacket of a man who was supposed to bring it home.

“Fine,” she said to the car. The car didn’t answer. It never had been much help in conversations.

✦ ✦ ✦

Big Wu had said it in the van on the way up, twice, and he said it again at eight o’clock by the scrutineering bay with his arms folded, glaring up at the mountain.

“No run-off. No gravel. You go off at the Needle, you sit in the gravel and cry on your sister. You go off up there, you go off the mountain.”

“You said this in the van.”

“Twice.”

“Three times, Wu.”

“Then this is four, and four’s bad luck, so listen to it.” He glared at Gilded. Matte black. White 7 on the door. AURELIA in gold across the bonnet. A little grey toy taxi glued to the corner of the dashboard. “Circuit car. Circuit tyres. Against a field of specials built for nothing but this. It’s a waste of good tyres.” The glare got worse. “His tyres.”

She patted his enormous arm. The Baizhang climb went up eleven hundred metres in a little over twelve kilometres, from the tea village at the bottom to a concrete car park and a temple at the top, through a sequence of hairpins and stone-walled bends and two blind crests, and the field was strong: lightweight open-wheel specials, a handful of modified road cars, a couple of expensive things whose owners looked as if they’d never touched a tyre in their lives. Gilded, roofed and wide and built for a flat circuit, looked out of place among them. She liked it better that way.

Two bays down a man in a white suit was standing beside a red open-cockpit special. Lau Kam-wing. Forty-seven, silver at the temples, with the easy manner of somebody who’d been winning long enough not to have to announce it. He had held the outright record up the pass for four years. He looked at Gilded, and then at her.

“Song? First time here?”

“First competitive run.”

“Big car for this mountain.”

“It’s a big mountain.”

He smiled. “Fair answer. Good luck.”

“You too.”

“That’s Lau Kam-wing,” said Mouse, when he’d gone. “Four years.”

“That’s why it’s a record.”

“Do you want to beat him?”

“I want a clean run.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“Then yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The pressures weren’t quite where she wanted them. She knelt by the front left with the borrowed gauge, read the display, unclipped it, and tapped it twice out of habit. Nothing happened. Mouse crouched beside her.

“It’s digital.”

“I know.”

“You don’t have to hit it.”

“I wasn’t hitting it.”

“You were about to.” She did all four, and then all four again, slower than usual, checking every valve twice. Then she put her palm flat against the tyre wall. Not because it told her anything. Because it reminded her of a cardigan and a cold morning in Milan, and her grandmother holding the brass gauge between two fingers. Don’t trust the number until you trust the way you got it. She’d been twelve. She hadn’t understood. She did now.

At half past ten the first run was for seeding. The marshal checked her transponder, and the flag went up, and came down, and Gilded went. She kept the car tidy through the opening bends and didn’t attack before the tyres had come in. Third. Fourth. The road opened for a breath and closed again. She braked a little later than in practice at the third hairpin, not too late, just enough, and the car rotated clean, and for a second the whole drop opened up beyond the stone wall and she didn’t look at it, she looked at the exit. At the top the surface went bad and the steering went light and she kept her foot in. One minute, forty-eight point seven six. Second, eight tenths behind Lau.

“Good,” she said.

“Good?” said Mouse.

“Now I know where the time is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two minutes past four on Sunday morning, in the lobby of a hotel in Lisbon, Fernando had been working nights for thirty-one years, and he knew which guests wanted conversation and which wanted silence, which were waiting for somebody who wouldn’t come, and which had come down because the rooms were too quiet. The man in the white shirt belonged to the last kind. He had appeared at nineteen minutes to four, with no luggage and no coat, and asked whether the television could get a particular stream, and Fernando had shown him how.

Now they sat at opposite ends of the lobby sofa. On the screen a mountain road wound up through dark trees. BAIZHANG PASS HILL CLIMB — LIVE. Seven hours ahead, it was late morning there, and the last runs were starting.

“Your friend?” said Fernando.

“My fiancée.”

“Ah.” He thought about it. Then he brought a second coffee over. “Then you should sit closer.”

The stream was terrible. The camera wandered from the start line to the paddock to the timing board, the sound came and went, the picture broke up into blocks of colour every few minutes. The man watched every second of it.

“Which one is she?”

He pointed. A woman in a dark suit beside a big low black car, talking to a girl with a ring in her nose, holding a pressure gauge. She put the gauge down and reached for something else in a bag, and stopped. The man’s hand moved towards the inside pocket of his jacket, which was over the back of the sofa, and took out a small round brass thing.

“Yours?” said Fernando.

“Hers. She lent it to me.” He turned it over. It was warm. “I have to give it back.”

“Then take good care.” Fernando watched him close his hand on it. “My daughter races bicycles.”

“Professionally?”

“No. Very badly. She falls off all the time. I used to stand at the side of the road and shout at her to slow down. She never listened.”

“Did she stop?”

“No. She got faster.” He drank his coffee. “Now I tell her to ring me when she gets home.”

“Does she?”

“Usually.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven minutes past twelve, at the start line at Baizhang, Lau was ahead by three tenths after the second runs.

“First split you’re up two hundredths,” said Mouse, reading off the tablet. “Second you’re down five. Third you get four back. You’re lifting in the long left.”

“Surface?”

“Dry. Same as before. Light crosswind at the top.”

Lau came past on his way to his car. “Don’t force the middle,” he said, conversationally. “The mountain takes time off people who get greedy.”

“Everyone?”

“Eventually.” He smiled and went.

“Good advice,” said Mouse.

“Annoyingly.” She got in. Harness. Engine. Mirrors. On the timing board: LAU KAM-WING, RECORD 1:48.41, 2019. She smiled to herself. “Let’s go.”

The flag dropped and Gilded went. She was measured in the first section, the car steady under braking, and in the long left she held it. Didn’t lift. Felt the front begin to push, and corrected, and waited, and opened the throttle. At the fifth bend she took a tighter line than before and gave up a breath of entry speed to get the exit, and the car pulled hard uphill and she went up through the gears with the stone wall going by in a grey blur on her right. The crosswind found the bodywork at the top. She caught it, not too much, eyes on the road, and the last sequence came fast, and her hands moved, and the engine screamed, and she was over the line.

For one second there was nothing on the radio at all.

“One minute, forty-seven point nine one.”

Then Mouse, shrieking. “Serafina! Serafina, you did it! Half a second! You beat the record by half a second!”

In the paddock Mouse grabbed her by both shoulders. On the board: 1:47.91. A new record up Baizhang, and the first roofed car ever to win it outright. Serafina stood still, and then laughed, a sharp disbelieving bark that set Mouse off too. Lau came over and looked at the board and then at her, and held out his hand.

“Half a second.”

“Thank you.”

“You drove well. Next year?”

“If Gilded survives the season.”

“Then I’ll see you next year.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-nine minutes past five in Lisbon, Fernando was on his feet first. The man on the sofa hadn’t moved. On the screen, in big white numbers, 1:47.91.

“Is that good?”

“She broke the record.”

“Then you should be happy.”

He didn’t answer. The camera had found her in the paddock, helmet still on, with the girl with the nose ring talking at her fast and pointing at the board. She looked straight into the lens. She lifted her left hand, deliberately, and the ruby on it caught the light even through that terrible picture. Then she mouthed two words.

Bring it back.

He looked down at the brass gauge in his hand, and laughed helplessly. “She wants something back.”

“Something expensive?”

“No. Important.”

“Then you must return it.”
