He wanted to be there. Not in a hotel lobby watching a stream that kept breaking into squares, but beside her car, hearing her laugh without glass in between, with his hand on the back of her neck, telling her she’d driven beautifully and letting her complain about the borrowed gauge. He took out his phone and opened the airline and found a flight with one change. He could be home by night if he left now. The operation was set for that morning. The folder was upstairs. Tianyi would already be up.

On the screen she was holding up a trophy with her left hand still where he could see it. He closed the app.

“You’re not going?” said Fernando.

“No.”

“Why?”

He put the gauge back in his pocket. “Because I said I’d come back. Not that I’d come back early.”

Fernando nodded and picked up his coffee. “Sometimes the way home is not the shortest road.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Hao: I saw it.

Sera: All of it?

Hao: Every run.

Sera: Half a second.

Hao: I saw.

Sera: You should have been here.

The answer took longer.

Hao: I know. I’m proud of you.

She looked up the mountain. It smelled of hot brakes and fuel and wet earth, and Mouse was arguing with a photographer about where to stand.

Sera: Did you bring my gauge?

Hao: Yes. I’m keeping it safe.

Sera: Bring it back.

Hao: I will.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past six, upstairs, Tianyi was waiting with the folder open on the desk and two photographs beside it: a narrow street of old apartment buildings, and a yellow house with blue shutters and a small tree by the gate at the bottom of a sloping road.

“You were downstairs?”

“Yes.”

“Watching the race?”

“Yes.”

“Congratulations to her.” Mo Tianyi had shared a dormitory with him under a roof that leaked, and had a face that laughed with all of it, and wasn’t laughing now. “The local man’s got the flat across the street from the house. We can move in at seven and start watching tonight.”

“Neighbours?”

“Both sides. It’s narrow. Civilians everywhere.”

“Then we don’t use the back road.”

“What about the target?”

“He’s alone,” said Haozhen. “He lives alone. It’s in the file.”

Tianyi looked at the page. “That’s not confirmed.”

“It’s in the file.”

“Files are wrong. You’ve been looking at the same photograph for three minutes, Qin.”

He had. A yellow house with blue shutters. A place where somebody made coffee in the morning and left shoes by the door. He thought of a garage under a railway bridge, and a chipped mug, and a mountain record, and how easy it would be to leave the folder on the desk and go to the airport after all. Then he put the photograph down.

“He has a wife and a son,” he said. “Seven or eight. The contact saw a boy with a football at the gate yesterday. They’re not in the file.”

Tianyi stared at him. “Then why tell me he was alone?”

“Because I wanted to see whether you’d take the easy version.”

“And?”

“You didn’t.”

Tianyi’s jaw went tight. “That isn’t a game you play with me. People get hurt.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t do it again.” He shut the folder. “We account for the family. If he moves, we reassess.” He studied Haozhen’s face. “You’re thinking about her.”

He didn’t deny it.

“You watched a woman drive up a mountain at four in the morning from a hotel lobby and then came up here to plan this.” Tianyi gave a small tired laugh. “Just come back in one piece. I don’t want to be the one who tells her I lost you in Lisbon.”

Haozhen put his hand in his jacket and found the brass gauge and held it.

“Neither do I,” he said.

chapters.title: The Target Has a Family
chapters.desc: Lisbon. Twenty-three days in a chair by a door, counting a boy’s keepy-ups. Then the job.
chapters.epigraph: “Not in front of the house. Please. That’s my son’s window.”
chapters.content:
The boy had done eleven keepy-ups. Haozhen knew because he had counted them.

It was eighteen minutes past six on the fourteenth morning in Lisbon, and he was in the passenger seat of a parked car across the street from the yellow house with a paper cup of coffee going cold in his hands. Tianyi was beside him reading the morning briefing on his phone. Across the road a boy in a yellow football shirt was trying to keep a scuffed ball in the air. One, two, three. He sent it too far on the fourth, chased it across the pavement, trapped it before it went into the road, and started again.

“Fourteen,” said Haozhen.

Tianyi looked up. “What?”

“The boy.”

“He’s been at it twenty minutes. Are you counting?”

“Yes.”

Tianyi looked at him and went back to his phone. “Your priorities have got strange.”

The front door of the yellow house opened. A woman came out with a shopping bag and called something in Portuguese, and the boy answered without looking up. A man came out behind her. Gong Ruiming was thinner than his photograph, with a receding hairline and the careful, slightly hunched way of walking of a man who had spent years not being noticed. Blue shirt. Ordinary watch. He kissed his wife’s cheek. Then he crouched to say something to the boy, and the boy kicked the ball straight at him, and he caught it on his chest and pretended to stagger, and the boy laughed.

Haozhen looked away.

“Forty-six,” said Tianyi. “Financial controller for the group for nine years. Walked out six months ago with four of their ledgers. The originals.”

“And the family?”

“Wife, Inês, local. Son, Tomás, seven. No involvement known.”

“Then they’re not the job.”

“They’re part of the ground.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No,” said Tianyi. “It isn’t.”

Gong handed the ball back, waved, and walked off down the hill. The boy started again. “Twenty-one,” said Haozhen, when the man had gone round the corner.

“I’m not counting with you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat they were using had two bedrooms and a kitchen and a view of the house, and curtains that wouldn’t quite close. Tianyi had complained about the curtains on the first night. By the fifteenth day he’d stopped.

Gong was predictable. The bakery at seven. Home. The little football court by the river with his son some afternoons. The market with his wife on Thursdays. Tuesdays the wife took the boy to the early market on her own. He didn’t look like a man getting ready to run. He didn’t seem to talk to anyone but his family. In every ordinary way, he looked like a man trying to have a life.

“The Director announced your engagement,” said Tianyi, putting down his pen. “Section dinner, before we flew. Stood up and did it herself.”

Haozhen looked up.

“She said you’d finally found something you couldn’t put on a transfer form.” Tianyi grinned. “Then she showed everyone the result from Baizhang on her phone. She said your fiancée had a good head for engines and a dangerous head for decisions.”

“That sounds like her.”

“You’re not embarrassed?”

“She gave us a wedding present. A silver pen with a seven on it.”

Tianyi stared, and laughed. “That’s absurdly specific. What did Serafina do with it?”

“Entered a hill climb.”

“Of course she did.” The laugh went. “Does she know how long we’ll be here?”

“She knows it could be longer.”

“And she’s all right with that?”

“No.” Haozhen turned a page. “She understands.”

It wasn’t the same thing. Tianyi didn’t press.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes to midnight on the seventeenth day, Tianyi put a small key on the kitchen table, with a faded blue plastic tag and a number stamped into its head.

“Where did you get that?”

“A man’s pocket.”

“Was it legal?”

Tianyi considered. “Not particularly.”

For two days they’d been following the trail of a left-luggage locker at the station, rented under a name that wasn’t Gong’s by somebody who’d worked hard to hide it. The ledgers had been moved there after he left, away from his house and away from the people looking for him. The key was the last link.

“Tomorrow we get the books,” said Tianyi. “Then Gong. We’ve got the authorisation. Man and records together.”

“I know.”

“You’ve been quiet.”

“I’ve been listening.”

“To what?”

Down in the street, somewhere in the dark, a ball bounced against a wall. “Nothing,” said Haozhen.

✦ ✦ ✦

The station at sixteen minutes past ten was full of suitcases and announcements and a child crying by the ticket machines. Haozhen stood by a pillar, watching the crowd without appearing to watch anything. Tianyi came back from the lockers with a canvas bag and walked past him without a look. “Four. Originals.” They left by different doors.

On the kitchen table, under gloves, the ledgers were old account books with soft corners and worn covers: payments through a chain of companies, transfers between accounts, names and coded references kept deliberately out of anything electronic. The fourth was the thinnest. Haozhen turned the pages slowly, and stopped.

One line had been marked in pencil, in a small neat hand. Three initials. D.Q.Y. And beside them, one word. Private.

He read it again. Beside it was a date, a reference and a sum that had gone through two accounts on its way somewhere. Nothing else. He knew the name behind those letters. Not from this job. From a file he had read years ago, before he knew Serafina, before he had ever slept in the passenger seat of anybody’s car, in a building by a river, upside down across a clean desk.

“What?” said Tianyi, from the sink.

Haozhen closed the ledger. “Nothing.”

Tianyi came over. “Those initials. Do you know them?”

“Could be an internal reference.”

“Do you know them, Qin?”

“No.”

Three letters and one word. A small lie. He knew exactly what he was doing when he told it. He had recognised them, and he had decided, standing at a kitchen table in Lisbon with a pair of borrowed gloves on, not to say so.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six minutes past two on the twentieth night he couldn’t sleep. The ledgers were locked in the case by the table. Tianyi had gone to bed. He sat by the window that wouldn’t close and looked down at the dark street.

He had rung her the evening before. Eleven minutes. Gilded needed new rear dampers. Mouse had somehow lost an entire socket set. Mr. Kwok had accused her of driving like somebody who had no plans to get old. He’d asked about the garage, and she’d said the mug was still there. He’d asked if she’d eaten, and she’d said yes, and he’d believed her, mostly. Before she rang off she’d asked if he was all right.

“Yes.”

She’d been quiet. “Hao. Don’t make me guess.”

He’d shut his eyes. “I’m tired.”

“That’s better.”

He had almost told her about the three letters in the ledger. Instead he’d asked to see the prototype, and she’d laughed and sent six photographs. He looked at the last one now. Gilded under the garage lights with the bodywork half off, and on the corner of the dashboard, still there, the little grey taxi. He made it bigger with two fingers and looked at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-second morning the boy was out early, in a blue shirt this time. His keepy-ups had got better. Haozhen counted twenty-seven before he lost it.

“Thirty-one yesterday,” said Tianyi.

“Twenty-seven today.”

“You’re keeping a record.”

“No.”

Gong came out with a backpack. His wife fixed the strap on his shoulder at the gate and kissed him. The boy ran up with the ball and said something, and Gong touched the top of his head and smiled and went off down the hill, and the boy stood and watched him go.

“Tomorrow,” said Tianyi.

“Yes. It’s a Tuesday. She takes the boy to the early market on Tuesdays. They’re never back before eight. He’ll be on his own at seven when he goes for bread.”

“You’re sure?”

“I’ve watched three Tuesdays.”

“If you’ve got a problem with this, say it now.”

“I haven’t.”

“Then don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you think I’m going to ask you to do something you can’t.”

“I can do it,” said Haozhen, and watched the boy kick the ball against the wall and run after it, and go inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past seven on Tuesday, the twenty-third day, the street was bright and quiet except for a car going past and somebody opening shutters. The wife and the boy had gone down to the market at half past six with the shopping bag. The front door opened and Gong came out alone, and locked it, and checked it twice, and turned round, and Haozhen was standing on the pavement in front of him.

“Mr. Gong.”

Gong went white. He didn’t run. Haozhen had known he wouldn’t. After ten years you could tell who would, and Gong was a man who had walked out of a building with a briefcase and known every day since that one morning somebody would be standing on his pavement saying his real name.

“Yes,” he said, in the northern language, a capital accent gone soft at the edges by the sea. “All right.” He looked past Haozhen’s shoulder at the window above the door. “Not in front of the house. Please. That’s my son’s window.”

“All right.”

They walked down the hill side by side, close, like two friends leaving a party, Haozhen’s hand at Gong’s elbow, not hard. Gong walked the way he wanted to walk, towards the market, away from the window, into the narrow lane behind the stalls where the bins were, because it was the quietest place he knew. Tianyi brought the car round to the end of it. And at the far end of the lane, where it met the market, a small boy in a yellow shirt came round the corner at a run with a football under his arm, the way he did every Tuesday at seven when he’d left his ball at home and his mother sent him back for it.

He stopped. He looked at his father, and at the man holding his father’s arm.

“Tomás,” said Gong.

“Papá?”

Gong pulled. Haozhen’s grip changed. He turned the elbow and brought the arm up behind Gong’s back in one short movement, high, until the man went up on his toes with a gasp and couldn’t pull any more.

“Go home,” said Haozhen to the boy, in Portuguese.

The boy didn’t move. “Papá?”

“Please,” said Gong. “My son. He’s just a child.”

“I know.”

“Let him go.” The boy came a step. Another. “Let him go!” He dropped the ball, and it rolled across the stones, and he ran at them, and Haozhen walked Gong the last ten metres to the car with the man’s arm locked up between his shoulder blades and his own body between the father and the son. Tianyi had the back door open. Gong twisted once more and Haozhen put him in, hand on his head, and got in after him.

Something hit the window beside Haozhen’s face with a hard hollow crack. The football. It bounced off the glass. The boy was a metre away, both fists clenched, his face scarlet and wet.

“LET HIM GO!”

He picked the ball up and threw it again, and it hit the door, and Tianyi got in and the car moved, and the boy ran beside it with his palm slapping the glass, and then behind it, in the road, the yellow shirt getting smaller in the rear window, still running, until the lane turned and he was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes to nine Gong had stopped speaking. He sat with his hands together, looking at the floor. Tianyi drove. Neither of them mentioned the boy. The ledgers were secure. Gong was alive. Everything was where it was supposed to be. Haozhen’s hands were perfectly steady, and he looked at them, and there was a smear of dirt on his right cuff from the lane, and he rubbed at it with his thumb, and it didn’t come off.

At seventeen minutes past nine, at a pontoon on the river below the old docks, a boat was waiting with two men on it: one in a dark jacket despite the heat, one older with a grey beard and a cigarette. The ledgers went first, four cases, checked and signed for. Then Gong. At the edge of the boards he looked at Haozhen and spoke for the first time since the lane.

“My son.”

Haozhen said nothing.

“Tell them I didn’t hurt anyone.”

“I’ll report what happened.”

It wasn’t an answer, and Gong understood that. He stepped down onto the boat. The grey-bearded man took his arm and took him below. The boat backed off the pontoon into the brown water, and Haozhen stood and watched it go, and a gull called somewhere overhead. Then he turned away from Tianyi and was sick over the side.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi didn’t come close at first. When the heaving had stopped he held out a bottle of water, and Haozhen rinsed his mouth and spat into the river.

“You all right?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t.” Tianyi stood beside him at the rail. “That’s three, Qin.”

Haozhen looked at him.

“The hotel. He’s alone. The ledger. Don’t, I saw your face when you shut it. And Tuesday.” His voice stayed quiet. “You’ve watched three Tuesdays. You knew he comes back for his ball.”

Haozhen heard it again: the hollow crack of a football on glass beside his face. Let him go.

“Yes,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to know if I could still do it.”

“Do what?”

“Take him. After three weeks of that boy. With the boy there.” He looked at the water. “I wanted to know what I was.”

“And?”

“I could.” He swallowed. “I did.”

Tianyi’s face went through anger into something tired. “You put me in a lane with a child in it and didn’t tell me. You don’t get to decide that on your own.”

“I know.”

“Don’t do it again.”

“I won’t.” It was a long time before either of them said anything else. Then Tianyi said, much more, “Do you want to go home?”

Haozhen’s hand went to the inside of his jacket. The brass gauge was there. “Yes.”

“Then we finish the paperwork and go.”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because I don’t know what I’m going to say when I get there.” He drank. The water tasted of metal.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past ten, on the edge of the hotel bed, he had three messages from her. A photograph of the prototype with its new front clam taped on. A complaint about Mouse. A picture of the chipped white mug on the bench. Your mug’s still here. I think it misses you.

He typed The job’s finished and deleted it. He typed I’m all right and deleted that too. The brass gauge lay on the bedside table with the light on its scratched face, and he remembered her holding it out to him at four in the morning. He remembered a boy in a yellow shirt and a ball against glass and a man’s voice saying my son. He typed: I’m coming home as soon as I can. He sent it before he could change it.

The answer came in under a minute.

Sera: I’ll be here.

He looked at it, and bowed his head. For twenty-three days he had sat by a window and counted a little boy’s keepy-ups. On the twenty-third day he had taken the boy’s father away in front of him. And for the first time in a long time he didn’t know whether going home would make him feel any better. He only knew that he wanted to go.

chapters.title: He Comes Home Wrong
chapters.desc: He comes home, sits in her passenger seat and says nothing for two days. Her father’s company is falling apart, and in the end he tells her about the boy.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to ask. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say.”
chapters.content:
The photograph came at sixteen minutes past nine on Friday night, while he was looking at the brass gauge on the hotel table. Nonna’s dashboard, the little compartment underneath it hanging open and empty.

Sera: Your passenger seat is getting impatient.

He looked at it.

Hao: Sunday. Four in the morning.

Sera: I’ll be there. And Hao? You don’t have to be all right before you come home.

The room was quiet. Tianyi was downstairs with the last of the transfer papers. The ledgers had gone where they were going, the operation was closed, and the report was waiting for his signature. He should have felt relieved. He felt as though he’d left something behind in a narrow lane in Lisbon. Something small, in a yellow shirt. He put the gauge in his jacket. He’d promised.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three minutes past four on Sunday morning she had been waiting in the arrivals hall for twenty-seven minutes, and knew it because she’d checked the clock every three. She had two coffees. His was going cold.

She saw him the moment the doors opened. Dark trousers, black jacket, small case. Thinner. Not so much that anyone else would see it. But she knew the exact set of his shoulders and the way he carried his weight and the little tilt of his head when he was looking for someone, and he found her, and stopped. He didn’t move at all. Then he walked to her.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

Neither of them smiled. She put her arms round him, and his came round her slowly, and he held her, but not the way he did. No tightening. No hand at the back of her head. He stood in it.

“You’re home,” she said into his chest.

“Yes.”

“Have you slept?”

“A little.”

“How much is a little?” He didn’t answer. She took his case. “Come on.” At the doors she reached for his hand, and he gave it to her, and his fingers were cold.

In the car park, before they reached the car, he took the gauge out of his jacket and held it out. She stopped and looked at it, and took it. The weight settled into her palm. The scratch across the glass, the bent needle, a new tiny mark near the rim. She tapped it twice and the needle moved.

“Still works.”

“Good.”

“Thank you for bringing it back.”

He nodded. She put it in her coat pocket, and opened Nonna’s passenger door, rebuilt and painted while he’d been gone, and he got in and sat with his hands on his thighs.

“Do you want to go home?”

He looked through the windscreen. “Can we drive?”

✦ ✦ ✦

So she drove the loop, gently, the way she had all winter. Bridge. Tunnel. Coast road. The ferries and the cranes. He didn’t sleep.

“Remember this bit?” she said. “You always go here. Every time.”

At the bend on the coast road where his head always slid off the window and onto her shoulder, he stayed upright. She went round three times. Four. The sky began to go grey over the water. Nothing. She pulled into the lay-by above the harbour, where they’d watched the fireworks, and turned the engine off, and it ticked.

“I’m not going to ask,” she said, with her eyes on the windscreen. “I want you to know that. I’m not going to ask where you went or what happened or what you did. I’m not going to ask. I’m going to sit here. You talk when there’s something you can say. If that’s tomorrow, it’s tomorrow. If it’s next year, it’s next year.”

He didn’t answer. After a while his eyes closed, and his head tipped towards the glass, and his hands stayed on his thighs with the fingers not quite loose. He wasn’t asleep. She knew the difference. She didn’t say anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At fourteen minutes past seven he got out of the car in the garage and stood beside it, looking. The shutter half up. A work lamp on Gilded’s front end. Tools across the bench. His mug where he’d left it. She put the kettle on and made coffee and put it by him and came back to find him exactly where she’d left him. She showed him the clean towels. He came down from the shower in an old shirt of hers that hung off him and sat on the sofa again.

She stood in front of him. “Can I touch you?”

Something moved in his face. “Yes.”

She put her hands on his face. His skin was warm now. She brushed her thumbs under his eyes and kissed his forehead, and he shut his eyes. Then she went and made breakfast, and he didn’t eat much of it, and he didn’t talk. When the morning turned into afternoon he went back out to Nonna and sat in the passenger seat with the door open and one foot on the concrete, looking at the dashboard. She found him there an hour later and didn’t ask him to come in. She sat in the driver’s seat. They stayed there until the light went.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday she had stopped asking whether he wanted anything. She brought it. Water. Toast. Coffee. A blanket. Sometimes he took it. He spent the day in the passenger seat and didn’t sleep.

At noon Mouse came in, shouldering the side door with a plastic tub in both hands. “Soup. From Big Wu’s mother. She’s made enough for a regiment. Apparently this is the portion for one very stubborn man.” She looked across the garage at Nonna, and at the man in it with his head against the seat and his eyes open. “Oh,” she said, and didn’t say anything else. She put a bowl on the bench and covered it and left a spoon beside it. Then she went over to the car.

“Qin.”

“Mouse.”

“Welcome back.” She held out a little bag. “Clementines. You look like you need vitamins. Don’t argue. They’re from the good shop.” He took the bag. “You don’t have to tell us anything,” she said. “But you have to eat something.”

Something almost like a smile crossed his face. “All right.”

She went back to her screens. He peeled one slowly, and ate a piece. Then another. It was the most he’d eaten since he came home.

At a quarter to four Mr. Kwok came in through the side door with a newspaper under his arm, nodded at Serafina, and walked to the car. “Qin.”

“Mr. Kwok.”

“I’m reading.” He pulled up a stool by the open door, unfolded the paper, and began to read aloud. It was a long article about a planning dispute over a car park, written in the kind of language that makes an argument between neighbours sound like a border war, and he read every word. The headline twice. The subheading. He stopped to complain about the reporter’s grammar. After twenty minutes he turned to the sports pages. After thirty, the football results. He didn’t ask a single question. At one point Haozhen’s eyes closed, and Mr. Kwok lowered his voice and carried on. When he reached the bottom of the page he folded it.

“Tomorrow I read the next one.”

“All right.”

“Make him eat,” said Mr. Kwok to Serafina, and left.

“Did you like the article?” she said, when the door had shut.

He thought about it. “Not particularly.”

“Neither did I.” And for the first time since he’d come home, the corner of his mouth moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four minutes to nine her phone rang upstairs. Aurelia.

“Is he there?”

“Downstairs. Why?”

“It’s the Group.” Her sister’s voice was controlled, the way it went when it was holding something up. “The towers across the bay. The bridge approach. The banks have started asking for meetings and nobody will tell me what the numbers are. Father won’t talk to me. If it goes the way I think it’s going, it doesn’t stop at the towers. The houses are pledged. The Peak.”

Serafina sat down on the bed. “The house?”

“Maybe. Not yet. I’m telling you because I want you to hear it from me first.” A pause. “And Sera. Don’t let Haozhen get involved.”

“Why would you say that?”

“Because I know the kind of man he is. He’ll see a problem and decide he can make it disappear.”

“He won’t.”

“I hope not.”

When she’d rung off, Serafina sat for a while with the phone in her lap. The house on the Peak. The staircase. The floor that creaked outside her old room. The room off the garage where her mother had put Nonna’s toolbox and photographs when the old woman died in Milan, and never once opened the door again. The house their father had said they would always be able to come back to, whatever happened.

She looked at the ring on her finger, and went downstairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in Nonna. She stood by the open door. “Aurelia rang. The company’s in trouble. The house might have to go.”

His face changed, slightly. “I’m sorry.” He looked at the dashboard. Then: “Do you want me to help?”

He wasn’t offering to take it over or promising to make it vanish. He was asking.

“Not yet.”

“All right.”

“You’re not going to ring someone? Or move money? Or look into the banks?”

“No.”

“Thank you.”

“You don’t have to thank me for listening.” She leaned on the door. “Hao. You’ve sat in this car for two days. You don’t sleep. You barely eat. You look at the door every time somebody comes in. I’m not asking you to tell me anything you can’t. But I’m frightened for you.”

He rubbed his thumb along the seam of the seat. He didn’t speak. She nodded and turned to go.

“Serafina.” He was still looking down. “Can you stay?”

She got in the driver’s side. He moved over a little, though there was plenty of room. The strip lights hummed. After a long time his hand came across the console and lay there, palm up, and she took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes past four on Tuesday morning, in the dark, he said, “The boy was called Tomás.”

She turned her head. He was looking through the windscreen. She didn’t interrupt.

“He had a yellow football shirt. I watched him for twenty-three days. He lived in a yellow house with his mother and father, and every morning he came out and did keepy-ups by the gate, and I counted them. At first he could do ten or eleven. Then twenty. The last day I saw him he got to thirty-one.” His voice was even. Far too even. “We were there to take his father, and four account books. We watched the house for three weeks. We knew when the family went out, when Gong went for bread, when the boy played. On Tuesdays his mother took him to the market early and he always came back at seven on his own, for the ball. I knew that. I told Tianyi they’d be gone till eight.”

“Did you take him?”

“Yes.” It broke slightly on the word. “In the lane behind the market. Tomás came round the corner and saw us. He kept shouting for his father. He threw his football at the car. It hit the window by my face. He was crying. He kept telling me to let him go.” His hand had started to shake in hers. “I put his father in the car, and he ran after us, and I watched him till the road turned.”

She waited.

“I’ve done it before. I’ve taken people from their families. I’ve put men in cars and handed them to people whose names I didn’t know, and told myself the job was finished when the transfer was. But I knew his son’s name. I knew what shirt he wore. I knew how many times he could kick a ball without dropping it. I knew he’d be waiting for his father to come home. And I let him see it. On purpose. To find out if I still could.”

The first tear came before he seemed to know it. He wiped it away at once. Another came. He turned his face to the window. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t.”

“I shouldn’t—”

“Hao. Look at me.” She didn’t let him go into the glass. He looked at her, and there was no control left anywhere in his face. No careful distance. No level voice. Just a man who had held something in for too long and had no idea where to put it.

“I don’t know what happened to him,” he whispered. “I don’t know where they took his father. I don’t know if he’ll ever come home. I don’t know anything.”

She put her arms round him. He stayed rigid. Then something in him gave way, and he bent into her and put his face against her shoulder and sobbed. Not quietly, not neatly. His whole body shook with it. She held him as hard as she could, one hand behind his head and the other spread on his back, and she didn’t tell him it was all right, because it wasn’t. She didn’t tell him he’d done the right thing, because she didn’t know that. She didn’t tell him the boy would be fine. She held on.

“I can’t do it again,” he said into her shirt. “I can’t take another father away from a child. I can’t sit outside another house counting some boy’s football and then—” He couldn’t finish.

“Then don’t.”

“I’ll have to tell them.”

“Then tell them.”

When he finally lifted his head his eyes were red and he looked ashamed of it. She touched his cheek. “Don’t look at me as if you’ve done something wrong by crying. You came home. That’s enough for this morning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when his breathing had come down, he said, “There was something in one of the books. One line, marked in pencil. Three initials. D.Q.Y. And the word Private.”

“Do you know them?”

“Yes. From another file, years ago. I can’t tell you the name yet. I lied to Tianyi when he asked.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to understand what I was looking at before anyone knew I’d seen it.”

“Is it to do with the Group?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t do anything with it until you do. And don’t try to fix my family on your own.”

“I’ll talk to you first.”

“Better.” He put his head back against the seat. “Are you frightened?” he said. “About the house?”

“Yes. My grandmother’s things are there. Her tools. Photographs. All the little things nobody remembers until they’re gone. And it’s the idea you can go back. That whatever else changes, that place is still there.”

“You’ll still have somewhere to go.” He took her hand. “And if you haven’t, you’ve got me.”

He didn’t say it like a solution. He didn’t offer money or a plan. He just meant it. She kissed his cheek.

“I’m tired,” he said. “Can I sleep? Here?”

“Where else?” She put the seat back and laid the blanket over him, and he turned his head towards her, and this time he slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six hours and four minutes. Mouse brought coffee and took the soup tub away without a word. Mr. Kwok came with the next newspaper, saw him asleep, and left it on the bench unread. Big Wu’s mother sent another pot. Nobody asked what had happened. They just made room.

At eleven minutes past eleven he stirred in the bright late-morning light and blinked, lost, and then found her beside him.

“Hi,” she said. “Welcome back.”

“How long?”

“Six hours and four minutes.”

“You counted.”

“Of course I counted.”

He took her hand and kissed her knuckles. His eyes stopped on the ruby. Then he leaned over and kissed her temple, once, and stayed there with his mouth against her skin, and she shut her eyes. When he drew back she turned her face to him. He looked at her mouth.

“You can,” she said.

He kissed her slowly, without any hurry at all, his hand along her jaw, as though he were learning how to be in a room again. “I’m sorry I was quiet.”

“You were allowed to be quiet.”

“I don’t want to shut you out.”

“Then don’t disappear behind it.”

“I’ll try.” He put his cheek against her shoulder. Outside a toolbox went over, and Mouse swore, and Mr. Kwok shouted about people who couldn’t put things back where they found them. The garage went on round them, and he listened to it. For the first time in twenty-three days he wasn’t watching a door.

“Sleep more if you need to,” she said.

“No. I want to sit with you.”

“Then sit.” On the bench beside his mug, the brass gauge lay where she’d put it down. Back where it belonged.

chapters.title: Her Family Opposes the Match
chapters.desc: Her mother writes for the first time in seven years: bring him. The house on the Peak has lot numbers on everything, and her mother asks him nine questions.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody keeps her, madam. I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for.”
chapters.content:
The envelope came with the post at half past ten on Wednesday the ninth of August: thick, cream, her name on the front in green ink in a hand she hadn’t seen on anything addressed to her for seven years. She knew it before she turned it over. On the flap, embossed: Vittoria Conti Song.

“Bad news?” said Mouse, halfway through a packet of biscuits.

“Possibly.”

“Bill?”

“Worse.”

“Tax?”

“My mother.”

Mouse put the biscuit down slowly. “Oh.”

There hadn’t been a birthday card. Not this year, six days ago, and not for the six before. Her mother hadn’t rung when Serafina left the house at nineteen, or when she started at Granny Shum’s, or when she drove her first race, or when she put Nonna into the barrier at the container yard and spent a night in a ward. She had come to the circuit in the north once, four years ago, with a policeman at her elbow, and hadn’t come down to the pit lane. Seven years of nothing. And now cream stationery.

Haozhen came in through the side door with two coffees, took one look at her, and put them down. “What’s happened?”

She held up the envelope. He read the name and looked back at her. “Do you want to open it?”

“No.” She turned it over. “Yes.” Inside was one sheet of heavy paper.

Serafina. I understand you are engaged. Bring him to the house on Saturday at four o’clock. We should meet. Vittoria.

“That’s it?” said Mouse. “Not even congratulations?”

“No.”

Haozhen read it once and laid it carefully beside her tools. “Do you want to go?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then we don’t have to.”

She laughed shortly. “She hasn’t spoken to me in seven years, Hao. If I don’t go she’ll send a second letter.”

“Would that be worse?”

“Depends on the stationery.” She looked at the sheet again. “It’s the house. She doesn’t invite people to the house. She summons them.”

“Then we’ll go.”

“You don’t have to. She’ll be unpleasant.”

“I’ve met unpleasant people.”

“My mother’s very good at it. Are you frightened?”

He considered. “Of your mother? No.”

“That’s because you haven’t met her.”

“Should I be?”

“Absolutely.”

He picked up his coffee. “Then I’ll prepare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday night she changed three times. The first was too formal. The second too casual. The third, she said, was an invitation for her mother to discuss her upbringing.

“Wear the first one,” he said from the edge of the bed.

“Why?”

“Because you liked it before you started thinking about what she’d say.” It was a plain dark green dress she’d bought for a dinner that never happened. She stopped with it in her hands.

“Do you notice everything?”

“More than I’d like.” He caught her hand as she passed and brought her to stand between his knees. “What do I tell her about my work?”

“The truth.”

“I’m a security guard.”

“That’s a very small part of the truth.”

“It’s the part I can say.” He looked up at her. “What’s she like?”

“Very polite when she wants to hurt someone. She’ll offer you tea. She’ll ask if you’re comfortable. Then she’ll ask you something that makes you wish she’d just slapped you.”

“Do you want me to answer, or keep quiet?”

“Answer. Truthfully. Especially truthfully.” She touched his face. “And if she says something about me—”

“I won’t let her speak to you like that.”

“Don’t start a fight with my mother.”

“I’m going to meet your family,” he said, and kissed the inside of her wrist, “not arrest them.”

“That’s less reassuring than you think.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eighteen minutes to four on Saturday he drove the grey estate up through the hairpins to the Peak and stopped at the gate. The gate had a camera. Under the camera was a small white sticker with a number on it in black. P-01.

“She’s labelled the gate,” said Serafina.

“Maintenance?”

She didn’t answer. The drive curved up between clipped hedges to the house, pale stone and dark glass above the harbour, beautiful and somehow impersonal, as though it were waiting to be photographed for someone else. As they walked up she saw the stickers everywhere. A white square on a stone planter. G-04. On the air-conditioning unit. M-12. By the garage door. P-03. She slowed down.

“Lot numbers,” she said.

He looked at her.

“I spend half my life at auctions. That’s how a valuer tags a house. The garden’s G. Plant’s M. P is the property itself.” She looked up at the windows. “Somebody’s already been round with a clipboard.”

At the door Pina, who had kept the house since Aurelia was fifteen and had sent Serafina birthday cards in secret for three of the seven years, put her hand on her arm for a second. “Miss Serafina.” She looked at Haozhen. “Mr. Qin.”

“Good afternoon.”

The drawing room was immaculate. Flowers arranged with mathematical exactness. No family photographs on the mantelpiece, only a porcelain figure and a silver clock, and under the clock, small and white, L-07. Serafina looked at it and then at him, and he said nothing, and she nearly smiled.

Her mother came in at four o’clock exactly. Ivory silk blouse. Tailored trousers. Hair pinned back, jewellery quiet and expensive. Still beautiful, and Serafina hated that she noticed.

“Serafina.”

“Mother.”

“Mr. Qin.”

He stood. “Mrs. Song.”

She offered her hand after a moment, and he took it. Nobody sat until she did. Pina brought tea. Vittoria waited until the cups were down.

“I understand you are engaged to my daughter. How long have you known each other?”

“Since October.”

“Less than a year. And you think that’s enough time to marry?”

“I think it’s enough to know I want to.”

Vittoria set her cup down. “I have nine questions.”

Serafina nearly choked. “Mother.”

“Mr. Qin, I’d appreciate direct answers. First. What do you do?”

“I’m a security guard.”

She waited. He didn’t add anything. “Private?”

“Some of the work is private.”

“Government?”

“Yes.”

Serafina looked at him. He was perfectly composed.

“Second. Who employs you?”

“A government security division. I can’t tell you its name.”

“Convenient.”

“It’s a condition of the work. Not a preference.”

“Third. Your income.”

He gave her a figure. It was the true one. Her eyebrows moved. “Not very high. Is it enough to keep a wife without my daughter’s money?”

“Yes.”

“Fourth. Do you own property?”

“No.”

“Savings?”

“Yes.” He told her that too. Her expression changed again.

“From a salary like that?”

“Ten years of not spending it.” He paused. “Rather less of it since the spring. I put some into a racing team.”

Serafina made a noise into her tea. Vittoria’s eyes went to her daughter and back. “Fifth. Have you ever been arrested?”

“No.”

“Investigated?”

“Yes.”

“For what?”

“Incidents at work.”

“Cleared?”

“Some were closed. Some are restricted.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one I can give you.”

Her mouth tightened. “Sixth. Have you been married before?”

“No.”

“Seventh. Debts? Obligations to anyone who might come looking for you?”

He paused. “I have obligations at work. I don’t have private debts.”

“Eighth. You’ll go on working after you marry her? Even if it puts you in danger?”

“Yes.”

Serafina’s fingers tightened on her cup. Vittoria saw it. “Then you mean to expose her to that danger.”

“I mean to be honest with her about what I can tell her and what I can’t.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

“I know. My work can be dangerous. I won’t pretend it isn’t, and I won’t promise you nothing will happen to me. I can promise I won’t make decisions about her life without her.”

“Ninth.” Vittoria let it sit. “If my daughter becomes a burden to you, what will you do?”

“Mother, that’s enough.”

He didn’t answer at once. “You think I want to keep her,” he said. “You’re looking at a man with no house and no name you can find, who’ll probably still be standing at a door at sixty waiting for somebody important to come out of it. You’re right. I’m not important. I don’t own anything.” He glanced at Serafina, once, and back. “But I’m not asking you to let me keep her. Nobody keeps her, madam. I’ve watched her for ten months. Nobody is ever going to keep her.”

“Then what are you asking for?”

“I’d like to be wherever she is. That’s all I’m asking for.” A beat. “And I’m not really asking you.”

The room went completely quiet. The clock under its sticker ticked once.

“You answer very carefully,” said Vittoria at last.

“I try to answer truthfully.”

“Are you always this controlled?”

“No.”

Serafina looked at him. That answer, at least, was new.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Your father is upstairs,” said Vittoria, at twenty-one minutes to five. “He knows you’re here. He prefers not to be involved in this conversation.”

“Of course he does.”

“I have had someone watching you.”

Serafina went still. Beside her, Haozhen’s eyes moved to her mother and stayed there.

“For how long?”

“Seven years. Since you left. A friend in the traffic police. I knew where you lived. I knew where you worked. I knew when you began racing on the roads, and when you put that car into a barrier.”

“You knew when I was in hospital?”

“I was informed.”

“And Baizhang?”

Vittoria’s eyes went to the window. “I watched the hill climb.”

Something cold went through Serafina. “You watched. And you didn’t ring. Not once.”

“Watching you was not the same thing as approving of you.”

“You watched me race. Watched me build cars. Watched me leave this house and make a life and get engaged, and you never said one word.”

“You were very determined to prove you didn’t need this family.”

“I didn’t need someone following me.”

“Don’t be childish.”

“Don’t call me childish.”

“You have always mistaken independence for maturity.” Vittoria’s voice didn’t rise at all. “You have made a series of poor decisions. I have watched you throw away every chance this family gave you. You ran away. You embarrassed us. And now you bring a man I’ve never met into this house and expect me to accept that you intend to marry him.”

“You don’t have to accept anything. You’ve had your questions.”

“Then I’ll ask you one.” She seemed to consider it. Then she said, in exactly the same tone, as though it were something entirely ordinary, “You were a mistake I made in August.”

The clock ticked.

“You were impulsive before you were born,” said Vittoria. “I should have known what kind of child you would be.”

Serafina didn’t move. Beside her the stillness in Haozhen turned into something else.

“That’s enough,” he said.

“I beg your pardon?”

“You’ve made yourself clear.”

“This is a family matter.”

“She’s your daughter. She should be spoken to with respect.”

Vittoria stood. “I don’t need a security guard to tell me how to speak to my own child.”

He stood too, and stepped forward, and put himself between them. He didn’t touch her. He didn’t raise his voice. He stood where she would have to look at him before she could say anything else.

“Then speak to her as her mother,” he said.

“Move.”

He didn’t. Behind him Serafina’s eyes had filled. She put her hand on his arm. “Hao. Let’s go.” He nodded, and stepped aside for her, and they walked out together.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got as far as the first bend in the drive before she stopped with her back to him and pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes.

“Serafina.”

“Don’t.” She breathed. “I knew she’d be unpleasant. I knew she’d ask about money and your job and whether you were good enough. I didn’t think she’d say that.” Her voice shook. “Seven years of knowing exactly where I was. Watching me. And she never once rang. She watched me win at Baizhang. I was looking into that camera thinking about you, in Lisbon, bringing my gauge home. And she was watching too.”

“You wanted her there,” he said.

It wasn’t a judgement. She lowered her head. “Yes.”

Behind them a door banged. “Serafina!”

Song Weiren was coming down the drive faster than a man of sixty-two who disliked being seen in a hurry should. His shirt had come untucked on one side. He looked older than she remembered. “Wait. You can’t leave like that.”

“Why not?”

“I wanted to speak to you.”

“You had seven years.”

He flinched. “I know.”

“Did you know she was having me watched?”

“Yes. I didn’t agree with it. But I knew.”

She laughed once, a small hurt sound. “Wonderful.”

“Did you watch Baizhang?” she said.

“Yes. The whole thing. Practice too. I wanted to see you drive.” He swallowed. “I didn’t understand half the commentary. I understood the last run. The car was magnificent.”

Her face crumpled for a second before she got hold of it. “Even the bit where I nearly spun?”

“I was frightened,” he said, and looked embarrassed by it. “I didn’t know whether I was allowed to be.”

“You could have come. You could have rung. You could have said you were proud of me.”

“I was.”

It came too late. She turned her face away.

“I don’t know how to fix this,” he said.

“Neither do I.”

He looked at Haozhen. “Mr. Qin. Thank you for bringing her.”

“She brought herself.”

Weiren’s eyes went back to his daughter, and something in his face gave. “Will you come again? Without your mother. To talk.”

“Not today.”

“Not today.” He stepped back. Then, as if he couldn’t help it: “The car was magnificent.”

She gave the smallest nod. “Thank you.” It wasn’t forgiveness. But it was something.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the foot of the drive, by the estate, she was trying hard not to cry again. He lifted his hand and brushed the wet from under her eyes with his thumb.

“Look at me.”

She did. He kissed one cheek, then the other, without any hurry. His thumb stayed along her jaw, and he bent and kissed the corner of her eye where another tear had come.

“You don’t have to be strong right now,” he said.

“I hate that she can still do this to me. I hate that I wanted her to be proud of me.”

“There’s nothing wrong with wanting that.” He kissed her forehead, and then her mouth, slowly, with his hand along the side of her face, and she held his jacket lightly between her fingers. It wasn’t an answer to anything her mother had said. It couldn’t undo seven years or make the house a home again. But he had stood beside her in that room, and walked out with her without asking her to explain.

“Thank you,” she said. “Nine questions.”

“Nine.”

“What would you have said if she’d asked whether you were frightened of me?”

He considered. “The truth. Sometimes.”

“Hao!”

“Especially when you drive.”

She gave a wet laugh and hit his chest, and he caught her hand and kissed her again.

✦ ✦ ✦

She drove. On the way down the hill her phone lit up on the console: a number she didn’t know.

It’s your father. I know you may not want to talk to me. I watched the race from the start. You were very good. I’m sorry I wasn’t there.

She read it twice. She didn’t answer. She didn’t delete it either.

“Your father?”

“Not yet,” she said, and put the phone face down. “Do you think he means it?”

“I think he watched your race.” He rubbed his thumb over her fingers. “That’s something he chose to do.”

“That’s a very careful answer.”

“I’m trying to be truthful.”

“You did very well today. Nine questions. Not one lie.”

“Not one.”

“I’m glad you came.”

“There’s nowhere else I’d rather have been,” he said, and she drove them down towards the harbour and left the house on the Peak behind, with its numbers on everything.

chapters.title: A Getaway Car Nobody Knows
chapters.desc: Rule four, at the kettle: he wants out. That means a car nobody knows, so they go to Jinx.
chapters.epigraph: “One order. No questions. And you never bring it back here with a hole in it.”
chapters.content:
The kettle was boiling. It was eighteen minutes to eight on Tuesday the fifth of September, and Serafina was at the bench trying to work out how Mouse had returned her socket set with three pieces missing and one that definitely wasn’t hers.

He was by the kettle, and he had been quiet all evening. Not the empty quiet from July, and not the far-off silence after it. This was different. On the bench beside him lay Saturday’s paper, folded to a photograph he had looked at when Mr. Kwok brought it in: a vice-minister at six in the morning, walking down his own front steps with a man at each elbow. Not ours, he’d said, and nothing else. For the past twenty minutes he’d been watching her, and now and then the door, as though he were waiting for somebody to come through it.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been looking at me.”

“I know.”

The kettle clicked off. He didn’t move. Then he said, “Sera.”

“Hmm?”

“I want out.”

The socket slipped out of her fingers and rang on the steel.

He hadn’t raised his voice. He’d said it the way he told her the road was wet. But the words filled the whole garage. She crossed it.

“Say that again.”

“I want out.”

“Of the Bureau?”

“Yes.”

She took his face in both hands and kissed him, hard enough to knock his head back against the cupboard. He caught her round the waist, and she pulled him closer and kissed him with all the months of wondering whether he’d ever choose to leave, and her elbow caught the kettle, and it went over, and hot water ran across the counter, and neither of them noticed until the steam reached them.

“Serafina. The kettle.”

“Oh.” She grabbed a tea towel. He turned the switch off. For a few seconds they mopped in silence, and then she looked up. “Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Not because of Lisbon?”

“Not only.”

“Not because of my mother?”

His mouth moved. “No.”

“Then why now?”

“Because I don’t want to live as if the next call matters more than everything else. I don’t want to be available every hour of every day. I don’t want to keep leaving without knowing when I’ll be back, being useful to people who only remember my name when they need something done.” He held her eyes. “And I don’t want you to keep wondering whether I’m coming home.”

“You know it won’t be simple. They won’t necessarily let you go quietly. You might lose your pension. You might have to explain things.”

“I know.”

“And you’re still sure?”

“Yes.”

“Then we’ll work it out.” She took his hand.

“You don’t have to solve it for me.”

“I’m not solving it for you. I’m standing next to you while you do it.” He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Now,” she said. “Do you want to leave the country?”

“No.”

“Change your name?”

“No.”

“Burn your whole wardrobe?”

He thought about it. “Possibly.”

“Good. Because rule four says I have the car outside. And I don’t have one that nobody knows. But I know somebody who can make one.”

“Who?”

“Jinx.”

He was quiet. “That sounds worrying.”

“It is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Jia Cao, who had been Jia Lin since Friday and hadn’t told anybody, and whom nobody but her husband had called anything but Jinx since she was nine, arrived at eighteen minutes past eleven on Wednesday with a packet of crisps, a toolbox, and no interest in being there at all.

“I’m not building a getaway car.”

“You haven’t heard what it is,” said Serafina.

“I heard getaway on the phone. That’s plenty.” She was small and sharp, in an oil-black vest with her hair scraped back, and she had grown up in her father’s chop shop under the flyover taking apart things the Syndicate had brought in at night. She looked at Haozhen. Then at Serafina. Then at him again. “Oh. It’s him. The quiet one. The one who looks like he knows where the bodies are.”

“Good morning,” said Haozhen.

“That’s worse.” She threw the crisps on the bench and sat. “Four minutes.”

Serafina told her. Something ordinary. Something nobody would look at twice. Reliable, comfortable, able to carry the two of them away from something without turning into a spectacle. No flash bodywork. No odd exhaust note. Nothing that tied it to either of them.

“Are you robbing a bank?” said Jinx to Haozhen.

“No.”

“Kidnapping someone?”

“No.”

“Disappointing. I had a speech.”

“It’s for leaving,” he said.

Her face changed. “Leaving what?”

“My work.”

She looked at Serafina. “Does he mean it?”

“Yes.”

“Does he know people who do his kind of work don’t always get to walk off because they feel like it?”

“Yes,” said Haozhen.

Her eyes went to Serafina’s hand. The ruby. “That’s new.”

“Engaged.”

“To him?”

“To him.”

Jinx got up and walked to the back wall, where she’d pinned one of her own drawings when she’d last borrowed Serafina’s bench: a motorbike in pencil, every bolt and spoke, and underneath in neat architect’s capitals, J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021. She stood in front of it with her arms folded.

“One order. No questions.” She didn’t turn round. “I don’t want to know where. Or who’s chasing. Or your name. And you never bring it back here with a hole in it.”

“Agreed.”

“And you.” A black-nailed finger at Serafina. “Wash my floor. Every night. Good soap.”

“What do we call it?” said Serafina.

“I’m not responsible for whatever stupid name you give it.”

“Nobody,” said Haozhen.

Jinx stopped. “What?”

“The car. Nobody.”

Serafina smiled. Jinx rubbed her face with both hands. “I’ve made a terrible mistake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They found it on the third Saturday in September, behind a fleet yard on the docks road. A silver-grey 2006 saloon that had been a taxi for eleven years. Faded paint, a dent over the rear wheel arch, a driver’s seat that had seen better decades, a crack in the dash by the glovebox, and a back seat that smelled of cigarettes and lemon cleaner. Serafina thought it was perfect.

“It’s ugly,” said Jinx.

“That’s the point.”

“It’s old.”

“Also the point.”

“It’s a taxi.”

“Exactly.”

“Your fiancée has terrible taste,” Jinx told Haozhen.

“She likes it.”

“That’s what frightens me.” Serafina opened the driver’s door. The old meter was still bolted under the dash. She switched it on and the little screen flickered and showed a fare. “Don’t,” said Jinx. “I’m taking that out before she gets attached.”

“Too late.”

They worked on it for six weeks in Jinx’s place by the docks, a garage under a flat with a roll-up door and a floor Serafina washed every night with good soap. Jinx stripped it to the shell and found the engine healthy and the gearbox tired and the suspension shot. Out came the old interior in pieces. In went the drivetrain from a big saloon of the same family that somebody had written off against a lamp post, and brakes off something much faster, and a cooling pack, and a set of dampers Serafina chose and Jinx argued with, and all of it went in so quietly that from the outside the car still looked like what it was: tired, silver, a taxi nobody would hail twice. Jinx did the body and the paint, and the things she said weren’t optional if you wanted a car to survive being driven by a Song. Serafina did the mechanical work. Haozhen helped where he could, and was careful, every day, not to make it into something it wasn’t. Nobody would race it and nobody would fear it. It was a car that would start on a cold morning and carry them away if they had to go. A car that belonged to nobody. That was the whole point.

Under the passenger seat Jinx found the old registration papers in a plastic sleeve. “It’s got a history.”

“Every car’s got a history.”

“This one’s is very boring.”

“That’s good,” said Haozhen.

Jinx looked at him. “Have you thought about being a comedian?”

“No.”

“Keep it that way.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth Saturday in September, at twenty-six minutes to three, a tall untidy man in a paint-spattered jumper came in with a drawing tube under his arm and stopped dead at the sight of the taxi.

“That’s the car?”

“Don’t laugh,” said Jinx.

“I wasn’t going to.” Raiden Lin looked at the dent over the wheel arch. “I was thinking about how much work you’ve given me.” He put a hand on the back of Jinx’s neck as he passed her, lightly, the way you’d touch something that was yours, and she let him, and Serafina saw it and filed it away.

He spread the sheet across the bench. A cutaway of the whole car in pencil and ink: the structure, the cabin, the drivetrain, every part they’d renewed, in clear small annotations. Serafina leaned over it. “This is beautiful.”

Raiden looked pleased. Haozhen found the passenger seat on the drawing, and then the driver’s seat, and looked for a while at the space between them.

“Something wrong?” said Raiden.

“I’m imagining her driving.”

“That’s a terrifying image,” said Jinx, and Serafina elbowed her.

“What are you calling it?” said Raiden.

“Nobody,” said Haozhen.

“That’s a strange name.”

“It’s the right one.”

Raiden wrote it in the corner of the drawing in his neat capitals. NOBODY. “I want it recorded that I objected,” said Jinx.

The first drive, a week later round the industrial estate, was uneventful, which was exactly what Serafina wanted. It started without complaint. The steering was honest. The brakes were predictable.

“It’s pulling left,” said Jinx from the passenger seat.

“I know. I’m seeing if it changes under braking.”

“Can you do that without sounding like you’re interrogating the car?”

“No.”

Back at the roll-up door Haozhen walked round it once, and opened the passenger door, and sat down. The seat was clean and new enough to be comfortable without looking new, and the old taxi smell had gone.

“Comfortable?” said Serafina, leaning on the roof.

“Yes.”

“You haven’t even driven it.”

“I don’t need to.”

“Please don’t make it sentimental,” said Jinx. “I’ve spent three weeks on a taxi.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody was finished on the last Saturday in October. Not perfect, not new. Finished enough. At twenty-one minutes past five it stood on the docks road with the low orange sun on its paint, looking like a hundred other cars that had been through the docks that day.

“Everyone ready?” said Serafina, behind the wheel.

“No,” said Jinx, outside.

“Yes,” said Raiden.

“Whenever you are,” said Haozhen, beside her.

She drove out past the warehouses, and along the coast, and up onto the approach road to the new bridge across the bay. It had been finished in the spring, three lanes each way and lit all night, and closed ever since; the work had stopped in the summer when the money stopped, and the towers at the far end stood half-glazed against the sky, and nobody had driven it in months but security patrols and the odd lost lorry. Jinx and Raiden followed in Jinx’s van. At the barrier at the bottom, which Jinx had taken a good look at in the week, nobody was standing.

At first Serafina drove normally. She felt the steering, listened to the engine, let the tyres come in. He knew the look on her face. It was the one she wore when she was no longer driving. She was measuring.

“Serafina.”

“Hmm?”

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Whatever you’re considering.”

“I’m not considering anything.” She glanced at the speedometer. “It’s a good car.”

“Yes.”

“Very stable.”

“Yes.”

“Would you say it was capable?”

“Sera.”

She grinned. The approach opened out ahead of them, straight and lit and empty for four kilometres. The engine note rose. The old taxi gathered itself with a composure that had no business being in it, and the steering stayed steady and the suspension held its line, and it didn’t feel like a machine trying to prove anything. It went. Two hundred. Two hundred and twenty. Two hundred and forty. Then, with the far end of the bridge coming up fast in the windscreen, two hundred and sixty-four.

She lifted. The speed came down. The engine settled.

“Did you see that?”

“I was in the car.”

“Two hundred and sixty-four! That’s a hundred and sixty-four miles an hour. In a taxi!” She pulled into the empty toll plaza at the far end and stopped, laughing. “An old taxi!”

“I noticed.”

“Are you going to tell me off?”

“I’ve got several things I’d like to say.” He looked at her. Then he smiled. “I’m glad you’re happy.”

Her face softened. She leaned across the console, and the gearstick was in the way, and it was awkward, and she didn’t care. She took the front of his jacket and hauled him over to her.

“Serafina—”

She kissed him. He turned as far as the seatbelt would let him and caught her round the waist, and she kissed him harder and laughed into his mouth when the gearstick dug into her hip.

“You’ll hurt yourself.”

“Then move.”

“I can’t.”

“Try.”

Three hard bangs on the roof. They broke apart. Jinx was standing outside, one hand flat on the car, with a face like murder.

“ARE YOU TWO FINISHED?”

Serafina wound the window down.

“THAT IS NOT A BEDROOM. I BUILT A CAR. NOT A PRIVATE SUITE.”

“It’s a very comfortable car!”

“I’M SELLING IT!”

“You can’t. It’s ours.”

“I’LL SELL MY HALF!”

“You don’t own half!”

Jinx pointed at Haozhen. “YOU. CONTROL HER.”

He looked at Serafina, and back. “No.”

Serafina put her forehead on the steering wheel and laughed so hard she couldn’t breathe. He reached over and lifted her head off it, gently. “Careful.” Behind Jinx, Raiden had his hand over his mouth.

“Leave them alone,” he said, and took his wife by the shoulder.

“They’re abusing my craftsmanship.”

“They’re testing the upholstery.”

“THAT’S NOT WHAT THE UPHOLSTERY IS FOR!”

Serafina wound the window up, and the two of them went out of sight round the van. She was still smiling. “What?”

“Nothing.” He looked round the cabin. The plain dash. The ordinary seats. The silver bonnet in the last of the light. A car that had nothing to do with his old life, that carried none of the Bureau’s weight and none of the people who knew where to find him. “Yes,” he said, before she’d asked.

“Good. Because we’re keeping it.” She took his hand. “Home?”

And for once there was nowhere else he needed to go.

chapters.title: The Mission He Didn’t Take
chapters.desc: A grey building in the capital that isn’t on any map. A seventh-floor office with a radiator that knocks. A thin folder about a journalist in Singapore. For the first time in eleven years, he says one word to the state.
chapters.epigraph: “Do you know what happens to people who say no, Haozhen?” “Yes, Director. I’ve driven them.”
chapters.content:
“Your hair’s getting ridiculous.”

He looked up from the papers. She was standing behind him at fourteen minutes past eight on Monday the sixth of November with a pair of scissors in her hand.

“Is that a threat?”

“It’s an observation. You look like you’ve been sleeping in airports.”

“I have been sleeping in airports.”

“Exactly. It’s affecting your appearance.”

He looked at her a moment longer, and then leaned back in the chair. “Go on.”

She fetched the little barber’s cape she’d bought when she worked out that cutting his hair was easier than getting it off his collars, and fastened it at the back of his neck, and combed his hair off his forehead. “Head down. More. Good.” The garage was quiet except for the scissors. Nobody sat under the lights across the floor, silver and unremarkable, still smelling of new upholstery. He watched her in the black glass of the window: her lower lip caught in her teeth, a loose strand pushed off his forehead now and then with the back of her fingers.

“Stop moving.”

“I’m not.”

“Your eyes are.”

“I’m allowed to look.”

“Not at me. I’m working.” She did round his ears. “You’re going tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“To the capital. Do you know what they want?”

“I have an idea. I think they’ll offer me something.”

“And if they do?”

“I’ll say no.”

She put the scissors down on the bench and came round in front of him and took his face in both hands and kissed him, once, fast and hard. He barely had time to answer before she did it again, just as fiercely. His hand came up to her waist. When she pulled away, his eyes stayed shut for a second.

“That’s twice,” he said.

“I’m aware.”

“Is there a third?”

“Depends whether you behave.” She brushed a bit of hair off his cheek. “Come back to me.”

“I’ll do everything I can.”

“Good. Now sit still. I’m not sending you into a government building with one side shorter than the other.”

“Would that be embarrassing?”

“For you? No. For me? Catastrophic.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The building in the capital wasn’t on any map. It sat back from a broad grey road between two bigger ministries, behind a plain wall with no sign and no flag and no name by the door. At six minutes past nine on Tuesday the clerk checked his card and gave him a visitor’s pass, and the lift took him to the seventh floor, along a corridor that smelled of old carpet and radiator dust, to a grey door at the end.

Duan Qiuyan was knitting by the window. The long red scarf had grown since May. On the desk lay a thin folder, a glass of water, and a slim silver pen exactly like the one in Serafina’s jacket pocket, except that the number engraved by the clip was 11.

She saw him look at it. “I had two made. Sit.”

He sat. The radiator behind her knocked twice. Then again.

“Singapore,” she said, and slid the folder over without stopping the needles. A man in his late thirties in glasses, tired, photographed outside an office. “Xu Zhenyu. A journalist. Ours, by passport. Living there two years. We’d like him home.”

“Voluntarily?”

“He has information we require.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“He’s refused contact.”

“Then he doesn’t want to come.”

“People change their minds.” Click. “He’s been publishing things that make difficulties for several people. He has documents and sources and financial records that oughtn’t to be loose.”

“Is he a threat?”

“He’s a journalist.”

“That isn’t what I asked either.”

She looked at him over her glasses. He read it. Background, a list of his articles, photographs, contacts. Sensitive individual. Potential source of instability. Recovery preferred. No crime. No sign he’d hurt anyone or threatened anyone. Only a list of people who didn’t like what he’d written. He closed it.

“No.”

It came out. It was still the wrong word, in that room. Not because it was untrue, but because in eleven years he had never once said it to the state.

The needles stopped. Duan laid the knitting on the desk, the long red ribbed scarf with her needles across it, and folded her hands on top. She took her glasses off. Without them her eyes were smaller, and tired, and older than he’d let himself see.

“Do you know what happens to people who say no, Haozhen?”

“Yes, Director. I’ve driven them.”

The radiator knocked three times, like somebody wanting in. She put her glasses back on and picked up the needles and found her place. “You haven’t heard the offer.”

“I don’t want anything.”

“Your release?” He didn’t move. “You’ve been thinking of leaving. And you imagine refusing this makes it easier?”

“No. I’m not bringing a man home because somebody dislikes what he writes.”

“You’re judging a situation you don’t fully understand.”

“Possibly.”

From a drawer she took a second file. “Gong Ruiming. The transfer was completed. His cooperation was not. Nothing about the ledgers, the accounts, or the people who helped him. Not a word since he arrived.” Click. “His son has written to our embassy in Lisbon. That his father was taken in a lane. That he wants to know where he is.”

“How old?” said Haozhen, though he knew.

“Seven.” She watched his jaw. “Does that mean something to you?”

“No.”

“You’ve been difficult since Lisbon. Gong’s son isn’t your responsibility. Neither is the journalist.” Click. “Your fiancée is. Serafina Song. The woman who beat Lau Kam-wing up a mountain. Who has turned one of my best into a man who spends his evenings rebuilding taxis.”

His face went blank. “Leave her out of this.”

“I’m not threatening her. I’m reminding you that you have a life. A future. Things worth protecting. And your mother.”

“My mother sews curtains in a town that isn’t on your maps.”

“It’s on mine, Qin.” She didn’t look up. “Think about her. Think about Serafina. A man in your position understands that his decisions don’t stop at himself. You have until the New Year.”

“I won’t change my mind.”

“You have until the New Year,” she said again, and the needles went on. “Don’t mistake my patience for permission.”

He put the visitor’s pass on her desk, and walked out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tianyi was by the lift with a paper cup of coffee, looking at his phone, and put it away when he saw him. “Well?”

“No.”

“What?”

“I said no.”

Tianyi’s face changed. He looked down the corridor towards the grey door. “Not here.” He walked them into the stairwell and let the door close and leaned on the wall. “You refused. To her face. One word.”

“Yes.”

“That’s brave.”

“It’s a refusal.”

“In this building they’re not always different.” He turned the cup in his hands. “She’s already talked to the section.”

“About what?”

“About your leaving. They’ll send someone.” He looked at Haozhen. “That’s how it’s done. If the man they want won’t take a job, they send somebody he trusts. Somebody who can get close.”

“Who?”

Tianyi didn’t answer. He didn’t need to. They had been sixteen together under a roof that leaked onto bed eleven, and Haozhen had given him the dry bed and taken the wet one, and Tianyi had never forgotten it.

“You,” said Haozhen.

“Me.”

“Don’t accept it.”

“You think I can refuse?”

“Yes.”

Tianyi smiled, small and tired. “You’ve just found out how that works.”

“It’s a journalist. There’s nothing against him.”

“I read the file.”

“Then don’t.”

“I’m not saying I’ll take it. I’m saying they’ll ask. And I haven’t decided.” His face softened. “Go home, Qin.”

“I’m sorry. For leaving you with this.”

“Don’t make your decision into an apology for me.” Somewhere outside the lift chimed. “Go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-four minutes to eight that evening Serafina was on the floor beside Nobody looking for a washer, Jinx was on the phone by the door, and Raiden was on the sofa with his tablet. Haozhen came in through the side door and stopped.

“Hi.”

“Hi.” She got up and looked at his face. “How was it?”

“Fine.”

“That’s a terrible answer.”

He took his jacket off. “I said no.”

She came to him. “And?”

“They’ve given me until the New Year to think again.”

“Can they stop you leaving?”

“I don’t know.”

“What did they want?”

“A journalist. In Singapore. Brought home.”

“Does he want to come?”

“No.”

“Then why ask you?”

“Because I used to be good at getting people to go where they didn’t want to.”

Her hand closed on his arm. “Used to be.”

“I don’t want to do it any more.”

“Then you won’t. You said no. That’s where it starts.” He breathed out slowly and bent and kissed her forehead, and by the door Jinx lowered her phone.

“Are you two going to do that every time he comes in?”

“Yes,” said Serafina, without turning round.

“Then I’m charging rent.”

“You don’t own the building,” said Raiden.

“I own the emotional atmosphere.”

“Congratulations,” said Haozhen to her.

Jinx blinked. “For what?”

He took his phone out and showed Serafina the screen. A marriage registration record. Lin Raiden. Cao Jia. Dated the first of September.

Serafina stared at it and then at the two of them. “You got married?”

“Apparently,” said Jinx.

“And you didn’t tell us?”

“We were going to.”

“When? It’s been two months!”

“Time’s a social construct.”

“We registered in September,” said Raiden, putting the tablet down. “It wasn’t a secret. We just didn’t announce it.”

“I checked the registry,” said Haozhen.

Jinx turned on him. “You what?”

“To confirm.”

“Confirm what?”

“That you were married.” He looked at her with complete seriousness. “Congratulations.”

“Your fiancé is terrifying,” said Jinx.

“He’s thorough,” said Serafina, and hugged Raiden, and then Jinx, who stood it for about three seconds before patting her shoulder and saying, “All right. Enough.” Haozhen watched them. A married couple pretending not to be pleased with themselves. A friend making too much noise. A woman who’d cut his hair and was now smiling at him as if the day hadn’t been hard. He wanted to stay inside it. He knew it wouldn’t last.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve minutes to midnight, in the office, his phone lit.

Tianyi: They’re moving fast.

Tianyi: I haven’t accepted anything.

Hao: Don’t.

Tianyi: I know.

He rang. Tianyi answered on the second ring. “Where are you?” said Haozhen.

“Home.”

“Have you talked to her?”

“Not since this morning.”

“Don’t go in there alone.”

A pause. “You sound like you. You used to say that to me.” Tianyi breathed out. “Go home to Serafina.”

“I am home.”

“Then go upstairs.”

She was asleep when he went up, her hair over the pillow and one hand outside the blanket with the ruby catching a line of streetlight. He got in carefully. She moved towards him without opening her eyes.

“Hao? Did you say no?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and was asleep again. He stayed awake.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday at two minutes past eight, an unknown number. He answered.

“Have you reconsidered?”

“No.”

“You’ve had four days.”

“I don’t need more.”

“Then think carefully about what comes next. Your mother would want you to be sensible.”

His face didn’t change. “My mother isn’t part of this.”

“Everyone is part of something, Qin.”

“Not everyone gets to choose what.”

A silence. “New Year,” said Duan Qiuyan, and the line went dead.

He put the phone down and went to the bench and picked up the silver pen with the seven on it, and turned it in his fingers, and put it down again. He had spent eleven years being available. Now he was trying to become a man who could say no and mean it. He knew the state wouldn’t take the word. He also knew he’d already said it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday night he flew back up to see Tianyi in person, because some things couldn’t be said on a phone the section listened to, and at nineteen minutes to seven on Monday morning, in the rain, he stood in a telephone box three streets from the grey building because he didn’t want the call tied to his number. He’d already said everything he could say to Tianyi, in a noodle shop at midnight, and it hadn’t been enough. Now he needed to hear her.

She answered on the fourth ring. “Hello?”

“It’s me.”

“Hao? Where are you? Are you all right?”

He looked through the glass at the empty street. “No.”

She went quiet. He heard a cupboard open on her end. “What’s happened?”

“Nothing I can explain properly on the phone.”

“Are you coming home?”

“Yes. On the train. It gets in at four.”

“Then I’ll be at the station.”

“Even if it’s late?”

“Especially if it’s late.” A pause. “Hao.”

“Sera.”

“I’m here.”

“I love you.”

There was a silence. Not surprise. She’d understood he was saying it for a reason. “I love you too.”

“I don’t know what they’ll do.”

“Neither do I.”

“I don’t want you to be frightened.”

“Then come home and let me be frightened next to you. You don’t have to manage my feelings from another city.”

He held the receiver closer. He wanted to tell her about the radiator and the red scarf, and the pen with eleven on it, and his mother on someone else’s map, and Tianyi in a noodle shop looking at his hands, and a journalist in Singapore who had a name and a face and maybe a family. He wanted to tell her he was afraid. Instead he said, “I love you,” again, and she said at once, “I know. I love you too. Come back,” and he put the receiver down, and stood there a moment with his hand on the cold metal, and went out into the rain.

At two minutes past seven he bought a ticket south and took a seat by the window. When the train began to move he looked at her last message, I’ll be at the station, and put the phone away. The radiator in the grey office had knocked all through the morning. The train made a different sound: a steady rhythm under the floor, something heavy going along a track, something that knew where it was going. He rested his head against the window, and listened.

chapters.title: A File on the Workbench
chapters.desc: A Saturday afternoon. He’s in the north for his mother’s birthday. A woman of fifty-five in a grey coat ducks under the shutter with a shopping bag and her knitting, asks very politely for hot water, and sits on his stool. When she leaves, there’s a file on the bench. Forty photographs. One of them was taken that morning.
chapters.epigraph: “I thought I was watching out for her.”
chapters.content:
On Thursday the seventh of December, at twenty to six, the station car park was busy with people going home for the weekend, and the light was already thinning into winter grey. Serafina had driven him there in Nobody, and there was a bunch of yellow chrysanthemums on the passenger seat that she’d bought on the way because she refused to let him turn up at his mother’s door for her birthday with nothing but a paper cup of coffee in his stomach.

“You could come,” he’d said, on the bridge.

“Next time. When she knows who I am.”

“She knows who you are. I told her in March.”

“She knows I exist. That’s different.” She’d looked at him sideways. “Go on your own this once. Tell her I’m nice.”

Now he stood by the driver’s door with his overnight bag, and she reached up and straightened his collar, and he caught her hand before she could take it back and kissed her. Slowly. Not the quick kind they swapped when one of them was late, or the hungry kind that sometimes happened at the bench when they forgot what they’d been doing. Quiet. His hand along her cheek, his thumb moving once along her jaw. She leaned into it and kept her eyes shut after he’d lifted his head.

“Go,” she whispered.

“Drive carefully.”

“I’m an excellent driver.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“I’ll drive carefully.”

“And eat. And don’t stay in the garage too late.”

“Now you’re being unreasonable.” She kissed him once more. “Go and see your mother, Hao.”

At the station entrance he turned. She was still by the car with one hand on the roof, and she lifted her fingers, and he lifted his, and went in. He didn’t see the woman in the grey coat by the ticket machines, with a shopping bag over one arm. He didn’t see her watch him all the way to the platform.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning, in a mining town in the north that the maps had more or less stopped bothering with, he spent forty minutes in a narrow shop between a chemist and a tailor’s on the main street, choosing thread. The air outside smelled of coal smoke and damp stone.
