The woman behind the counter assumed at first he was buying for somebody who embroidered, and when he said his mother had an old Japanese sewing machine and made curtains and quilts for half the street, she brought out a long wooden drawer of silk thread in every colour.

“Does she like bright colours?”

“She likes blue.”

Three blues went on the counter. “What else?”

He thought about it. “Grey. Cream. Green. Red. She makes things for other people.”

“Then she must be generous.”

“Yes,” he said. “She is.” He bought thirty spools, wrapped in tissue in a paper bag, and knew exactly what she’d say: that he’d spent too much, that she didn’t need so many, that thirty was ridiculous. Then she’d put them away in the drawer under the machine in colour order and use them one at a time for the next five years on other people’s children’s coats.

At nine forty-one he was in the market behind the square, carrying her bags. Liang Shufen was sixty-three, small and square, in a dark blue coat, and she had stopped at the vegetable stall to ask whether the spring onions were really from that morning, and to pick them up one by one and feel them before she chose, while he stood two steps behind her and watched the road. She had already told him he walked too fast. He had slowed down.

“Is she nice?” she said, to the spring onions. “The one who sent the flowers.”

“Yes.”

“Is she patient?”

“No.”

His mother laughed, and paid for the onions, and handed him the bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past three that afternoon, the garage under the railway bridge was empty, its shutter half up the way Serafina always left it when she went out for an hour, however many times she’d been told not to. A woman in a grey coat came along the alley with a shopping bag and a knitting bag, and ducked under it without asking anyone.

The lights were off. Nobody sat in its place under the bridge girders. Nonna was out. The bench had been cleared. The woman stood a moment just inside, looking round as though she were visiting someone’s home, and then she sat down on the stool by the bench. His stool. She took out a long red scarf on two needles and knitted a row, and then another.

After a while she looked at the kettle. “Is there any hot water?” she asked the empty garage, politely.

Nobody answered. She knitted another row. Then she put the needles away and stood, and went to the bench, and picked up the plain white mug with the chip by the handle, and turned it over and looked at the name written on the bottom. She put it down again with the name to the wall. Beside it she left the shopping bag. Then she ducked out under the shutter and pulled it down carefully behind her, all the way, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina got back at two minutes past six with a box of brake pads from the supplier on the docks road and a bag of oranges, thinking about dinner and about whether Haozhen would remember to eat, and found the shutter down, which she never left it, and inside, on the bench, a plain brown shopping bag she thought at first was Mouse’s.

Then she saw the mug.

She put the oranges down. “Hello?”

Nothing. She looked at the mug, with its handle turned the wrong way, and the name on the bottom facing the bricks. She knew that mug. The chip, the faint ring it left on the steel, the way he always set it down so the writing couldn’t be seen, and the way she always turned it back. Somebody had been in. Somebody had touched his things.

In the bag was a thin black file. She opened it.

The first photograph was Haozhen coming out of the alley. The second was her getting into Nonna. The third was Nobody outside Jinx’s roll-up door. She turned the page. More. Him at a station. Her at the circuit in the north. Him buying coffee at the stall under the flyover. Her carrying a box of parts. The two of them outside Da Gianni. Him at the airport drop-off with his case, and her across the roof of the car with her mouth open, shouting. She counted them. Forty. She counted again because the number seemed too big to be real. Some were from far off. Some through windows. Some close enough to show the ruby on her hand, and the little grey taxi on Gilded’s dashboard, and the white mug on the bench.

One was Haozhen asleep in Nonna’s passenger seat with his head against the glass. She knew the road. The coast road, the third loop, the night in December he’d slept two hours and eleven minutes. Somebody had been on that road too.

At the back was a single sheet. A phone number and a name. Li Zhenhua. Traffic police. And one last photograph: a small square woman in a dark blue coat at a market stall, holding a bunch of spring onions, taken from behind a parked van. In the corner, the time. 09:41. And today’s date.

Serafina didn’t know her. She looked again. She still didn’t. She didn’t need to. She put the photograph down and only just made it to the sink.

When she’d finished she held on to the edge of it and tried to breathe. Her throat burned. The garage tilted. Then she wiped her mouth and went to Mouse’s laptop on the shelf, the one that took the feed from the little camera over the side door that Mouse had put up in January after she’d found the other one in the roof, and found three o’clock, and watched a woman of about fifty-five in a grey coat duck under the shutter and sit on his stool and knit, and look at the kettle, and ask the empty room politely for hot water.

She turned his mug back round, so that his name faced the room. Then she rang him.

“Sera?”

She couldn’t speak.

“What’s happened?”

“Somebody came to the garage.” She heard her own voice, flat. “A woman. Fifty-five, maybe. Grey coat. She sat on your stool and knitted and asked the camera for hot water. She turned your mug round. She left a file.”

Silence. “What’s in it?”

“Photographs. Forty. You asleep in Nonna. Us at the airport. Everything.” She looked at the last sheet. “A number. A name. Li Zhenhua. Traffic police.”

“Don’t ring it.”

“I wasn’t going to. Hao.” She held the photograph. “The last one’s from this morning. Nine forty-one. A woman at a market. A blue coat. Spring onions.”

The line went completely quiet.

“Hao?”

“That’s my mother,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was sitting in his mother’s front room above the tailor’s, with her sewing machine under its cloth by the window and the thirty spools still in their tissue on the table, when the phone rang, and he listened to all of it without interrupting. When she said nine forty-one he looked at the clock on the wall.

He knew exactly where he’d been. Two steps behind her at the vegetable stall with her bags, watching the road. She had felt the spring onions one by one. She’d told him he walked too fast and he’d slowed down. He remembered the colour of her coat and the paper bag and the way she’d laughed when he said Serafina wasn’t patient. He had been there, watching for anything, and someone else had been there too, and he hadn’t seen them.

“Was there anything else?”

“The number. Hao, I know that name. My mother said a friend in the traffic police. It’s him, isn’t it? The one she had watching me.”

“Yes.”

“I’m scared.”

“I know.”

“No. I don’t think you do.” Her voice shook. “I don’t know how long they’ve been doing this. I don’t know how many of these were taken with us standing right there. I don’t know if your mother was on her own in that market before you got there or whether somebody had been behind her all morning.”

“I was behind her,” he said. “At nine forty-one. I was standing behind her with the bags. I remember the moment. Not the camera. I didn’t see a camera. I remember her choosing onions.” His voice was quiet. “I was there, Sera. And I didn’t know.”

She breathed in sharply. “They were watching you.”

“Yes.”

“And her.”

“Yes.” The word tasted like metal. “Don’t go anywhere on your own. Don’t answer the door. Don’t ring anyone from that sheet. Ring Mouse and tell her to come and stay, and to bring her brother.”

“Are you coming home?”

“On the last train. My mother’s neighbour’s a retired shaft foreman with four sons who all still live on this street. He’s sitting up in her kitchen tonight, and she thinks it’s because his wife’s away.” He looked at his mother, in the doorway now, with her arms folded, who had heard every word and was pretending she hadn’t. “Stay on the phone till Mouse gets there.”

“I will,” she said, and didn’t hang up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came under the shutter at twenty to two in the morning. Mouse was asleep on the sofa with her brother snoring in the chair. Serafina was at the bench with every light on. She had laid the photographs out in order, not to study them but because she couldn’t bear them scattered.

He stopped and looked at the bench. At the mug. At her. She was pale.

“Come here,” he said.

She didn’t move, so he went to her. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t. Don’t apologise as if you knew this would happen.” She looked down at the forty photographs. “Who is she?”

“Duan.”

“Your director? She came here herself?”

“I know the coat. And the knitting.”

“She sat on your stool. She asked for hot water. She turned your mug to the wall.” She pointed at it. “I turned it back.”

He looked at it, and his face was completely still. Then he picked up the photograph of his mother and studied the angle, the distance, the van, the time, and turned it over. Nothing on the back.

“She’s telling me she can reach anyone,” he said. “My mother. You. This room. And your mother’s policeman with her number on it, so I know whose cameras she borrowed.”

“That isn’t a warning. That’s a threat.”

“I know.”

“Then what are you going to do?”

He didn’t answer at once. He gathered the photographs up one by one and squared them into a neat stack.

“What are you doing?”

“Making a copy. Because this isn’t the only file. She’s been keeping records. On me, on everyone she’s ever sent me after, on whatever was in that line in Lisbon. I need to know what she has, who supplied it, and how far it goes.”

“You’re going to investigate your director.”

“Yes.”

“Alone?”

“No.” He looked up at her. “I won’t use the garage. I won’t keep anything here. I won’t bring anybody here. And I won’t keep anything from you that touches you.”

“You’ve said that before. And then you decided things without me.”

“I know.”

“I’m not asking you to tell me what you can’t. I’m asking you not to pretend this is only your problem when they’re putting my photograph in a file.”

He took her hand. “You’re right.”

“So what happens now?”

He looked at the stack under his other hand. “Now I build my own file.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sleep much. She got him upstairs in the end. He wouldn’t have the file in the bedroom. He locked it in the office drawer, and washed his hands at the little sink, and then washed them again.

“You don’t have to wash them again,” she said from the bed.

He looked at his fingers. “I know.” She held out her hand and he took it and lay down facing her, and she put her palm flat on his chest. He looked at the ceiling.

After a while she said, “Did your mother like the thread?”

“She said thirty was too many. Then she put them in the drawer under the machine in colour order.” A breath that was nearly a laugh. “She asked if you were nice. I said yes. She asked if you were patient. I said no. She said good, she’d never liked patient women.”

“I like her already.”

He turned on his side and drew her in, and lay listening to her breathe. Then “I was standing behind her.”

“I know.”

“I thought I was watching out for her.”

“You were.”

“And someone was watching me.”

She moved closer. “Then we’ll find out who.”

“We?”

“Yes.” He didn’t argue. She kissed his forehead. “Happy birthday to your mother, Hao.”

“Thank you.” He shut his eyes. And in the dark, with her hand over his heart, he began to remember everything he’d ever been trained to notice. Not to make anybody disappear. Because this time, for the first time, he wanted to know who was watching the people he loved.

chapters.title: Leverage
chapters.desc: Eleven years of black notebooks in his own code, hidden under a laundry cat’s heated bed. One line in a stolen ledger: two initials and the word “Private”. A month of nights at the workbench, Mouse at the end of it finding companies, and three copies of a file nobody in the capital knows exists.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re starting to exist.”
chapters.content:
The first thing he brought home in the new year was a laundry basket.

It was twenty past seven on Tuesday the second of January, and Serafina was on her back under Gilded with a lamp in her teeth when she heard the side door and saw his resoled oxfords cross the floor and stop. She rolled out. He was holding a blue plastic basket against his hip, the kind the laundry under his old flat lent to customers who’d forgotten their bags.

“Have you finally decided to do your own washing?”

“No.”

“Shame. I was going to put the flags out.”

He set it on the workbench. A folded towel, two old shirts, a grey blanket that smelled of fabric conditioner and cat. Under the blanket, a black notebook. Then another. He kept lifting them out and laying them in rows, the way he laid out anything he meant to account for, until there were twenty-three on the bench: thin ones worn white at the corners, fat ones held shut with rubber bands, one with a water stain like a map of somewhere, one whose spine had been mended with black tape.

“You said you wouldn’t keep anything here,” she said.

“I’m not keeping them. I’m showing you. Then they go somewhere else.”

“Where were they?”

“Under the cat.”

She looked at him.

“The laundry woman’s cat sleeps on a heated pad in the storage cupboard. Nobody moves a cat off a heated pad. Not a search team, not the woman herself. I put a board under the pad in my second year.” He opened the first notebook. Small square handwriting, dates and numbers, initials, little marks that looked like nothing. “My own code. No names in full. Places as references. Payments by date and amount.”

“Payments to who?”

“To me. And around me.” He turned pages. “Eleven years. Everything I was told, and everything I saw that I wasn’t told. I didn’t trust the official version. Not because I knew it was wrong. Because it was never the whole of it.”

She sat down across from him and didn’t touch them. “Hao. When you said you’d build your own file. I thought you meant you’d start one.”

“I started one at eighteen.”

He took out the fourth notebook and opened it where a strip of paper marked the page. In the margin, in pencil, three letters and a word. D.Q.Y. Private.

“Lisbon,” she said.

“I wrote it down there first. Then I went back through the others and found it four more times, in different ways. A job that came by phone instead of on a docket. A transfer with no receiving unit. A week where I was told to forget the dates.” He laid his palm flat on the page. “Private isn’t a classification. It’s a client. Work the Director took for people who paid her, and ran through us as if the state had asked.”

“Paid jobs.”

“Yes.”

“And you did them.”

“Some of them.” He didn’t look away. “I didn’t know which. That’s what this is for.”

She looked at the twenty-three notebooks and then at him, and she said what she’d been wanting to say since the side door opened. “You should have asked me before you carried eleven years of that into my garage.”

“Yes.”

“And you’ll need Mouse. And you haven’t asked her either.”

“No.”

“Then ask her. Properly. And let her say no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mouse said yes in about four seconds, which Serafina had expected, and then asked who’d be in danger if she was caught, which she hadn’t. Haozhen told her. Mouse listened with her hood up and her hands round a coffee, and at the end she said, “Fine. But not here.” So the notebooks went to her cousin’s farmhouse in the hills behind the reservoir, into a chest freezer that had stopped freezing in 2019, and for three weeks the three of them drove up after dark and worked at the kitchen table under a bulb that buzzed.

He read his shorthand aloud. Mouse typed. Serafina, who had spent seven years making invoices look like art for Granny Shum’s sponsors, sat between them and asked the stupid questions that turned out not to be stupid. Why does a consultancy pay for storage. Why are these two invoices the same except for the name. Why does everyone in this column have the same registered agent.

On the eleventh night Mouse turned the laptop round.

“Northgate,” she said.

Haozhen went still.

“Northgate Advisory. Not your Northgate. Yours is Northgate Services. You set it up in November ‘22 to pay her tyres and entry fees from your salary account, and Aurelia’s husband’s man found it in a morning.” Mouse scrolled. “So why’d you call it that?”

“Because it was on my payslips.” He said it. “Every few months a second line came into my salary account. Northgate Advisory, allowance. I thought it was a payroll cover. Overtime for things that didn’t have overtime. When I needed a name for a company nobody would look at twice, I used the one I’d been looking at for years.”

“Right.” Mouse’s voice had gone flat. “Northgate Advisory isn’t payroll. It’s an invoice house. Money comes in from outside as consultancy fees. It goes out through three firms with no staff. One of those firms pays your allowance.” She put two columns side by side. “Your allowance dates. Your notebook dates. And here,” another column, “the fees coming in. A customs officer in Rotterdam. A port authority man. A shipping consultant. All of them paid into Northgate, or paid by it, the month before you took someone near them.”

The bulb buzzed. Serafina found she was holding the edge of the table.

“There’s one more.” Mouse didn’t want to say it. “Port contract. A terminal concession nobody’s heard of. Two companies fighting over it in Antwerp courts. One of them pays Northgate in September ‘22. The other one’s lawyer is a man called Lucien Marchal.”

Haozhen sat down. He had already been sitting, and somehow he sat down further.

“He wasn’t national security,” Mouse said. “He was a lawsuit. Somebody paid to have him out of a court case, and the Director sold them you.”

“And I was paid for it.” He looked at the column with his allowance in it, and the date. “In November. Sixty thousand.” He’d told Aurelia that number over dinner at Da Gianni’s as if it were a good thing. “I bought your brakes with it.”

Serafina reached across the table and turned his face toward her with one hand.

“You didn’t know.”

“I should have.”

“You wrote it down for eleven years because you knew something was wrong. That’s what knowing looks like when they’ve had you since you were sixteen.” She held on until he looked at her and not at the screen. “We’re going home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t speak on the drive back. At the garage he went straight to the bench as if there were something on it, and stood there with a glass of water he didn’t drink, and she watched him read nothing for a full minute.

“Come to bed.”

“One more page.”

“There isn’t a page. They’re in a freezer on a hill.”

He looked down at the empty bench. Then at her. She held out her hand, and he took it, and halfway up the iron stairs to the loft he stopped and said, “Sera,” and she turned on the step above him, which put her eyes level with his.

“Thank you for staying.”

“You don’t thank me for that.”

“I know.”

“Do you?” She kissed him. It was meant to be short. He made a low sound against her mouth, as if something in his chest had given way, and then he bent and put one arm behind her knees and the other round her back and lifted her clean off the stairs.

“Hao—”

“I’ve got you.”

“I’m wearing boots.”

“I noticed.”

He carried her up the last of the steps and across the loft with her arms round his neck and laid her on the bed, boots and all, and stood over her breathing hard. Then he knelt on the end of the mattress and unlaced the left boot and pulled it off, and the right, and dropped them over the side one after the other, the second hitting the floor just as the eleven-fifty passed under the bridge and the whole loft hummed.

She reached for his shirt. He let her open it. She pushed it off his shoulders and put her mouth to the notch of his collarbone, and felt him shudder, and pulled him down by the waistband. He came down on his forearms and kissed her as if he were trying to put the whole evening somewhere it couldn’t follow them. Her jumper went. Her bra went, and he looked at her in the light from the stairwell and closed his eyes for a second, and opened them, and bent and took her breast into his mouth, slowly, until her back came off the sheets.

“Don’t be careful,” she said. “Not tonight.”

“I’m always careful.”

“I know. Stop.”

He lifted his head. Then he put his hand flat on her stomach and slid it down inside her jeans, under the cotton, and found her already wet, and she watched his face change. He touched her with two fingers, slow, then not slow, and when her hips began to move he didn’t let her set the pace. He held her down with the other hand on her hip and kept going until she was gasping and pulling at his hair, and he said into her neck, “Look at me,” and she did, and came apart with her eyes open on his.

She was still shaking when she got his belt undone. He kicked his trousers off with none of his usual tidiness. She pulled him over her and wrapped her legs round him and guided him into her with her hand, and they both stopped breathing at the same moment. He went in slowly, all the way, and stayed there, forehead to hers.

“Sera.”

“Move.”

He did. Long, deep, deliberate, the way he did everything, until she dug her heels into the backs of his thighs and he lost the rhythm altogether and took her hard, the iron frame of the bed knocking against the wall, her nails in his back, his breath ragged in her ear. She felt him start to break and held his face and said his name, Haozhen, the whole of it, and he came with a sound she’d never heard him make, buried deep in her with his arms locked round her as though the bed might go.

Afterwards he didn’t move off her. She stroked the back of his neck. Another train went over, and the bulb in the stairwell trembled.

“You said my whole name,” he said into her shoulder.

“It’s a good name.”

“It’s on a lot of things it shouldn’t be.”

“Then we’ll take it off them.” She turned his head and kissed his temple. “Sleep.”

He slept for six hours, and she knew because she woke twice, and both times he was still there, one hand open on her hip.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the twentieth Mouse had a spreadsheet nobody was allowed to see and a habit of not making jokes. Forty-one entries. Of the people in his books, nine sat on a line that ran through Northgate. Nine where money had come in from someone who wasn’t the state, and gone out to him.

“It doesn’t touch her,” Mouse said. “Not on paper. The money stops one company short of a name. But D.Q.Y. Private sits next to every single one in your books. And your allowance lands three weeks after every one of them.”

“It’s enough,” he said.

“For what?”

“For her to know that I know.”

He wanted copies. Not on a drive, not in a cloud, nothing that could be read from a room in the capital by someone pressing a key. On paper, in his hand. Three of them.

“That’s weeks,” Mouse said.

“Yes.”

“I’m never complaining about spreadsheets again.”

He wrote them at night, at the kitchen table on the hill and then at the end of the workbench after Serafina went up, in the same small square hand, with a line drawn down every page: what he knew on the left, what he only believed on the right. He wrote nothing about her. He wrote nothing he couldn’t stand behind. When he finished, on Monday the twenty-ninth, he checked every copy against the notebooks, and then checked them again, and she found him at one in the morning with his eyes red and the last page under his palm.

“Where are they going?”

“One in Gilded. Inside the roll cage, behind the left door bar. Big Wu will seal it in with the foam. Nobody opens a roll cage that’s passed scrutineering.” He turned the second envelope over. “One under Nobody’s seat frame. Jinx built a box in the floor for a spare phone. It fits.”

“You said nothing in the garage.”

“They’re not in the garage. They’re in cars. Cars leave.” He touched the third. “And this one goes to Chen Si’s safe.”

“You trust Chen Si.”

“I trust him to know what it is.” He considered. “He told me once not to make you carry things on your own. I’d like someone outside the two of us to be carrying this.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Qian Yu came on the last afternoon of January in a dark coat with his work bag over his shoulder, and nodded to Serafina first, as he always did, and then held out his hand to Haozhen without saying what for.

Haozhen gave him the envelope. Qian looked at the seal, and at the name on the front written in that careful hand, and at the man.

“What is it?”

“Payments. Private assignments. Northgate Advisory. Handwritten copy. The originals are somewhere else.”

“Where?”

“He doesn’t need to know that yet.”

Qian put the envelope in the inside pocket of his coat, not his bag, and buttoned it. Then he stood a moment longer than he needed to.

“For eleven years,” he said, “you’ve been a name on a pass that gets taken back at the door. Nobody wrote down what you saw. Now somebody has.” He looked at the bench where the notebooks had been, and back. “You’re starting to exist, Mr. Qin. It’s uncomfortable. It wears off.”

He went. The side door swung to. Haozhen stood looking at the place where the envelope had been, and Serafina came and stood beside him and took his hand.

“Will he give it to him tonight?”

“Within the hour.”

“Will he believe it?”

“He’ll read it.” She laced their fingers together. “And then he’ll decide what it’s worth.”

A train went over, eleven minutes after the last. On the far side of the floor Gilded sat under her cover with three hundred pages of somebody else’s sins behind her door bar, and the little grey toy taxi on her dashboard looking out at the shutter. For eleven years he had written everything down because he was afraid the truth would disappear.

Now, at least, it wouldn’t disappear with him.

chapters.title: The Resignation Letter That Took Ten Years
chapters.desc: The New Year comes and goes and nobody calls. Lunar New Year comes and goes. So he goes to them, uninvited, on a Monday in February, with one sentence on a page torn from his notebook and the first page of an index. A quiet office, a radiator that knocks, and a woman who doesn’t stop knitting until she reads the word Northgate.
chapters.epigraph: “I resign. — Qin Haozhen.”
chapters.content:
The new year came and went, and nobody called.

He had expected a summons. A warning, or a polite request to reconsider, delivered by somebody senior who would pretend it was a courtesy. The first week of January he checked his phone more often than he admitted. The second week he stopped checking it in front of her. By the end of the month, when the last of the copies was gone and there was nothing left to write, he had started to recognise the particular quiet that comes before a door is opened.

No door opened. No strange cars under the bridge. No numbers he didn’t know. Nothing from Tianyi. Lunar New Year fell on Saturday the tenth of February, and Big Wu’s mother fed him fish belly again and called him thin, and still nothing came from the capital. Not a card, not one of the Director’s carefully worded invitations.

On the evening of the first day of the new year Serafina found him at the garage window, watching a delivery van that had been parked across the road for twenty minutes.

“You’re doing it again.”

“He hasn’t moved.”

“He’s eating noodles.”

“He could be waiting.”

“Then I hope they’re good noodles.” She put two bowls down on the bench. “Sit.”

He sat. She waited until he’d picked up his chopsticks, and then she waited some more, because he didn’t use them.

“Say it.”

“They haven’t asked me to come back.”

“You resigned.”

“I said I’d take no more assignments. That isn’t resigning. And they haven’t asked.” He turned the bowl a quarter turn. “Not to stay. Not why. Nothing.”

“And you wanted them to.”

He didn’t answer, which was an answer.

“Hao.”

“I spent eleven years being useful.” He said it to the noodles. “I thought it would add up to something. And it turns out that when you stop, they don’t even ring.” He looked up. “So I keep wondering what happens when you work it out.”

“Work what out?”

“That I’m not much use for anything else.”

She put her chopsticks down. She wanted to throw the bowl at him, and he saw it, and was almost relieved.

“You think I’m with you because you’re useful.”

“I think it’s what I know how to be.”

“You can’t strip a gearbox,” she said. “You loosened one bolt for me in two years and you still look pleased about it. You change a wheel like it’s a magic trick. You aren’t here because you’re useful. You’re here because I want you.” She came round the bench and stood between his knees and took his face in her hands, not gently. “And if the people in the capital don’t know what to do with you once you stop being their tool, that’s a fact about them. Not about you. Say it back.”

“It’s a fact about them.”

“Not about you.”

“Not about me.” He turned his face into her palm. “I don’t believe it yet.”

“I know. You’ll say it every day till you do.” She kissed his forehead. “Now eat. Then tell me how many times you’ve looked out of that window.”

“Four.”

“Seven.”

“Five.”

“You’re a terrible liar.”

The van left before they’d finished. Neither of them watched it go.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Sunday of February he came up to the loft late, with his hair still wet from the shower and the old black T-shirt she had taken from his flat and then declared hers. He stood in the doorway.

“You look like a man delivering bad news.”

“Tomorrow.”

“I know.” She put her phone face down. “You’re going to see her. Uninvited. With one sentence and one page.”

“Yes.”

“Are you frightened?”

He sat on the edge of the bed. “I don’t know what she’ll do.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“I don’t want to go back.” He looked at their hands. “And I don’t know what happens after. I might not come home tomorrow.”

“Don’t.”

“I only mean—”

“I know what you mean.” She pulled his hand against her chest. “You might be kept waiting. You might be questioned. You might have to explain yourself to people who have never had to explain anything to anyone. And then you’ll come home and tell me she was horrible.”

“That’s likely.”

“And if they try to keep you, I’ll come and get you.”

“You’d need an appointment.”

“I’ll bring a tyre iron.”

He laughed. It came out of him unexpectedly, and his shoulders dropped half an inch, and she pulled the T-shirt over his head while he was still laughing and threw it at the chair.

He kissed her slowly at first, as if he were trying to learn something by heart. She didn’t let him keep it slow. She pushed him onto his back and climbed over him and sat across his hips in nothing but her knickers, and took his wrists and pressed them into the pillow above his head.

“Leave them there.”

“Sera.”

“You spend all day deciding things. You’re not deciding this.”

He left them there. It cost him; she could see what it cost him. She kissed down his throat, over the healed line on his forearm, across his chest, and felt him go rigid under her and then begin, slowly, to give. She took his hand from the pillow herself and put it between her legs and held it there and moved against it, showing him exactly what she wanted, until his breathing was louder than hers.

Then she let go of his hand, rose up, and sank down onto him in one long movement.

He swore, which he never did. She stayed still on purpose, all of him inside her, and watched his face.

“Look at me,” she said. “Not the ceiling. Not tomorrow. Me.”

“I’m looking.”

She rode him slowly, then less slowly, her palms flat on his chest, his hands clamped on her thighs. The bed creaked. A train went under the bridge and she didn’t hear it. When he tried to sit up and take over she pushed him back down, and he made a sound like begging, and she gave him more. He came first, which he never did, with his head pressed back and her name torn out of him, and before he’d finished he had his thumb on her and wouldn’t stop until she fell forward onto his chest and shook.

Afterwards he lay with his head on her breastbone. She traced the line of his shoulder.

“You’re allowed to be glad about leaving,” she said. “And angry. And sad. All three. You gave them eleven years. They didn’t deserve them. You still gave them.”

“I thought I’d feel freer.”

“Maybe it takes a while.”

“Maybe.” He closed his eyes. “Say the other thing.”

“It’s a fact about them.”

“Not about me,” he said, and slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he chose a plain dark-blue shirt and pressed it himself, and fastened the cuffs, and put on the watch he had worn to the Autumn Reception sixteen months before.

“You’re dressing for a funeral.”

“Mine, if it goes badly.”

“Try again.”

“An administrative meeting.”

“Better.”

On the bench lay two things. One was a page torn from one of his old notebooks, with one line in black ink, no date and no explanation:

I resign. — Qin Haozhen.

The other was the first page of the index. Not a report, not a confession. A way in: dates, payment references, three company structures, the notebook and page where each entry could be found. NORTHGATE across the top, in capitals, with Advisory and Services side by side beneath it. Left of the line, what he could prove. Right of it, what he believed.

She straightened his collar. Then a crease that wasn’t there.

“You’re fussing.”

“I’m arming you.” She caught his wrist when he reached for his jacket. “Come back.”

“I will.”

She didn’t make him promise. He had made too many promises in his life to people who meant something different by them. She kissed him once and let him go, and he took the half-past six flight to the capital with the page inside his jacket and nothing in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building on the broad grey road still had no sign. The clerk downstairs still gave him a visitor’s pass, though this time she looked at his name before she did. On the seventh floor the radiator knocked twice, paused, and knocked again.

Duan Qiuyan was knitting by the window. The red scarf had grown since December; it lay folded on the desk in ribs as neat as a staff list and ran in a long tail off the edge into a basket on the floor.

“Qin.” She didn’t look up. “You’re early.”

“I didn’t want to keep you.”

“You’re not keeping me. Sit.”

He stayed standing and put the torn page on her desk.

The needles paused. She read the line, and he watched her read it more than once, though it was only five words long.

“You understand that resignation isn’t a private matter.”

“I understand.”

“Your position isn’t ordinary. Your record can’t be closed because you’ve decided you’d like a different life.”

“I know.”

“Then what do you expect to happen?”

“I expect it to be received.”

Something that was almost amusement crossed her face. “You’ve become very literal.”

“I’ve always been literal. You used to like it.”

He took out the second page and laid it beside the first.

She stopped knitting. For a while she didn’t move at all. He watched her eyes go down the page, find the word at the top, go down the dates, stop at September 2022 and stay there. Her hand came to the edge of the paper and didn’t quite touch it.

“Where did you get this?”

“From my records.”

“There are no records.”

“There are now.”

The pleasant office face slipped, and what was under it was colder and much more attentive, and older. For the first time since he’d known her he thought she looked like someone who could be frightened.

“Northgate Advisory,” she said.

He said nothing.

“Do you understand what you’re carrying, Qin? These names aren’t connected the way you think.”

“Then the index will be useful. The entries underneath are available. The copies are kept somewhere else.”

“Where?”

“I’m not discussing that.”

It was the old reflex, he could see it in her: the expectation that he would answer because she had asked. He didn’t.

“You’ve been talking to Chen Si.”

“Yes.”

“And the woman.”

“She has nothing to do with these records.”

“She has everything to do with them. You made her part of this when you let your personal life become a weakness.”

“Don’t speak about her as an operational problem.”

“She’s a risk.”

“To whom?”

“To you.”

“No,” he said. “You are.”

The radiator knocked, three times, like someone who wanted to come in. Duan took her glasses off and folded them and laid them on top of the index.

“This goes upstairs,” she said. “They’ll read it. They’ll decide what can be done. And they’ll send someone.”

“Who?”

“Someone.”

“From this office?”

“Not a stranger.” She put the glasses back on. “They never send strangers. You know that. You’ve been the friend at the door yourself.”

Not a threat, quite, not a comfort. Someone who knew him. Someone whose arrival would be hard to refuse.

“Is it Tianyi?”

She picked up the needles, found her place in the red, and made a stitch.

“Then tell whoever it is to come to me,” he said. “Not her. Not my mother. Me.”

“You still think you can set terms.”

“No. I think I can make mine clear.”

She looked almost disappointed. “You were very good at this.”

“I know.”

“You could have had a long career.”

“I had one.” He turned for the door. “Now I have somewhere to be.”

He didn’t look back. He didn’t need to. He could hear the needles, and then he couldn’t, and then the radiator knocked again behind a closed door.

✦ ✦ ✦

His phone had one message on it when he came out into the grey. A photograph of the workbench: his chipped white mug turned upside down so the word on the bottom faced the camera. HAOZHEN.

Your mug is behaving. Come home.

He typed: I resigned.

I know. Are you all right?

Yes.

Suspiciously short.

I’m coming home.

Good. Bring food.

She was waiting at arrivals at ten to four, in short-stay, leaning on Nonna’s door in her black jacket with his old scarf round her neck, because if he was coming home after eleven years he would be collected in a car with a personality. He saw her before she saw him and stood still in the stream of people with suitcases. No radiator. No file. Just her, looking at her phone, and the small red car behind her.

She looked up. She didn’t run, or call his name. She put the phone in her pocket and straightened, and smiled.

“Well?”

“She took the letter.”

“That isn’t the same as accepting it.”

“No. It goes upstairs. They’ll send someone. Someone I know.”

Her hand paused on the door. “Tianyi.”

“She didn’t say no.”

“All right.” She took it in without trying to make it smaller. “Then we’ll find out when we find out. You don’t have to solve the next six months in a car park.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were.”

She got in. He went round to the passenger side and had just folded himself into the seat and reached for the belt when she leaned across the gearstick, took his jacket in her fist, and kissed him.

Not carefully, not the quick kind they traded across a bench when one of them was holding a spanner. She kissed him with one hand hard at his jaw and her elbow in the steering wheel, and the horn gave one short, outraged beep, and a man with a trolley said something rude, and neither of them stopped. He forgot the belt. He forgot the man. He put his hand in her hair and kissed her back as if he’d been holding his breath since half past six.

When she let go her forehead stayed against his.

“Welcome home.”

He couldn’t say anything. She reached across him and pulled the belt down and fastened it, and patted his chest once, satisfied, and started the engine.

He laid his hand over hers on the gearstick as they pulled out. The index was on a desk in the capital. Someone would come. He hadn’t brought Marchal home, or given Gong Ruiming back to his son, or undone a single thing he’d done because somebody had told him it was necessary. He didn’t mistake a letter for absolution.

But it was signed. And he was in the passenger seat of a little red car, with her driving and her hand under his, and for once he didn’t need to know where the road ended.

chapters.title: They Send Someone
chapters.desc: The season opener at the circuit in the north. Eleven thousand people in the grandstand, a black car with a gold name, and in the pit lane, with a hospitality lanyard and a stick of cinnamon gum, the boy from the next bed in a dormitory of forty, who once gave his window seat to nobody but him.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re already here.”
chapters.content:
The first thing he noticed was the cinnamon gum.

A man stood in the pit lane at the circuit in the north with a hospitality lanyard round his neck, one hand in the pocket of a dark jacket and the other round a paper cup, watching mechanics roll tyres between garages. Every so often he chewed. Two slow movements of the jaw, a pause, two more.

Haozhen knew that rhythm. He had heard it at night in a dormitory of forty beds where the heating never worked and the windows rattled when the wind came off the mountains, from the next bed along, the dry one, which Haozhen had given away on the first night when the roof leaked onto bed eleven. The boy in it had paid him back for two years by keeping him the window seat on the academy bus every Sunday without being asked. He had heard it in the back of transport vans. He had heard it five months ago in a corridor in the capital, outside a grey door on the seventh floor.

Tianyi.

Nothing had changed since November except one thing. There was a thin pink line now beside his left eyebrow, not yet faded to white, the kind of scar a person gets from a car door or a ring. He still chewed as if he had all the time in the world.

It was half past ten on Saturday the thirteenth of April, the first round of the season. Across the garage Serafina was arguing with Mouse about a tyre blanket.

“I didn’t say the temperature was wrong. I said someone unplugged it.”

“Why are you looking at me?”

“Because you’re standing next to it.”

“I was supervising.”

“You were eating.”

Tianyi saw him looking. He didn’t wave. He lifted the paper cup an inch: a greeting between colleagues, or a reminder.

Haozhen took his phone out. Someone’s here.

She read it, and her face changed at once. Who?

Tianyi.

She didn’t ask if he was sure. She looked down the pit lane, found the man with the lanyard, and took him in from shoes to scar. Then she walked across and kissed Haozhen on the cheek, quick and ordinary, the way anyone might.

“Don’t disappear,” she said.

“I won’t.”

“You can’t promise that if you don’t know what’s happening. So tell me when you do.”

“I will.”

“Good. Now come and look at the front-left. Mouse has been supervising it with her teeth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The circuit hadn’t changed much since the year before. The same long grandstand, the same peeling paint round the service doors. They had resurfaced two corners over the winter and put new barriers in at the Needle, the long tightening left at the end of the back straight where she’d cracked a splitter a metre from the wall thirteen months before. Eleven thousand people had come for the opener. The noise rolled over the pit lane in waves every time a car went out.

Gilded sat in the garage with her covers off: matte black, a white seven on the door, AURELIA in gold across the bonnet, and on her dashboard the little grey toy taxi that had been riding there for a year. Serafina had spent the winter on the car’s balance and argued with everyone who said it should be made more forgiving.

“It doesn’t need to forgive me,” she said, crouched at the front wheel with the gauge. “It needs to understand me. Pressure?”

He read it off.

“That’s not a number. That’s a mood.” She checked it herself and tapped the gauge twice. Then she stood and wiped her hands and leaned close enough that only he could hear. “Is he here for you?”

“Yes.”

“Do you know what he wants?”

“I can guess.”

“Don’t guess at me. Tell me when you know.” She kissed his jaw and went to get her helmet.

Tianyi had moved to the end of the pit wall. His lanyard said hospitality guest. His shoes said otherwise: plain, black, rubber-soled, broken in at the heel by somebody who walked on concrete for a living. And he hadn’t come alone.

There were five of them in the grandstand. Not together, not in the same colours. A man with a programme folded on his knee who never opened it. A man by the stairwell with a camera he didn’t lift. A woman in a pale cap who had been looking at the pit lane for six minutes without taking a single photograph. Two more he found on the second count, one high in the main stand and one at the end of the row nearest the garages.

They weren’t watching the race. They were watching her garage, the way he would have, from the angles he would have chosen.

He counted them again. Five. He looked at Tianyi, and Tianyi chewed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The race started at two. Haozhen stood on the pit wall with a headset on and one hand flat on the barrier. He wasn’t allowed to speak on it; on Team AURELIA only Mouse talked to the driver, one calm voice in her ear, because two voices in a helmet at a hundred and sixty kilometres an hour was how people ended up in walls. He listened.

She started third. The first two laps were clean. She held position through turn one, stayed out of the dirty air behind the leader, waited for the tyres to come in. The leader was driving scared, protecting the inside into the long right and then leaving his exit open because he cared more about stopping a pass than about his own lap.

She noticed. He could tell she’d noticed because she stopped trying.

“She’s got him,” Mouse said, off the radio, to nobody.

“Not yet.”

“She has. Look at his rears.”

The leader’s car was starting to step out on exit. Lap after lap she sat a few car lengths behind him, close enough to fill his mirrors, never close enough to give him a reason to shove her wide. The gap came down two tenths, three, nearly half a second.

On lap nineteen, at the end of the back straight, he did what she’d been waiting for him to do. He moved to the inside to cover the Needle.

“Outside’s open,” Mouse said into the radio, flat and quick. “Your call.”

Serafina didn’t answer. She stayed flat a fraction longer than anyone in the grandstand believed was possible, braked at the marker, and went round the outside of him in the long tightening left with two wheels on the very edge of the new kerb. He tried to close the door on exit. She was already alongside. The two cars ran level, close enough to swap paint. Then Gilded’s tail cleared his front wing and she was through.

The grandstand made a noise like weather.

Haozhen didn’t move. He watched the next sector, and the next. She had the cleaner exit and the better traction, and by the final sector the gap was two seconds, then three. She crossed the line four point zero eight two seconds clear.

The garage went mad. Big Wu threw a towel in the air and it landed on someone else’s car. Mouse was shouting, really shouting, the headset crackling with it. Haozhen took the headset off and stood in eleven thousand people’s noise, and felt something in his chest unclench that had been clenched since February.

Then he looked for Tianyi, who hadn’t cheered.

He was by the hospitality entrance, looking at Haozhen. And the five in the grandstand were moving. Not towards the podium. Towards the exits, unhurried, one by one, each down a different stair. They’d come to make sure he saw them. They’d done it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony was loud and bright and sticky with champagne. She stood on the top step with the trophy in one hand and the bottle in the other, and found him across the paddock straight away, and her smile changed. Not smaller. More private. She mouthed something. He couldn’t hear it. He knew what it was. Four seconds.

When she got away she came round behind the tyre stack at the garage entrance with her helmet under one arm and champagne still running out of her hair.

“Well?”

“Very good.”

“Very good?”

“Four point zero eight two.”

“You sound like you’re reviewing a gearbox.”

“Would you rather have the analysis?”

“I’d rather you kissed me.”

She didn’t wait for him to decide. She caught his jacket and pulled him down behind the stack of black tyres, and he tasted champagne and salt and sweat and the inside of a helmet, and her fingers were cold from the bottle on the back of his neck. He kissed her the way he hadn’t let himself in public before, with both hands in her wet hair, his back against the warm rubber. She laughed into his mouth.

“You’re soaking.”

“Your fault. You let me win.”

“I didn’t let you do anything.”

“You never do.” She kissed him again, slower.

Then she felt him go still, and opened her eyes.

Tianyi was standing at the end of the tyre stack. The lanyard was gone. So was the coffee. The gum moved slowly between his teeth.

“Congratulations,” he said.

“Thank you,” said Serafina, not letting go of Haozhen’s jacket.

“Can we talk?”

“No,” said Haozhen.

“Alone.”

Haozhen moved half a step, so that he was between them. “Say it here.”

Tianyi’s jaw worked once. Something went across his face that wasn’t anger. Disappointment, perhaps, the kind you feel for someone you’d taught better.

“Tonight,” he said. “You come in tonight. There’s a car at the north gate at nine. You get in it.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then things start being reviewed that have been left alone.” He looked at Serafina, quite politely. “Her racing licence. National licences are renewed every year, and renewals can be delayed. Her sister’s company, which imports a great deal of gold. And your mother.” He let that sit. “A woman of sixty-three, living alone above a tailor’s, without a pension in her own name, on a street where everybody knows everybody. It would be a shame for her landlord to find out who her son works for.”

“Don’t,” said Haozhen.

“I’m telling you what will happen.”

“You’re threatening my family.”

“I’m telling you.” Tianyi turned his eyes on him at last. “You didn’t leave the Bureau, Haozhen. You walked into its office with a list of its sins and left it on the desk. Nobody upstairs has been asked to forgive that before. They sent me because I’m the one you might get in the car with.”

“Who sent you?” Serafina said.

“You know who.”

“Does she know you’re threatening my licence?”

“I wouldn’t call it that.”

“No. You wouldn’t.”

Haozhen’s hand had found her wrist. Not tightly, only so she’d know he was there. She looked down at it and then at him, and he let go.

“Nine o’clock,” said Tianyi.

“No.”

“Don’t make me come back for you.”

Haozhen looked at the boy from the next bed. The one who’d split a stick of cinnamon gum in half on the second night because the new boy had never tasted it. The one who’d stood beside him on a pontoon in Lisbon and said nothing at all while a child threw a football at a car window.

“You’re already here,” Haozhen said.

Tianyi looked at him a moment longer. Then he turned and walked into the crowd, and was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t go straight to the car. She changed out of her suit and into jeans and a dark jacket. She thanked the team, all of them, one at a time, and told Big Wu to take Gilded home in the transporter and lock the shutter and not open it to anyone, not even her.

“Why not you?”

“Because if someone says it’s me and it isn’t, you’ll have already decided.”

Big Wu looked at Haozhen. Haozhen nodded once. Big Wu touched the wooden bead on his mirror for luck and didn’t argue.

They walked to the car park side by side.

“You’re going to tell me everything,” she said. “Not the version you think I can handle.”

“Yes.”

“Not the one without the parts where you look bad.”

“Yes.”

Nonna was at the far edge of the car park, small and red and patient. He looked in the mirrors before he got in. She saw him do it.

“How many?”

“Three.”

She looked. A dark saloon two rows back with a man in it who wasn’t on his phone. A silver estate rolling along the next lane at the speed of somebody not looking for a space. A third, a white hatchback, just turning onto the exit road ahead of them.

“From the grandstand?”

“Some of them.”

She started the engine. “So we don’t go home.”

“No. There’s a switch,” he said. “If we’re followed.”

Her hands stopped on the wheel. “Planned by who?”

“Me.”

“When?”

“In December. After she put forty photographs on our bench.”

“You made a plan without telling me.”

“Yes.”

“Does it use my garage?”

“No.”

“Does it involve you deciding where I go?”

He thought about it before he answered, which was why she believed him. “Not unless you say yes.”

She looked at him. Then she put it in gear. “Tell me.”

He told her. Not in shorthand. The route, and why it wasn’t the obvious one. The self-service car wash on the old coast road where the camera over bay three had been broken since autumn. Jinx in the bay behind with a coat, a cap and a wig, waiting to take Nonna north up the expressway with her lights on so the three cars had something to follow. And in the bay beyond that, with its engine already warm, a silver-grey 2006 ex-taxi nobody in the world would look at twice.

“Nobody,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Jinx knows?”

“She knows the car might be needed tonight. She doesn’t know why. She said she didn’t want to.”

“Good.” Serafina checked the mirror. The saloon had moved up. It was two cars behind them now. “Three.”

“Yes.”

The exit road opened onto the public road past the gate. Families were leaving with flags tucked under their arms. A boy in a miniature helmet. Someone still waving a foam hand. The world looked ordinary, and that was the part he hated most.

“Are you all right?” she said.

“No.”

“Me neither.” She took her hand off the gearstick and held it out, palm up, without looking, and he took it. “Then we’ll be frightened together. Then we’ll be clever.”

The marshal lifted the barrier. Nonna went through. For a few seconds the road behind them was empty.

Then the dark saloon came out of the gate. The silver estate after it. The white hatchback joined from the slip road a little further on.

“Still there?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and changed up. “Now we know.”

He watched them in the mirror all the way to the coast road. For the first time since he’d put that page on the Director’s desk, he understood exactly what they meant to do with his freedom. They meant to take it back, with her in the car.

chapters.title: Shoot the Tyres
chapters.desc: A closed service station on the old coast road, a car wash, and a grey taxi with the engine already running. Three cars behind them, then two, then one. She drives. He shoots out tyres. Nobody dies who didn’t have to, and one man who nearly does is pulled out of the fire by the friend he was sent to bring in.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not asking you to be brave. I’m asking you to stay awake.”
chapters.content:
The first car stayed behind them for six minutes. The second joined at the roundabout by the cement works. The third came up just before the turn for the old coast road, a white hatchback with dipped lights and enough distance to pretend it wasn’t there.

“Three,” she said.

“I see them.”

“All Bureau?”

“The silver estate is. The others are hired.”

“How do you know?”

“The estate isn’t trying to look like it isn’t following us. That’s a man who wants to be seen.” He watched the mirror. “That’s Tianyi.”

The car wash stood at the far end of a service station that had been closed for a year. The sign above the forecourt still promised petrol, hot food and clean facilities. The pumps were gone, the shop was boarded, and weeds grew through the cracks in a long line where the drain ran. She swung Nonna into the self-service bay with the broken camera and the shutter came down behind her with a clatter, and for a second there was nothing but dripping pipes and their breathing.

Jinx was standing in the next bay in Serafina’s own black jacket and a short dark wig, holding a paper cup. Beyond her, in the third bay, Raiden sat at the wheel of a silver-grey 2006 ex-taxi with its engine idling and its roof sign long since unscrewed.

“You’re late,” said Jinx.

“Traffic.”

“Three cars of it.” Jinx held out her hand for Nonna’s keys. “Is this the part where I ask what’s going on?”

“No,” said Haozhen.

“Excellent. I hate the answers.” She looked at Serafina’s car with real love. “If they scratch her, I’m coming after them myself.”

“Take her north on the expressway. Lights on. Don’t speed. Let them keep you in sight for forty minutes, then go to your father’s yard under the flyover and put her inside.”

“Yes, Dad.” Jinx got in. Nonna’s engine caught, that familiar uneven bark, and Serafina felt it in her own chest as the shutter went up and the little red car rolled out into the dark with someone else’s hands on her wheel and turned north.

They watched through the gap under the shutter. The saloon followed her. Then the hatchback. Then the silver estate came level with the entrance, and paused, and Haozhen didn’t breathe.

It went on after the others.

“Now.”

Raiden got out of Nobody and held the door. “She’s ugly,” Serafina told him, sliding behind the wheel.

“She’s meant to be ugly. Jinx spent three weekends on it.” He handed Haozhen an envelope. “The numbers you wanted.” Then, to her: “Be careful.”

“Always.”

“That isn’t what I’ve heard.” He hauled up the back shutter. Nobody rolled out onto the rear service road, past the bins and the old tyre cage, and onto the coast road going the other way.

✦ ✦ ✦

For twelve minutes they had it to themselves. The road wound between black hills and the sea, patched and repatched, the white lines nearly worn away. She drove with both hands. Nobody was heavier than Nonna and softer at the front, the steering vague around the middle, the brakes good but long. She learned all of it in the first three bends and stopped noticing it by the fourth.

“Any sign?”

“Not yet.”

Then a single pair of headlights came round the long bend behind them, closing fast, one of them flickering where the lamp had been knocked.

“That’s not Nonna.”

“No.” He knew the shape before he could see it. “He worked it out.”

“Or he never believed it.”

“He never believes anything I do the first time.” He reached under his jacket.

Her eyes went to the gun and back to the road. “Are you going to shoot him?”

“I’m going to shoot his car.”

“Don’t miss.”

“I don’t.”

The silver estate came up until its lights filled the mirror. Then it pulled out, on the straight before the hairpin above the old salt pans, and drew alongside them with a metre of air between the doors, and she could see Tianyi at its wheel, chewing, looking straight ahead as if he were driving to work. He was going to put his nose in front of hers on the hairpin and make her stop.

Haozhen put his window down. Salt wind roared in.

“Brake a little,” he said. “Now.”

She lifted. The estate shot half a length ahead of them, and for one second its front wheel was right there, three metres away, turning.

He fired twice. The first round went into the tyre and the second into the rim, and the sound in the small car was so loud it was like being hit. The estate’s front end dropped and it slewed across the road in front of them, its rim screaming on the tarmac and throwing a fan of orange sparks, and she went round its tail through the hairpin with the rear of Nobody stepping out and caught it and was past.

“Did you hit him?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.” He was watching the mirror. The estate was coming again, slower, lurching, sparks pouring off the bare wheel. “He’s still coming.”

“On three tyres?”

“On three tyres and pride.”

“Where’s the tunnel?”

“Two minutes. Then the road climbs.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw the van before she did.

It was parked across the mouth of the tunnel at an angle, a white panel van with its rear doors open and its hazard lights going, as if someone had broken down there. There was a gap between its front corner and the tunnel wall. Two men stood behind the open doors.

One lifted something long.

“Down,” he said, and put his hand on the back of her neck and pushed.

The windscreen starred above her head. Something hit the road and went whining away into the dark. He had his arm out of the window and was firing back at the gap between the van doors, two, three, four, the brass jumping off the dashboard. One of the men spun round and sat down hard against the van with his hand clamped to his shoulder. The other kept firing. A round punched through the door beside Haozhen’s hip and another through the pillar, and then he made a small sound, not much of one, and his gun hand dropped.

“Hao.”

“Drive.”

She put her head up. The van filled the tunnel mouth. The gap between its bumper and the wall was the width of a car and almost nothing else.

Two metres, she thought. Nobody’s a metre seventy-eight. The mirror goes.

She didn’t lift. She did the thing her body knew how to do better than anything else in the world: she put her eyes on the far side of the gap and nowhere else, and kept the wheel dead straight, and let the speed carry her. The needle sat at a hundred and sixty. The man still standing threw himself sideways. The passenger mirror went with a crack like a branch, metal screamed down the right side of the car, the van rocked, and then the tunnel swallowed them and its lights went past in long yellow streaks and there was nothing behind them but noise.

“Are you hit?”

“Yes.”

“Where?”

“Left arm. Above the elbow.”

She looked. His sleeve was black and shining all the way to the cuff. He had his right hand clamped over it and blood was coming out between his fingers.

“That’s a lot of blood.”

“It’s through. I can feel both holes.” His voice was perfectly level. “Keep driving.”

“Don’t tell me to keep driving.”

“Serafina.” He waited until she looked at him. His face was grey under the tunnel lights, but his eyes were steady. “Please.”

She drove.

✦ ✦ ✦

The road came out of the tunnel and began to climb in long switchbacks above the sea. She took them as fast as she dared and no faster, because every jolt went into his arm and she could see it go.

Behind them, headlights. The saloon had come back from the north, or another car like it. And behind that, slow and terrible, the single knocked lamp of the silver estate, still throwing sparks.

“He’ll kill himself,” she said.

“He’s trying to keep up so he can say he tried.”

On the third bend, the estate tried to pass the saloon. Its bare front wheel caught the edge of the road where the tarmac broke away, and the car went sideways into the low barrier, and over it. She saw it in the mirror: it rolled once, twice, the roof coming round white in the saloon’s headlights, and slid down into the gully below the road, and a second later something under its bonnet caught and the dark went orange.

She braked.

“Keep going.”

“He’s in there.”

“Sera—”

“He’s in there.” She was already turning into the lay-by behind a stand of pines, cutting the lights. The saloon went past them without slowing. Its brake lights glowed once at the next bend, and then it was gone.

He caught her wrist as she reached for the door. She looked at his hand, and at him.

“He came here to take you.”

“I know.”

“Then let go.”

He let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gully stank of petrol and burning rubber. The estate lay on its side against a tree, the front of it folded up like paper, flames running along the bottom of the engine bay. Behind the broken driver’s window something moved.

She went down the slope on her heels and her hands. Haozhen came after her with his bad arm jammed against his ribs.

Tianyi was hanging in his belt, his face streaked with blood from a cut above the new scar, his left leg wrong under the dashboard. He saw them and his eyes went wide.

“Go.”

“Shut up,” said Serafina. “Where’s the release?”

“Jammed. Go.”

Haozhen knelt in the broken glass and reached in with his one good hand. The belt had twisted in the buckle under Tianyi’s weight. He worked it with his thumb, once, twice, the heat on the side of his face, while Serafina wedged her shoulder under Tianyi’s and took the weight off it, and the buckle let go and Tianyi fell against her and screamed, because his leg had stayed where it was.

“It’s trapped.”

“I know.” Haozhen put his good hand on the dashboard and shoved, and the plastic gave a centimetre. Flames came up through the floor near the pedals. “Pull. On three. One, two—”

They pulled. Tianyi came out of the window all at once with a sound she would hear, and the three of them went over backwards onto the gravel. She got her fists in his jacket and dragged. Haozhen got him under one arm. They were halfway up the slope when the fire got into the fuel line, and it wasn’t an explosion the way films had told her, it was a great soft punch of heat and light, and Haozhen turned his body between her and it without thinking.

For a while there was only the crackle.

Tianyi coughed. “You’re both mad.”

“You’re welcome,” said Serafina, and found she was crying.

Haozhen knelt over him and ran his good hand down the leg, quickly, the way he’d been taught. Broken below the knee. Not through the skin. Tianyi’s pupils were the same size.

“Who’s at the tunnel?”

“Not mine.” Tianyi turned his head. “I was told to bring you to the main road. If you wouldn’t come, keep you there till somebody else arrived. I wasn’t told who. I wasn’t told about guns.”

“You saw the guns.”

“I saw them when you did.” He shut his eyes. “There’s another car past the top of the climb. Two men. I don’t know who sent them. Not her, I think. Upstairs.”

“Come with us.”

“No.”

“Your leg’s broken.”

“And I’m the Bureau’s man in a burnt Bureau car on a public road. When they come for me, I’ll tell them you shot my tyre and I lost it on the bend. That’s true.” He opened his eyes. “If I come with you, I’m a hostage or a deserter. If I stay, I’m only a fool.”

“Tianyi.”

“You took the wet bed for me,” Tianyi said. “Bed eleven. The first night. I’ve owed you for twelve years.”

“You kept me the window seat. Every Sunday.”

“That was the bus. It doesn’t count.” Something went across Tianyi’s bloody face that might have been a laugh. “Go, Haozhen. Before I remember what I’m for.”

Haozhen looked at him a moment longer. Then he nodded once. Nobody forgave anybody and nobody promised anything: two men who had once shared a leaking room, with no idea how to save each other.

They left him on the gravel by the road, propped against a stone with Haozhen’s jacket under his head, conscious and breathing, with the fire lighting the bottom of the clouds.

✦ ✦ ✦

In Nobody she tore the sleeve off his shirt with her teeth.

Two holes, front and back, high in the meat of the arm. Ragged where it had come out. Blood running steady, not spurting. She packed both holes with gauze from Jinx’s kit under the seat and he made no sound at all, which was worse than if he’d shouted, and she bound it as tight as she could and tied his forearm to his chest with the torn sleeve.

“Fingers.”

He moved them. All four, and the thumb.

“Dizzy?”

“A little.”

“We need a hospital.”

“A hospital reports gunshot wounds. In an hour they’d know where I am, and you.”

“Then where?”

He leaned his head back against the seat. “Mr. Kwok told me once, if I ever needed to be nowhere, there’s a house. His brother’s. In the mountains past the reservoir. Above the tea at Yunwu. His brother died the winter before last. A cousin looks after it.”

“You’ve known about a safe house for a year and you didn’t tell me.”

“I didn’t think I’d need it.”

“After tonight we’re having a very long conversation.”

“I know.”

“With diagrams.”

“I’ll prepare,” he said, and his eyes closed.

“Don’t you dare.” She grabbed his chin. “I’m not asking you to be brave. I’m asking you to stay awake. Talk to me.”

He opened his eyes and talked to her. For two hours, up and up, past the dark water of the reservoir and through villages with no lights and onto a road that was barely a road, he talked about nothing: the cat under his old flat, the names of the five people in the grandstand as he imagined them, Big Wu’s mother’s fish. Every time he stopped she said his name, and he started again.

Once he said, “You went through at a hundred and sixty.”

“Yes.”

“With the mirror scraping the van.”

“Yes.”

“You were extraordinary.”

“I was terrified.” Her hands were tight on the wheel. “When I saw your sleeve I thought I was going to drive home without you.”

“I’m here.”

“Don’t make me do that again.”

He didn’t say he wouldn’t. He knew her too well to lie. He lifted her hand off the gearstick with his good one and kissed her knuckles. “I’ll do everything I can not to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was stone, with a blue door, at the top of a lane between tea terraces that ran down the hill in black stripes under the moon. One light burned in a kitchen window. It was nearly two in the morning.

The door opened before she could knock. A man in his late sixties in a cardigan over pyjamas, with a torch, looked at her, and at the car, and at the shirtsleeve tied round the arm of the man she was holding up.

“Kwok’s girl,” he said. “The one with the red car.”

“I’m sorry to come like this.”

“Lok.” He held the door wide. “Kwok rang an hour ago and said someone might. Bring him in. Mind the step, it’s older than me.”

No questions. Just a door held open, and the smell of tea and woodsmoke, and on the shelf in the front room, in front of a small dish of oranges, a photograph of a man who looked exactly like Mr. Kwok if Mr. Kwok had ever learned to sit still.

She got Haozhen onto the narrow bed in the back room. Uncle Lok brought a basin of warm water and a clean towel and a jar of salt and set them down without a word. Then he went to the window and drew the curtain, and stood there with his hand on it for a while.

“Is anyone coming after you?”

“I don’t know,” said Serafina.

“Then I’ll sit up.” He went to fetch a chair.

Haozhen’s eyes were on her. Not the window, not the door. Her.

“You came home,” she said. Home was a long way off. This was a dead man’s house on a mountain, and both of them were covered in someone else’s blood and their own. She said it anyway.

“Yes,” he said. “I came home.”

chapters.title: The Safe House in the Mountains
chapters.desc: A stone house above the tea terraces at Yunwu, a dead man’s photograph on the shrine, two deaf neighbours who bring eggs and ask nothing, a stray dog that stops dead in front of you, and rain on a tin roof. A fever, and then fourteen days with nowhere to be. The best two weeks of their lives.
chapters.epigraph: “The garage. Under the bridge.”
chapters.content:
The house above Yunwu had a tin roof, which they found out at three in the morning on Sunday, when the rain came.

By then the arm had been cleaned twice. The old doctor from the village below had come up the lane at half past four on the first morning with a leather bag and a torch, because Uncle Lok had woken him, and he’d looked at the two holes in Haozhen’s arm and grunted, and said he had stitched up tea pickers and miners and once a man who had argued with a tractor, and he didn’t write things down. The round had gone through the meat above the elbow and missed the bone and the big vessel by the width of a finger. He left the exit wound open to drain, put three stitches in the front, and gave Serafina a brown bottle of tablets, a bag of gauze, and instructions.

“Boil water. Cool it. One spoon of salt to the cup. Wash it out twice a day, morning and night, and look at it every time. Red spreading, smell, pus, call me. Fever tonight, expect it. Fever on the third day, call me.” He looked at Haozhen. “You’ll want to argue with her. Don’t.”

Serafina wrote it all on the back of a fuel receipt and stuck it to the wall above the bed with a piece of tape.

She did it exactly. Twice a day she boiled the water in Uncle Lok’s dented pan and let it cool and measured the salt with a spoon, and knelt by the bed and peeled the dressing back, and washed the holes out with a clean cloth while he looked at the ceiling.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

She looked at him.

“Some.”

“Thank you for being honest.” She dabbed. His jaw tightened and nothing else moved. “You’re allowed to make a noise.”

“I know.”

“I’d prefer it. When you’re quiet I think you’ve died.”

He made a noise, small and dry. She laughed in spite of herself, and wrapped it, and kissed the inside of his good wrist.

The fever came that night, as promised, and the next, and the one after.

On the first night he was only hot and restless, kicking the blanket off and asking for it back. On the second he talked. Not to her. In fragments: a time, a street, a number, stay down, don’t cross, not that door, and once in a voice she’d never heard from him, high and young, I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I didn’t look. He tried to get up with his bad arm and she caught his shoulder and held him down with her whole weight.

“Hao. It’s me.”

His eyes were open and didn’t see her. “Stay in the car.”

“I’m here. Look at me.”

“Don’t cross.”

She put her palm flat on his burning cheek and turned his face to hers. “Haozhen. You’re in a stone house on a mountain. There’s a dead man’s photograph in the front room and a man called Lok asleep in a chair. It’s raining. You’re with me.”

Slowly, something came into his eyes. “Sera.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her as if he had to make sure. Then his face broke, not into tears, quite. Something in it let go, and he turned his mouth into her hand.

“Don’t go.”

“I’m not going anywhere.”

He fell asleep with her fingers in his fist. She didn’t take them back until it was light.

On the third night he was quiet, which was worse. She sat by the bed with a book she didn’t read a word of and took his temperature every hour with the glass thermometer Uncle Lok had found in a drawer, and wrote the numbers under the doctor’s instructions. Thirty-nine point one. Thirty-nine point four. At two in the morning, thirty-eight point six. At five, thirty-seven nine. At six he opened his eyes and said, in his own voice, “Have you slept?”

“You’re in no position to ask.”

“You’re lying.”

“So are you. Shut up.” She put his good hand against her cheek. “Sleep.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth day he slept for eight hours in a bed. She knew because she had meant to lie down for ten minutes beside him and woke at ten in the morning in full sun, with the rain gone and the room bright and his breathing slow and even next to her, and not a mark of struggle on his face.

She lay still and looked at him.

When he woke he looked at the window, and frowned. “What time is it?”

“Ten.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Because you’re an idiot.” She kissed him. “Eight hours, Hao.”

He thought about it. “That seems excessive.”

The dog came that afternoon. She found it in the courtyard, a thin brown thing with one white front paw, standing exactly in the middle of the flagstones and staring at her as if she’d arranged the weather. She put down a bowl of rice and fish scraps from Uncle Lok’s pot. It ate everything and stayed.

When Haozhen came out, moving slowly, with his arm in its sling and one hand on the doorframe, the dog walked straight up to him and stopped dead in front of him. Not a step closer, not a step back. Exactly in his way.

He sat down on the stone step. The dog sat too. They looked at each other.

“He’s suspicious,” said Haozhen.

“You’re projecting.”

The dog leaned forward and smelled his good hand. Then it put its head on his knee and shut its eyes.

Haozhen went still. “What do I do?”

“Nothing. He’s chosen you.” She folded her arms. “What’s he called?”

“Brake,” he said, after a moment.

“Why?”

“Because he stopped in front of me.”

“That’s terrible.”

The dog’s tail went once against the flagstones.

“Brake it is,” she said.

By the third day Brake had decided the courtyard was his. By the fifth he had appointed himself to Haozhen’s recovery and barked whenever Haozhen tried to walk further than the wall.

The neighbours came every morning: an old couple from the house below the terraces, both deaf, who talked to each other with their hands so fast it looked like weather. The woman brought eggs, too many eggs, and the man brought spring onions and greens tied with grass. They never asked a single thing. Once a jar of honey appeared on the step with a note in shaky capitals, FOR COUGH, though nobody had coughed. Haozhen tried to pay them. The woman pointed at him, then at the house, then at the bed, then made a short chopping gesture with the side of her hand that Serafina translated as lie down before I hit you with this basket.

He lay down.

Uncle Lok came up the lane at seven every evening with a pot of soup and sat with them while they ate it, and told them about the brother, Mr. Kwok’s elder brother, who had grown tea on these terraces for forty years and liked to fish and had never once in his life learned to drive.

“Kwok did all the driving,” he said. “For both of them. Forty years in a taxi. His brother said one wheel in the family was enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth day the doctor took the stitches out and said he could get it wet if he didn’t do anything stupid.

The pool was below the terraces, where the stream came down through the rocks into a bowl of grey stone, so clear she could see every pebble on the bottom and so cold that when she stepped in to her knees she swore out loud.

“No,” he said, from the bank.

“The doctor said wet.”

“He said nothing stupid.”

“Standing in water isn’t stupid.”

“It is when it’s that colour.”

She waded out to her waist and turned round and looked at him. Then she took her shirt off, and threw it at the rock beside him, where it landed on Brake.

He looked at her. Then he unbuttoned his own shirt one-handed, folded it on the rock with great care, and came down into the water with his left arm held up against his chest like a man carrying something he couldn’t put down, and his breath went out of him in a shocked white rush.

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Liar.”

“Yes.” He came to her anyway. He stood in front of her up to his waist in the moving water with his bad arm lifted clear, and she put her hands on his shoulders and felt him shaking, and it wasn’t only the cold.

“Hello,” she said.

He kissed her. His mouth was warm and the water was freezing and she laughed into it and he made a sound and pulled her in with his good arm so hard that a small wave went over the rocks. She wrapped her legs round his waist under the water. He held her up one-handed with his palm spread under her, the other arm still held out to the side like a wing, absurd and careful, and kissed her throat, and her collarbone, and her mouth again, until she couldn’t feel the cold at all.

When they came out, Brake had the towels. One was in his mouth.

“Thief,” said Haozhen.

Brake sat on the other one.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night the rain came back. It drummed on the tin, ran in the gutters, filled the courtyard with the smell of wet earth. The lamp by the bed was on its lowest, and the mosquito net hung round them from the hook in the beam, pale and stirring when the wind found the window.

He lay on his back. She lay along his side with her hand on his chest, careful of the sling.

“Are you awake?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” She sat up and pulled her T-shirt over her head.

He looked at her in the low light and didn’t say anything at all.

“Don’t move your arm,” she said. “Don’t help me. Don’t decide anything. Lie there.”

“Sera—”

“That’s an order.” She took his good hand and put it on the pillow above his head, and leaned down and kissed him, slowly, the way you would kiss someone you had nearly lost and found again on a mountain. Then she moved down.
