She kissed the bruise that had spread yellow and green along his ribs from the seatbelt, and the old white scar on his forearm, and the place under his navel where the hair began, and pulled the drawstring of his trousers with her teeth.

His breath stopped. She took him in her hand and then in her mouth, unhurried, while the rain came down on the roof, and his good hand left the pillow and came to her hair and didn’t push, only held on. She looked up at him once. His head was back, his throat working, his eyes shut tight.

“Look at me.”

He looked.

She sat up, and slid her knickers off, and straddled him, mindful of the arm, one hand flat on his chest to keep him there. Then she lowered herself onto him slowly, all the way, and they both made the same sound.

She didn’t hurry. She rode him in long slow strokes, her other hand braced on the wall above his good shoulder, his palm spread on her hip, feeling him try not to move up into her and fail and try again. When he tensed she stopped and waited, and kissed him, and began again. The net swayed round them. Somewhere below, Brake turned over in his sleep and sighed. She felt it start in her like a long bend taken flat, and leaned back with both hands on his thighs and let it come, and came hard with her head back and his name in her mouth, and his hips came up off the bed once, twice, and he followed her with a hoarse sound that was nearly a sob.

She lay down on his good side with her heart going like an engine.

“I like this,” he said, after a long time. He sounded surprised.

“Being looked after?”

“Not having to earn it.”

She kissed his shoulder. “You’ll get used to it.”

“I don’t think so.”

“Then I’ll keep doing it till you do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The radio was on in the kitchen when she came down the next morning, an old portable set on the shelf with its aerial taped. The local station, the weather, the price of tea. Then: The driver injured in Saturday night’s collision on the old coast road has survived. The man, in his thirties, suffered a broken leg and burns to one hand, and remains in hospital. Police are asking any witnesses to come forward.

Nothing about a van. Nothing about a tunnel. Nothing about a Bureau.

Haozhen was on the stairs. He had heard it.

She turned it off. “He’s alive.”

“Broken leg.”

“And a hand.”

He came down the rest of the way and sat at the table, and she put tea in front of him. He looked at it.

“I thought he was dead,” he said. “On the gravel. Before he spoke.”

“So did I.”

“I don’t know what I feel.”

“You don’t have to. Not today.” She sat opposite and put her hand over his.

On the eleventh morning she came down and found him at the kitchen table with one of the two notebooks he had brought in his bag, writing, slowly, with his bad arm resting in its sling on the wood.

She read over his shoulder. At the top of the page, in his small square capitals: WEDDING.

Date. Guests. Food. Registry. Venue.

“We’re hiding on a mountain,” she said.

“We’re staying somewhere private.”

“That’s hiding.”

“It’s temporary.” He turned the page. There was one line on it.

The garage. Under the bridge.

She sat down next to him without meaning to.

“There’s a leak over the lift,” she said.

“We’ll fix it.”

“There’s an oil stain on the floor that’ll never come out.”

“It’s where I knelt.”

She stopped. It was. The eleventh of March, last year, by the glovebox, in her oil, with a ring on her little finger because he’d guessed her size wrong.

“Mr. Kwok will want nine courses. Granny Shum will bring clementines. Mouse will complain about the chairs. You’ll have to wear a proper suit.”

“Yes.”

“Then that’s where.”

He wrote Yes next to it, which she thought was unnecessary, and like him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourteenth day, a car came up the mountain.

Brake heard it first and stood up with his ears flat. Then she heard it: a big engine taking the bends slowly. A black car with tinted windows stopped at the bottom of the lane where the tarmac ended, and two men got out.

The first was Chen Si, in a plain dark coat, with his still hands in his pockets. The second was taller and broader, in a beige suit with the collar open, rings on his fingers, one strand of black hair falling over his forehead that he pushed back as he came up the lane between the tea. Serafina had seen him twice, at her sister’s parties, always by a door.

“Zhao Zhendong,” Haozhen said, low. He stood up. Brake planted himself in front of him.

Chen Si came into the courtyard and looked first at the sling, then at the dog, then at Serafina.

“He’s being treated?”

“By a man who writes nothing down.”

“Good.” He looked at Haozhen. “You’ve been hard to find.”

“That was the point.”

“Two weeks. Aurelia hasn’t slept.” Chen Si glanced round the courtyard, at the tin roof, at the deaf couple’s eggs in a bowl on the step. Something in his face eased by a degree. “Kwok’s brother’s house. I should have guessed sooner.”

Zhao Zhendong had stopped at the gate and was looking back down the lane, the way Haozhen would have. He turned round.

“You were looking for a door,” he said. “When you went into her office with that page. Si told me.” He pushed the strand of hair back again. “We think we’ve found one.”

“What door?”

“Not out here,” said Chen Si.

Haozhen felt the old reflex rise in him: send her inside. Decide what she should know. Go and meet the danger somewhere she wasn’t. He looked at the open notebook on the kitchen table through the doorway, and the one line in it.

“Here,” he said. “With her. Or not at all.”

Chen Si looked at him. Then at Serafina, whose hand had found Haozhen’s good one.

“All right,” he said. “Here.”

“Tea first,” said Serafina. “Then you can tell us why you drove up a mountain. And nobody gets anything stronger until I like the answer.”

For the first time, Zhao Zhendong smiled.

chapters.title: A Truce in the Tea Terraces
chapters.desc: A black car in the tea terraces. A minister who has tea with Aurelia on the first Thursday of every month. A month of waiting, and then a quiet room in the old town where everything he ever wrote down goes into a stove. Two prices. He pays them both without asking. That night, at last, she asks him for the number, and he tells her.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m not going to tell you it was fine.”
chapters.content:
“There’s a man who taught the minister,” Chen Si said, “before the minister was anybody.”

They were at the kitchen table in the stone house, the four of them, with Uncle Lok’s teapot between them and the rain starting again on the tin. Zhao Zhendong had taken the chair facing the door without asking. Brake had taken the space under it.

“He’s eighty-one. He grows orchids. He has no office and no title, and nobody in the capital does anything that matters without wondering what he’ll think of it.” Chen Si turned his cup a quarter turn. “Aurelia has tea with the minister on the first Thursday of every month. Has done for six years. They talk about his granddaughter’s violin and her gold. She has never once asked him for anything.” He looked at Haozhen. “Three weeks ago she asked.”

“She showed him the index.”

“She showed it to his teacher. My copy. Not your notebooks. Nothing with her sister’s name on it.” He looked at Serafina, and back. “He read it at his kitchen table in an afternoon. Then he rang the minister and said one word, which I’m told was Northgate, and put the phone down.”

“And?”

“And the people above Duan would very much prefer an internal review to a scandal. They’re frightened. Not of you. Of what’s under you.” Chen Si laid a thin folder on the table. “These are terms. Not a promise. You’d be a fool to trust it.”

“Then why bring it?”

“Because terms are better than a van in a tunnel.”

He read it twice. Resignation accepted. Records sealed. An independent review of every payment through Northgate Advisory, under the teacher’s eye. The private cases reopened. And a name, typed in a column by itself: Gong Ruiming. Release to be confirmed.

“He’s alive.”

“He’s been in a building in the north since July. He told them nothing. Not one name.” Chen Si watched him read it again. “And the Director retires. Quietly. With a pension, and an orchid from the old man, which I’m told is not a compliment.”

“What do they want?”

“Two things.” Chen Si didn’t look away. “I’ll tell you the first when it’s time. The second is mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove home in Nobody on the first day of May with Brake on the back seat, his head out of the window, ears flying, and Uncle Lok waving from the lane until the bend took him. The deaf couple had left a dozen eggs on the bonnet.

Jinx was waiting in the garage when they came under the shutter, sitting on Nonna’s bonnet with her arms folded, and Raiden beside her with a box of pastries. She got down without a word and walked round the taxi once. She stopped at the front passenger door. Two holes, neat as punched paper, one below the window and one through the pillar.

“Two,” she said.

“I know.”

“In my car.”

“I know.”

“I built her to be invisible.” Jinx put her finger in the lower hole. It went in to the knuckle. “Somebody looked at her anyway.”

“She was invisible,” Haozhen said. “Until I put my arm out of the window.”

Jinx turned away and walked three steps toward the workbench and stood with her back to them. Her shoulders moved.

“Oh, Jinx.”

“I’m not crying. I’m angry. It’s different.” She wiped her face on her sleeve, furiously, and turned round and walked straight into Haozhen and put her arms round him hard enough to make him grunt, then let go of his left side as if it had burned her, and grabbed Serafina instead and held on.

“Don’t,” she said into Serafina’s hair. “Either of you. Ever again.”

“We’ll try.”

“Try harder.” She stepped back. “I’m not filling them. The holes. I’ll paint round them. People should know she’s been shot at and kept going.”

Raiden opened the pastry box. Brake ate one before anyone saw him move.

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother rang on the Monday, at twenty past nine in the morning, which she never did.

“There’s a man been,” she said. “In a good suit. He carried a sewing machine up my stairs.”

He was standing at the workbench. He put down what he was holding carefully. “What man?”

“From your office, he said. For your years of service. A big electric one, a proper one, the kind the factory had. He set it up for me by the window and threaded it.” She sounded pleased, and puzzled, and far away. “He knew which stair creaks. He stepped over it.”

“Ma. Did he leave a card?”

“For the hands that taught you. Nice handwriting.” A pause. “Haozhen. You told me you guard doors.”

“I do.”

“He asked if you still came for my birthday. I said every year. He said that was good. That a son should know where his mother lives.” Another pause. “I didn’t like how he said it.”

“Don’t use it,” he said. “Don’t touch it. Put the old one back where it was. Lock the door at night.”

“I always lock the door.”

“Lock it twice.”

When he put the phone down Serafina was already beside him. She had heard half of it, and the half she heard was enough.

“They walked into her flat.”

“They threaded it for her.” He was looking at nothing. “They put it by her window. So they’d know which window.”

She took his phone off the bench and turned it face down. Then she took both his hands.

“They aren’t sending her a machine. They’re telling you she’s in reach. And you’re going to let them think it worked, and you’re going to ring the tailor downstairs, and he’s going to photograph it and carry it out of her flat by lunchtime and put it in his back room with the suit lengths.”

“Yes.”

“And you are not going to drive north tonight and sit on her stairs with a gun.”

He didn’t answer.

“Hao.”

“No,” he said. “I’m not.”

“Say why.”

“Because that’s what they want.”

“Good.” She put her forehead against his. “They’re using the fact that you love her. Don’t let them make you ashamed of it.”

The tailor had the machine out by half past twelve. Liang Shufen rang again at one to say he’d been polite and had taken his shoes off at the door, which was more than the first man had done.

✦ ✦ ✦

May went slowly. Chen Si went to the capital and came back and went again. Aurelia had her tea on Thursday the second, and talked about the violin, and on her way out the minister walked her to the lift himself, which he had never done. Mouse kept working through what was left of the money trail. Jinx painted round the holes. Serafina tested at the circuit in the south and kept her days short, and Haozhen sat in the garage and was forbidden by everyone to lift anything heavier than a cup.

In the third week a photograph came through on Chen Si’s phone. A man in a plain room with a cup of tea in his hands. Thinner. Older. Shaved too close by someone else’s razor. Alive.

Haozhen looked at it.

“His son?” Serafina said.

“In Lisbon. With his mother.” He put the phone down. “He’ll be home by June.”

He didn’t call it a victory. He had no right to. But somewhere a boy would have a father in the doorway again, and the football would hit the wall instead of a window.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Tuesday in May, Chen Si took them to a tea house in the old town after it closed.

It had a back room with a cast-iron stove, cold since March. A man of about sixty in a grey cardigan was sitting on a hard chair beside it with his hands on his knees. He didn’t give his name. He had a typed list and a pencil.

“The first price,” said Chen Si. “The review keeps sealed copies of everything it needs. Your index. Mouse’s map. Under the old man’s eye. Nobody else keeps anything. No private record of state work exists anywhere outside that room in the capital. Not under a cat. Not behind a door bar.”

“So they burn,” said Serafina.

“So they burn. In front of him.”

Haozhen had brought them in a holdall. Twenty-three notebooks, worn at the corners, one with a water stain like a map, one with its spine taped. Big Wu had cut the copy out of Gilded’s roll cage that afternoon and sealed the foam again. Jinx had unscrewed the box under Nobody’s seat. Qian had brought the third himself, from the safe on the forty-fourth floor, and handed it over without a word.

The man in the cardigan ticked each one off his list. Then he lit the stove.

The first notebook caught slowly. The edges went brown and curled back and the small square handwriting stood out black against the flame for a second before it went. He fed in the second, and the third. The room filled with the smell of old paper. Serafina stood with her shoulder against his and didn’t speak.

He held the fourth a moment longer. D.Q.Y. Private, in the margin, in pencil. Then it went.

When the last copy had burned he took the index page out of his jacket. NORTHGATE across the top. He held it until the man in the cardigan looked up.

Then he let go of it, and watched it fold in on itself and disappear.

“That’s the first,” said Chen Si.

“And the second.”

“The second is mine.” Chen Si looked at Serafina, and then at him. “You tell her. Everything. Before you marry her. Not what you think she can carry. Not names; I don’t care about names. The number. And the part you’ve never said out loud.”

“That’s between us.”

“It is. That’s why I want it said by you, and not read in a file in ten years’ time by a woman who thinks she was lied to.” He stood and buttoned his coat. “Everything else could be negotiated. This couldn’t. Goodnight.”

He went out. The man in the cardigan raked the ash, and nodded to them both, and went out after him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t ask in the car. She didn’t ask when they came in under the shutter, or when she put the kettle on, or when he stood at the workbench with his hands flat on it for long enough that she knew he was waiting to be asked.

She asked at eleven, sitting on the bottom step of the iron stairs with a cup going cold in her hands.

“How many?”

He’d been waiting for it since January the fourteenth of last year. He told her.

“Thirty-eight. People I took, or moved, or handed to someone. That’s the ones I touched. Not everyone the work reached.”

She held the cup. “And you killed.”

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Two.”

“With your own hands.”

“Yes.”

“Tell me.”

He sat on the floor with his back against Gilded’s door, facing her, and told her.

The first time he was twenty-one. A man who had got out of a holding flat in a port city with a kitchen knife and a guard’s pistol. A concrete stairwell. The light on a timer that went off every forty seconds. They were on the landing between the fourth and fifth floors when the light went off, and he heard the man come down at him in the dark, and he fired once, upward, from the hip, and when the light came back on the man was sitting against the wall with his hands in his lap as if he’d been waiting for a bus. He had been twenty-six. He’d had a photograph of a woman in his shoe.

“I sat with him till the team came,” Haozhen said. “Nobody told me to. I thought somebody should.”

The second time he was twenty-five, and nobody had ordered it. A man in a car park with a girl of nineteen in the boot of his car, and a phone call telling Haozhen to wait for a second team, ninety minutes out. He hadn’t waited. He’d come up behind the man while he was lighting a cigarette and put him on the concrete, and the man had gone for something under his jacket, and Haozhen had broken his neck. It had taken less time than lighting the cigarette.

“The first, I was sorry the moment it happened,” he said. “The second took me three years. I don’t know if I’m sorry for him or only for what it taught me I could do.”

She didn’t say anything. The fridge hummed. A train went over.

“Did you ever want to?” she said. “Not because of an order. Just want to.”

“Once.”

“Who?”

“The woman who put forty photographs on our bench,” he said. “In December. For about an hour.”

She looked at him then, a long, white, steady look, the look she gave a corner she’d never driven before. She was trying to put the man on the floor next to the one who’d slept two hours and eleven minutes in her passenger seat, and discovering that she didn’t have to put them next to each other, because they were the same man. That was the hard part.

“I’m not going to tell you it was fine,” she said.

“I know.”

“I’m not going to tell you that loving you makes them any less dead. And I’m not going to spend my life making you feel forgiven. That isn’t my job.”

“No.”

“Don’t call the bullet even. Or the fever. Or the years of not sleeping. You don’t get to suffer your way to square.”

“I know.”

She put the cup down on the step. She stood up and walked away from him, across the floor, past Nonna, to Gilded’s open door, and looked at the little grey toy taxi on the dashboard. Then at the chipped mug by the sink. Then at the oil stain where he’d knelt.

He didn’t move. He had imagined this a hundred ways. In some of them she shouted. In some she walked out under the shutter. In the worst one she looked at him with the careful politeness of people who had worked out that he wasn’t safe to be near.

She came back and stood over him.

“I’m deciding again,” she said. “Not because of Chen Si. Not because of thirty-eight or two. Because I know who I’m deciding about now.”

“Sera—”

“Let me finish. I don’t know if I’ll ever be comfortable with all of it. I don’t think I’m supposed to be.” She crouched in front of him, so their eyes were level. “But I want you. I want the man who sat in that stairwell till the team came. I want him to marry me in this garage under that bridge. And I want him to ask me properly, because the first time he asked me he hadn’t told me any of this.”

He looked at her. His eyes had gone bright.

Then he got up onto one knee on the concrete, on the same stain, and took the ruby off her finger, and held it.

“Serafina Song. I’ve told you everything. Will you marry me?”

“Yes,” she said, and held out her hand, and he put it back where it belonged. “Yes, Haozhen. Get up. You’ll ruin your trousers.”

He didn’t get up. He put his face against her stomach and held on, and she stood in the middle of her garage with her hands in his hair while another train went over, and let him.

chapters.title: Disavowed
chapters.desc: Nine quiet months: a championship, a prize in Geneva, a man learning to sleep six hours and cook. Then a registered letter from the capital informs him that no person called Qin Haozhen has ever existed, and asks him to sign to confirm he received it. For the first time in years, he laughs until he can’t stand up. And with it comes a parcel, two metres long, in red wool.
chapters.epigraph: “For the first who walked out.”
chapters.content:
By the end of June he could make an omelette.

It wasn’t a good omelette. The edges were ragged and the middle was sometimes still wet and once, answering a question about tyre pressures, he burned the bottom of it black. But it was edible, and Serafina, sitting on the bench in one of his shirts with her bare heels against the cupboard door, ate the whole thing and said, “Acceptable.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t get confident. It’s brown.”

“Eggs go brown.”

“Not that brown.” She stole the crispest corner off his plate while he watched, which was the other thing he’d learned: she liked hers soft, she needed salt in before the pan and not after, and she would always take the best bit of his if he wasn’t paying attention.

He started paying attention so he could let her.

There had been a time when a morning like this would have felt like something he was getting away with. A morning with no operational phone, no report to file, nobody waiting at the far end of a car park. He’d have found a reason to leave before the coffee. Now he made the coffee, in a machine he’d bought because the old one had leaked onto her invoices for four years.

“You asked me if you could buy it,” she said, looking at it.

“Yes.”

“It was already on the counter when you asked.”

“I wanted to see if you’d changed your mind.”

He spent money that summer on things that didn’t protect anyone or hide anything or lead to an exit. A heater for the office. New strip lights. Steel shelving for her tools so that she would stop keeping torque wrenches in the bread bin. The roof over the back bench mended properly, not with the patch she’d sworn was fine. A mattress for the loft, because she’d once said the old one was trying to kill her. He showed her every invoice before he paid it, and paid it from his own account, which was now only his own account, with no second line coming into it every few months marked allowance.

He learned to sleep. Not every night, not without waking. Some nights he still came up out of the dark at four with his heart going, reaching for a sound that wasn’t there. But six hours became possible, and then usual. Once, after a fourteen-hour day helping Big Wu with a gearbox, he slept for seven hours and eleven minutes, and Serafina photographed him with his mouth open and sent it to Mouse.

Rare species, Mouse wrote back. Do not disturb habitat.

He deleted the photograph from her phone. She had already sent it to Aurelia.

He bought a cookbook. A fat one with pictures, written for people who had an ordinary relationship with food. She found it by his mug and opened it and looked at him.

“So you don’t have to,” he said, before she could ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

The season went the way she liked best, which was badly for her nerves. The Asian series was close all year. Every round mattered. A blown tyre, a poor qualifying lap, one lock-up at the wrong corner, and the title could go.

He went to every round he could and learned to sit in the garage and do nothing, which was the hardest thing anyone had ever asked of him. He learned that when she came in angry she didn’t want advice. Sometimes she wanted water. Sometimes she wanted him to hold her helmet while she explained, at length and with diagrams drawn on a tyre in chalk, why the car had pushed through the last sector. He learned to tell which.

At the second-to-last round she climbed out of Gilded and pulled off her helmet and stared at the timing tower.

“Four points.”

“Between you and him?”

“Four points between me and the whole year.” She pushed her hair back. “I need four more.”

“Then you need to finish ahead of him.”

“That’s all? You’re a genius.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By who?”

“Nobody.”

“That’s a taxi.”

“She’s a good judge of character,” he said, and she laughed for the first time all weekend and leaned against him with her face in his shirt.

The final round was at the circuit in the south at the end of September. She didn’t need to win. She needed to beat one car, a white works coupé driven by a man who had been racing since she was six, and he qualified in front of her. For forty laps she sat behind him and didn’t waste her tyres on a move that wasn’t there, and Mouse said almost nothing on the radio, because there was nothing to say, and Haozhen stood on the pit wall with his hands behind his back and didn’t look at his phone once.

On the last lap, at the long right-hander before the pit straight, the white car ran a fraction wide. She was on the inside before he had finished making the mistake. He tried to come back at her on the exit. She had the better drive and held him by a nose to the line.

Second in the race. Champion by four points.

The garage came apart. Mouse shrieked down the headset so loud the engineer from the next team flinched. Aurelia hugged Qian, who allowed it. Jinx climbed onto a tyre trolley to see better and fell off it. Mr. Kwok, who had said all weekend that he wasn’t nervous, sat down on an upturned crate and said something to the sky that made Big Wu cover his mother’s ears.

Haozhen didn’t move. Then she came down the pit lane with her helmet in one hand and her hair stuck flat to her forehead and saw him, and he opened his arms, and she ran the last ten metres and hit him so hard he took a step back.

“Champion,” he said into her hair.

“By four points.”

“Four points.”

Somebody shook a bottle and sprayed it over both of them. He felt it run down the back of his shirt. She took his face in her wet hands and kissed him in front of the team, the cameras, the white works car’s whole crew, and he didn’t turn his face away from any of them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Geneva was in October. Aurelia’s eleven pieces had been made from every second-place medal she’d ever been given, and she’d been shortlisted for the oldest prize in the jewellery world, and Serafina flew out with Haozhen two days before the ceremony and spent them walking round the lake and not talking about the one thing.

Their parents would be in the front row. Aurelia had sent them each an envelope with a card that said only I’d like you to be there, and both had answered. Serafina had been sent the same card, and had said yes, and booked the flight, and then spent fourteen months not deciding whether she could sit three seats from her mother in a dark hall and be polite.

On the night, in the hotel, she sat on the end of the bed in a borrowed dress with her shoes in her hand.

“I can’t go in.”

“Then don’t.”

“She’s my sister.”

“She’s your sister,” he agreed. “She’ll be the same sister in the foyer.”

They watched it on the screen in the lobby outside the main hall, side by side on a leather bench with the doors closed and the noise coming through them, he in a dark suit and no tie with his back to the wall and both exits in view, she with her shoes still in her hand. He had chosen the bench because no photographer would think to stand there. She had chosen it because nobody in the front row could turn round and see her.

When the presenter read the name, Serafina stood up so fast she dropped both shoes.

On the screen Aurelia walked to the stage in black with nothing at her throat. She talked about a shoebox. She didn’t mention a bridge, or four towers, or a pen engraved 7, or a man called Northgate. She didn’t need to. Serafina cried in the lobby with her hand over her mouth, and a waiter with a tray of glasses looked at her and at the man beside her, and sensibly walked the other way.

Aurelia came out twenty minutes later with the medal in her hand, and looked at them both on the leather bench, and didn’t ask why they hadn’t been in the room.

“You heard?”

“Every word,” said Serafina, and put her arms round her, medal and all.

Over her sister’s shoulder she saw, through the closing door, the back of a woman in dark blue in the front row, upright, alone. Her mother didn’t turn round. Serafina didn’t call out. The door swung shut.

“Next time,” Haozhen said, as they walked back along the lake.

“Maybe.”

“Maybe is a word.”

“Don’t quote me at me.” But she held his hand all the way to the hotel.

✦ ✦ ✦

By winter he was a competent cook. Not an adventurous one. He could make rice without reading the packet, soup that tasted of something, fish that wasn’t dry. He could tell when she was pretending not to be hungry. He still hated supermarkets. He still sat facing the door. He was no longer waiting to be sent somewhere.

The wedding moved twice. Once for the championship calendar. Once because of a form.

The registry wanted his identity card, his household register and a certificate saying he wasn’t already married. His identity card had come in an envelope from the Bureau at eighteen, along with his first pay. He had never seen a household register in his life. When Serafina rang the registry office in November to ask what to do, a woman read the number off his card, put her on hold for nine minutes, and came back to say there must be some mistake, because that number didn’t belong to anybody.

“They’re wiping him,” Mouse said, when Serafina told her.

“They’re tidying,” said Haozhen. He didn’t seem surprised. “It’s what you do when somebody leaves who was never there.”

The letter came on Monday the seventeenth of February 2025, by registered post. A thick cream envelope with the crest of a ministry in the capital, his name in capitals on the front. Serafina signed for it at the shutter and brought it in to him at the shelving, where he was putting up a bracket.

He wiped his hands and opened it standing up.

It was two pages. The language was immaculate. Following the conclusion of the relevant administrative review, the institution’s records had been reconciled. No person by the name of Qin Haozhen had at any time been employed by, contracted to, paid by, or known to the institution. Any document suggesting otherwise was to be regarded as erroneous. The recipient was asked to sign the enclosed slip, confirming receipt and understanding of this notice, and return it in the envelope provided.

He read it once. Then again.

“What does it say?”

He handed it to her. She read it and her face went perfectly blank.

“They’ve erased you.”

“Apparently.”

“They’re saying you never existed. And they want you to sign to say you got a letter telling you you don’t exist.”

He looked at the signature slip. The small box. The line for a name.

“Administrative efficiency,” he said.

Then she saw his mouth move.

It started as a breath. A small, disbelieving sound in his chest. He looked down at the letter again, at the box, at the line for the name they had just told him he didn’t have, and the sound came out of him properly.

He laughed.

He couldn’t stop. He put one hand flat on the bench and bent over it and laughed until he had to put the paper down, and his shoulders shook, and he slid down the front of the workbench and sat on the floor with his back against it and laughed until there were tears running down his face. Eleven years of writing down what they wanted forgotten. Thirty-eight people moved out of the world by a man who had now officially never been in it. A stamped, numbered, registered letter, sent at the state’s expense, so that a man who didn’t exist could confirm in writing that he had received it.

She stared at him. Then she sat down on the floor in front of him and started laughing too. Not because it was funny. Because he was laughing, the way she’d never once heard him laugh, with his whole body, like a boy.

The side door banged. Mouse came in with a box of cable ties.

“What happened?”

Neither of them could answer. Mouse picked the letter up off the bench and read it, and read it again, and put the box down slowly.

“They want you to sign?”

He nodded, helplessly.

Mouse made a sound like a kettle and sat down on the floor too.

She sent one message: Garage. Now. You need to see this. Within the hour Aurelia was there, and Qian, and Jinx and Raiden, and Big Wu with his mother’s thermos, and Mr. Kwok with his reading glasses. The letter went round. Aurelia read it white with fury and then had to turn her back. Qian read it and said, thoughtfully, “That’s actually very good drafting.” Jinx read it twice and said, “Brilliant. So he doesn’t pay tax,” and Raiden said that wasn’t how tax worked, and Jinx said, “How would they know? He doesn’t exist,” and Big Wu laughed so hard he had to sit on Nonna’s bumper.

Haozhen was still on the floor. He reached for Serafina without getting up, and she came, and he pulled her down into his lap and wrapped both arms round her waist and kissed her while their entire team laughed around them, a long, warm, unhurried kiss with the letter crushed somewhere under her knee, until Mouse made a retching noise and threw a cable tie at them.

“You’re officially nobody,” Serafina said against his mouth.

“Then nobody loves you.”

“That’s a terrible line.”

“I’ve been saving it.”

The slip stayed on the bench, unsigned. It still is.

✦ ✦ ✦

The parcel came on Tuesday morning. Nearly two metres long, in brown paper tied with red string, propped against the shutter by a courier who hadn’t waited for a signature. No return address. His name in a hand he knew.

It was light. Inside, under a layer of tissue, folded back and forth on itself, was the scarf.

It was finished. The long ribbed red he had watched grow in a grey office in May, and in December on their bench while she laid out forty photographs of his mother, and again in February on the seventh floor while she read the word Northgate. It ran through his hands like a long red road. At one end, where it finished, she had worked a small change into the rib in darker wool: a figure seven.

A card was tucked into the fold.

For the first who walked out.

No signature. He didn’t need one.

“Is it from her?” Serafina said.

“Yes.”

“What does it mean?”

He looked at the seven. Serafina’s number. The number on the pen in her jacket. “I don’t know. Goodbye. Or sorry. Or I can still find you.” He turned it over. “Or that she’s been in that room for thirty years, and nobody ever walked out of it before.”

“Do you want to keep it?”

He thought about burning it. He thought about it for some time.

“Yes,” he said.

“Why?”

“Because she made it with her own hands while she was deciding what to do with me. And she finished it.” He folded it carefully, the seven on top. “I’d like to know that she knows I left.”

He didn’t put it on. He laid it on the workbench, folded, beside the chipped white mug with his name on the bottom, and left it there. The letter that said he had never existed lay beside it, unsigned.

In the morning he made her an omelette. It was too brown. She complained, and ate it.

chapters.title: A Man With No File
chapters.desc: A mining town that the maps stopped bothering with, a registry clerk who remembers a boy on the wall by the winding gear, and his mother at her Japanese sewing machine, who has never once believed he was a security guard. Then a driving test he fails for checking his mirrors too often. And Harbour Road, on a Friday afternoon, holding her hand where anyone can see.
chapters.epigraph: “Now I exist.”
chapters.content:
The town was smaller than he remembered every time he came back, and he said so every time, and this time she was there to hear it.

“Maybe it shrank,” she said.

“Buildings don’t shrink.”

“How would you know? You only come once a year.”

It was the second Saturday in March, grey and cold, and the road narrowed after the last petrol station into a main street of shuttered shops and one bus stop with a timetable bleached white. Above the roofs the old mine stood against the hill, the headframe rusted the colour of dried blood, the great wheel at the top of it stopped. Once there had been three schools here, two cinemas and a railway station. Now the maps barely bothered with the name.

She had offered him the last stretch. He’d said no. Not because he didn’t trust himself to drive it. Because for once in his life he wanted to arrive as a passenger.

“Are you nervous?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said. “I was afraid you’d pretend.”

His mother lived above the tailor’s on the main street, up a flight of outside stairs with a pot of chrysanthemums on every third step and the fourth step from the top that creaked. He stepped over it without thinking. Serafina saw him do it and remembered why.

Liang Shufen opened the door before he knocked. She was small and square, sixty-four now, in a dark blue cardigan with a tape measure round her neck and a faint blue stain of tailor’s chalk on one thumbnail. She looked at her son.

“You’ve lost weight.”

“Hello, Ma.”

“Don’t hello me. Your face is thinner.”

“I’m older.”

“Older doesn’t make a face thinner.” Then her eyes went past him. “And you’re the one who isn’t patient.”

“Serafina.”

“I know your name. I’ve had it on the telephone every Sunday since December before last.” She looked her up and down, exactly as she’d looked at her son, and stepped aside. “Come in. Take your shoes off. Both of you.”

She saw the scar on his arm before he’d got his coat off. A pale pucker above the elbow at the front, a wider one behind.

“What’s that?”

“An accident.”

“What kind?”

“A car.”

She looked at him. He looked back.

“That’s a very poor explanation,” said his mother.

“I agree,” said Serafina, hanging up her coat.

Liang Shufen turned and regarded her with something that might, in time, become approval. “Good. Somebody in this family has sense.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat smelled of tea and rice and machine oil. Photographs on the wall: a boy of eleven with his hair cut far too short, scowling in a white shirt outside a railway station that no longer existed. A young woman in a factory overall at a bench of machines. No man in any of them; Serafina didn’t ask, and saw that he saw her not ask.

“He cried when I made him wear that shirt.”

“Ma.”

“And he wouldn’t smile.”

“Some things don’t change,” said Serafina, and his mother made a small sound that was nearly a laugh.

She looked at Serafina’s hands over the tea. “Do you sew?”

“Badly.”

“Show me.”

Serafina held out the cuff of her jacket, where she’d mended the lining herself in January. Liang Shufen turned it to the light from the window and examined it as if it were a piece of evidence.

“Uneven,” she said. “Too big here. Pulled too tight here, so it puckers. You sew like you drive.”

“How do I drive?”

“Your sister sent me the recording of the mountain race. You drive like somebody’s chasing you.” She put the cuff down. “I’ll show you how to do it properly after lunch. You can learn.”

He drank his tea and kept his face still. In every version of this he had ever imagined, bringing her here, nobody had criticised her stitches before lunch. He found he liked it more than any of them.

The machine sat by the window, under its fitted cover: the old heavy Japanese one with the black enamel body, the one she’d bought secondhand the year the factory closed. The new electric one was gone; Chen Si’s man had carried it down the stairs in May. She lifted the cover and turned the handwheel once, and it clicked, the same small sound he’d fallen asleep to on the floor beside it for most of his childhood.

“You still have the thread?”

“Thirty spools,” she said to Serafina. “He spent far too much. They’re in the drawer in colour order.” She threaded the needle without looking. “Where did you tell her you work, Haozhen?”

He was quiet. “She knows.”

“Good. Then you can stop telling me you guard doors.”

He went still.

“You were eighteen. You came home and said you’d found work in security, very important, protecting important people, sometimes you’d travel and couldn’t telephone.” She guided a strip of blue cotton under the foot. “I didn’t believe a word of it. Not for one day.”

“Why not?”

“Because you never looked like a boy who was protecting anybody.” The needle went down. “You looked like a boy waiting to be told what to do. You’ve looked like that since you were sixteen and they came to the school with a letter.” She didn’t look up. “Every time I asked, you said not to worry. So I stopped asking. I didn’t stop worrying.”

“Ma—”

“And then a man in a good suit carried a machine up my stairs, and stepped over the bad step, and I knew for certain.” She turned the cloth. “I don’t want to know all of it. I’m your mother, not your priest. But you can stop lying to me now. I’m sixty-four. I haven’t got time to be lied to.”

Serafina’s hand found his under the edge of the sewing table. He held on to it hard.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“You’re here.” She snapped the thread. “That’s sorry enough.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning they went to the registry office in the old municipal building.

He had no file. His identity card had come in an envelope from the Bureau at eighteen. In November, when the woman at the city registry had rung the number through, it belonged to nobody. In February, the state had written to tell him he had never existed. His licence had been issued against the same dead number, which meant that in law he had been driving without one since he was nineteen.

The clerk was in her sixties, with a grey bun and glasses on a chain. She looked at the forms, and then at his face over the top of them, and her own face changed.

“You’re Liang Shufen’s boy.”

“Yes.”

“You used to sit on the wall by the winding gear after school. Every day. Watching the wheel.” She was already getting up. “Never the men. Just the wheel.”

She came back from a back room with a ledger as long as her forearm, its cloth cover gone soft with handling. The old paper register, she said. From before they put everything on computers in 2003. When the town had been computerised every entry was copied across, and the paper kept in the cupboard, because nobody ever throws a register away.

She turned the pages. Her finger stopped.

Qin Haozhen. Male. Born 12 January 1994. Household: Liang Shufen. Place of birth: this district. In blue-black ink that had gone brown at the edges, in a careful hand, entered by somebody long retired on a February morning thirty-one years ago.

“Somebody’s been very busy on the computer,” the clerk said, and looked at him over her glasses. “Nobody’s touched the cupboard.”

He reached out, and stopped.

“May I?”

She nodded. He put one finger beside his name. A line in a book. It was older than every false document anyone had ever made for him. It had been there before the academy and the dormitory with the leaking roof, before the first van, before the first person anyone had told him to watch.

“Three weeks,” said the clerk. “Maybe four. There are a lot of forms.”

There were. Certified copies. Verification letters. Photographs. A statement from his mother, who wrote hers in ten minutes at the counter in a hand that put the clerk’s to shame. A box on page six asking whether the applicant had ever held another identity.

He looked at it for a while. Then he ticked Yes.

“Is it still in use?”

“No.”

“Do you wish to retain it?”

“No.”

The new number came in a sealed envelope on Thursday the third of April. He opened it at the garage table and looked at it and passed it to her without a word.

“Hello, Mr. Qin,” she said.

“Hello.”

“Do you feel different?”

“No.” He folded it. “Less temporary.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His mother had given her the quilt on the last morning, spread across the sewing table: dark blue and grey and cream and a green like the hills round the town. It looked like an ordinary patchwork until Serafina saw the stitching. A road wound through the middle of it in pale thread, climbing. A hairpin. A long left. A short straight. A tightening right over a crest, and a small embroidered flag at the top.

“Baizhang,” Serafina said. She couldn’t get any further.

“I watched it four times,” said Liang Shufen. “Your sister sent it. I wanted to see what my son was looking at.” She folded it into Serafina’s arms. “The stitches on the hairpin are uneven. That’s where you were going too fast.”

“I was going exactly fast enough.”

“I know. I was frightened anyway.” She turned to her son. “Carry it for her. And eat before you drive. And drive carefully.”

“Yes, Ma.”

“Don’t answer me like a clerk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He failed his driving test on Monday the seventh of April.

It was Serafina’s idea. “You need a licence,” she’d said, and he’d said he’d been driving for twelve years, and she’d said, “Under a dead number, with a relationship to traffic law that I’d describe as creative. Prove it.”

The examiner was a calm woman with a clipboard. Thirty-eight minutes. He reversed into a bay without looking at the camera. He did the hill start. He took the dual carriageway at exactly the limit and not a kilometre over.

At the debrief she was kind about it.

“Your observation is thorough,” she said. “Too thorough. You check your mirrors every three or four seconds even on a straight road with nothing behind you, and you looked over your shoulder twice at a red light. That isn’t a fault in itself.” She turned the sheet round. “But at the T-junction on the market road, with a clear gap to the right, you waited for a second clear gap, and then a third, checking your mirror each time. The car behind had to brake. I’ve had to mark that as undue hesitation, and because another road user had to react, it’s a serious fault.” She looked at him with real curiosity. “Can I ask what you were waiting for?”

He thought about it honestly. “Somebody to come round the corner.”

She wrote nothing down. “Try to wait for what’s actually there.”

Serafina was leaning on Nonna in the car park with two coffees. She took one look at his face.

“You failed.”

“Mirrors.”

She stared. Then she laughed so hard she had to put the coffees on the roof.

“You sat next to me at two hundred and sixty-four on the new bridge without blinking. You’ve been shot in a taxi. And you failed your test for looking.”

“For waiting.”

“For what?”

“For someone who wasn’t coming.”

She stopped laughing. She came and put her arms round him in the car park and held on.

He passed on Thursday the tenth. He’d spent the week practising nothing but a T-junction on the industrial estate, at night, with her in the passenger seat counting under her breath, one look right, one look left, one mirror, go. No less careful, only no longer driving as if he expected someone behind him with a gun.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday afternoon they walked down Harbour Road.

The sky was high and bright. The cafés had their tables out on the pavement. A cyclist rang his bell at a delivery van, two children went round and round a bench, and a man with a long lens by the railings was photographing the old ferry terminal.

He had one hand in his coat pocket. The other held hers. Not in a car, not behind a tyre stack or under a railway bridge. On the open pavement in the afternoon, with his thumb over her knuckles, where anyone could see.

“You’re doing it,” she said.

“I’ve held your hand before.”

“Not here.”

The man with the lens turned as they passed, and lifted the camera, and she felt it go through him: the half-step, the shoulder, the old turn of the face away. He didn’t turn. He didn’t let go.

The shutter went. Once. Twice.

“All right?” she said.

“Let him.”

At the railings he stopped, and looked at the water, and then at her, and there was no reason to check behind them and no reason to count the people going past. He put his hand on her cheek and bent his head and kissed her, on Harbour Road on a Friday afternoon, with strangers walking past and a man with a long lens three metres away and the gulls going over. She laughed against his mouth and caught his lapel and kissed him back.

“What was that for?”

“Now I exist,” he said.

“You always existed.”

“Not on paper.” He rested his forehead against hers. “My name is Qin Haozhen. I was born on the twelfth of January 1994 in a mining town. My mother thinks your stitches are terrible.”

“She’s right.”

“I’ve got a licence. You’ve got a championship. And you’re going to marry me.”

“Yes.”

The shutter went once more. This time he looked straight at it, and didn’t look away, and the photographer lowered his camera a little uncertainly, as if he’d been caught at something, and nodded, and went back to his ferry terminal.

chapters.title: Her Family Was Not Invited
chapters.desc: Now that he exists, Mr. Kwok says, there has to be a proper engagement dinner. Six dishes, trestle tables, borrowed chairs, two mothers who have never met, and the trains every eleven minutes. Her parents were not invited. At eight o’clock, they come in under the shutter anyway, and her mother is carrying a folder.
chapters.epigraph: “To the top.”
chapters.content:
Mr. Kwok announced the engagement dinner with a pair of kitchen tongs in his hand.

“Now that the boy exists,” he said, “we do it properly.”

Haozhen looked up from the gearbox on the bench. “We’re already engaged.”

“Engaged is a ring. A dinner is a fact.” Mr. Kwok pointed the tongs at him. “Both families. Your mother meets hers. Six dishes. Not some ridiculous restaurant with a bill like a phone number. Here. Saturday the seventeenth. And nobody goes home hungry.”

“Six is a lot of food.”

Mr. Kwok stared at him. “You’re marrying my girl and you think six dishes is a lot of food?”

“No,” said Haozhen, after a moment’s thought.

“Good.” The tongs swung toward Serafina, who was sitting on the bench with her coffee. “And her parents?”

The garage went quiet. She looked at her mug.

“No,” she said. “Not them.”

Mr. Kwok looked at her, and didn’t argue, and went back to the wok.

✦ ✦ ✦

By five o’clock on the Saturday the garage was a dining hall. Two trestle tables under the bridge, covered with white cloth from the laundry under Haozhen’s old flat. Borrowed chairs from the noodle shop on the corner, Granny Shum’s yard and the back office, no two alike. A string of warm bulbs along the girders. The cars pushed to the far end under their covers, except Nobody, who stood just inside the shutter with a white ribbon on her one remaining mirror and two holes in her side that nobody had filled.

“It’s a rehearsal,” said Jinx.

“It’s a taxi,” said Haozhen.

“It’s a taxi with a ribbon on it. That’s a rehearsal.”

Aurelia came first with Qian, and moved three chairs, and found the place card Serafina had written for Mouse: MOUSE. NOT NEAR THE BOTTLES.

“Fair,” said Aurelia.

Chen Si came with Zhao Zhendong and Elowen. Chen Si brought tea. Zhao brought an envelope and gave it to Serafina with a little bow that was mostly mockery. Inside was a print: a man in a dark coat and a woman with her hand tucked into his at the harbour railings, his face turned to hers, the ferry terminal behind them going gold in the late light.

“The photographer sent it to a picture desk,” Zhao said. “The picture desk works for a paper. The paper’s owner owes Si a favour. It won’t run.” He pushed back his strand of hair. “But it seemed a shame to burn it.”

Serafina looked at it for so long that Haozhen came and looked over her shoulder. He was holding her hand in it. He looked like an ordinary man on a Friday.

“Keep it,” he said.

Elowen put a jar of flowers on each table, informal on purpose, she said, because a garage wasn’t a ballroom and she refused to pretend. Jinx and Raiden argued about the angle of Nobody’s ribbon. Mouse arrived with a bag of oranges and a bottle she swore wasn’t champagne, and Mr. Kwok confiscated it without looking round from the stove.

Liang Shufen came on the four o’clock train from the north with a cloth bag and her best dark-blue jacket. Serafina met her at the shutter.

“Hello, Auntie.”

“Have you been practising?”

Serafina held out her sleeve. Liang Shufen turned the cuff to the light.

“Better,” she said. “Still too tight on the turn.” Then she looked past her at her son, who had come to take the bag. “Have you eaten?”

“We’re about to.”

“Then why are you standing at the door?” She surveyed the garage: the tables, the bulbs, the mismatched chairs, the trains. “You’ve made a good place.”

“She made it.”

“I can see that,” said his mother, and took Serafina’s arm, and sat her down beside her as though she’d been doing it all her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

Six dishes became eight before anyone counted. Mr. Kwok said two of them weren’t dishes, they were necessities. A whole steamed grouper with ginger and spring onion. Roast duck, lacquered dark. Prawns in their shells with garlic and chilli. Greens. A clay pot of chicken and mushrooms that had been in the oven since noon. Soup. Rice. And a plate of salt-and-pepper squid that appeared from nowhere and that he refused to explain.

He stood at the head of the table with his glass.

“Both families,” he said. “Old friends. New friends. People who have caused me trouble.” Jinx looked up. “You know who you are. To the two of them. A long life. Enough food. Fewer bullets.”

“Fewer bullets,” said everyone, and Big Wu’s mother crossed herself, though she wasn’t anything.

Then Serafina ate the fish.

Not some of it, not the polite part. The whole fish. She took the belly first, the way she always had, and then the cheeks, and then she lifted the spine out in one long clean piece and laid it on the side of the plate and went on to the other side, while the conversation around her slowed to watch.

“You’re not even pretending to be polite,” said Aurelia.

“I’m hungry.”

“You’re eating like nobody’s fed you since Christmas.”

“Nobody has fed me like this since Christmas.” She took the other cheek. Haozhen moved the greens nearer her elbow without looking. She ate those too.

“She’s going to eat the plate,” Mouse said to Qian.

Qian moved the plate of squid out of Mouse’s reach. “At least she’s eating.”

Haozhen had taken the end of the table, as he always did, the one chair with its back to the wall and a clear view of the shutter. He sat there with his hand round a glass of tea he wasn’t drinking, watching her eat, and something in his face was so open that Elowen nudged Zhao and Zhao, for once, didn’t make a joke about it.

“What?” said Serafina.

“I like watching you eat.”

“That’s strange.”

“I’ve been told.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At eight o’clock the shutter rattled.

Nobody looked at first. The street was busy, the shutter was half up, people came and went under the bridge. Then it rattled again, and a man ducked under it into the light.

Song Weiren, in a dark suit, with his hair gone almost white at the temples and a small paper bag in one hand. Behind him, in a pale coat, with a leather folder held flat against her chest like a breastplate, Vittoria.

The table went silent so fast that the next train sounded like an explosion.

Serafina put her chopsticks down. Aurelia half rose. Chen Si put a hand on her arm and she sat again.

“Good evening,” said Vittoria.

“Mother.”

Song Weiren looked at the tables, and the lights, and the mismatched chairs. “Is this the engagement dinner?”

Mr. Kwok stood. “Yes.”

“Thank you for inviting us.”

“We didn’t,” said Serafina.

“We know,” said her mother.

Nobody moved. Haozhen watched Serafina’s hands, which had gone flat on the cloth on either side of the fish bones, and her face, which had gone white the way it had at the tunnel. Then he watched Vittoria, who hadn’t taken her coat off and was holding the folder so tight her knuckles showed.

He stood up.

He didn’t look at Serafina. If he had, she might have stopped him, and she might have been right to. He pulled out his own chair, the one at the end with its back to the wall and the whole room and the shutter in front of it, the one he had taken at every table he’d sat at for twelve years.

“Mrs. Song,” he said. “Please.”

Vittoria looked at the chair. Then at him. “That’s your seat.”

“Yes.”

“You’re giving me the one facing the door.”

He was surprised she’d noticed. Then he wasn’t. “You’ll want to see who’s coming.”

She studied him longer, as she might have studied a hem. Then she sat. He took the stool beside Serafina, with his back to the shutter for the first time in his adult life, and felt every hair on his neck go up, and stayed.

Song Weiren put the paper bag on the table. Tea, from the shop below the Peak, the tin with the crane on it. Serafina knew the label. He had bought it every month when she was small.

“Thank you,” she said, not quite to him.

Liang Shufen poured Vittoria a cup. The two mothers looked at each other over it, two women of nearly the same age from different ends of the world, and nodded, slightly, the way two drivers nod on a grid.

“There’s still fish,” said Mr. Kwok, who had decided that dinner would go on whatever anybody’s family thought, and sat down.

Vittoria looked at her daughter’s plate.

“You still eat fish like that.”

“Like what?”

“As if nobody were watching.”

“Should I stop?”

A long pause. “No,” said her mother. She picked up the chopsticks Mr. Kwok had put in front of her. “Go on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened the folder after the soup.

Cuttings. Printouts. Race reports in three languages, a magazine page, results tables torn from the back of sports sections, all of them in clear sleeves, in date order. Serafina at nineteen beside Nonna in a car park in a photograph so small and grainy it must have been taken from a phone. Granny Shum’s crossroads, from somebody’s video, a single frame. The track day. Baizhang, three pages of it. Gilded on the grid at the circuit in the north with the white seven on her door. A printout of the final championship table from last September, with the four-point margin circled in blue ink.

“Where did you get these?”

“Some were sent to me. Some I found.”

“All of them?”

“Every race since you left.” Vittoria turned a sleeve.

“Li Zhenhua,” Serafina said. The friend in the traffic police. The number in Duan’s file.

“He sent me what he found. The rest I looked for myself, at night, on a computer I didn’t know how to use.” Vittoria laid the last sleeve down. “I stopped him in December. When I found out who else had been ringing him.” Her mouth tightened. “I wanted to know whether you were all right. I didn’t want anybody else to know.”

“You could have rung.”

“Yes.”

“You could have come here. Any day. It’s twenty minutes from the Peak.”

“Yes.”

“Then why didn’t you?”

For the first time that evening, her mother had difficulty finding an answer.

“Because I was angry,” she said. “At you. At myself. Because you left without asking me to understand.”

“I did ask you. For years.”

“You asked me to accept it. I thought that was a different thing.”

“It isn’t.”

“No,” said Vittoria. “I know that now.” She put her hands flat on the folder. “There is something I said in August. In that room, with the stickers on the furniture.”

Serafina went still.

“I said you were a mistake I made in August.” Vittoria’s voice was perfectly level, and her hands weren’t. “I said it because I wanted it to hurt you as much as you’d hurt me. It was the cruellest thing I have ever said to anyone. And it wasn’t true. It was never true. Not for one day of your life.”

Nobody at either table was eating.

“I was proud of you,” her mother said. “I watched you win. I watched you lose. I watched you get back into a car when I thought anyone with sense would be afraid. I watched you build this, under a railway, out of nothing, with your own hands. I was proud. I didn’t know how to say it without also saying that I’d been wrong.”

“Then why make it so hard?”

“Because I thought if I made you frightened enough, you’d come home.”

“That isn’t love.”

“No.” It was barely audible. “I know.”

She didn’t say she was sorry. Perhaps she couldn’t yet. Perhaps the word was too small for the thing, or too big. But she had taken back the other word, at a borrowed table, in front of a garage full of strangers, and Serafina watched her do it and understood exactly what it had cost.

She took the Baizhang page out of its sleeve and looked at it, and put it back, and closed the folder.

“Thank you for keeping these,” she said.

It wasn’t forgiveness. But she didn’t push the folder away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Song Weiren had said almost nothing all evening. He had eaten slowly and asked Mr. Kwok about the clay pot and listened. Now he stood up with his glass.

“I’ve watched my daughter drive for a long time,” he said. “I watched Baizhang from a car park at the bottom, in the rain, where she wouldn’t see me. I watched her go over the crest at the top.” He looked at Haozhen. “I don’t know all of who you are. I know there are things I won’t be told. But I know that at the top of that mountain, the person waiting for her was you.” He raised the glass. “To the top.”

Serafina looked at her father. Then she lifted hers.

“To the top.”

The glasses went up all down both tables. Under the cloth, Haozhen took her hand and turned it palm up, and then, in front of everybody, in front of her mother, he lifted it and kissed her knuckles, just below the ruby.

Vittoria watched him do it. She didn’t look away.

The next train came over at nine-oh-two. The bulbs swung on their string and the cutlery shivered and the whole garage hummed, and everybody stopped talking for the length of it, as they always did, and then went on.

“Still on time,” said Liang Shufen, pleased.

Across the table, Vittoria had leaned in to look at the quilt Liang Shufen had brought down from the loft to show her, spread over the end of the table among the plates. The road on it. The hairpin.

“Very fine work,” said Vittoria.

“She’s learning to sew,” said Liang Shufen.

“She’s never been patient.”

“I can hear you both,” said Serafina.

Both mothers smiled, at exactly the same moment, and pretended they hadn’t.

He sat with his back to the door all night. Nothing came through it that he needed to see.

chapters.title: Last Race in the Industrial District
chapters.desc: A works team from Modena wants her for the rest of the season and all of next. Page nine of the contract says she gives up the road. So she goes back to Granny Shum’s for one last Saturday, against a kid in a purple coupé who was filming from a car roof the night she met the taxi, and a woman from Modena is standing in the crowd.
chapters.epigraph: “You’ve carried enough things that weren’t yours. Now you carry her home.”
chapters.content:
The call came on a Tuesday in June, which was an inconvenient day for anything that would change her life.

She was under Nonna at half past two on the tenth, arguing with a suspension bolt that had been fitted by someone who hated mechanics and happiness in equal measure, and her phone buzzed across the bench and stopped and buzzed again.

“Your phone,” said Haozhen from the office.

“I know.”

“It sounds upset.”

“So am I.”

He came and stood at the edge of the pit with the phone between two fingers and a faint crease between his eyebrows that meant he’d read the name. “Donatella Ferri. Fourth time.”

She slid out on the creeper. “Who?”

“Orsini Corse. Sporting director. Modena.” He held it out. “She doesn’t stop.”

The voice on the line was crisp, Italian, and completely untroubled by having been ignored three times. “Serafina Song. Finally.”

“Sorry. I was losing an argument with a bolt.”

“Are you going to win it?”

“Eventually.”

“Good. I don’t hire people who give up on bolts.”

Donatella Ferri had watched her for two seasons. Baizhang. The Asian title. The pass round the outside of the Needle at the opener last year. She had spent a week with the team’s technical director going through every lap of data Team AURELIA had ever filed with the series, and she wanted to talk about a seat. Not a guest drive, not one weekend. A works car for the rest of this season and all of the next, with a proper engineer, a crew of eleven, and a programme that went to Europe.

Serafina stopped wiping her wrist.

“That’s a big conversation for a telephone.”

“Then come to Modena.”

“I’ve got a garage.”

“I know. You’ve also got a habit of making cars do things the people who built them would prefer they didn’t.” A pause. “You haven’t asked about money.”

“I’ll ask when I know if I want the car.”

“Do you?”

Serafina looked across the floor at Gilded under her cover, and at the oil stain, and at the man in the doorway.

“I want to see it.”

“Good answer. I’ll send the contract.”

When she put the phone down the garage felt quiet. He came and crouched by the creeper and wiped a streak of grease off her cheek with his thumb.

“I’m proud of you,” he said. Not teasing, not making it smaller.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you mean it.”

“I do.” She caught his wrist and kissed the inside of it, below the watch, and went back under the car, because if she didn’t she’d cry, and it was only a Tuesday.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found page nine on Thursday night.

It wasn’t hidden. It sat between a clause about sponsor obligations and one about social media, in plain English and plainer Italian. The Driver shall not take part in any unsanctioned competitive motor event on a public road.

She took it into the office, where he was going through invoices.

“Page nine.”

He read it. “That seems reasonable.”

“Whose side are you on?”

“The road’s.”

“Traitor.”

“It’s a works drive, Sera.”

“I can read.” She dropped the pages on his desk. She wasn’t planning to spend her life racing on an industrial estate with bad tarmac and spectators on car roofs. She knew exactly what a works contract meant and how easily one could be torn up. But there was one Saturday she hadn’t finished with.

He looked at her face for a while.

“Granny Shum’s.”

“This Saturday.”

“Of course.” He let out a small breath through his nose. “Seven ways this goes wrong.”

“You’ve counted.”

“While you were reading page nine.” He folded the invoice. “I’m coming.”

“In the car?”

“In the car,” he said. “Awake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Saturday night the industrial district had turned back into itself. The warehouses dark except for their yellow security lamps, the loading bays gaping. Hot tarmac and oil and the harbour on the wind. Someone had a speaker going off the back of a pickup. Someone was selling skewers. Granny Shum was in her folding chair at the crossroads by the paint works with her flask of chrysanthemum tea and her police scanner on its string round her neck, and hanging off the back of the chair on its loop of wire was the board she’d painted twenty years ago, white letters on red: NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING.

Mouse was there with a stopwatch. “Look who’s come to retire.”

“I’m not retiring.”

“That’s what they all say before they start wearing team polo shirts.”

Then Serafina saw the purple coupé.

It was parked by a stack of tyres, an outrageous violet under the sodium lamps, and the boy leaning on it was nineteen at most, with a grin that had never met a consequence it couldn’t outrun. She knew him. On the last Saturday in November, two and a half years ago, he’d been on the roof of a parked van with his phone, filming, the night a man in resoled shoes first stood at this crossroads and watched her drive.

“Song,” he said.

“Ghost Pepper.”

“You remember me.”

“I remember you nearly falling off a van.”

“Best night of my life.” He looked past her. “That’s the taxi.”

Haozhen had come round Nonna’s tail. Dark jacket, jeans, the same expression he’d worn here the first time: composed, watchful, unimpressed by a crowd that thought a public road was a test bench.

“That isn’t my name,” he said.

“Everyone calls you that.”

“Everyone’s wrong.”

There was a woman at the back of the crowd by the loading bay who didn’t belong. Dark trousers, cream jacket, flat shoes made for walking a paddock, a small notebook. She met Serafina’s eyes and nodded once. Donatella Ferri had come to see what the contract couldn’t show her.

Granny Shum got up from her chair and took Serafina’s face between her hands. “You’re thin.”

“I’ve been racing.”

“Racing doesn’t stop you eating.” She turned to Haozhen and put a clementine in his palm without a word. He peeled it without argument.

✦ ✦ ✦

The boy wanted the loop. Four point oh two kilometres past the paint works, the container yard, the fish-ball factory, through the S-bends, and down the long straight past the gas works to the crossroads. She knew every metre of it. The dip by the container yard. The drain cover that sat proud by the fish-ball factory. The gas-works bend, resurfaced two winters ago with new tarmac running from the fifth lamp post on, so that braking at the fifth was right and braking at the fourth was early, on the old broken stuff, where you could hear the tyres.

Tonight she’d brake at the fourth.

Not because the road wanted it. Because she wanted to hear it.

He checked the passenger belt. The door latch. Her harness, which was his business only because she let it be.

“You’re not going to tell me to be careful?”

“Come back to me.”

“I always do,” she said, and got in.

He got in beside her. The first night he’d ever sat in her passenger seat he’d been asleep in four minutes. Tonight he sat with one hand on the door and the other flat on his thigh and his eyes on the road, and didn’t close them once.

“The left rear’s still loose over the drain.”

“Two clicks of rebound.”

“Three would be better.”

“Then bring your own car.”

That smile. “Drive, Sera.”

Granny Shum’s granddaughter, nineteen now and taller than her grandmother, walked out between the cars with the white scarf. The purple coupé revved twice and the crowd cheered. Serafina looked straight ahead and smelled petrol and hot brakes and for one second was nineteen again with nothing in the world to lose but a race.

Then she glanced to her right. He was watching the road. Awake. Beside her.

The scarf came down.

The boy launched hard, his rears chirping, and took the outside into the paint-works bend. He came in too hot; she heard his tyres complain. She held the inside, turned in early, let Nonna settle, and fed the power in, and Haozhen’s hand tightened once on the door. Not fear. Recognition. He knew that line.

Through the container yard the coupé twitched over the dip and the boy caught it. Past the fish-ball factory she let the left rear skip over the drain cover and felt it and didn’t fight it. Through the S-bends he was all over her mirror, and on the straight past the gas works, with the lamp posts going by in yellow bars, he pulled out to come alongside.

One. Two. Three.

At the fourth she lifted, and braked.

For one breath the engine note fell away and the tyres whispered on the old surface, a long rasping hiss like a held breath, and the crowd went somewhere far off. She heard the rattle in Nonna’s dash. The click in the passenger door. His breathing. The road.

The boy had expected her to stay on it to the fifth. He’d committed. He went past her into the gas-works bend a car’s length too deep, and his rear came round on the new tarmac, and he caught it, and lost his exit. Nonna came off the old surface already turning, already on the power, and was through and gone.

The crowd made the sound it always made. She brought the car down to a roll at the crossroads with her heart going and a grin under her helmet that hurt.

“Four,” he said.

“You noticed.”

“I was sitting next to you.”

“You were supposed to be terrified.”

“I was.” He let out a long breath. “I’m reconsidering everything.”

The boy came over with his helmet off and his face outraged. “You braked. You were ahead and you braked.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to.”

He stared at her. Then at Haozhen. “Did you know she’d do that?”

“Yes.”

“That’s worse,” said Ghost Pepper. “You both knew.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Donatella came through the crowd while the noise was still dying. She didn’t clap. She looked at Serafina, and then at the car.

“You lifted at the fourth.”

“I did.”

“The surface is better from the fifth. You know that. I watched your braking marker on three laps of your practice run.” She tilted her head. “Why?”

“Because I wanted to hear the car.”

“Most drivers would tell me they were managing the surface.”

“I was managing the surface. And him.” She nodded at the boy. “He was managing his ego.”

Donatella laughed, once, a short real laugh. Then she took a folder from her bag.

“The final version. Your changes are in. Your engineer is subject to the test. The seat’s yours if you meet the times.” She held out a pen. “Page nine is still there.”

“I know.”

Serafina didn’t take her pen. She took her own out of her jacket instead: slim, silver, with a small 7 engraved by the clip. The pen a woman in a grey office had given her two years ago and that she had used ever since, out of spite and then out of habit. She felt him see it, and say nothing.

She laid the contract on Nonna’s bonnet. The metal was still hot from the run, and the pages curled a little. She signed on page nine first, initials in the margin, and then the last page, Serafina Song, slightly slanted, because a bonnet isn’t a desk and because Mouse had started cheering before she’d finished the g.

“Welcome to Orsini Corse,” said Donatella, and shook her hand. “The car comes to you. Tuesday the eighth, the circuit in the north.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Granny Shum called them over while the last cars were leaving.

“You’re leaving my road.”

“Not forever.”

“No.” The old woman turned Serafina’s hand over and looked at it: the burn on the back, the little cuts, the grease that never came out of the creases. “You did well tonight. Not because you won. Because you knew where to stop.” She looked at Haozhen. “And you. You sat in that car with your eyes open.”

“Yes.”

“Good.” She reached behind her chair and unhooked the red board from its wire and held it out to Serafina. NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING. “Take it. Someone should keep it.”

“Granny, it’s yours—”

“I’m eighty-three. I know whose it is.” She pushed it into Serafina’s hands. Then she looked at Haozhen, and her face didn’t change at all.

“You’ve carried a gun,” she said.

The air went still. Serafina’s fingers tightened on the board.

“Yes,” he said.

“Did you ever bring it here?”

“No. Not once.”

“I know. I’d have seen.” She tapped two fingers on his chest, over his heart. “You’ve carried enough things that weren’t yours. Now you carry her home.”

“I will.”

“Don’t promise. Show me.” She turned away to shout at somebody’s cousin for parking on the paint-works verge, and that was all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The garage was dark when they came in under the shutter. She put the signed contract on the bench and the red board against the wall beneath the whiteboard, where it would stay. He hung his jacket on the chair.

She watched him do it.

“What?” he said.

“You were awake.”

“Yes.”

“The whole way round.”

“Yes.” He came and stood in front of her. “I’ve never been so frightened in a car in my life. And I’ve been shot in one.”

She hooked a finger in the front of his shirt and pulled. He came. The first kiss was light, the familiar one after a long night. When she began to draw back his hand came up to the back of her neck and held her there.

“Again,” he said against her mouth.

“Greedy.”

“Yes.”

She laughed, and he kissed her again, slower, and she got her hands under his shirt and felt him draw in his breath. Then she took his hand and walked him across the dark floor to Nonna, still ticking as she cooled, and opened the passenger door.

“Here?”

“You sat in it awake,” she said. “I want you awake in it.”

She got in first and pushed the seat right back on its runners and pulled him in after her. He came down over her in the small dark space with one knee on the sill and the door still open, and she laughed when his head hit the roof lining, and stopped laughing when he kissed her throat. His hands were at her jeans. Hers were at his belt. The gearstick was in his ribs and the seat belt buckle was under her hip and neither of them cared. She kicked one leg free and hooked it over his back, and he pulled the door shut behind him with a reach she hadn’t known he had, and the interior light went out.

In the dark it was all touch. The smell of hot oil and old leather and him. His mouth on her breast through her shirt and then not through it. Her hand round him, slow, until he swore against her collarbone. He moved down as far as the footwell would let him and put his mouth between her legs, with her heel braced on the dashboard and her hand flat against the cold glass of the window, and he didn’t stop when she said his name or when she said it again, louder, and the glass fogged under her palm, and she came with her other hand clamped in his hair and her whole body arching off Nonna’s seat.

“Now,” she said, when she could. “Now, Hao.”

He came up and over her and she guided him in, and they both went still. The car rocked once on its springs. Outside a train went over and the whole garage hummed and Nonna hummed with it, and he began to move with the long slow rhythm of it, and then faster than the train, his forearm braced on the headrest, her nails in the backs of his shoulders, the seat creaking, the window white with breath. She held his face and watched him the whole time. He kept his eyes open. He looked at her, only her, until the end, when he pressed his forehead hard to hers and shook and said her name like something he’d been told never to say aloud.

Afterwards they lay folded into a seat designed for one, in the steamed-up dark, with her leg over his and her head under his chin.

“I’m going to have to have this seat cleaned,” she said.

“Don’t.”

“It’s a race car.”

“It’s where you did eleven checks on me with fourteen stitches in my arm,” he said. “And now it’s this.”

She laughed into his neck. Then she reached up and drew a small square on the fogged window with her finger, and put a seven in it, and he watched her do it, and didn’t ask what it meant.

chapters.title: Overqualified
chapters.desc: Orsini Corse needs a head of security for its Asian operation. His CV is one line long and says “References: none available.” Donatella Ferri asks why she should hire him. He tells her eleven things wrong with her paddock that he noticed on the walk from the car park. Then the twelfth.
chapters.epigraph: “Only a small one.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she did when she saw the works car was forget how to talk.

It sat on its stands in the Orsini garage at the circuit in the north at eight in the morning on Tuesday the eighth of July, red and white, so low the splitter almost kissed the floor, with a rear wing that looked as if it could hold a small aircraft to the ground. A mechanic was torquing the front-left. Another was plugging a laptop into the car. A third, in his forties, with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair, was watching her stand there with her helmet under her arm.

“You can touch it,” he said. “I’m Matteo. I’ll be your engineer, if you’re as good as Donatella says.”

“I was being polite.”

“It’s a race car. It doesn’t know what polite is.”

She put her hand flat on the bodywork. Everything on it had a reason. Nothing was there to be looked at. She crouched and ran her fingers along the edge of the floor.

“Who looks after this?”

“Luca,” said Matteo.

“Luca’s good.”

“I heard that,” said a voice from under the rear wing.

“I meant you to.”

Seat fitting. The pedal box moved forward eleven millimetres. The wheel two closer. Installation lap, in, temperatures, out.
