On the first run she learned the brakes, which were more immediate than anything she’d ever driven, and the steering, which told her the truth a fraction before she was ready to hear it. On the second run she started to trust the front. On the third she stopped thinking of it as new and just drove it, and the numbers on Matteo’s screen began to get interesting.

“You’re carrying too much into sector two.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you doing it?”

“To see if I can.”

A pause on the radio. “That isn’t an engineering answer.”

“It’s a driver’s.”

When she came in, Donatella was standing by the timing screens with her arms folded.

“Well?”

“Your car’s very honest,” said Serafina, pulling off her balaclava. “It tells you what it’s doing even when you’re being stupid.”

“Your third run was your best.”

“The rear settled after the ride-height change. I’d like a click less rebound at the back. It’s still moving when I pick up the throttle. Not enough to lose it. Enough to make me wait.”

Matteo looked at his data, and then at her, and then at Donatella. “I like her,” he said.

“I noticed.”

Across the paddock Haozhen stood by the transporter with a coffee, a long way from the garage on purpose. He had spent the morning with the operations manager, asking about access lists and travel and who held the keys to what, and had been told twice that the team already had security. He’d said twice that he hadn’t asked whether they had security. Now he watched her talk to Matteo with her hands, explaining the rear, and smiling the smile she kept for things she loved.

She caught him looking. He lifted his cup. She lifted her water bottle, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

Donatella rang on Thursday.

“Are you still interested?”

“Yes.”

“Series office. Ten. Bring your CV.”

“I have one.”

“Then we’ll start there.”

The receptionist in the series office asked his company. “None.” His last employer. “None.” References. “None available.” She looked at him and decided not to ask anything else.

Donatella was in a glass-walled room above the pit lane with a laptop open and two coffees and a printout.

“This is your CV.”

“Yes.”

“It’s one line long. Qin Haozhen. Born 1994. References: none available.”

“Yes.”

“I need somebody to run security for our Asian programme. Drivers, engineers, eleven mechanics, logistics, hospitality, sponsors, two transporters, four cars, a lot of data, and people who want to stand in our garage for reasons that have nothing to do with racing.” She leaned back. “Your application tells me nothing. Why should I hire you?”

“Short answer, or long?”

“Surprise me.”

“Your paddock has eleven weaknesses I saw on the walk from the car park,” he said. “Twelve with this room.”

Her eyebrows went up. “Go on.”

He didn’t open a notebook. “One. The vehicle gate has one guard checking passes by eye, no live list. Yesterday at four he let in a catering van on accreditation that expired in June. Two. The walk-in gate by hospitality: anyone can follow an accredited guest through without showing anything. Three. The temporary fence behind the garages has a gap at the fourth panel wide enough for a man with a tool case. Four. The camera on that fence is pointed at the sky. Five. Your freight and your team kit share the loading bay, so anyone with a box gets to your transporters unchallenged. Six. Tomorrow’s guest list, with arrival times and access levels, is on the reception desk, face up. I could photograph it from the corridor. Seven. The briefing room door doesn’t latch. Eight. Your staff use the medical entrance as a shortcut. Nine. Catering has no map of restricted areas. Ten. Nobody inspects vehicles on the rear service road. Eleven. Your guards and your transport coordinators work off two different lists and don’t talk to each other.”

She hadn’t moved. “And twelve?”

He looked at the glass wall beside her.

“Anybody in the corridor can read your screen in the reflection. You’ve got your email open. The subject line of the message you received at nine twelve this morning is the name of a driver at another team, and the word terms.”

She turned her head. The laptop’s reflection sat in the glass like a second screen. She closed the lid.

“Seven minutes,” she said. “From the car park.”

“Seven.”

“Are you always this irritating?”

“Only when somebody asks why they should hire me.”

She laughed. Then she asked him whether he could run a team, and he said yes. Travel, yes. People who didn’t like being told what to do. “I’m marrying one.” She tapped the one-line CV.

“I can’t check a word of this.”

“No.”

“You won’t give me references.”

“Some of the people who could give them can’t be called. The others shouldn’t be.”

“That’s a very careful answer.”

“It’s the true one.”

She looked at him. Then she closed the folder. “Head of Security, Asia. You report to me. Access, personnel, incidents, travel. You work with the European director, not round him. You write everything down and explain it to people who don’t share your background. Your first job is to fix the eleven.”

“Twelve.”

“God help me. Twelve.” She held out her hand. “Your CV’s terrible.”

“I’ll ask Serafina to help.”

“God help us both.”

The pass came at noon. His photograph, the team’s crest, a red stripe. QIN HAOZHEN. HEAD OF SECURITY — ASIA. Not transferable. He turned it over in his hand in the corridor outside. Every pass he’d carried for twelve years had belonged to someone who didn’t exist, and had to vanish when the job was done. This one had his name on it, and a company behind it that knew he was real.

He found her behind the series office between two stacks of tyre cases, frowning at a set-up sheet with her phone to her ear. He waited until she’d hung up and held it out.

“Oh no,” she said, reading it.

“What?”

“You look like you’re about to ask the photographer where he was on the night in question.”

“I was told to look serious.”

“You look like a man who’s never been to a birthday party.” Then she read the title again, and her face changed. “You got it.”

“I found twelve things.”

“Only twelve?”

“She stopped me.”

She pressed the pass flat against his chest and curled her fingers in his shirt over it, and pulled him down, and kissed him behind the series office with the pass trapped between them and its plastic edge digging into her palm, until he forgot that he’d only come to show her the photograph.

“Your first official duty,” she said.

“Which is?”

“Being kissed by the driver.”

“Is it mandatory?”

“Absolutely.”

“I’m going to pretend I didn’t see that,” said Matteo, from the end of the tyre cases. “Since you’re employed: someone’s left a trolley in the fire exit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning, an hour before first practice, she saw a man at the back of the Orsini garage taking photographs.

He wore a team shirt. Not theirs: an old season’s, the crest faded enough that you’d have to know. He had a lanyard. He was pointing his phone not at the cars but at the keypad on the rear door, then the server rack in the engineers’ corner, then the locker where they kept the spare data drives.

She looked for Haozhen. He was already moving.

He came at the man from the side, not from behind, easy and unhurried, the way a man walks up to ask for a light.

“Can I help you?”

“I’m with the team.”

“Which part?”

“Technical.”

“Who’s your engineer?”

“Luca.”

“We have four Lucas,” said Haozhen pleasantly. “Which?”

The man looked at him a moment too long. “I don’t have to tell you that.”

“Then you won’t mind walking with me.”

She watched the space change. Nothing in his face moved. His voice didn’t. But he’d shifted half a step so the way to the rear door was still open and the man would have to go past him to reach it, and the man looked at the door, and at him, and understood.

“I haven’t done anything.”

“Then this will be easy.”

The man went for the door anyway. He made two steps. Haozhen’s hand found his elbow, and his other hand found the back of the man’s neck, and the man’s knees stopped working, as if someone had turned them off, and he would have gone down onto the concrete if Haozhen hadn’t held him up. It took about a second. Nobody else in the garage looked up from what they were doing. Haozhen leaned in close, his mouth at the man’s ear, and said something Serafina couldn’t hear. The man’s face went the colour of putty.

Then Haozhen took the phone out of his hand, and the lanyard off his neck, and walked him out of the back door with one hand on his elbow like a friend helping a friend who’d had too much.

He came back alone nine minutes later.

“Who was he?”

“Not ours. Not a fan. The lanyard belongs to a hospitality temp who reported it stolen on Thursday. He was photographing the door codes and the drive locker.” He held up the phone. “He’d already posted three pictures to an account with forty followers. Two of them work for a team two garages down.”

“Can you get them taken down?”

“They’re down.” He’d gone to the series media officer, and explained calmly that the images showed restricted security equipment and had been taken without authorisation, and that their circulation was a risk the series wouldn’t want to have to explain to its insurers. The media officer had made a call. The account was gone. Donatella had the man’s name and the event organiser had his face.

“What did you say to him?” she asked. “At the door.”

He thought about it.

“His address,” he said.

She looked at him. Then she held out half her banana, and he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum Hart asked her to dinner that afternoon.

He was the second Orsini driver: English, twenty-eight, quick, funny, with a habit of talking with his hands and a way of standing a little too close when he did it. They’d spent the afternoon comparing tyre wear and liked each other at once.

“There’s a place by the hotel. No forty-euro plates of leaves. Come. Matteo’s coming, a few of the lads.”

“Maybe.”

“I’ll keep you a seat.” He touched her shoulder as he went.

Haozhen was three metres away with the accreditation list. He didn’t look up. He didn’t need to. When she came over, he was still reading.

“Callum asked me to dinner.”

“I heard.”

“Team dinner.”

“Good.”

She waited. He went on reading. Then he lifted his head and looked past her, across the paddock, at Callum Hart’s back as Callum walked to the transporter. The look was short and measuring: a man fixing the shape of somebody else’s shoulders, and the way he moved, and which side he kept his phone on, so he could find him in a crowd in the dark. She’d seen him look at five people in a grandstand like that.

“Hao.”

“Yes.”

“Stop it.”

He brought his eyes back to her. “Second driver. Twenty-eight. Single. Lives up on the hill road. His last teammate left mid-season.”

“You read his file.”

“I read everyone’s file. It’s my job.”

“You read his twice.” She stepped closer. “You’re jealous.”

“No.”

“Hao.”

He looked at the list. Then at her. “Yes,” he said.

It took the laugh out of her. He’d said it like a man admitting to a weapon.

“I don’t like how he stands next to you,” he said. “I know it’s unreasonable. I’m telling you so I don’t do anything about it.”

“You’re allowed to feel it,” she said slowly. “You’re not allowed to read his messages, follow him to his hotel, or quietly get him moved to another continent.”

“I wasn’t going to move him.”

She waited.

“I wasn’t going to arrange for him to be moved,” he said.

“Hao.”

“I won’t touch your friendships. I promise.”

She took his hand and kissed his knuckles. “Then come to dinner. Sit next to me. Be nice.”

He was nice. He passed the bread. He asked Matteo about dampers. He laughed at one of Callum’s jokes, which Serafina thought was possibly the bravest thing she had ever seen him do. When Callum leaned across the table and asked how he’d ended up in motorsport, he said “Serafina,” and Callum looked between them and said, “Right. That makes sense,” and then, after a moment, “You look like you could take a building apart without changing your face.”

“Only a small one,” said Haozhen, and the whole table laughed, Callum loudest.

✦ ✦ ✦

The transporter was dark when they came back, apart from the light over the desk in the front office: two chairs, a printer, a battered sofa, a laptop still open on access rotas and a half-written incident report.

She closed the laptop.

“That’s confidential.”

“I didn’t read it.” She took hold of his pass by its clip and pulled him down by it. “You were jealous.”

“Yes.”

“Still?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and kissed him, and backed him into the desk chair until it hit the backs of his knees and he sat down hard. It rolled six inches and stopped against the filing cabinet.

“Callum,” he said, against her mouth.

She sat back on his knees and stared at him. “You’re asking me about Callum now?”

“I wanted to be clear.”

“Callum is a teammate,” she said. “You are the man I am about to have in your own office chair.” She took his face in both hands. “Clear?”

“Clear.”

The chair wasn’t built for two. It complained when she shifted into his lap and complained again when he pulled her shirt over her head. She undid his shirt button by button with the pass still hanging round his neck, and when she reached for the clip to take it off he caught her hand.

“Leave it.”

“You want to wear it?”

“I want you to see whose it is.”

She left it. It swung against his bare chest, cold, with his terrifying photograph on it, and she laughed and bent and kissed the skin above it, and he slid his hands down the back of her jeans and pulled her hard against him, and she stopped laughing. She stood long enough to get her jeans off and his open, and then she was back in his lap with her knees either side of his hips on the cracked seat, and she took him in her hand and sank down onto him so slowly that his head went back against the chair and he made a sound she’d never heard from him.

“Look at me,” she said. “Not the door.”

“There isn’t a door.”

“There’s always a door with you.” She rocked her hips. “Look at me.”

He looked at her. He kept looking. She rode him in his own office with the chair creaking under them and the pass knocking between her breasts and the paddock lights coming in through the blind in stripes, and he held her by the hips and let her set the pace and didn’t try to take it from her, not once, not even when she slowed to nothing just to watch his face. When he broke, it was with his hand flat between her shoulder blades, pulling her down to his mouth, and her name, and the chair rolling back into the filing cabinet with a bang that must have been heard in the next garage. She came a moment after, on him, with his thumb on her and his eyes open, and bit his shoulder to keep from shouting.

They sat there afterwards, wrapped round each other, the chair turned a little sideways.

“Your office furniture’s terrible,” she said into his neck.

“I’ll put it on the list.”

“Thirteen.”

“Thirteen,” he agreed, and she felt him smile against her hair.

chapters.title: Pit Wall
chapters.desc: Speed traces, brake pressure, throttle, steering angle: four coloured lines on a screen, a thousand times a second. He learns to read them the way he used to read rooms. He finds something in her data nobody else has seen. And at the end of the pit wall, after three years, Mouse finally says a word to him.
chapters.epigraph: “That was good.”
chapters.content:
By the end of the first week he had stopped asking what the colours meant. By the end of the second he had started asking why she did what they showed. Matteo said that was the difference between a tourist and an engineer, and that most engineers took two seasons to cross it.

The data room at the circuit in the south was a narrow box behind the Orsini garage, cold with air conditioning: three monitors, two desks, a timing screen on the wall, and enough cable on the floor that Serafina said the whole operation was held together by tape and Matteo’s religious faith. On the big screen, four lines ran across a map of the track. Speed in white. Brake pressure in red. Throttle in green. Steering angle in yellow. A thousand samples a second, every one of them a decision.

“It isn’t speed,” Matteo had told him on the first morning. “It’s what she does with speed. Where she chooses to lose it. Where she trusts herself to keep it.”

“And where she’s afraid?”

Matteo had paused. “Sometimes.”

That was familiar. For twelve years he had read rooms: where people stood, where their eyes went first, which hand they kept near the body, who everyone else looked at before they answered. The thing that mattered was almost never the thing people meant to show you. Telemetry was the same, only honest. A driver could tell you she was happy in a corner. The green line could show her lifting a tenth earlier every lap. Four lines weren’t four facts. They were a conversation, and the truth was in the pauses.

It was the Thursday before the race, the seventh of August, a month into his job. Big Wu and Mouse had come to Orsini with her, the two changes she’d written into page four of her contract in her own hand: one mechanic and one data engineer, non-negotiable. Mouse was at the second desk with her hood up, tracking a tyre-pressure sensor that kept reading two tenths high. Matteo was eating a sandwich.

“You’re staring at it again,” he said.

“I’m thinking.”

“That’s what worries me. Last time you thought, I had to rewrite the garage access procedure.”

“Can you put her lap from this morning against one from last year?”

“Which one?”

“Any from before the Needle.”

Matteo looked at him. Then he did it. Two laps stacked on top of each other, this morning’s in bright colour, an old one from February 2023 in grey.

He watched them run. Then he put his finger on the screen at the approach to turn six: a long, fast, downhill left that tightened at the end, with a gravel trap and a tyre wall beyond it.

“There.”

“Normal braking.”

“She lifts before she brakes. A tenth. Then she comes on the pedal softer and longer than she used to.” He traced the red line with his fingertip. “She’s slowing before the point where she used to start slowing. Six metres, near enough.”

“Fronts,” said Matteo. “She’s nursing the front-left.”

“Not every lap. Every lap since March 2023.” He tapped the grey trace. “That’s the last lap she drove before the Needle. Then this.” He pointed at the bright one. “Turn six here is the same shape as the Needle at the north. Long, fast, tightening, a wall at the end. She cracked a splitter a metre from that wall.”

Matteo put the sandwich down. He pulled up twenty laps from the last six months, one after another. The lift was there in every one. Five metres, six, six and a half.

“She doesn’t know she’s doing it,” said Haozhen. “Her hands know the corner’s safe. Her foot doesn’t believe them.”

“Christ.” Matteo rubbed his face. “She’s making it all back everywhere else. That’s why nobody’s seen it. She’s quick enough to hide it.”

“Don’t tell her she’s afraid.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“She’ll argue. And she’ll be right. It isn’t fear. It’s a memory.” He looked at the red line. “Show her. Let her decide what it is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was sitting on the pit wall in the heat with her race suit tied round her waist and a towel over one shoulder when they brought her the tablet. She looked at their faces.

“Why do you both look like that?”

“You’re braking early at six,” said Matteo. “About six metres. Since March last year.”

She took the tablet and looked at the two traces without speaking. He watched her face, and didn’t help her.

“That isn’t six metres,” she said at last. “That’s five and a half.”

“Depends on the lap,” said Haozhen.

“You found it.”

“Matteo checked it.”

“Don’t drag me into your relationship,” said Matteo.

She looked at the red line. She remembered March. The cold track. The splitter cracking. The wall coming at her. The long walk back to the garage, telling everybody it was nothing. She’d driven a hundred laps since and never once felt afraid at the Needle.

“It’s a habit,” she said.

“Probably.”

“I don’t feel nervous.”

“I didn’t say you did.”

He wasn’t looking at her as if she were damaged. He wasn’t trying to comfort her, or explain her own body to her. He’d shown her what he’d seen and was waiting for her to look at it. That was what made it possible to look.

“I can fix it.”

“Not tomorrow,” said Matteo. “Not in qualifying. Half a metre a run.”

“Of course,” she said, sweetly.

“You see?” Matteo said to Haozhen. “This is why I don’t sleep.”

When he’d gone she looked at Haozhen for a while.

“Two weeks.”

“Three.”

“And you found something nobody else had seen in a year and a half.”

“I’ve been reading people for a long time. She’s easier to read than most.”

“She?”

“You,” he said. “On the screen you’re she. It helps.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Saturday was hot enough to make the pit lane shimmer. The circuit lay in dry hills, brown grass and low mountains, and the air smelled of hot rubber and brake cleaner. She went back half a metre a run, exactly as she’d been told, and on the last run of qualifying, with the track at fifty-one degrees, she braked for turn six where she had braked in 2022.

Fourth. Three tenths off pole.

“Four,” she said, climbing out.

“Fourth,” said Matteo. “Half a second quicker than yesterday.”

“I can read.”

“Would you like me to say something encouraging?”

“No.”

“You’re learning.” She threw a towel at him.

She came to the back of the garage, where Haozhen was standing out of the way with his pass on his shirt.

“Don’t say it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Tell me I did well.”

“You moved it back six metres in a day without touching a wall.”

“That’s better than well.”

“I know,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday, on lap twenty-three, a line on the screen started to stutter.

Not the main timing, not the engine. On the third monitor, where Mouse kept the sensor health, the front-left wheel-speed trace dropped to nothing for a fraction of a second and came back.

“What was that?” said Mouse.

It did it again. Then again.

He was standing behind Matteo on the pit wall with a headset on that he wasn’t allowed to speak into. He leaned in.

“Where on the lap?”

Mouse put it against the track map. “Turn nine. And again at eleven.”

“Kerbs,” said Haozhen. “Both times she uses the inside kerb. When the suspension compresses.”

“Vibration. Bad connector.”

“Then it would drop out on the straight as well. It doesn’t.” He watched it happen again: the same corner, the same load, almost the same length. “Something’s moving when the wheel goes up. And rubbing when it comes down.”

Mouse looked at him. Then at Matteo. “If that sensor goes,” she said, fast, “the ABS loses the front-left. It’ll go into fault. She’ll have no ABS at all on the brakes at turn one. On old tyres. At two hundred and thirty.”

Matteo keyed his radio. “Serafina, box this lap for your stop, box this lap. Everything’s fine. Routine.” He let go. “Big Wu!”

Big Wu came off the wall with a light and the spare loom already in his hand, because Mouse had shouted his name too.

The series made every car sit in its box for at least sixty seconds at the compulsory stop, refuel or no refuel; it had been brought in years before, after drivers had gone back out with their belts half done. The tyre change took eleven of those seconds. Big Wu had the other forty-nine. He was flat on his back under the front-left before the car had stopped rocking, torch in his teeth, and on the second pass of his hand behind the upright he found it: the sensor lead where it ran past a bracket, its outer sleeve worn right through to bright copper on one side, rubbed raw by three races of kerbs.

“Chafed!” he shouted. “Nearly through!”

He cut out the bad section, crimped in the spare, wrapped it, and zip-tied it clear of the bracket with two ties instead of one. The lollipop man was counting under his breath. On fifty-eight seconds Big Wu slapped the bodywork twice and rolled out, and the jack dropped, and she went.

“What was it?” she said on the radio.

“Sensor wire,” said Matteo. “Fixed. Car’s safe. Go.”

“Copy.”

She’d come in fifth and gone out seventh. She took one car round the outside of the long right-hander on lap thirty and held another off for three laps with a line so tight that Matteo said something into his headset he’d later apologise for. On the last lap she took sixth back on the brakes into turn one, where the ABS worked exactly as it should, and crossed the line fifth.

Not the result they’d hoped for, but the best Orsini had finished in Asia in three years.

The garage exploded. Matteo threw his headset on the desk. Big Wu picked Mouse up off the floor and she hit him with a clipboard. One of the mechanics hugged the nearest body, who turned out to be a tyre engineer from another team. Donatella stood with both hands on the pit wall and looked at the timing screen without saying anything at all.

He stayed where he was, and looked at the last lap’s trace. Turn six, braking where it used to. The wheel-speed line clean all the way round.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came down the pit lane with her helmet off and found him at the end of the wall and put both hands on his shoulders.

“You found the wire.”

“Big Wu found it.”

“You told him where.”

“Mouse told him why.”

“You,” she said, and kissed him, hard, in her race suit, still smelling of hot tyres and sweat, in front of the whole pit lane. His hand came up to her cheek and for a few seconds the noise went somewhere else.

“Turn six,” she said against his mouth.

“I saw.”

“Six metres.”

“Five and a half.”

“Don’t ruin it.”

Then, from the end of the wall: “Good.”

Mouse was standing by the timing stand with her hood down and the old stopwatch she didn’t need any more round her neck. She was looking at him.

In three years she had talked to him about cameras and cables, money and shell companies and the wrong side of a spreadsheet. She’d let him into her cousin’s farmhouse at midnight and fed him biscuits. She had never once said a single word about him.

“Good,” she said again. She tipped her head at the screen. “That was good.”

He looked at her.

“Thank you,” he said.

She nodded once, as if something had been settled. Then she held the stopwatch up at Serafina. “Fifth. Still too slow.”

“Get lost,” said Serafina, and Mouse grinned and went.

He stood looking at the space where she’d been.

“She said good,” he said.

“I heard.”

“After three years.”

“I know.” She took his hand. “Some people take a while to look at you properly. Then they never stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Donatella found them at the back of the motorhome.

“Fifth,” she said. “Best in three years. Your security chief found a fault my data engineer missed.” She looked at Haozhen. “I want the incident report and the wiring report tonight.”

“You’ll have them.”

“And you have media in twenty minutes,” she told Serafina. Then she looked at her watch, and at the two of them, and at the closed door at the end of the corridor. “The drivers’ room is empty for the next ten. I’m going to the series office. I won’t be back for ten. Don’t make me regret it.”

She went.

The drivers’ room was small: a sofa, a locker, a mirror, a narrow window onto the paddock with the blind half down. Serafina shut the door and turned the lock and leaned back against it.

“Ten minutes.”

“You should change.”

“I will.” She pulled the zip of her race suit down from her collarbone to her navel, slowly, and his eyes went with it. “After.”

He crossed the room in two strides. She pushed off the door to meet him and they hit the locker together hard enough to rattle it. He had his mouth on hers and his hands inside the open suit, under the fireproof shirt, on her bare waist, and she was dragging at his belt with both hands.

“Your shoulder.”

“Fine.”

“Your neck—”

“Hao, I swear to God.”

He laughed into her mouth. Then he stopped laughing and pushed the suit down off her hips, and she kicked it free of one leg, and he lifted her by the backs of her thighs and she locked her legs round him with her back against the cold metal of the locker. She reached down between them and guided him, and he went into her in one long push, and she bit down on his shoulder through his shirt to keep quiet.

Outside, someone was shouting for a ten-millimetre socket. A scooter went past the window. The whole paddock was still celebrating three metres away through a thin wall. He held her up against the locker and moved in her, deep and hard and not careful at all, with his forehead against hers and his breath ragged, and every thrust rattled the locker door, and she didn’t care, she wanted it, she pulled him in deeper with her heels and said “harder” against his ear and he gave her that. She came first with her head thrown back against the steel and her hand over her own mouth. He followed her a few strokes later with a sound he buried in her neck and his whole body shaking.

He didn’t put her down at once. He stood there holding her, his face in her hair.

“You found it,” she said. “The fear. I didn’t know it was there.”

“You weren’t looking for it. You were driving round it.”

“That’s a horrible way to put it.”

“It’s accurate.”

“I hate how accurate you are.” She kissed him. “I’m proud of you.”

He went still. “For what?”

“For sitting on that wall for three weeks looking at four lines until they made sense.”

“They made sense before you did.”

“Excuse me?”

“Your data’s easier to read than you are.”

She laughed so hard he nearly dropped her.

His watch buzzed against her thigh. He looked at it over her shoulder. “Ten minutes.”

“Terrible system.”

He set her down. She did up her suit and he did up his belt and straightened his pass, and she pulled his collar straight, and he pushed her damp hair back off her forehead with both hands and looked at her for one second longer than the ten minutes allowed.

When they opened the door Donatella was at the end of the corridor with a clipboard. She looked at her watch.

“Ten,” she said.

“Exactly,” said Serafina, and went to talk to the cameras with her face burning and her smile impossible to hide.

chapters.title: The Needle
chapters.desc: The home round. Her parents in the grandstand for the first time. Lap thirty-one, the end of the back straight, a backmarker’s engine letting go a few seconds before she arrives. He sees it in the data before anyone sees it on the screens: brake pressure at maximum, and the speed not coming down.
chapters.epigraph: “Together.”
chapters.content:
Her mother had brought a hat.

Cream, wide-brimmed, entirely wrong for a racing circuit, where the wind carried grit and rubber and the smell of somebody’s burnt clutch. Vittoria wore it in the front row of the main grandstand at the circuit in the north on Sunday the fourteenth of September with the face she wore to charity luncheons, as if she’d been told this was a garden party and had decided not to argue. Song Weiren stood beside her holding two paper cups of coffee.

Serafina stared at them from the garage mouth.

“They came.”

“Yes,” said Haozhen.

“Both of them. In the stand. Where I can see them.”

She had come once before, Serafina knew now: four years ago, alone, at the far end of the stand, with a friend from the traffic police beside her. She’d never once let her daughter see her.

Her father saw her and lifted a hand, coffee and all. She lifted hers back. Then her mother turned her head, under the ridiculous hat, and looked down at the garage without moving at all.

Then she lifted her hand. Not a wave. Barely more than a hand raised from her lap.

Serafina felt something shift under her ribs. She put her own hand up higher, all the way, like a child at a school gate, and held it there.

Beside her he said nothing. He didn’t tell her it was a good sign or to make the most of it. He stood next to her and let her look.

“She’ll complain about the noise,” she said.

“Probably.”

“And ask why they have to be so close together.”

“Probably.”

“Good.” She took his hand. “She can complain in person.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The home round was the biggest weekend of Orsini’s Asian year. Eleven thousand in the stands by Saturday, sponsors, journalists, guests on lanyards, a hundred people who wanted to stand somewhere they weren’t allowed. He’d been on since six with a radio on his collar and a scooter for the perimeter road. The main gate had a live list now. The fence behind the garages was mended. The medical gate was locked to anyone who wasn’t medical, and the catering staff had stopped speaking to him.

He found Vittoria at the garage gate at noon, without her hat.

“Your people check a great many passes, Mr. Qin.”

“Yes.”

“Even for guests.”

“Especially for guests.”

She looked towards the track for a while. “My husband has been asking whether these cars are safe.”

“They’re inspected before every session. The cockpit is a carbon cell. She wears a device that holds her head to her shoulders in a crash. There are two medical cars on the circuit and a helicopter on the infield.”

“That isn’t what he wants to know.”

“What does he want to know?”

“Whether you think she’ll come home.”

“Yes,” he said.

She looked at him. He didn’t add anything to it.

“Good,” said Vittoria, and went back to the grandstand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Forty minutes before the start Serafina found him at the back of the garage, finishing with a marshal. She was in her suit with the top half tied round her waist, hair in a tight braid, the helmet on the bench behind her.

“Busy?”

“Not now.”

He made her drink water. He straightened the fold of her collar, which didn’t need it. He told her the strap on her helmet had been twisted that morning and she said she’d fixed it and he said, “I know. I checked.”

She took hold of his shirt. He knew what that meant. His hand came to her waist, and he kissed her, meaning it to be quick: something to carry with her into the car.

It didn’t stay quick. She came up on her toes and took his jaw in her hand and kissed him again, deeper, and his other hand went to the back of her neck, and he forgot about the race and the radio on his collar and eleven thousand people outside.

A whistle split the garage. Beppe, the chief mechanic, sixty and bald and beaming, standing by the tyre trolley with two fingers still in his mouth.

“Some of us are working!”

“Work harder!” she shouted back.

“Your boyfriend is distracting my driver!”

“Fiancé,” said Haozhen.

“Worse!” Beppe threw up his hands, and the whole crew laughed.

She rested her forehead against his for a second.

“See you after.”

“Come back.”

“Always,” she said, and took her helmet and walked to the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started sixth and was fifth by lap four. On lap seventeen the car ahead ran wide at the hairpin and she was fourth. Matteo was pleased. Donatella was pretending not to be. Haozhen stood behind Matteo on the pit wall with the headset on, silent, watching the screen.

He knew her lines now. Two months of them. The way she breathed the throttle through the fast right after the bridge. The small correction she made before the last chicane. The way she used the kerb at nine when the tyres were new and stayed off it when they were old. He knew what a good lap looked like and what a tired one looked like and what one looked like when she was pushing. Matteo had added a fifth line for him that morning, at his request: blue, under the white. The white was her speed from the car’s GPS, the speed of the car over the ground. The blue was her front wheels, how fast they were turning. On a clean lap the two lay on top of each other like a single line.

On lap thirty-one a backmarker at the end of the back straight, a lapped car from a privateer team in green, lost its engine.

He heard it on the television feed before he saw it: a hard mechanical bang, then a long grey plume rolling across the track. The green car coasted toward the run-off. A marshal’s yellow flag came out at the post before the Needle.

She was four seconds behind it. At two hundred and fifty.

He looked at the screen.

The red line, brake pressure, went up as she reached her marker. Up. Seventy per cent. Ninety. One hundred. Everything she had.

The white line, the car’s speed over the ground, barely moved.

The blue line fell off a cliff.

The front wheels had gone from two hundred and fifty to forty in a quarter of a second. And the car hadn’t.

“She’s locked,” he said.

“The ABS—”

“There’s nothing for the ABS to find.” He heard his own voice from a long way off. “The wheels have stopped. The car hasn’t. She’s on oil.”

On the second camera, under the drifting smoke, a dark gloss had spread across the racing line from the green car’s bleeding engine, exactly where every driver on the grid had been braking all afternoon. There hadn’t been time for the oil flag. There hadn’t been time for anything.

“Oil, oil, oil,” Matteo said into the radio, flat and fast. “Off line, Serafina, off line—”

She already knew. The yellow line jerked: she’d let go of the brake to get her steering back. For a fraction of a second the blue line leapt back up to meet the white, the wheels turning again, and the steering trace swung hard right, and he saw her try. She tried. She had the car pointed at the gap between the tyre wall and the gravel. She was braking again, on the grey surface at the edge, two wheels on dry tarmac, and the white line was coming down, finally coming down, two hundred, one-ninety-five—

Then the white line stopped. All the lines did. A last burst of numbers.

One hundred and ninety-one kilometres an hour.

The camera at the Needle shook. The picture went grey.

And on his screen, all five lines went flat.

Speed: zero. Wheel: zero. Brake: zero. Throttle: zero. Steering: zero.

Nobody on the pit wall said anything.

The car was in the tyre wall. The front of it was gone. A wheel lay in the gravel thirty metres away, still spinning. The tyres of the barrier had come down over the cockpit like a landslide.

Then the noise came all at once. Red flag. Red flag. Medical car one. Medical car two. Recovery to the Needle. Matteo was talking into the radio and getting nothing back. Donatella was already through the garage. Somebody was shouting at race control.

He didn’t remember putting the headset down.

He remembered the pit wall, and going over it in one movement. He remembered the scooter he used for the perimeter road, and the key in it, and the service road behind the barriers, and the wind, and a marshal at the gate at the back straight waving his arms, and going past him. He remembered the second medical car already there, its doors open, and the red flags, and the tyres, and the wreck.

He went over the barrier at the Needle.

“Sir! Stay back!”

He didn’t stay back.

A marshal caught his arm at the gravel. “Behind the line!”

“She’s in there.”

“The medical team—”

“She’s in there.”

He pulled free. The tyres had been dragged back off the cockpit now. The carbon cell had held: he could see the roll hoop, the window net still clipped in place on the driver’s side, the shape of her helmet inside, tipped forward. The doctor was at the other side, reaching in. Haozhen dropped to his knees in the gravel by the net and put his hand through it, and found her hand on her thigh, in its glove, and took hold of it.

It was warm.

“Sera.”

Nothing.

“Sera. It’s me. I’m here.”

Her head stayed forward against the head restraint. He couldn’t see her face. He held her hand in both of his through the net and talked to her. He didn’t know what he said. Her name, mostly.

“Sir, we need room.”

“She isn’t answering.”

“We know. Please. You have to move back.”

He didn’t move. He knew exactly what they needed. He had stood at the edges of a hundred emergencies with incomplete information and watched people work. He knew he was in the way. He knew that every second he knelt there was a second they didn’t have.

He couldn’t let go.

“Please,” he said. To her. To the doctor. To nothing. He bent his head until his forehead touched the edge of the broken cockpit. “Please.”

The doctor reached across and put her hand gently over his wrist.

“Sir. You have to let go of her now.”

He looked at the glove in his hands. He had held that hand at a crossroads in the industrial district, and in a hospital corridor with fourteen stitches in his own arm, and in a car park at the airport, and on Harbour Road where anyone could see. He had held it when she said she wanted him.

His fingers opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

They cut the net. They took her helmet off with two people and a collar, so slowly he wanted to scream. There was blood under her nose. Her eyes were shut. They put a mask on her face and a board under her and somebody said helicopter, and he heard that word before he heard the rest of the sentence.

He stood up. “I’m coming with her.”

A marshal stepped into his way. “Only crew.”

“I’m going with her.”

“Family only, sir.”

“I’m her fiancé.”

“I’m sorry. I’m sorry. Medical crew and family. There’s one seat and it’s for the doctor.”

He reached for the stretcher. A hand on his chest stopped him: the marshal, a small woman of fifty, white with it, who would have been knocked flat by one movement of his arm and who didn’t move.

“You can’t,” she said. “I’m sorry.”

He stood there with her hand on his chest while they lifted Serafina into the helicopter on the infield and the doors closed and the blades came up to a scream, and it rose and turned and went south over the grandstand, getting smaller, and he watched it until it was a dot in the pale sky, and then until it wasn’t.

For twelve years he had been good at getting people out. He had never once learned how to watch someone being carried away without him.

“Qin.”

He didn’t turn round.

“Qin Haozhen.”

Aurelia. Her face was white and her phone was at her ear. Behind her was Chen Si. Behind him was Zhao Zhendong with a car key in his fist.

“The big hospital on the hill,” Aurelia said. “In the city. They’ve got the trauma floor ready.”

“I’ll drive,” said Zhao. “Get in.”

He looked down at his hands. There was a smear of black across one palm from the tyre wall. He rubbed it once with his thumb. It didn’t come off.

“Come on,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria was waiting by the car.

She had come down from the grandstand the moment the screen went grey. Her hat was gone. Her hair had come down on one side. Song Weiren was a few metres behind her on the phone, saying yes, yes, which floor to somebody, with his free hand over his other ear.

She looked at Haozhen. Neither of them said anything.

Then she reached out and took his hand. The one with the black on it.

“Come,” she said.

Zhao drove. Aurelia sat in front with the phone, checking which entrance the helicopter would use and which surgeon was on. Chen Si sat behind her, speaking to someone at the circuit. Vittoria sat in the back beside Haozhen and held his hand.

He watched the road. He could still see the screen. The red line going up. The blue one falling. The white one that wouldn’t come down. The dark gloss under the smoke. Five flat lines.

“She’s strong,” Vittoria said.

He didn’t answer.

“She was stubborn as a little girl. When she fell over, she was up again before anybody could reach her. She would never let anyone see her cry.” Her voice was perfectly steady. Her hand wasn’t. “Mr. Qin. You must not decide what has happened until the doctors tell us.”

He turned and looked at her. She was frightened. He could see it now: the woman who had once called her daughter a mistake, sitting beside him in the back of a stranger’s car with her hand round his, trying to keep them both from coming apart.

“I know.”

“Then breathe.”

He tried. The first breath caught in his chest. The second one hurt.

“Again,” said Vittoria.

He breathed again.

Zhao drove faster than he should have and nobody told him not to. Somewhere on the expressway Aurelia turned round in her seat and said the helicopter was down, she was inside, they had her. He nodded. He asked if anyone had said anything. Aurelia said not yet. He looked at his hands.

Vittoria didn’t let go of him once. Not on the expressway, not on the ring road, not in the long climb up the hill to the hospital, where every light on the ninth floor was on.

When Zhao pulled up at the doors Haozhen had his own door open before the car had stopped. He took one step toward the glass.

Vittoria’s hand tightened on his.

“Together,” she said.

He looked at her. She looked back.

So he didn’t go on ahead. He walked into the hospital at her pace, with her hand in his, carrying five flat lines and the sound of his own voice asking a woman who had always come home to please, please come home again.

chapters.title: Hospital, Night Two
chapters.desc: The ninth floor of the big hospital on the hill. A collarbone, three ribs, a bruised lung, a brain that has been shaken very hard. A machine breathing for her. “Family only,” says the nurse. Her mother says something nobody expected. Thirty hours later, at two in the morning, she opens her eyes and asks about the car.
chapters.epigraph: “Car?”
chapters.content:
The windows on the ninth floor of the big hospital on the hill didn’t open.

He found that out at seventeen minutes past three on Monday morning, looking for air that didn’t smell of disinfectant. Beyond the glass the city was still going. The world had carried on. He found that offensive.

She was in intensive care, at the end of a corridor behind two sets of doors that only opened for a card.

They had told it to him in pieces, because they were busy keeping her alive while they told it. Left collarbone, broken in two places. Three ribs on the left. A bruised lung. A concussion, a serious one. Cuts and deep bruising across her chest and hips where the harness had held her. No spinal fracture. No bleeding in the abdomen. The carbon cell had held. The head restraint had held. The helmet had done exactly what it was built to do. Her chest had taken the rest.

The bruised lung wasn’t working well enough on its own. They had put her to sleep and put a tube down her throat and a machine was breathing for her, so that the lung could rest and the swelling in her head could go down, and they could watch both. At eleven the surgeons had put a plate in her collarbone. Now there were scans every few hours, and numbers on a screen, and waiting.

He had listened to every word the doctor said. He had asked about her oxygen, about pressure in her head, about what they’d be looking for in the next twenty-four hours, what would be a good sign and what would be a bad one.

He hadn’t asked whether she’d wake up. Not because he didn’t want to know. Because he couldn’t stand there and hear the answer.

At four a nurse told him to sit down. He sat. At half past four he asked if he could go in.

“Are you family?”

“I’m her fiancé.”

“I’m sorry. Only immediate family, in the unit. Her parents are here. They can go in.”

“I understand,” he said, and didn’t move from the glass.

He watched Vittoria and Song Weiren go through the doors. Then he sat down again on a plastic chair in the corridor, facing them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first night was long. The second day was worse.

He learned the floor. The nurses changed at seven and seven. The consultant came round at nine. The quiet chairs were at the far end by the fire door, the vending machine was round the corner, and the coffee was terrible even for a hospital. He didn’t learn how to leave.

At ten on Monday morning Vittoria came out of the unit with her eyes red.

“Still asleep,” she said. “They’re satisfied with the lung for now. They’ll keep her under.”

“Can I see her?”

Vittoria looked at the nurses’ station. Then at him. “Come with me.”

The nurse on the desk looked up. “Mrs. Song, you can go through. But he—”

“He’s her husband.”

He stopped dead.

The nurse looked from one to the other. “I’m sorry?”

“Her husband,” said Vittoria, without the smallest hesitation. “He is her family. I’m her mother. I’m telling you who her family is.”

“Do you have any documentation—”

“Would you like to see the ring? It’s on her hand. You took it off and put it on the locker.” Vittoria put both of her own hands flat on the desk. “He is the person she rings when she’s frightened. He knows how she takes her coffee and which shoulder hurts when she sleeps badly and which part of her car rattles in the rain. He was at the corner when she crashed. He held her hand through the net until your colleagues made him let go of it.” Her voice shook once. She steadied it. “He has been sitting on that chair since yesterday afternoon. If my daughter wakes up and asks for him, I will not be the one to explain why he wasn’t there.”

The nurse looked at him. He stood still.

There was a short conversation with the senior nurse. A look at a screen. A nod.

“With Mrs. Song,” the nurse said. “Ten minutes at a time. Don’t touch any of the equipment.”

“Thank you,” he said, and his voice came out wrong.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was dim and full of small sounds. The machine. The monitor. A pump ticking somewhere.

She lay with her head raised a little under a white sheet, a tube taped at the corner of her mouth, leads on her chest, a line in the back of her hand, a dressing over her left collarbone. Somebody had brushed her hair off her face and cleaned the blood from her upper lip. There was a bruise on her cheekbone already going purple. She looked terribly small.

He had seen her in a race suit and in overalls black to the elbow, with her chin up, arguing with a gearbox. He’d seen her laughing with her head back on a bonnet. He’d seen her asleep in a passenger seat. He had never seen her this still.

“Hello, Sera.”

He pulled the chair close. He didn’t touch anything. Then he touched her fingers, carefully, below the line.

“Your mother told them I’m your husband,” he said. “She was very convincing. I think the nurse is frightened of her.”

The machine breathed.

“I suppose we should have done the paperwork.” He looked at the ruby on the locker, where they’d put it when they cut her suit off. “You’re going to have to wake up and complain. Your mother’s decided we’re married and I haven’t even been allowed to argue about flowers.”

Nothing.

“Mouse rang eleven times. She says the car’s ugly and you should be ashamed of crashing it.” His mouth went tight. “She’s frightened. So am I.”

The nurse touched his shoulder at ten minutes. He bent and put his lips to the back of her hand, where there was no tape.

“I’m outside,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second afternoon the ninth floor had filled with people carrying things they didn’t know what to do with.

Aurelia came with a bag of clean clothes and a phone charger and sat beside him for an hour, not talking. Chen Si brought coffee that was better than the hospital’s and a quiet word with the hospital’s director, whom he seemed to have known for years. Zhao put a box of food on the table by the window without asking if anyone was hungry, and stood by the fire door with his arms folded as if the corridor were his.

Jinx came with Raiden in the early evening. She walked down the corridor with her jaw set and her hands shoved in the pockets of her jacket, and stopped in front of him.

“Where?”

“Through there. Her parents are in.”

Jinx looked at his face. “You look terrible.”

“I haven’t slept.”

“That isn’t what I meant.” She stepped in and put her arms round him, hard and graceless, the way she did everything that frightened her. He stood rigid for half a second. Then his arms came up.

“Don’t you ever,” she said into his shoulder. “Either of you.”

“I know.”

“I’m serious.”

“I know.” He let her go. “She’ll blame the car.”

“Good,” said Jinx, and wiped her eyes on her wrist. “Let her. I’ll defend it.”

They let her in for five minutes. She came out with her eyes wet and didn’t say what she’d said. Raiden took her hand and didn’t ask.

Donatella came at seven, out of team clothes but with her Orsini pass still round her neck.

“The chassis did its job,” she said. “The cell held. Medical car one was there in forty seconds. Matteo has the data locked. The circuit has the marshals’ reports and the footage. The green car’s engine dropped about four litres in under two seconds and they never had time to show the oil flag.” She looked at the unit doors. “We’ll handle all of that. Your job is here.”

“Yes.”

“She was driving beautifully,” Donatella said, more. “Before. It was going to be a podium.”

“I know,” he said. “I was watching.”

She touched his shoulder and left a folder with Aurelia.

Callum came at half past eight with two takeaway coffees and the face of a man who had argued with himself the whole way.

“I didn’t know what you drink.”

“Thank you.”

They sat side by side for a while, watching the doors.

“I was two cars behind,” Callum said at last. “I saw the smoke. I lifted. She didn’t have time to.”

“No.”

“I keep thinking somebody should have called it sooner.”

“There wasn’t a sooner. The engine let go four seconds before she got there. The oil was on the line before the marshal had the yellow out.” He looked at his coffee. “It’s in the data.”

“She’ll be back,” said Callum. “She’s too stubborn not to be.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The photographer came at twenty to ten that night.

Young, in a dark jacket, with a long lens on a camera half hidden under his arm, and a visitor’s sticker for a ward on the sixth floor. He’d come up in the lift with a woman carrying flowers and walked out of it as if he belonged.

Haozhen noticed him because he was looking at the wrong things. Everybody who came onto that corridor looked at the doors. This one looked at the reflections in the glass of the unit window, where you could see across the nurses’ station to the end bed if you stood at the right angle.

He lifted the camera. The shutter went.

Haozhen stood up.

“Put it down.”

“I’m press.”

“You’re on an intensive care corridor with a sticker for orthopaedics.”

“People want to know how she is—”

“Walk with me,” said Haozhen.

He didn’t touch him. He stood close, closer than strangers stand, and waited, and the young man looked at his face and found he had started walking. Down the corridor. Past Zhao at the fire door, who opened it for them without a word and let it close behind them.

The stairwell was concrete and cold and smelled of cigarettes somebody had smoked against the rules. The light on the landing was on a timer.

“Look,” said the photographer. “I’m just doing my job.”

“So am I.” Haozhen held out his hand. “The card.”

“I’m not giving you my—”

“You live on the third floor above the noodle shop on Ferry Street,” Haozhen said, quite gently. “You park your scooter in the alley at the back and you don’t lock it, because you think nobody would bother. You sold four pictures of a singer’s divorce to the evening paper in July. You’re very good at standing in the right place.”

The young man had gone white.

“So am I,” said Haozhen. “The card.”

The light on the landing clicked off. In the dark the photographer fumbled at the camera. The light came back on. He was holding out the card.

Haozhen took it, and bent it once between his thumbs, and it snapped. He gave the camera back.

“There’s nothing here you need,” he said. “There’s a woman in there who can’t say yes. Go home.”

Hospital security met the photographer at the bottom of the stairs, because Haozhen had sent the supervisor a message before he stood up from the chair. They walked him out of the building. By midnight the series press office had asked every outlet it accredited not to run a picture of her being treated, Chen Si had made one telephone call to the owner of the evening paper, and the two images that had already reached a gossip site had gone, as if they’d never been taken.

When he came back up, Aurelia was at the window. “Handled?”

“Yes.”

She looked at him. “Thank you,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty-six minutes past midnight Vittoria came out of the room. He stood up.

“Stable. The lung’s holding. They’ve started to bring the sedation down, very slowly, because of her head.”

“Can she hear?”

“They don’t know.” She sat down beside him. “I told her you were here. That you hadn’t gone.”

“She knows.”

“Perhaps. I wanted her to hear it from me.” She put her hand over his. “You should sleep.”

“When she wakes.”

“That isn’t a sensible arrangement, Mr. Qin.”

“No.”

She looked at him then the way Serafina looked at an argument she was deciding whether to have. “You’re stubborn too.”

“So I’m told.”

“Her father’s gone home for clothes. He’ll be back in the morning.” She looked at their hands. “You don’t have to prove anything to us.”

“I’m not.”

“Then what are you doing?”

He looked at the doors.

“Waiting for her,” he said.

She didn’t argue. She stayed beside him.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to two on Tuesday morning they let him back in.

He’d changed his shirt, because Aurelia had told him Serafina would be furious to wake up and find him in the same clothes for three days. He had eaten half a sandwich. He had slept eleven minutes in a chair at seven that evening and woken with his heart going.

The nurse turned the ventilator down a setting and explained that they were letting her breathe more for herself. The sedation was lighter. They’d be watching for her to move.

He sat by the bed and took her hand.

“Your mother says we’re married,” he told her. “I think the whole floor believes it. Your father went home for clothes. Mouse came. She sat on the floor in the corridor and did nothing for two hours, and then she said you’re stubborn, and I said I knew.” He looked at her face. The swelling on her cheek had gone down a little. “Jinx says Nobody’s still ugly. You’ll have to tell her yourself.”

He bent his head.

“I don’t know where you are,” he said. “I hope it’s somewhere with better coffee.”

The machine breathed.

“I miss you,” he said, so quietly he barely heard it. “Come back, Sera.”

At ten past two the monitor changed.

A small change. He felt it before he saw it: her fingers moved against his.

He went completely still.

“Sera?”

Her eyelids trembled. Then again. Then they opened, not all the way, unfocused, the eyes moving slowly under the heavy lids as if the light hurt them and the room made no sense.

“Don’t move. It’s all right. Don’t move.”

He reached for the call button. Her eyes found him, and he stopped with his hand in the air.

She looked at him. Her brow moved. Her lips moved round the tube.

“Don’t. There’s a tube. You can’t talk. Don’t try.”

Her eyes went to the machine, and back to him. Her fingers moved weakly in his.

“What is it?”

Her eyes went to the door, and back to his face.

“Your mother? She’s outside.”

The smallest shake of her head.

“Your father?”

No. Her eyes narrowed. She was concentrating with everything she had. Her lips moved again round the tube, one shape, then another. He watched them. He didn’t understand. She did it a third time, and a fourth, with enormous patience, as if he were a slow mechanic.

Then he understood.

Car?

He stared at her.

Car? she shaped again, and frowned at him, as if he was being deliberately difficult.

A sound came out of him. It might have been a laugh. It was broken and wet and caught somewhere in his chest between one thing and another, and he put his forehead down on the back of her hand on the sheet and held it there.

“The car’s gone,” he said into her hand. “The car’s in pieces. It doesn’t matter. Nonna’s fine. Gilded’s fine. Nobody’s fine. Big Wu’s fine. Everyone’s fine.”

He lifted his head. Her eyes were still on him.

“Except you.”

Her brow creased.

“No. No, don’t. You’re going to be fine too. You’re going to be fine.”

He pressed the button. A nurse came, then two, and a doctor in a cardigan over her scrubs, and they put a light in her eyes and asked her to squeeze a hand and she did, and to look to her left and she did, and to wiggle her toes and she did, and the doctor looked at the monitor and then at him and said, “That’s very good. That’s good.”

When they had done she was still looking at him. Her eyes went to the door again.

“They’re all here,” he said. “Your mother and your father. Aurelia. Chen Si and Zhao. Jinx and Raiden. Donatella came. Callum came.” He paused. “Mouse spoke to me. At the race. Before. She said good.”

A tiny crease between her brows. Then her fingers tightened round his. He felt it go all the way up his arm.

“You frightened me,” he said.

Her eyes softened.

“You don’t have to do anything. Rest.”

Her lids began to come down. He felt her hand loosen, and for one terrible second the fear came back up through him like cold water. Then the nurse looked at the monitor and nodded.

“She’s sleeping. Real sleep. That’s what we want.”

He bent and kissed her forehead. Her skin was warm.

“I’m not letting go,” he told her. “Not this time.”

Her eyes closed. Her fingers stayed curled round his.

He didn’t let go until the nurses changed at seven.

chapters.title: She Drives Again
chapters.desc: Four months. A plate in her collarbone, headaches that come like weather, a red arm sling with a mountain road on it, and a simulator where she freezes at the Needle every time. Then a January morning at the circuit in the north. He doesn’t stop her. He holds her helmet.
chapters.epigraph: “I won’t stop you. And I won’t push you.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she learned about getting better was that it had terrible manners. It came when it liked, left without saying goodbye, and came back just as she’d started to believe it had gone for good.

He brought her home on Thursday the twenty-fifth of September, eleven days after the Needle, with a plate in her collarbone and three ribs knitting and a lung that could manage on its own again, and a list of restrictions from the hospital that she considered a personal insult. No driving. No lifting. No screens for more than twenty minutes. Nothing that might knock her head.

She spent the drive home in an offended silence that broke at the garage, because the garage had changed.

There was a bed downstairs. A real one, with a new mattress and clean sheets and a lamp on a table, in the little back room behind the workbench where they used to keep the tyre racks, because she couldn’t manage the iron stairs to the loft and wouldn’t for weeks. The old sofa had been pushed over against the wall. A fridge by the door, full of water and fruit and the four foods she could keep down. Flowers in a jam jar.

“Who did that?”

“Your father.”

“Dad?”

“He said the room looked depressing. He also brought soup.”

“Was it good?”

“It was soup.”

“Hao.”

“It was very good,” he said, and took her bag.

She stood in the middle of the floor and breathed in. Oil and metal and rubber and coffee. The chipped white mug on the bench. Nonna under her cover. Gilded’s empty bay, where the transporter would bring her home on Saturday.

“Oh,” she said. “Home.”

The sling came two days later, in a parcel from the north. Red cotton, heavier and softer than the hospital’s grey one, and across the front of it in dark thread a mountain road wound up from one corner to the other, with a row of tiny trees along its edge and a small car near the top.

“Baizhang,” she said.

“She said the hospital one looked miserable.” He settled it round her neck, adjusting the strap so it didn’t press on the plate. “And that it’s for the driver who keeps trying to climb mountains before she’s healed.”

“That’s very specific.”

“She knows you.”

“Does she like me?”

He looked at her. “She sent you a road.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The headaches came worst in the late afternoon. After an hour of reading, or a conversation that went on too long, or a lorry going over the bridge at the wrong moment. Light made them worse. Noise made them worse. A bad night turned the next morning into a negotiation with her own skull.

The words were worse than the headaches.

She forgot Beppe’s name for a whole afternoon. She put her phone in the fridge, and spent twenty minutes looking for it, and found it beside the yoghurt, and stood with the door open looking at it with real outrage. He didn’t laugh until she told him he could.

One afternoon in October she stood in the middle of the floor and pointed at the bench.

“That thing.”

“Which thing?”

“That. The thing. With the—” She made a turning movement with her good hand.

“The torque wrench.”

“I know what it’s called.” Her face had gone red. “I know what it’s called. I’ve held one every day for nine years.”

“I know.”

“Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re waiting for me to remember.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.” She swept it off the bench with her good arm. It hit the concrete with a crack that made them both flinch. “I don’t want to sit here practising words like a child. I don’t want you watching me forget things. I don’t want—”

She stopped, because she’d run out of breath, or of words, and both of those were the same thing now.

He didn’t shout back. He stepped back two paces and stood there, and let her be angry at him, and it made her angrier.

“Say something!”

“What would you like me to say?”

“I don’t know!” She put her hand over her eyes. “I can hear an engine and tell you it’s at nine thousand and one cylinder’s misfiring. And I can’t remember what you call a wrench.”

“It’s a difficult wrench.”

“Don’t.”

“No,” he agreed.

She sat down hard on the stool. He picked the wrench up off the floor and put it back on the bench, handle towards her. Then he sat on the other stool, opposite, a little way off.

“I just shouted at you.”

“You’re having a bad day.”

“That doesn’t mean you have to put up with it.”

“No,” he said. “It means I can sit here while you have it.”

He didn’t reach for her. He waited until she held out her hand. Then he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The prototype disappeared in the third week of October.

She noticed on a Monday morning, sitting on a stool sorting the invoices Aurelia had brought round. She looked up at the far end of the garage and the space under the back window was empty. The burnt 1991 endurance car she’d bought in March two and a half years before, the one she’d stood in front of and said two hundred miles an hour to as if it could hear her, the one that had sat there scorched and patient through the worst months of her life: gone. Even the oil stain under its sump had been scrubbed.

“Where’s the prototype?”

He was at the bench with a delivery note. He didn’t look up at once. “It’s gone.”

“I can see it’s gone.”

“It’s been taken away.”

“Where?”

“Somewhere it isn’t here.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“I know.” He put the paper down. “I didn’t sell it. I didn’t scrap it. I didn’t give it to anybody.”

“Then where is it?”

“I’ll tell you.”

“When?”

“Not yet.” He saw her face change, and spoke before she could. “I’m not hiding it to keep you safe. And I’m not asking you to stop asking. I want to tell you properly. That’s all.”

She looked at him. There was something in his face she couldn’t read. Not guilt. Something nearer to nerves.

“I’m not angry,” she said. “I’m curious.”

“That’s worse.”

“Much worse.” She pointed at him with her good hand. “You haven’t got away with it.”

“I wouldn’t dare.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first proper kiss after the Needle happened behind a curtain in the fracture clinic on Thursday the sixth of November.

The consultant had looked at the X-ray and said the bone was knitting well and the plate was where it ought to be, and gone to find a form. Haozhen was helping her back into the red sling when she caught his wrist.

“Come here.”

“Your shoulder.”

“Hao. Come here.”

He bent. She kissed him. It was careful at first, a little clumsy, because of the sling and the bruises that had gone yellow down her side, because neither of them knew any more how much was safe. He kissed her back with one hand lightly on her cheek, and when she tried to pull him closer he stopped.

“Slowly.”

“I am going slowly.”

“You’re not.”

“I’m allowed to kiss my fiancé.”

“Yes.”

“Then kiss me.”

He looked at her a moment longer. Then he did, still carefully. She made a small impatient sound against his mouth and he smiled and kissed her again, less carefully, his fingers moving to the side of her neck, her good hand fisted in his shirt, and she bit his lower lip, and he made a sound that wasn’t careful at all. A nurse’s shoes squeaked past the other side of the curtain. They both froze.

“Very professional,” she whispered.

“Extremely.”

“You’re blushing.”

“Your powers of observation are recovering.”

“One more.”

He gave her one more. Then another. The shoes came back. He straightened and looked at the ceiling. She laughed until her ribs hurt.

✦ ✦ ✦

By December she could walk the length of the garage without sitting down. By the middle of the month she could use her left arm for ordinary things, though the plate ached after an hour. The headaches came less often. The words came back. Not all at once. Sometimes she still stopped in the middle of a sentence, looking for something. Sometimes a dropped spanner made her jump. He learned not to react to every pause. She learned to ask for help without treating it as surrender. They argued about it. They also, sometimes, laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The simulator in Modena was worse than anything.

It was meant to be the safe way back. No car. No tyres. No wall. A full cockpit on a moving platform in a dark room at the team’s factory, with a curved screen and the engine coming through speakers and a wheel that fought back. Matteo had built the sessions with the team doctor and a performance psychologist: short, slow, nothing heroic. She’d flown out on the eighth of January and had been looking forward to it for a month. She wanted to sit in a cockpit. She wanted the wheel in her hands.

For twenty minutes it was wonderful. The circuit in the north came up on the screen, perfect to the last kerb, and she drove the first sector clean and the second sector clean, braking early, but steady.

Then the back straight.

The marker came up at the end of it. Two hundred metres. Hundred. She lifted.

And then she stopped.

Not her hands. Her hands stayed on the wheel. Her feet stayed on the pedals. But she stopped driving. The car on the screen kept going toward the corner.

“Serafina?” Matteo’s voice, in her ears. “Brake.”

She saw the screen. She also saw the dark gloss on the tarmac, and grey smoke, and the white line on a screen that wouldn’t come down.

“Serafina, brake.”

Her foot went down. The car on the screen slowed. She didn’t see it. She saw the tyres coming at her.

She tore off the headset.

“Stop!”

Matteo killed it. The engine noise vanished. The screen froze on the mouth of the Needle.

“Stop it! Stop it!”

“It’s stopped. Serafina. It’s off.”

She was gripping the wheel so hard her knuckles were white. She couldn’t let go of it. She screamed, one long sound with no words in it, and the psychologist half stood up and Matteo put out his hand and stopped her.

He was through the door from the observation room before anyone called him.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t touch me.”

He stopped two metres away. “All right.”

“I can’t.”

“All right.”

“I saw it.” Her voice cracked. “I saw the oil. I couldn’t stop it. I couldn’t stop the car.”

He came a little closer, slowly. “Look at me.”

She shook her head.

She lowered her hands. His face was calm. Not because he wasn’t frightened. Because she needed something in the room that didn’t move.

“It’s a screen,” he said. “You’re in Modena. Nothing is moving. You’re safe.”

“I know that.”

“I know you know it.”

“I hate it,” she said, furious and terrified at once. “I hate that I’m afraid of a corner.”

“You’re not afraid of a corner.”

“Don’t tell me what I’m afraid of.”

“All right.” He crouched in front of the cockpit, below her. “You don’t have to finish today. You don’t have to do it again this week. You don’t have to prove anything to Matteo, or Donatella, or me.”

“What if I can’t ever do it again?”

“Then we’ll find out what comes next.”

“You make it sound easy.”

“It isn’t.” He took her hand off the wheel, one finger at a time, and held it flat against his chest. “But you don’t have to decide it today.”

She leaned forward out of the seat. He put his arms round her, carefully, away from the shoulder, and she cried into his shirt. Not quietly, not prettily. She cried like somebody who’d had something taken from her that she wasn’t ready to give up, and he didn’t tell her she’d be fine, and he didn’t promise she’d race again. He stayed until her breathing came back to her.

She didn’t go back in for four days. Then she drove two sectors and stopped. The next day she reached the marker, braked, and stopped the session, and called it a humiliating waste of expensive machinery. On the fifth day she drove the Needle in the simulator nine times in a row. She didn’t scream once.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday the twentieth of January it was cold enough at the circuit in the north that her first breath outside the garage came out white.

A private test. Not a race. The team doctor had signed her off. The series doctor had signed her off. Haozhen had been careful enough for all of them. But it was hers to decide.

The collarbone had healed round its plate. The ribs didn’t hurt when she breathed in. The headaches had almost gone. Almost. She rolled her shoulder once by the car, and he saw her do it.

“Pain?”

“Are you going to read me the whole questionnaire?”

“If necessary.”

“I’m fine.”

Haozhen had her helmet. He knew its weight, and the dent in the shell from the day she’d hit it with a spanner.

“What?” she said.

“Your braking.”

“Of course.”

“Your first marker today is six metres before your old one. Matteo’s put a cone there. Take it at your own pace. You don’t have to chase anything.”

“I know.”

He held the helmet out. She didn’t take it.

“You’re not going to tell me to stop?”

“No.”

“Even if I’m slow?”

“Yes.”

“Even if I come in after one lap and tell you I can’t?”

“I’ll listen.”

“I won’t stop you,” he said. “And I won’t push you. I’ll hold this.”

She took the helmet. Then she leaned in and kissed him, and a mechanic turned away with great deliberation, and Matteo studied his tablet. He did up the strap under her chin, and his fingers stayed there a second longer.

“Come back,” he said.

She gave him a thumbs-up through the visor.

The first lap was slow. The second was slower. She came in, and they looked at the data, and he stood behind Matteo and read her the way he’d read rooms. The red line, clean. The green, smooth. The yellow a little cautious, but not one correction he didn’t understand.

“Again?” said Matteo.

She looked out of the garage at the empty track. “Again.”

On the next lap she carried more speed through the first sector. On the back straight the white line climbed. He watched the cone go past on the onboard camera and the old marker come up behind it, and his hand closed on the edge of the desk.

The red line went up.

The white line came down. The blue line came down with it, lying on top of it like a single line.

She turned in. The yellow line moved smoothly. The car held its line all the way round the long tightening left, and came out of the Needle, and went on.

He breathed out.

“Good?” said Matteo.

“Good.”

She came in after the lap and sat in the cockpit with the engine off before she lifted her visor.

“How did it feel?” said Matteo.

“Like driving.”

She climbed out, pulled the helmet off, and her face was flushed and her eyes were bright.

“I braked on the marker,” she said to Haozhen.

“I saw.”

“Not the cone. The old one. Mine.”

“I saw.”

She looked at him for a second more. Then she took the front of his jacket in her fist and kissed him, properly, in the middle of the garage, in front of Matteo and Beppe and Big Wu and Mouse and half the Orsini crew. Somebody whistled. Somebody clapped. Beppe shouted, “Again! That one was too short!” and she laughed into his mouth, and he held her by the waist and the back of the head and kissed her again because Beppe had asked.

“You didn’t tell me to stop,” she said.

“No.”

“You didn’t even look worried.”

“I was terrified.”

“Liar.”

“I was holding your helmet,” he said. “It’s hard to look worried with a helmet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria was at the fence on the far side of the pit lane, on her own.

No hat. She had come up on the early train and stood there since nine, out of everyone’s way. She didn’t understand the coloured lines that the men behind the pit wall watched as though they were reading scripture. She didn’t know what brake pressure ought to look like.

But she had watched the car come down the back straight, and seen its brake lights come on at the end of it, and had held the wire of the fence so hard it had marked her palm. And she had seen her daughter climb out and pull off her helmet and kiss the man who’d held it.

This time she didn’t lift her hand half an inch from her lap.

She waved.

Across the pit lane, Serafina looked up and saw her. She didn’t move. Then she raised her hand high, the left one, the one with the plate in the shoulder, all the way up above her head, and held it there.

Haozhen, with the helmet under his arm, followed her eyes to the fence, and saw her mother smile.

chapters.title: Just Married at Three Hundred and Twenty-Two
chapters.desc: A registry office at ten past nine, where he finally gets a piece of paper that says what he is to her. Nine dishes in a garage under a railway bridge, and the middle of a wedding, at last, from the inside. Then rice, and a grey taxi, and the old military airstrip at sunset, where something red is waiting under a tarpaulin with his handwriting on its nose.
chapters.epigraph: “I get to go home with you.”
chapters.content:
At ten past nine on Saturday the twenty-fifth of April, Qin Haozhen became somebody’s husband.

He had been somebody’s fiancé for three years, somebody’s son for thirty-two, and for one unpleasant stretch, somebody who had officially never existed. The registry office didn’t care about any of that. It cared about two identity numbers, two signatures and two witnesses, and whether the couple in front of the registrar understood what they were signing.

He understood. He’d read the forms three times.

“Twice,” he said, in the corridor.

“Three. I watched you.” She was in ivory, a plain dress fitted at the waist that stopped just below the knee, no veil, nothing at her throat, and flat shoes because she’d said she might need to run. Her hair was pinned back loosely over the scar the stitches had left at her hairline. The ruby was on her hand. She took his left hand between both of hers. “You’re cold.”

“It’s air-conditioned.”

“Liar.” She rubbed his knuckles. “Are you frightened?”

“I’ve never done this before,” he said. “I’ve stood outside eleven weddings. Always at the door. Always watching the exits. I’ve never once been inside.”

She lifted his hand and kissed it. “Then today you go inside.”

The registrar opened the door. “Mr. Qin? Miss Song?”

“Not for much longer,” said Serafina.

It took eighteen minutes. A small room, a table, a window onto a row of ordinary buildings, a registrar in a grey cardigan, and two witnesses: Aurelia, who had sworn she wouldn’t cry and was already holding a handkerchief, and Chen Si beside her. The registrar read the declarations. Serafina answered clearly. So did he. When it was time to sign he took the silver pen out of his breast pocket, the one engraved 7 that she’d given him that morning to carry, and wrote his name.

Qin Haozhen. Not an alias. Not a designation, not a line in a file someone could reach in and delete. His name, in his own small square hand, in a marriage register, beside hers.

“Congratulations,” said the registrar. “You’re married.”

He didn’t move.

“Hello, husband,” said Serafina.
