The word reached him slowly, the way light reaches a room when somebody opens a shutter. He looked down at the certificate, then at her hand next to his on the desk, and then at her. The registrar was saying something about copies and collection.

He kissed her. At the registrar’s desk, in front of the registrar. It wasn’t a restrained kiss. Aurelia made a sound that could have been a laugh or a sob. Chen Si looked out of the window with the expression of a man giving two newlyweds privacy in a room that held five people.

The registrar cleared her throat. He kissed his wife once more anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside on the steps it was chaos. Zhao Zhendong had brought an armful of white peonies he insisted weren’t from him. Elowen had brought Eliana, now twenty-three, in round glasses and a claw clip, who asked to see the certificate and studied it with enormous seriousness. Raiden and Jinx had come, and Evangeline in silver with an orchid, and old Lin Jian in the black suit he wore to every important thing.

“So you’re married now?” said Eliana.

“Apparently,” said Serafina.

“Apparently,” said Haozhen, and held up their joined hands.

Chen Si came down the steps and held out his hand. Haozhen took it. They just looked at each other.

“Welcome to the family,” Chen Si said.

Something changed in Haozhen’s face. Serafina saw it. He’d been let into a hundred rooms. Given access and passes and the temporary protection of people who had decided he was useful. Nobody had ever said welcome.

“You’ve stood outside enough doors,” said Chen Si, holding on a moment longer. “Come in now.”

“Don’t make him cry,” said Aurelia. “He’ll ruin my photographs.”

“I’m not crying,” said Haozhen.

Serafina looked up at him. His eyes were bright. “Not yet,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

By eleven the garage under the bridge had stopped being a garage.

Strings of warm bulbs ran along every girder. Trestle tables in long rows under white cloth. Two hundred borrowed chairs. Flowers in old glass bottles. The benches cleared of tools and laid with dishes. Over the shutter, on a sheet, in Mouse’s capitals: QIN & SONG. And under it, smaller: JUST MARRIED. PLEASE DON’T ASK ABOUT THE CARS.

“Accurate,” said Haozhen.

Two hundred people. The team, old and new. Beppe and Matteo and Luca and Donatella and half of Orsini, who had flown in on Friday. Mouse and Big Wu and his mother. Granny Shum in the middle of the first table, with her red board propped against the wall behind her where Serafina had hung it. Liang Shufen on one side of her and Vittoria on the other, discussing the stitching on the table runners. Song Weiren at the end of the table with his hands folded, watching his wife lean across a borrowed tablecloth towards a seamstress from a mining town.

“Your mother’s showing mine how to tie off a knot,” Serafina said.

“Yours is pretending to listen.”

“She’s actually listening.”

“Then that’s new,” he said, and Liang Shufen put another piece of cake on Vittoria’s plate, and Vittoria ate it.

Mr. Kwok had insisted on nine dishes, and there were nine. A whole steamed grouper with ginger and spring onion, set in the middle of the top table. Roast duck. Prawns in the shell. Braised mushrooms. A slow-cooked chicken in a clay pot. Greens with garlic. A soup he’d stood over since dawn. And two more that appeared after everyone said there couldn’t possibly be more. Serafina took the belly of the fish before anyone else could reach it, and Haozhen put his own piece beside it.

“You don’t have to bribe me any more. I’ve married you.”

“It isn’t a bribe,” he said. “It’s a habit.”

Big Wu stood up first with his glass. “To Serafina, who can take a perfectly good car apart and then complain that it doesn’t feel right. And to Haozhen, who has finally found a job he can’t resign from.”

Granny Shum stood, slowly, and the garage went quiet for her. “To the girl who always wanted to go faster,” she said, “and the man who learned he didn’t have to chase her. Now he can sit in the passenger seat.”

“He’s very good at it,” said Serafina.

“I had a good teacher.”

Mr. Kwok lifted his glass last, and looked round at the bulbs and the girders and the two hundred people, and the shutter, and the trains. “To the garage,” he said. Then, more: “And to the people who made it a home.”

The eleven-forty-one went over the bridge in the middle of it. The bulbs swung. Everyone stopped, as they always did, and then cheered.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had kept a dark blue folder beside his chair all morning. After the third toast he slid it across to her.

“More paperwork? On my wedding day?”

“Possibly.”

A title deed. The arch and land at the eastern end of the railway viaduct, it said, under a lot of language about easements and drains and the right of the railway to send trains overhead every eleven minutes in perpetuity. And two names on it. Qin Haozhen. Song Serafina.

She read it twice.

“The railway sold off the arches in October,” he said. “To raise money. I bought this one. At the auction. In my own name, the week my number came through.” He looked at her. “I didn’t want you to think it belonged to me. Or that it depended on me. It’s ours.”

“You bought the garage.”

“Half of it is yours. It always was. I just made the railway agree.”

“You could have told me.”

“I wanted to give it to you today.”

She looked down at the deed, and up at the girders, and at the oil stain where he’d knelt twice, and at the sofa he had slept on, pretending he wasn’t tired, the night he first turned his mug to the wall. Her eyes filled.

“I’d have married you without it.”

“I know.”

“I’m not marrying you for a building.”

“I know.”

She put the folder down and took his face in her hands and kissed him long enough that someone at the next table whistled. She ignored them.

“Then we keep the sofa,” she said against his mouth. “And the mug. And the grey taxi on the dashboard. Everything.”

“Everything,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The envelope came during the second round of toasts. A boy from the Orsini crew brought it over: somebody at the shutter had given it to him and gone. No name on it. No stamp.

Inside was a small packet of cinnamon gum. And a folded slip of paper with two words.

Window seat.

Serafina saw his face change. “Tianyi?”

“Yes.”

“Did you tell him?”

“No.”

She turned the paper over. Nothing on the back.

He took one stick of gum out of the packet and held it between his fingers. For two years, every Sunday, a boy from the next bed had kept him the window seat on the academy bus without being asked, so that a new boy who couldn’t sleep with his back to a door could at least see the road.

He put the gum in his breast pocket, next to the pen.

“Do you want to ring him?”

“Not today,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four they threw rice.

It started with a handful from Eliana and became a cupful from somebody at the back, and Serafina shrieked and he put his arm over her head, and he was laughing, actually laughing, with rice in his hair and on his collar. She threw a handful back at him. He threw some at her dress. She chased him across the garage and he let her catch him at the shutter.

Nobody was waiting outside, polished till the silver-grey paint shone. Raiden had replaced the mirror the van had taken. The two holes in her side were still there, unfilled.

“Don’t scratch her,” said Jinx. “Don’t put her in a ditch. Don’t let her put her in a ditch.”

“I’m standing here,” said Serafina.

“I know,” said Jinx, and kissed her cheek, and kissed his, and stepped back.

He opened the passenger door for her. She shook her head.

“I’m driving. It’s my wedding.”

He got in beside her. Brake was already on the back seat, where he’d been since the soup, his white paw on the window. She started the engine, and Nobody rolled out from under the bridge with two hundred people behind it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Hengling airstrip had been closed since the air force left in 2011. It lay beyond the industrial district behind a rusted fence: three point two kilometres of concrete runway, faded markings, grass in the cracks. The sun was low when they came through the gate. A fire tender stood at the halfway mark. An ambulance by the old tower. Mouse at a folding table with a laptop, and Big Wu, and Beppe, and Matteo.

At the far end, under a long tarpaulin, something waited. Low and wide. The front of it unmistakable.

She stopped the car.

“Hao.”

“Go on.”

She walked to it in her wedding dress and took the edge of the tarpaulin and pulled.

The prototype. Not burnt, not a pile of scorched panels and an expensive dream. Rebuilt around a new carbon safety cell, the bodywork finished in deep red, the cooling new, the suspension new, the cockpit stripped and refitted with two seats: the driver’s, and the second one the 1991 rules had insisted on and nobody had ever sat in. On the nose, painted in his small square hand, two words.

TWO HUNDRED.

“What have you done?”

“Rebuilt it.”

“Since October?”

“Since October. A workshop outside the city. Big Wu. Beppe flew in twice.” He stood beside her. “I did the brakes.”

She turned.

“I designed the system with them and did every test. Carbon discs. New ducts. I didn’t want to give you a car that looked beautiful and stopped badly.” He paused. “I didn’t want to give you anything that wouldn’t stop.”

She crouched in her ivory dress and looked at the front corner: the lines, the routing, the heat shielding round the calipers. It was beautiful work.

“You did this.”

“Yes.”

“Two hundred what?”

“Miles an hour,” he said.

She laughed, a small disbelieving sound, and then she was crying, and she threw her arms round him.

“You can’t keep giving me cars.”

“I’ll try to stop.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ran it properly. The runway had been swept. The fire crew briefed. The wind measured: nine knots straight down the strip. Mouse had a GPS logger in the car and two timing beams across the measured kilometre. Three runs, building up. Brake marker boards at one thousand, seven hundred and five hundred metres to go.

She changed into her suit by the tower. He checked her harness, then his own, in the second seat.

“Shoulder?”

“Fine.”

“Head?”

“Do you want me to fill in a form?”

“No,” he said, and pulled his belt tight.

The first run was a hundred and eighty and stable. The second, two-sixty, and the nose stayed down and the brakes came in at the seven-hundred board exactly as he’d built them to. “Consistent,” he said, looking at the display. “Of course they are,” she said.

On the third run the engine climbed and kept climbing. The runway narrowed in the windscreen. Two hundred. Two-forty. Two-eighty. The car felt planted, like a train on rails. Three hundred. Three-ten. The measured kilometre went under them in eleven seconds.

The display read 322 km/h.

Two hundred miles an hour. The number she had said out loud to a burnt car three years ago, as if it could hear her.

She lifted at the thousand board. Braked at seven hundred, hard and progressive, and his brakes took the car down from three hundred and twenty to nothing as if it were a hand closing. She stopped it on the centre line with four hundred metres to spare.

Neither of them spoke.

“Two hundred,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Did you see?”

“I was here,” he said, and she leaned across the narrow cockpit and kissed him, helmets knocking, and he laughed against her mouth.

At the table by the tower, Mouse looked at the logger, and then at the car, and then at him, climbing stiffly out of the second seat with grease on his sleeve and a wedding ring on his hand. In three years she had called him the guard, him, your man, and once, memorably, the coat.

“Good work, Haozhen,” said Mouse.

He looked at her.

“Don’t get used to it,” she said, and went to look at the brakes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The sun was nearly gone when they climbed back into the cockpit. The crew had gone to the tower for the bottle Beppe had brought. The runway lay in long pale bands of last light, and the car ticked as it cooled.

She sat sideways in the driver’s seat with her suit open to the waist and the white vest under it, and he sat in the seat nobody had ever sat in.

“My husband,” she said.

“My wife.”

“Say it again.”

“My wife.”

She reached for him across the gap. The kiss was slow this time. There was no speed left to chase. He kissed her forehead, her cheek, her mouth, the scar at her hairline. She got her hands inside his shirt. He pushed the suit down off her shoulders and kissed the line of the plate under her collarbone, gently, and then the hollow of her throat, not gently at all. The cockpit was designed for restraint, not comfort, and they were careful of the switches and the edges and clumsy and laughing, and she climbed half over the centre tunnel into his lap with her knees either side of him in the narrow seat and her back against the curve of the roof, and undid his belt, and he lifted her by the hips and she sank down onto him in the warm dark with the smell of hot metal and fuel and him all round her.

“My wife,” he said into her neck.

“That’s one.”

“My wife.”

“Two.”

She moved on him slowly, as slowly as the light going, his hands spread on her back, his mouth at her breast, the car rocking slightly on its springs. She held his face and watched him. He didn’t look at the door. There wasn’t one. When it broke over her it was quiet, a long shudder and his name, and he followed her with his forehead pressed hard to her collarbone, below the plate, saying it again. My wife. She’d lost count.

Afterwards she lay against him with her head on his shoulder. The display still showed the last number. 322.

“We’re married,” she said.

“Yes.”

“We’ve got a garage.”

“Half.”

“Don’t correct me.” She kissed his jaw. “Have you anything else to say?”

He thought about it. “I get to go home with you,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove to Yunwu in Nobody, in the dark, with Brake asleep on the back seat and the packet of cinnamon gum on the dashboard. Uncle Lok had left the outside light on above the blue door, and a basket of food on the kitchen table, and his mother’s quilt with the mountain road on it folded at the foot of the bed.

That night, for the first time in his life, he didn’t take the side of the bed nearest the door. He took the side beside her.

chapters.title: First Podium
chapters.desc: A whole season without one. Fourth, fifth, fourth, sixth. Then the finale at the circuit in the north, a year and a month after the Needle, with two mothers and Granny Shum in Stand B and a red works car in her mirrors on the last lap. Third place. Champagne in his face. He lets it happen.
chapters.epigraph: “Come home. I’ll be here.”
chapters.content:
The first thing she learned about a season without a podium was that fourth place could become a personal insult. The second was that fifth was somehow worse.

By the last round of 2026 she had two fourths, a fifth and a sixth, and Callum had almost exactly the same: quick enough to be dangerous, steady enough to keep Orsini respectable, never in the right place when the flag fell. The team hadn’t stood on a step all year. Donatella had stopped using the word potential. Matteo had stopped saying unfortunate. Beppe had started calling their results “the usual disappointment,” which Serafina considered a poor motivational strategy.

And Haozhen had learned to say nothing at all when she came back from a race, which was the most annoying thing of all.

“You’re supposed to tell me I drove well,” she said one night at the end of September, sitting on the bench with her race boots dangling.

“You drove well.”

“You’re supposed to tell me I was unlucky.”

“You qualified ninth.”

She stared at him.

“What?”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am.”

“Then why are you agreeing with Matteo?”

“Because he’s right.” She threw a roll of masking tape at him. He caught it. She looked away.

He put the tablet down and came and stood between her knees and waited. He’d learned that too: when she was angry about a race there was nearly always something under the anger that needed longer to come up.

“I’m tired of fourth,” she said to her boots. “I’m tired of being told we had good pace. I’m tired of watching the same three cars disappear into the champagne.” She picked at a thread on her sleeve. “And I’m frightened.”

His face changed. “Of what?”

“Of how much I want it.” She swallowed. “I used to want to win because it was fun. Because I loved the car and the corner and getting it exactly right. Now I want that step so badly I can’t think about anything else. I lie awake and drive the last lap. The flag. Climbing out.” Her fingers tightened on the edge of the bench. “And then I think of the Needle. I’m not scared every time I brake any more. But part of me thinks I have to go faster to prove I’m not. And I hate that part.”

He looked at her.

“You don’t owe the track anything,” he said. “You don’t owe the team a podium. You don’t owe the people in the stand a result. And you don’t owe me a single tenth.”

“Even after you rebuilt a car for two hundred miles an hour?”

“Especially then.” He put his thumb on her knee. “I want you to race because you love it. Not to pay something back.”

“What if I want the podium because I love it?”

“Then go and get it.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Come home,” he said. “I’ll be here.”

She put her forehead on his chest. “That’s very inconvenient.”

“Why?”

“It makes it hard to stay angry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The final round was at the circuit in the north on the third Sunday in October. A year and a month after the Needle.

She hadn’t meant to remember the date. She didn’t keep it in a calendar. But the track looked the same, and the back straight still ran down to the same tightening left, and on Sunday morning she stood by the Orsini garage and watched the support race go through it, the approach, the brakes, the turn-in, the exit, and felt the sound in her chest without the old blow behind it.

That was something.

“Cold?” He held out her jacket.

“No.”

He held it out anyway. She took it.

“Your family’s here,” he said.

In the main grandstand, in the middle of the second row of Stand B, Aurelia had got three seats together, and three women sat in them with different degrees of enthusiasm. Vittoria had a pair of field glasses her husband had given her in 1998 for the opera. Liang Shufen had a flask of tea. Granny Shum had a bag of clementines and her police scanner, tuned, for reasons nobody could establish, to the race-control channel.

“What’s my mother doing with binoculars?”

“Teaching mine to use them,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“No. You turn this,” said Vittoria. “The little wheel in the middle. Both eyes open.”

Liang Shufen held the glasses up to her face. “Everything is grey.”

“You’re looking at the wall. Lower.” Vittoria put a hand on the barrel and tipped it down. “There. The pit lane. Count the garages from the left.”

“Which is hers?”

“Blue and white. Number seven.”

Liang Shufen counted. Then she was quiet for a while. Through the lenses, small and sharp, a woman in a blue-and-white race suit was standing by a car with her helmet under her arm, talking to a man in a dark shirt with a red-striped pass on it. The man put his hand on the woman’s back, just.

“That’s him,” said Liang Shufen.

“I asked you to find her.”

“I found both.” She lowered the glasses. “She looks small.”

“She isn’t.”

“I know. She’s always been like that,” said Vittoria. “Small, and impossible to move.”

Granny Shum laughed and handed them each a clementine.

✦ ✦ ✦

Qualifying had been bad. Fifth for her. Seventh for Callum. Donatella looked at the screen and said nothing for almost a minute.

“Our long-run pace is better than our one-lap pace,” said Matteo. “We have a reasonable tyre window.”

“Reasonable.”

“Better than poor.”

“Thank you.”

The start was clean. She held fifth through turn one and sat behind the two cars ahead for a whole stint, launch good, no room, tyres coming in properly, never overheating the fronts. On lap twenty a safety car bunched the field and Orsini called her in. A clean stop. Fresh tyres. She came out fifth with the cars ahead close enough to see.

Then the car in fourth began to struggle with its rears, and she took it at the hairpin without anyone noticing it happen.

Ahead of her now was a red works car that had been in front of her for most of the year. An old driver, quick and cunning and good at being wide. He covered the inside into turn one. He took the middle of the road through the second sector. He made his car as broad as a bus on the straights. She tried once, at the hairpin, and there was nothing. She tried at the chicane and he moved across, and she stayed behind.

Her breathing stayed level. The tyres were warm. The car was talking to her.

“Pace is good,” said Matteo in her ear, the only voice she heard. “Keep the pressure on. Watch your rears.”

“Copy.”

He was standing on the pit wall behind Matteo, next to Donatella, with a headset on that he wasn’t allowed to speak into. He watched the screen. The white line and the blue one, lying on top of each other on every braking zone. The red, clean. The yellow, sure.

Lap thirty-eight. The back straight. The red car half a second ahead.

The Needle came up at the end of it.

He watched her eyes go to the marker on the onboard camera. The same marker. The same corner. For one fraction of a second he saw the tiniest lift on the green line, and his hand closed on the barrier.

Then it was gone.

She stayed flat. The red car moved over to cover the inside, the way he’d covered it all year. She went to the outside. She braked at her marker, on it, not before it, and the white line and the blue line came down together, one line, and she turned in later than he had, carrying more speed round the long tightening edge of the corner, with two wheels on the very last of the kerb. The red car held the inside. Its fronts began to slide.

For a fraction of a second the two cars ran side by side through the Needle, close enough to touch.

Then she was through.

“Position confirmed,” said Matteo, and his voice wasn’t calm any more. “P3. That’s third, Serafina. Third.”

“I heard you.”

“Bring it home.”

“I’m trying,” she said, and he heard her laugh inside the helmet.

The last lap was the longest of her life. The red car was in her mirrors at every braking point and through every exit. She didn’t overdrive it. She made no sudden moves. She put the car exactly where it needed to be and nowhere else, and at the last corner she braked on the marker and turned in and opened the wheel and went.

The flag fell.

The radio exploded. Matteo was shouting. Beppe was shouting. Somebody behind them was shouting something that sounded like a prayer. She was laughing so hard her voice cracked. “P3! P3!”

“That’s a podium,” said Matteo. “Your first.”

“I know!”

She looked toward the pit wall as she went past. He was standing beside Donatella. He wasn’t shouting. He wasn’t waving. His hands were clasped in front of him and his face was still, and she knew that face, and she knew exactly what it cost him to stand there in the open and let the cameras on the pit wall look at him.

She lifted her hand from the wheel.

He lifted his.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the step she held the trophy against her chest and couldn’t stop looking at it. Third. After a season of fourths. After the hospital. After the simulator. After the January morning in the cold. The anthem played. Eleven thousand people in the stands. A medal round her neck.

Then the bottles.

The driver in second sprayed her first, and she ducked and sprayed him back, and the winner caught her from the side, and she was soaked and laughing and blind. Then she looked down past the barrier, at the strip of tarmac below the podium where the teams stood.

He was there, beside Donatella, looking up at her.

She pointed the bottle at him.

He saw it coming. He could have moved. He could have stepped behind Beppe, or turned his face, or done what he had done his whole adult life, which was to stay out of the middle of anybody else’s photograph.

He stayed where he was.

She squeezed. It hit him full in the face. His hair. His shirt. His pass. His eyes shut and his mouth came open in shock and the whole Orsini crew roared.

He wiped his face with one hand.

Then he looked up at her and smiled.

Not the small private smile he kept for the two of them in the garage, not the careful one he wore when he knew he was being watched. A real smile, wide and helpless and unguarded, with champagne running off his chin. The cameras on the podium caught it. The photographers below caught it. Eleven thousand people saw it on the big screen over the main straight.

She came down the steps before the ceremony was quite over, with the trophy in one hand and her hair dripping.

“You’re wet,” she said.

“I noticed.”

He held out his arms, and she walked into them, and he lifted her clean off the bottom step with her trophy and all. Her feet left the ground. She threw an arm round his neck and laughed into his hair. Somebody shouted his name. A dozen lenses swung round.

He didn’t look away from any of them. He kissed her, in front of the podium, in front of the team, in front of eleven thousand people and every camera at the circuit.

When he put her down she held his face in her wet hands.

“I passed him at the Needle.”

“I saw.”

“On the outside.”

“I know, Sera.”

“I’m not frightened of it any more,” she said.

“Good,” he said.

“Thank you for holding my helmet.”

“Always,” he said, and she kissed him again, and this time he let the cameras have all of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Stand B was still on its feet when they got there. Vittoria had been crying and said she hadn’t. Liang Shufen had been crying and said so at once. Granny Shum was eating a clementine and telling the strangers in the row behind that she had always known the girl could drive, since she was nineteen and stupid.

Her mother held out her arms and Serafina went into them, champagne and race suit and trophy, and Vittoria held on carefully, minding the shoulder.

“You drove beautifully.”

“I was driving.”

“You were brave,” said her mother. “You can be both.”

Then Liang Shufen took her face between her hands and kissed both her cheeks and said “Very good,” and looked past her at her son. “You watched?”

“Yes, Ma.”

“Good.”

Vittoria turned to him and held out her hand. He took it.

“Thank you for bringing her home, Mr. Qin.”

He looked at her.

“Haozhen,” he said. “We’ve been related for six months.”

Something moved at the corner of Vittoria’s mouth. “Haozhen,” she said, as if trying the weight of it. Then she looked at his wet shirt. “You ought to change.”

“He was sprayed with champagne, Mother,” said Serafina.

“I can see that. He didn’t move.”

“No.”

“Good,” said Vittoria, and turned away.

“You’ve been approved,” Serafina said.

“I’ve been married to you for six months.”

“Doesn’t count.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The sports pages came out on Monday. The first photograph was Serafina on the step with the trophy over her head and champagne in her hair. The second was the pass, round the outside of the red car at the Needle. The third was him: under the podium, soaked, eyes shut, mouth open, laughing. The fourth was him lifting her off the steps.

Vittoria cut out the third. Liang Shufen, who had come down on the Sunday-night train and stayed, cut out the fourth. They met at the kitchen table at the back of the garage that afternoon, Vittoria with her good scissors and Liang Shufen with an envelope, and laid them side by side.

Serafina came in with two coffees. “What are you doing?”

“Keeping this,” said Vittoria, and held up the third photograph.

“Why?”

“It’s a good photograph,” said Vittoria.

“He looks happy,” said Liang Shufen.

He was at the bench going through the prototype’s service schedule. He looked up. “What?”

“Nothing,” said Serafina.

“Your husband is handsome,” Vittoria told her daughter, without looking at him.

“Very,” said Liang Shufen.

He went red and looked back at his schedule. Serafina put the coffees down and slid her arms round his waist from behind and rested her cheek on his back.

“They’re making a collection,” she said.

“Apparently.”

“Are you happy?”

He put the schedule down and turned round. He looked at her, and at the two women at the table, each sliding a newspaper photograph of him into a clear plastic sleeve.

“Yes,” he said. “Very.”

A train went over. On the bench beside the chipped white mug, the right way round, the first podium trophy Orsini had won in Asia in four years caught the afternoon light.

chapters.title: A Garage With Two Names on the Door
chapters.desc: Epilogue. Two years on. The garage under the railway bridge has a sign at last. There’s a team, and a junior driver who used to film from a car roof, and three postcards on the whiteboard. One of them has a football drawn on it, and a number. And at three in the morning, someone different is driving the loop.
chapters.epigraph: “My road.” “Our road.”
chapters.content:
The sign took three attempts.

The first was too small. The second was too expensive, according to Aurelia, who read the quotation and informed her sister that no reasonable business needed letters you could read from the far side of the railway viaduct. The third arrived on Friday the twentieth of October 2028, two years after her first podium, wrapped in cardboard and carried by two men who regretted it all the way up the service lane.

He stood by the shutter with the instructions. She stood on the other side with a drill.

“You’re reading it upside down.”

“I was checking the back.”

“There is no back.”

They got it up at a quarter to four. Dark metal on the old brick, no gold, nothing extra, the ampersand a little smaller than the rest.

SONG & QIN
RACING · ENGINEERING

She stepped back into the lane. He stood next to her. Neither of them said anything for a while.

“Two names,” she said.

“Yes.”

“On the door.”

“Yes.”

“Officially.”

“Very.” He looked at it. “I like that it’s ours.”

A train went over. The letters trembled slightly on their brackets.

“It’s not going to fall down?”

“I checked the bolts.”

“Three times?”

“Four,” he said, and she laughed and leaned against him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It had grown in ways neither of them had planned. A garage with a handful of friends and too many cars and too many people eating dinner under a bridge had become, over two seasons, a racing team. Two cars in the Asian series. Matteo, who had left Orsini in the spring because, he said, he wanted to work for people who argued with him properly. Big Wu, and Beppe two weeks a month, and Mouse at three screens in the office with the old stopwatch hanging off one of them. A transport schedule Aurelia made them keep. A small engineering shop next door, in the arch the railway had sold in the second auction. And a junior driver who had once been famous for filming illegal races from the roof of a van.

Ghost Pepper came in at twenty past eight on Monday morning with his helmet under his arm. He was twenty-two now, still thin, still quick, and still had the purple coupé, which he had repainted black and swore he didn’t miss.

“Morning.”

“You’re late,” said Serafina, without looking up from a damper chart.

“I’m four minutes early.”

“Then you’re four minutes late for being on time.”

He looked at Haozhen. “Is she always like this?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said Ghost Pepper, relieved. “I thought I’d done something.”

“You probably have,” said Serafina.

His first season had been a revelation and a disaster in about equal parts. He was fast, too fast sometimes, and wanted every pass to look like a highlight. She had spent three months teaching him that a race wasn’t a list of chances to impress people. Haozhen had spent the same three months teaching him the things that happened outside the car. The difference between a gap and an invitation. The difference between a mechanic at the pit wall waiting and a mechanic at the pit wall because something was wrong. Where the fire extinguisher was in every garage he walked into. And that a driver who didn’t bring the car back in one piece wasn’t fast. He was just early.

“Installation run,” she said, and gave him the sheet. “Then balance. You’re not chasing a time. You’re not impressing the engineers.”

He looked at Matteo.

“I don’t need impressing,” said Matteo.

“See,” she said. “He already dislikes you.”

Haozhen held out a bottle of water. “Drink it before you get in.”

“Thanks, boss.”

She watched that. It was nothing. A man handing a boy a bottle of water. But she remembered a boy on a van roof with a phone who thought the way to be seen was to do something stupid and make sure it was filmed, and now he had a seat, and a sheet with his name typed on it, and people who would tell him when to lift.

“Proud?” she said, under her breath.

“He’s learning.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were three postcards on the whiteboard, beside the red board that said NO GUNS NO DRUNKS NO CHILDREN NO CRYING. He had never taken them down.

The first had come in March, in a plain envelope addressed to the garage. A railway station in winter, snow on the platform. On the back, in an upright hand she didn’t know:

I resigned too. They made a fuss. I let them.

And underneath, smaller:

The window seat is better than I remembered.

No name. He hadn’t needed one. Serafina had read it twice. Haozhen had read it many more times than that, standing at the board with his coffee in the mornings. There had been no letter after it, no explanation of what had happened after the coast road, no apology. Just a man who had once kept him the seat by the glass on a bus, sitting by a window of his own somewhere.

He hadn’t written back. Not yet.

The second had come in May. A small walled garden with tomato plants trained up the brick. No signature. One line:

These survived the first frost.

A paper packet of seeds had been tucked inside.

“She’s sending you vegetables,” Serafina had said.

“She’s sending seeds.”

“That’s worse. That’s an apology with planting instructions.”

He’d planted them in two pots in the yard behind the garage, by the kitchen door. One had grown. The other hadn’t. He never said which pot he had thought of as which.

The third had come in August, from Lisbon. A steep street of yellow houses with blue shutters. On the back, in a hand Haozhen knew at once from four account books:

Home.

And underneath:

Tomás did 32 keepy-ups yesterday. He says he could have done more if the ball hadn’t hit the wall.

A small drawing of a football. The number again, in a circle. 32.

He had stood in front of the board the day it came. Serafina had come and stood next to him.

“Thirty-two,” she’d said.

“He was at thirty-one. The day before.”

The day before a man in a dark coat came round the corner of a lane behind the market and took his father, and a seven-year-old boy threw a football at a car window by the face of the man in the passenger seat. Five years. A boy of twelve now, counting kicks against a wall in a steep street. A father in the doorway shouting that it was time for dinner.

“That’s a good number,” she’d said.

“Yes.”

“Keep it.”

He had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain at Monza had come out of nowhere, two springs before.

Orsini had taken her to Europe for three rounds in 2027, and on the Thursday of the Italian one it rained so hard during the last practice that they packed up early. She’d wanted to walk up to the old banking, the high concrete oval at the edge of the park that nobody had raced on in fifty years, which stood in the trees like the ruin of a cathedral. Of course he’d gone with her.

They climbed it on foot from the inside, where the angle was gentle enough to walk. Halfway up she stopped. Below them the empty track lay in the rain, the trees black, fine silver lines of water moving down the old surface.

“Imagine doing two hundred miles an hour up here,” she said.

“I don’t need to imagine.”

She turned. He was looking at her.

“You’re supposed to say something romantic.”

“I thought I had.”

“That was a technical observation.”

“It was accurate.”

“Try again.”

He took her hand. “It’s beautiful.”

“Better.”

The rain came down harder. He reached for the hood of her jacket. She caught his wrist.

“Don’t.”

“You’ll get soaked.”

“I’m already soaked. I’m happy.”

He put his hand down. They stood on the slope of the banking with the rain coming down on them and the empty circuit below, and then she turned round and kissed him. His hand went to her waist. She laughed into his mouth when he tried to pull her closer and his shoe skidded on fifty years of wet moss and he nearly sat down on the old concrete.

“Careful.”

“You told me not to stop you.”

“I didn’t tell you to fall over.”

He kissed her again anyway.

No race won. No record. Nothing decided. Just rain and old concrete and wet asphalt, and her laughing with both hands on his face. Mouse had taken a photograph from the bottom of the banking with the long lens and never told them, and given it to them framed for Christmas. Years later, when he looked at it, he would remember the sound of her laugh before he remembered the weather.

✦ ✦ ✦

The two mothers had at last come to an arrangement about the stool.

It was a low wooden stool beside the kettle that Liang Shufen had brought down from the flat above the tailor’s when she’d started staying at the garage for a week every month. Vittoria had said it was too low. Liang Shufen had said it was the correct height for sitting on. Vittoria had said it was uncomfortable. Liang Shufen had said that in forty years nobody had complained. The argument had lasted the best part of a year.

On Saturday afternoon Serafina came in from the yard and stopped in the kitchen doorway. Behind her, Haozhen stopped too.

Vittoria was sitting on the stool with a cup of tea. Liang Shufen was standing at the stove beside her, telling her how to make the soup he liked.

“Ginger first.”

“I know.”

“Not too much.”

“I know.”

“Then wait.”

Vittoria looked into the pot. “How long?”

“Until it smells right.”

“That isn’t a measurement.”

“It is a measurement,” said Liang Shufen. “It’s mine.”

“You northerners never measure anything properly.”

“We use our noses. It’s worked for many years.”

Haozhen looked at his mother at the stove, and his mother-in-law on the stool, arguing about ginger.

“Looks normal,” he said.

“Very normal,” said Serafina.

Vittoria looked up. “Your husband’s here.”

“Is he?”

“Have you eaten?” said Liang Shufen, to both of them.

“Yes.”

“What?”

He answered before Serafina could. “Rice. Fish.”

“Enough?”

“Yes.”

“You’re both terrible at eating properly,” said Vittoria, and Liang Shufen nodded.

He made four cups of tea. He knew which mug had the crack in the handle. He knew his mother took hers black and Vittoria wanted milk, a lot of it, put in first, which Liang Shufen considered a crime. He knew the kettle’s switch had to be pressed twice because it didn’t always catch. He’d learned all of it without writing any of it down. Without being told to. Without anyone asking him to keep watch. It was only his kitchen.

Serafina rested her chin on his shoulder. He gave her the cup.

“Careful. It’s hot.”

Vittoria watched them. Then she turned to Liang Shufen. “He still makes her tea.”

“He always will,” said his mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning she woke because the bed was moving.

Not much. Just enough to know he was getting dressed. She opened one eye.

“Where are you going?”

He stopped. “Sorry. Did I wake you?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the keys in his hand. Then at her. “Drive,” he said.

She pushed herself up on one elbow. “You?”

“If you’d like.”

“You’re taking the loop?”

“Yes.”

For six years the three-in-the-morning drive had belonged to her. She’d picked him up. She’d driven the harbour road with the music off and no sudden brakes. She’d watched him sleep two hours and eleven minutes in his own passenger seat, the first time, because he needed it more than he knew.

Now he was standing at the side of the bed with the keys.

“Are you sure?”

“I want to,” he said, and held out his hand. “Come with me.”

He helped her into a jacket. She was still half asleep when they reached the shutter.

“Which one?”

“The grey one.”

“Good.”

He opened Nobody’s passenger door for her, and fastened his own belt, and checked his mirrors, once each, and started her up.

The city was quiet. The harbour lights lay across the road. He drove without hurrying. No hard acceleration. No sudden brakes. At the first lights he looked across.

“Comfortable?”

“Mm.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

He turned the heater up a notch anyway. She smiled without opening her eyes.

They went past the garage, and the new sign above the shutter, SONG & QIN, and down to the water, and along it: the harbour road, the old bridge, the tunnel, the coast road, the loop. The same road she’d once driven alone while he followed two cars back. The same road she’d driven the night he first slept. The same road where they’d sat two wheels in a ditch on a New Year’s Eve and made promises about a life neither of them knew how to want.

Her head slid against the window. Then, at a bend, onto his shoulder. He kept the car steady. At the next red light he put his hand over hers.

“Still there?” she mumbled.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

The light went green. He drove on. Once round. Then again. He didn’t hurry. He didn’t need to be anywhere.

When the sky over the harbour began to go pale he turned for home. He parked under the bridge. The engine ticked as it cooled. She stirred, and opened her eyes.

“Home?”

“Yes.”

She looked at the clock on the dashboard. “Two hours?”

“Two hours and eleven minutes.”

“You counted.”

“I noticed,” he said. “I looked twice. When you fell asleep, and now.”

She lifted her head off his shoulder and touched his face.

“You drove.”

“Yes.”

“My road.”

“Our road.”

She kissed him, a sleepy, unhurried kiss, and he rested his forehead against hers.

“Next time,” she said, “I’ll drive.”

“Next time.”

“And you can sleep.”

“Deal,” he said.

They walked to the shutter together. The sign over it caught the first light. Inside, three postcards waited on the whiteboard under a framed photograph of a red car on a runway: a railway station, a walled garden, a yellow street with a football drawn on the back. A tomato plant in a pot by the kitchen door. A chipped white mug on the bench with his name on the bottom, the right way round. A life that hadn’t needed to be hidden.

A train went over.

For once, at three in the morning, he had been the one to bring her home.

chapters.title: He Learns to Lose at Karaoke
chapters.desc: December 2023. The team Christmas, in a karaoke room above Mr. Kwok’s favourite bar. Big Wu scores forty-one. Mr. Kwok sings for his late wife. And a man who has spent eleven years being forgettable tries very hard to sing badly, and she catches him lifting at the gas works.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re allowed to be bad at something, Hao.”
chapters.content:
The Christmas party was Mr. Kwok’s idea, which was unfortunate, because Mr. Kwok believed a proper Christmas needed three things: enough food for a small army, enough to drink that the army forgot how much it had eaten, and karaoke.

“Since when is it tradition?” said Aurelia.

“Since I decided.”

Nobody argued.

So on Saturday the twenty-third of December the whole team was crammed into the private room above the Golden Phoenix, Mr. Kwok’s favourite bar, on red leather sofas round a low table crowded with roast duck, fried noodles, prawn dumplings and an alarming quantity of mince pies that Big Wu’s mother had made because somebody had told her the English ate them. A plastic tree leaned to the left in the corner. Somebody had put a Santa hat on the microphone.

Big Wu took the first song. He sang with the confidence of a man who had never once asked himself whether he was any good. The machine awarded him forty-one.

He stopped with his arms half raised. “Forty-one.”

“Out of a hundred,” said Mouse.

“I know how numbers work.” Big Wu stared at the screen with real horror. “It’s got a four in it.”

“It’s got a one in it as well.”

“The four’s first.” He jabbed the button on the machine. “Again. I’m not taking a four into the new year.”

He sang it again. It was worse. The machine, which seemed to have a sense of humour, gave him thirty-nine. He bowed to the room as if he’d won a championship and sat down relieved.

Serafina was laughing so hard she had to hold on to Aurelia when Haozhen came back from the bar with two glasses of water and put one in front of her.

“You’re not drinking?”

“Later.”

“You’ve said later for an hour.”

“I’ve been busy.”

“Doing what?”

“Making sure nobody falls down the stairs.”

“It’s karaoke. Not an evacuation.”

“Is there a difference?” he said, and she pulled him down onto the sofa beside her.

He didn’t sing. He sat with one arm along the back of the sofa behind her and watched everyone else. He smiled when Big Wu went for a third. He laughed when Mouse chose a song in a key no human throat could reach on purpose. He clapped when Aurelia turned out to sing beautifully, and pretended not to see Qian filming her from the corner.

He was there. He was polite. He was also somewhere else.

She saw the way his eyes went to his phone every time it lit up. She saw his smile go out like a lamp whenever he thought nobody was looking. Fourteen days ago a woman in a grey coat had sat on his stool in the garage and left forty photographs on the bench, the last of them his mother at a market stall at nine forty-one in the morning. The file was locked in the office drawer. The Director’s deadline was the new year. He’d been quiet for two weeks in the way a held breath is quiet.

She leaned her head on his shoulder. He put his cheek against her hair for a second.

“Having fun?” he said.

“Very much. Are you?”

“Yes.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“Liar,” she said.

“That’s a serious accusation.”

“I’m very serious.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then Mr. Kwok picked up the microphone, and the room went quiet without being asked.

He stood by the screen with one hand on the back of a chair. “I don’t have a good voice,” he said.

“Nobody does!” shouted Big Wu.

Mr. Kwok ignored him. He chose an old song, a slow one. Serafina knew it. On the nights he shut the bar early he sat alone at the end of the counter with a pot of tea and this song on the little speaker by the till, and she’d never once asked him why.

He sang it. Not to the room, not to the machine. His voice was rough in places and he missed some of the notes, and he knew every single word, the way you know something you’ve sung a thousand times, sometimes with somebody beside you and then for a long while alone. His wife had been dead nine years. Nobody in the room moved until he finished.

The machine gave him seventy-three. Big Wu started clapping first, loudly, and then everybody did.

“Enough,” said Mr. Kwok, waving them down, his eyes wet. “Eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She felt Haozhen looking at the microphone.

“You could sing,” she said.

“No.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I’ve heard myself.”

“Have you?” She smiled at him sweetly. “Prove it.”

He said no again, and she watched him say it, and watched him look at the screen, and the list of songs, and the machine, and something clicked.

“Oh,” she said.

“What?”

“You’re going to sing badly.”

His face didn’t change at all. “I don’t know what you mean.”

“You’re going to pick something easy and miss every note on purpose, so it’s funny, and then everyone laughs and forgets it.”

“Why would I do that?”

“So nobody remembers you,” she said, and the smile went a little softer. “You’re allowed to be bad at something, Hao. You don’t have to arrange it.”

“I’m aware.”

“You’re not.” She picked up the microphone off the table, Santa hat and all, and stood up and held out her hand. “Qin Haozhen. It’s Christmas.”

He looked at her hand. Then he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

His first song was a disaster. A beautifully engineered disaster.

He chose a pop song from ten years before with an easy range, held the microphone at exactly the right distance from his mouth, and sang it as if the melody had personally insulted him. He came in a beat late. He went flat on every long note. He missed a whole line and stood looking at the screen with polite interest while it went past. On the last chorus he found a key that appeared to have been invented specifically to inconvenience everyone in the room.

The machine struggled. Then: TWENTY-THREE.

Big Wu fell sideways on the sofa. Mouse had tears running down her face. Aurelia covered hers with both hands.

“Twenty-three,” said Haozhen gravely, and put the microphone back on its stand.

Serafina caught his sleeve before he could sit down.

“Wait.”

He looked at her.

“You were breathing properly the whole time,” she said, quiet, under the noise. “Your timing was perfect till you decided it wasn’t. You changed key in the middle of the chorus. You don’t do that by accident. You have to know where the key is to miss it like that.” She held on. “You lifted.”

“Lifted?”

“At Granny Shum’s. The first night. At the gas works. You braked at the second lamp post, a whole lamp post early, so I’d win, and when I shouted at you, you said I was having fun.” She looked at him. “You just did it again.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“I don’t need to win everything,” he said at last.

“I know.” She touched his cheek. “But you don’t have to lose on purpose either. Not with us.”

Around them the room went on: Big Wu demanding another go, Mouse arguing with the machine, Mr. Kwok telling somebody to stop spilling beer on his sofa.

“What if I’m not good?”

“Then you’re not good.”

“And?”

“And I’ll still like you.” She smiled. “Besides, I want to hear you.”

He looked at the microphone. This time he picked it up himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t choose a song he knew. He chose one she liked: a slow old love song with a plain tune and a chorus that rose gently and asked nothing much of whoever was singing it. She’d played it in the car once, in October, on the harbour road at two in the morning, with him half asleep in the passenger seat, and she’d thought he hadn’t heard.

The room went quiet when the first notes came in.

He stood a little too straight by the screen, as though he were waiting for someone to give him instructions. Then he looked across at her, on the sofa, with her chin in her hand.

He began.

His voice was low. Not showy, not trained, but warm and steady. He knew how to breathe. He knew where the notes were, all of them. He didn’t have to push for the high part. He just went there.

And he wasn’t trying to disappear.

He sang the first verse to the screen. By the chorus he was singing it to her. The words were simple: a promise to come home, a promise to stay, a promise that somebody would still be there at the end of the road. She sat on the red sofa with her hand over her mouth and her eyes bright.

When it ended nobody said anything for a second.

98.

“NINETY-EIGHT!” Big Wu was on his feet.

Mouse looked betrayed. “That’s not possible.”

“Apparently he can sing,” said Aurelia.

“Good,” said Mr. Kwok, and clapped once.

Haozhen put the microphone down. He looked at the score. Then at her. She was smiling at him as if he’d done something far more important than sing a song in a room above a bar.

He walked across.

“Don’t you dare—” she began.

He got there first. One hand at her waist, the other on her cheek, and he kissed her. Not one of the small careful kisses he gave her in front of other people. He kissed her properly, in front of the whole team, with his hand in her hair, as if ninety-eight points had given him permission to be ridiculous.

She laughed against his mouth and took a fistful of his shirt and kissed him back.

Something flew past his ear and burst against the wall behind him.

A mince pie.

Big Wu was standing with another one in his hand. “GET A ROOM!”

Haozhen looked at the crumbs on the wallpaper. Then at Big Wu. “That’s food. Your mother made that.”

“YOU’RE WELCOME!”

She laughed so hard she had to sit down. He sat beside her and she tucked herself under his arm.

“You could have had a hundred,” she murmured.

“I missed a note.”

“You noticed?”

“The second chorus.”

She laughed and kissed the corner of his jaw. “Next Christmas, we’ll try again.”

“Together?”

“Obviously.”

“Then I’ll practise,” he said.

And for the rest of the night, even with a file locked in a drawer and the new year eight days off, he didn’t look at his phone once.

chapters.title: She Teaches Him to Change a Tyre
chapters.desc: December 2022, the week after the track day. She decides that any man who sits in her passenger seat should be able to change a wheel. He says he’s never done it. She times him: fourteen minutes. Then, one wet night in the alley, she sees him do it in ninety seconds.
chapters.epigraph: “It was how quietly he could arrange to be taught.”
chapters.content:
She found the gap in Qin Haozhen’s education on Wednesday afternoon, four days after the track day, when she asked him to pass her the wheel brace.

He’d brought the grey estate in because the left-rear caliper was sticking again, the same one she’d freed for him at two in the morning in November, and he had been leaning on the bench for an hour with her coffee in his hand, watching her work, which he seemed to consider an occupation. He handed her the brace without looking. She ran the last nut down on Nonna’s front wheel, let the jack down, checked the pressure.

“Have you ever changed a tyre?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Recently.”

“On what?”

He paused. “A car.”

She put the gauge down. “That isn’t an answer.”

“It was a car.”

“Have you, personally, with your own two hands, ever taken a wheel off and put one back on?”

“No,” he said.

She stood up. “Unbelievable.”

“What?”

“You drove the north circuit in one fifty-eight on Saturday and beat me by six hundredths on one lap and you can’t change a wheel?”

“I’ve never needed to.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“What’s the point?”

She took the coffee out of his hand and put it on the bench. “Anybody who sits in my passenger seat can change a wheel.”

He considered this. “Is that a rule?”

“It is now.”

“Does it apply to everybody?”

“Especially you.” She pointed at the estate. “Front left. Come on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first lesson took fourteen minutes. She stood beside him with Mouse’s stopwatch.

“Somewhere flat. Handbrake on. Hazards if you’re anywhere near traffic. Don’t start in the middle of a road because you’re in a hurry. Then crack the nuts before you lift it. Not off. Just break them.”

He fitted the brace.

“Your weight. Not your back. You’ll do your back in.”

He leaned. The nut gave. He went round the others.

“Jack. Do you know where the lifting point is?”

“Yes.”

“You’ve never done this.”

“I can read a manual.”

“Show me.”

He found the reinforced point under the sill and set the jack under it. She crouched beside him.

“Not there. Further in. There.”

He moved it. He checked it. He checked it again before he lifted the wheel off the floor. His hands were careful, almost too careful, and she watched them with more attention than the job required.

“You’re cautious.”

“Is that bad?”

“Not with a car in the air.”

He took the nuts off and laid them in a neat row on the concrete. He pulled the wheel. He looked at the spare.

“Don’t drop it on your foot.”

“I won’t.”

“Everybody says that.”

He lifted the spare to the hub and couldn’t get the holes to meet. She reached over his shoulder and put her hand over his on the rim.

“Here. Hold it level. Otherwise you’re fighting the weight.”

Her fingers lay over his. He didn’t move at all.

“Like this,” she said, and turned his grip a little. “Feel that?”

“Yes.”

“Nuts on by hand. Opposite sides, not round in a circle, or you’ll pull it on crooked. Then down. Then tight.”

He did it exactly as she said. When the car was back on the ground he tightened them with the brace in a star, and she checked every one, and pressed the stopwatch.

“Fourteen minutes.”

He looked at it. “Is that acceptable?”

“It’s terrible.”

He looked at her.

“I’m joking.”

“You’re not.”

“I’m a little bit joking.” He stood up. There was a streak of grease across his cheekbone. She reached up and wiped it off with her thumb before she could think better of it. His eyes followed her hand all the way.

“Will there be another lesson?”

“Tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow?”

“And Friday.”

“Should I bring a notebook?”

“You’re already unbearable,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he did it in six minutes and twelve seconds. She was impressed and tried not to show it.

The nuts were seated, the spare true, the jack on the right point first time. He’d remembered the order without being told. He’d stopped checking the jack every three seconds. He’d got grease right across his palm and hadn’t wiped it off.

“Good,” she said.

“Good?”

“Good.” She took his hand and turned it over and looked at the black across it. “You usually keep your hands so clean.”

“Not always.”

He was watching her with that quiet, slightly amused look that always made her forget what she’d been going to say. She let go of his hand.

“Tomorrow we do it again. Five minutes.”

“I’ll try.”

“Don’t try. Do it.”

“Yes, instructor.”

She pushed his shoulder, and he let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It rained on Sunday. It had been raining since the afternoon, the kind of steady winter rain that turns the roads to black glass and the gutters into rivers, and they were coming back from Granny Shum’s yard in the grey estate at half past nine with a box of second-hand bushes on the back seat when they heard it: the soft, sick thump-thump-thump of a tyre going down.

He slowed. “Flat.”

“Rear left,” she said. “Sounds like it.”

He pulled into the service alley beside the old gas works. It was nearly empty. Rain ran in sheets along the gutter into a choked drain. A yellow lamp flickered over a steel shutter.

She reached for her phone. “I’ll ring—”

He already had his door open. “Stay in the car. It’s raining.”

She looked at him. Then she smiled slowly. “Oh?”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

He got the spare out of the back. She stayed in the car for about three seconds. Then she got out, put up her umbrella, and took Mouse’s stopwatch out of her coat pocket.

He looked over his shoulder. “What’s that for?”

“Quality control.”

“It’s wet. The ground isn’t level. The nuts may be tight.”

“Are you nervous?”

“No.”

“Then go.”

She pressed it.

He crouched by the wheel. He looked once along the alley, both ways. Then his hands began to move, and she forgot to watch the stopwatch.

They moved fast. Not quick-for-a-beginner fast. Fast the way her own hands were fast on a gearbox she’d stripped a hundred times. The brace went on and the nuts cracked one-two-three-four-five without a pause. The jack went under the sill blind, straight onto the point, in the rain, in the dark, and the car came up in eight strokes. The nuts came off into his palm and into his pocket. The wheel came off. The spare went on, first time, true. Nuts, star pattern, by hand. Down. Brace, star pattern. He stood up with the flat in one hand.

She looked at the stopwatch.

01:31.

She looked at it. Then at him. Then at the wheel.

He picked up the punctured tyre. “What?”

“Ninety-one seconds.”

“Good.”

“Good?” She crouched and checked the nuts, every one, in the rain. Seated. Tight. In the right order. She checked the jack point. She checked the spare. It was perfect. It was better than she’d have done it.

She stood up.

“You’ve done this before.”

He didn’t answer.

“Haozhen.”

“Yes,” he said.

“How many times?”

He thought about it, and she saw something go across his face that wasn’t amusement at all: a van on a ring road at three in the morning with somebody in the back, a tyre gone, and ninety seconds before a patrol came by.

“Enough,” he said.

“You told me you hadn’t.”

“I said I hadn’t done it.”

“You said you’d never personally—”

“On that car,” he said. “I’d never done it on that car.”

She opened her mouth. She shut it. Then she pointed at him.

“You pretended you couldn’t. On purpose. For four days.”

The corner of his mouth moved.

“Why?”

He put the flat in the back and shut it. Rain was running down his hair and into his collar. He looked at her.

“Because you were teaching me,” he said. “And I liked it.”

She stared at him.

“You stood close,” he said, as if he were giving evidence. “You put your hand over mine on the wheel. You kept correcting my grip. Every time I got something wrong, you touched my hands.” He looked at her fingers on the umbrella. “So I got things wrong.”

She didn’t say anything at all. Then she laughed. It came out of her bright and helpless and too loud for the alley, and it made him smile properly.

“You did all that so I’d keep touching your hands.”

He nodded once.

“You could have just held my hand.”

“I did. Fourteen minutes on Wednesday.”

“You’re impossible.”

“I’m learning,” he said.

The umbrella slipped out of her fingers and fell into the flooded gutter. Neither of them looked at it. She stepped in and took both his hands, wet and cold and black across the knuckles, and lifted them, and put them flat against her own cheeks.

He went completely still.

“Here,” she said. “You don’t have to be bad at something to make me touch you.”

His thumbs rested beside her ears. “I know.”

“Do you?”

There was only the rain.

Then he bent his head and kissed her, hard. His hands slid from her face to the back of her neck and pulled her in, and she caught the front of his jacket in both fists and pulled him against her, and the rain came straight through both their coats. Water poured round their shoes. A car went past the end of the alley with its lights on full and neither of them saw it. She bit his lip. He made a sound into her mouth that she would think about for a week.

When he drew back, she was smiling against his mouth.

“Ninety-one seconds,” she whispered.

He pushed the wet hair off her forehead. “I can do better.”

“Don’t you dare.”

“Why?”

“Because next time I’m timing you properly,” she said, and he kissed her again.

He fished the umbrella out of the gutter. It was broken, two spokes snapped and the cloth inside out.

“Your fault,” she said.

“I know.”

“You owe me an umbrella.”

“Of course.”

“And dinner. And you are never allowed to pretend you can’t change a tyre again.”

He thought about it. “Can I pretend I can’t do something else?”

She narrowed her eyes. “What?”

He leaned close. “Dance,” he said. “You could teach me to dance.”

She laughed so hard she had to hold on to his jacket. “You’re a menace.”

“I’m a quick learner.”

When they got back into the grey estate she sat in the passenger seat with his cold hand in hers on the gearstick all the way to the bridge. The tyre was changed. The umbrella was ruined. And she had learned that the most dangerous thing about Qin Haozhen wasn’t how fast he could learn anything.

It was how quietly he could arrange to be taught.

chapters.title: The Security Guard Who Smiled Once
chapters.desc: August 2025, the Orsini paddock, as told by Callum Hart. There is a pool. Forty-one people have put money on who can make the head of security smile first. Callum tries jokes, a video of a goat, and an Italian mechanic in a wig. Witnesses are still recovering.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody was paying her.”
chapters.content:
The first mistake was making it a competition. The second was telling Callum Hart.

By the Saturday morning of the third weekend in August, at the circuit in the south, forty-one people in the Orsini paddock had put money into a small unofficial pool whose only purpose was to make the new Head of Security, Asia, smile.

The rules were written on the back of a tyre-pressure sheet and pinned inside the door of the tyre bay. A real smile counted. A polite nod didn’t. A movement of the mouth that might have been indigestion didn’t. Photographic evidence was preferred. Beppe held the money, because Beppe had started it.

Beppe was also the first to lose.

He walked into the security cabin at nine in a red nylon wig, a pair of enormous sunglasses and a yellow dress borrowed from a girl in hospitality, and stood in front of the desk with his hands on his hips.

“Buongiorno, signore.”

Haozhen looked up from the overnight access report. He looked at the wig. At the dress. At the wig again. At Beppe.

“Your pass expired on Thursday,” he said. “And you’re in a restricted area.”

Beppe left. The wig was found in the medical centre twenty minutes later. Beppe wouldn’t discuss it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum Hart considered himself a funny man. He had once made an entire press conference laugh by answering a question about tyre degradation with a story about his grandmother’s cat. He was confident.

At two in the afternoon he found Haozhen beside the transporter with a tablet.

“Qin. I’ve got one for you. Why did the racing driver bring a ladder to the circuit?”

Haozhen waited.

“Because he wanted to get to the top of the podium.”

Silence. Callum smiled encouragingly.

Haozhen nodded once. “Good.”

“Good?”

“Positive attitude,” said Haozhen, and went back to his tablet.

Callum went and found Matteo. “He didn’t even blink.”

“You told him a joke about a ladder.”

“It was a good joke.”

“It wasn’t.”

At four Callum tried again with his phone: a video somebody had sent him of a small goat in a child’s racing helmet running in circles round a paddock trolley and then into a stack of tyres, getting up, and running into the same stack of tyres. Callum had watched it six times and laughed six times.

Haozhen watched it to the end without any change of expression. Then he handed the phone back.

“Does the goat have a handler?”

“It’s a video.”

“Still,” said Haozhen.

Callum went back to the hospitality unit and sat down. Forty-one people. He was beginning to understand that none of them would see their money again.

At half past five Mouse tried, which nobody had expected, because Mouse had put in more money than anyone and claimed to have a method.

Her method was data. She came to the security cabin with her laptop and turned it round and showed him a chart: every lap Serafina had driven that weekend, the braking points at turn six plotted in a neat descending line, five and a half metres, four, two, nothing, her old marker.

“Look,” said Mouse. “Look what she did.”

He looked at it. Something went across his face. Mouse leaned in, her phone already up for the evidence.

“That’s very good work,” he said gravely, to Mouse. “Send it to Matteo.”

Mouse lowered the phone and shut the laptop. “You’re not human,” she said.

“I’ve been told.”

She left. Behind her, through the cabin’s small window, Big Wu saw him look at the closed laptop longer, and nearly do it, and not.

What none of them knew was that he had found the pressure sheet pinned inside the tyre-bay door at ten past seven on Saturday morning, on his first round, and read the rules, and the forty-one names, and the amount, and put it back exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle. He was Head of Security. Nothing went on a door in that paddock without his seeing it.

He had decided at once, on principle, that none of them were going to win.

✦ ✦ ✦

Callum took it to Serafina on Sunday morning, while she was checking front-left temperatures on the grid stand with a probe, when Callum came and leaned on the car beside her with a face of deep personal suffering.

“Has he ever smiled?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

“Yesterday.”

“Where?”

She pointed vaguely at the garage. “Here.”

“At what?”

“Something.” She read the probe. “Why?”

He told her. The pool, the rules on the back of the pressure sheet, the wig, the ladder, the goat. She listened as if it were all news to her, her face getting steadily more delighted. When he’d finished she looked across the paddock.

He was by the garage entrance talking to a contractor about a gate, composed and attentive, with his hands behind his back. He looked exactly as he always looked when he was being looked at.

“Forty-one people,” said Callum. “We’ve tried everything.”

“Have you?”

She gave the probe to Matteo and walked across the paddock to him.

Callum watched. He saw Haozhen register her coming before she was halfway: the slight turn of the head, the way he finished his sentence to the contractor and handed back the clipboard and turned toward her as if a compass had swung. He saw her stop in front of him and say something. One word, it looked like. Callum couldn’t hear it. Nobody could.

“Eleven,” she said.

She knew about the pool. Of course she knew. Beppe had tried to sell her a share at breakfast, and she had told him that she didn’t bet on things she’d already won. She also knew, because she knew him, that he’d seen the sheet on the door the moment it went up, and decided that nobody in the paddock was going to get his face for money.

Nobody was paying her.

For a second Haozhen’s face stayed perfectly neutral.

Then he smiled.

Not politely, not a small acknowledgement for the cameras. His whole face changed. His eyes went soft at the corners and his mouth went up and he looked, about twenty, and he looked at her as if she were the only person standing anywhere in the southern hills.

Callum stood absolutely still.

She reached up and straightened Haozhen’s collar. He said something back. She laughed. He smiled again.

“Did you see that?” said Callum, without turning round.

“Yes,” said Matteo.

“What does eleven mean?”

“I have no idea.”

The pool closed before lunch. Beppe paid out the whole pot to Serafina, who gave it straight back and told him to buy the mechanics dinner.

“She cheated,” Callum told anyone who would listen. “She had prior knowledge.”

“She has a prior relationship,” said Matteo. “It’s a significant advantage.”

That evening, between the two transporters, in the last of the light, with the paddock almost empty, Callum came round the back of the Orsini truck with a bag of ice and stopped dead. Haozhen had her against the side of the transporter with one hand flat on the panel beside her head and the other at her waist, and he was kissing her. Slowly. Not a kiss stolen between jobs. A long, unhurried kiss, as if the paddock had dissolved round them and there wasn’t a single camera in the world. She had his shirt in both fists.

When they came apart, she said something, and he smiled again.

Callum turned round and walked the long way to the motorhome.

“I hate this place,” he told Beppe.

Beppe patted his shoulder. “You lost money.”

“I lost my dignity.”

“That’s more expensive,” said Beppe.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the wedding, nine months later, under the bridge, with two hundred people eating Mr. Kwok’s soup, Callum finally asked.

It was late in the afternoon, after the toasts. Serafina was at the drinks table with a glass of something sparkling, still in ivory, a little rice in her hair.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Is this about the goat?”

“No. Though I still think the goat should have worked.” He lowered his voice. “Eleven.”

“Ah.”

“What did it mean?”

She took a sip. “Eleven minutes.”

“What?”

“Donatella had given us ten minutes in the motorhome. The week before, after the race. Ten minutes, exactly, with the door locked.” She smiled. “That Sunday morning I told him I’d asked her for eleven.”

Callum looked across the garage. Haozhen was standing with Chen Si, listening to something Aurelia was saying, entirely composed and respectable, a man with nothing at all on his mind.

“You made him smile,” said Callum slowly, “by promising him one extra minute.”

“One extra minute alone with me,” said Serafina. “And he was very happy about it.”

Callum shut his eyes. “I don’t want to know.”

“You asked.”

He walked away. Behind him she laughed. Across the garage Haozhen heard her and looked over, and caught her eye, and smiled at her, the real one, wide open, in front of two hundred people.

Callum saw it, and decided once and for all that forty-one people had never stood a chance.

chapters.title: Who Is Faster: the Car or the Bike?
chapters.desc: August 2024. An argument at Lunar New Year that has been going on for six months. A track day, the main straight at the circuit in the north, a matte black car and a motorbike Jinx built from nothing. Everybody has a bet. Raiden is holding the money, which is the first mistake.
chapters.epigraph: “You won, Sera.”
chapters.content:
The argument started over lunch at the Lin house on the second day of Lunar New Year, when Jinx looked out of the dining-room window at Gilded on the gravel, and then at her own black motorbike beside it, and made the mistake of saying, “Your car’s fast. But it’s got four wheels.”

Serafina slowly put down her chopsticks.

Across the table Raiden shut his eyes. He knew that tone.

“Meaning?”

“Meaning my bike’s quicker.”

“The one you built in your garage.”

“From nothing.”

“That’s a very elegant way of saying you bought parts.”

Jinx pointed her chopsticks across the duck. “Outside. Now.”

“After lunch,” said Serafina, and picked hers up again. And that was how it stayed for six months, through a bad winter and a worse spring, through a car wash and a coast road and a stone house in the mountains, while neither of them forgot it for a single day.

✦ ✦ ✦

By August it had witnesses, money, and a set of rules more complicated than the series’ sporting regulations. Jinx had booked the circuit in the north for the second Saturday, a test day with the main straight closed off, timing beams at the start and at a kilometre, and marshals at both ends.

Gilded sat on the grid in her matte black with the white seven and the gold across the bonnet, mapped for a straight line, tyres warmed. Beside her stood Jinx’s bike, equally black, low and furious, with a frame she’d bent herself and an engine she’d built on her kitchen table over two winters while Raiden ate dinner off the ironing board.

Raiden stood between them with a small notebook.

“I’ll hold the bets,” he announced.

“Why you?” said Aurelia.

“Because I’m trustworthy.”

Chen Si looked at him.

“Because I’m holding the money,” Raiden amended.

Zhao Zhendong put his on Jinx. Aurelia put hers on her sister. Chen Si put money on the bike, explaining that he respected mechanical simplicity. Elowen put hers on Gilded because she liked the colour.

“It’s black,” said Zhao.

“Exactly,” said Elowen.

“Finally,” said Jinx. “Somebody understands.”

Haozhen stood behind Serafina with her helmet. He looked at the car, and the bike, and the two women.

“Are we doing this safely?”

Jinx held up a hand and counted on her fingers. “Closed circuit. Closed straight. Full kit. Proper timing. Nobody near the run. Marshals both ends. Fire crew at the pit exit.”

“Good,” he said.

Serafina held her hand out for the helmet. He gave it to her, and then “Don’t let her get in your head.”

“I’m faster than her.”

“I know.”

“You sound very sure.”

“I’ve seen you drive,” he said.

“Good answer,” she said, and put it on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first run was from standing.

Lights. Three. Two. One.

The bike went like a thrown knife. Its front wheel lifted a hand’s breadth off the tarmac and came down, and it was a car’s length clear before Gilded’s rears had finished deciding what to do, and Serafina laughed inside her helmet and said “Show-off” to nobody and changed up.

At the first timing board the bike was still ahead.

Then the car began to pull. Gilded didn’t leap. She gathered herself, steadily, relentlessly, the power coming in like a tide, and the gap closed. At the halfway mark Serafina was level. For a few seconds the two black machines ran side by side down the long straight, close enough to see the rivets on each other. Then Gilded’s nose edged in front, and stayed there, and she crossed the kilometre beam a length and a half clear.

Jinx came back into the pit lane and pulled her helmet off. “Again.”

“You lost.”

“Off the line, I won.”

“Off the line, yes.”

“That’s cheating. You’ve got four wheels.”

“You built a motorbike.”

“Exactly!”

Raiden wrote something in his notebook.

The second run was rolling, both of them at sixty behind the pace car and a green flag at the line. The bike still jumped first, but not by as much. Gilded pulled harder the faster they went. At three hundred metres she was in front. At the beam she was clear by most of a second.

Jinx came back with a face of profound betrayal.

“Your car’s ridiculous.”

“Thank you.”

“I built a perfectly good bike.”

“You did.”

“And you still beat me.”

“Over a kilometre,” said Serafina.

“Don’t say it like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re enjoying it.”

“I am,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden gathered everyone at the timing board with the notebook and, crucially, all the money.

“After careful consideration,” he said, “I’ve reached a decision. The bike won the launch.”

“Correct,” said Jinx.

“The car won the kilometre.”

“Also correct,” said Serafina.

Raiden closed the notebook. “So it’s a draw.”

There was a pause.

“That’s not how racing works,” said Aurelia.

“It’s how this bet works.”

“Who decided that?”

“Me. I’m keeping the pot as my drawing fee.”

“Raiden,” said his wife.

“Yes, darling?”

“Give it back.”

“I performed an administrative service.”

“You stood there.”

“An important service,” said Raiden, already walking, and Chen Si said, “I’m going to have a conversation with you,” and followed him, and Raiden walked faster.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later Serafina found Haozhen beside Gilded, checking a front tyre that had been checked twice already. She leaned on the open window.

“Who did you bet on?”

“Neither.”

“Coward.”

“I had a private bet.”

“Oh?”

He put a hand on the roof and leaned down to the window. “If you won, I’d give you something. And if you lost, I’d give you the same thing.”

“That isn’t a bet.”

“No,” he said. “It’s an excuse.”

“For what?”

“To have you to myself tonight. For as long as I like.”

Her face changed. “You could just ask.”

“I know.”

She reached through the window and took him by the collar. “Then ask.”

“Come home with me,” he said.

“I’m already going home with you,” she said, and he bent and kissed her through the window with one hand on the roof and her fist still in his collar.

“You know I won,” she said against his mouth.

“I know.”

“By a lot.”

“You won, Sera.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night he didn’t hurry.

The loft was quiet, the garage below them dark and empty after a day of engines and arguments. She had just taken out her earrings at the little mirror by the window when he came up behind her and kissed the back of her neck, below her hair. She watched him do it in the dark glass.

“Still thinking about the race?”

“No.”

“Liar.”

He turned her round. “I’m thinking about you.”

He took her jacket off her shoulders as if it were made of something that could tear. Then the buttons of her shirt, one at a time, slowly, the way he’d fasten a seat belt, looking at her and not at the buttons.

“You’re being very deliberate,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I can.”

There was something in his voice that took the laugh out of her. He had spent his whole life moving fast, answering before anyone else could, measuring time in seconds and exits and the distance between a door and a car. Tonight there was no clock. Nobody waiting. Nowhere he had to be.

He knelt and took her boots off. He kissed the inside of her knee, and her thigh through her jeans, and undid them and drew them down, and she stood in the window in nothing at all while he looked at her for a long, long time as if he meant to remember the exact light.

“Hao.”

“Wait.”

He put his mouth on her where she stood. She caught at the window frame. He held her hips in both hands and took her apart slowly, without mercy, every time she was close easing off until she said his name in a voice she didn’t recognise, and only then letting her have it, and catching her when her knees went.
