He laid her on the bed and undressed himself while she watched. He came down over her and into her so slowly that she thought she’d die of it, and stayed there, still, his forehead on hers, his weight on his forearms.

“I think,” she managed, “you’re enjoying this more than you’d have enjoyed winning.”

“Possibly.”

“Admit it.”

“I’d rather not,” he said, and began to move.

He made it last. Every time she tried to hurry him, he slowed further. Every time she pulled at his back, he caught her wrists and pinned them gently over her head and kissed her until she stopped. The eleven-forty went over, and the eleven-fifty-one, and the twelve-oh-two, and he was still taking his time, and by the end she was begging and he was shaking with the effort of it and when he finally let go they went over together with her heels locked behind his back and his name and hers tangled up in the dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Jinx sent one message. REMATCH.

Serafina showed him over the coffee.

“Will you?”

“Obviously.”

“Good luck.”

“You’re supposed to say I’ll win.”

“I’ve seen the bike.”

“You’ve seen me.”

He thought about it, and bent and kissed her. “I’ve seen you,” he agreed.

Her phone went again. AND TELL RAIDEN TO GIVE ME BACK MY MONEY.

“Unlikely,” said Haozhen, reading it upside down. “His fee’s probably gone up.”

She laughed so hard she spilt the coffee. Somewhere across the city Raiden was almost certainly hiding the money, and Jinx was already building something faster.

chapters.title: He Checks the Perimeter Before Breakfast
chapters.desc: Spring 2027. Every morning, before the egg sandwiches, he walks the garage: shutter, side door, alley, loft window, the roof hatch, the stairs. Every morning. She starts timing it. Four minutes and twelve seconds on day one. She keeps a chart on the whiteboard for a month. Then one morning he forgets.
chapters.epigraph: “I just don’t need to go and look.”
chapters.content:
At eight minutes past six every morning, Qin Haozhen checked the perimeter.

Serafina found this out by accident on Thursday the first of April 2027, because he had stolen the blanket in the night and she woke up meaning to take it back, and found his side of the bed empty and cool.

The loft was dark. Below it the garage lights were on.

She leaned over the iron rail in his T-shirt and watched.

The main shutter first. He crouched and ran his hand along the bottom rail where the steel met the concrete, then stood and tried the lock. The side door into the alley: the handle, the frame, the bolt, and then the door open six inches and his head out, looking up the alley and down it, and the door shut and bolted again. Along the length of the floor past Nonna and Gilded, pausing under the loft window to look up at the catch. The iron stairs, every tread. The roof hatch over the office, by the ladder.

He did each one with the same quiet attention, his face giving away nothing at all.

Then he went to the kitchen and put the kettle on.

She looked at the clock on her phone. Six twelve.

“How long have you been doing that?” she said, coming down.

He turned with the kettle. “Doing what?”

“Walking round.”

“Checking the doors.”

“Why?”

He looked toward the shutter. “Habit.”

“Is everything all right?”

“Yes.” He came and kissed her forehead and reached for the bread. “Egg sandwich?”

She said yes. He made two. She said nothing about the four minutes and twelve seconds.

She wrote it down.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fifth she had a column of times. By the seventh Mouse had turned it into a chart on the whiteboard in the back room behind the office, where he never went before nine, with a column for each door and a total and a small neat graph.

MORNING CHECK — APRIL.

“Why is there a graph?” said Serafina.

“Numbers are easier to understand arranged properly.” Mouse pushed her hood back. “1 April, four twelve. 2nd, four oh nine. 3rd, four oh seven. 4th, four oh five. 5th, four oh three. 6th, four oh one. 7th, three fifty-eight.”

“Why’s it getting shorter?”

“Either he’s getting faster, or he’s skipping something.” Mouse looked at her. “He isn’t skipping anything. I checked.”

“You checked?”

“I watched on the side-door camera.”

“That’s slightly creepy.”

“You asked me to help.” Mouse picked up the marker. “Do you want weather? Whether the shutter sticks? Whether he looks tired?”

Serafina looked at the graph.

“Yes,” she said. “Whether he looks tired.”

Mouse wrote it down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the ninth Big Wu came into the back room with his tea, and stopped in front of the board, and read it.

“What’s this?”

“Nothing,” said Serafina, from the invoices.

“That’s a big nothing.”

“Haozhen’s morning check,” said Mouse.

Big Wu read the times. He looked toward the iron stairs. He put the mug down on the bench, carefully, as if it might go off.

“When I was inside the second time,” he said, “I had a cellmate who touched the walls.”

Serafina put the invoices down.

“Every morning. Before the bell. Same wall first. Same order. He’d run his hand along the concrete, every corner, the door, the hinge, the little window. Then he’d sit on his bunk.” Big Wu turned the mug round on the bench. “He’d been in fourteen years. He couldn’t sleep unless he’d done it. Couldn’t eat breakfast till he knew where the screws were. I asked him once what he was looking for. He said he was making sure the walls were still there.” He picked the mug up. “People learn ways of staying alive that don’t make sense once they’re safe. They do it anyway. Don’t make a joke out of it.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“I know,” said Big Wu. “That’s why I told you.” He went back to the workshop.

She stood in front of the board. Then she heard him on the stairs, and turned, and he came down in a clean shirt with her coffee in his hand.

“Eat,” he said, and kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

The times kept falling. A few seconds here, a few there. By the middle of April he was done in three minutes twenty. By the twentieth he was under three. Mouse wrote it all down. Serafina stopped asking her about it. She didn’t want him to know she was watching; not because she was ashamed of it, but because she wanted to see what happened if nobody asked him to stop.

Some mornings she watched from the rail. Some mornings she lay still and pretended to sleep and listened to him go: the shutter rattling under his hand, the side door, the stairs. Some mornings she came down and stood by the kettle while he did it, and he didn’t seem to notice, or noticed and let her be.

On the twenty-seventh Mouse wrote 2:41 and looked at it, and then at Serafina, and neither of them felt pleased.

On the thirtieth he woke before her, and lay for a while listening to rain on the roof of the arch. She was asleep with one hand on his chest. He looked at her. Then at the clock. Six oh eight.

He lifted her hand gently off his chest. She made a small sound and caught his wrist.

“Where are you going?”

“Down.”

“Why?”

“Coffee,” he said.

“Bring it back.”

“I will.” He kissed her forehead and went down and did the doors in two minutes and thirty-five seconds, and came up with two cups.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first of May was a Saturday.

He woke at six oh eight. He looked at the clock. Then at her.

She was asleep on her side, facing him, her hair all over the pillow, one hand open between them on the sheet. The rain had stopped. Outside a train went over and the building hummed with it, long and low, and faded.

He looked at her.

Then he moved closer, and slid his arm round her waist, and she settled back against him without waking. He was warm. He was comfortable. There was nowhere he needed to be.

He shut his eyes, and slept.

At seventeen minutes past eight she woke and looked at the clock, and then at him, with his arm still round her and his face tucked into her hair and his breathing slow, and she lay still so as not to wake him.

Downstairs, nothing had been checked. The shutter was locked. The side door was bolted. The alley was empty. The window was latched. The roof hatch was shut. And Qin Haozhen was asleep.

She reached for her phone, slowly, and sent Mouse one message. No check today.

The reply came at once. Leave the row blank?

She looked at him. Yes.

Understood.

He stirred and tightened his arm. “Mm?”

“Nothing.”

“What time is it?”

“Eight.”

His eyes opened. “Eight.”

She saw it come back into his face: the old alertness, the glance at the window, at the bedroom door, at the stairs. Then she watched him stop it. He didn’t get up. He looked back at her.

“Did I miss something?”

“Breakfast,” she said, and pushed his hair off his forehead.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. Stay.”

He stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the chart that afternoon. Mouse had left the back-room door open and he came through looking for a gearbox invoice and stopped in front of the whiteboard and read the heading, and the dates, and the times, and the little graph. Then he read it all again.

Serafina found him standing there.

“You timed me,” he said, without turning round.

“For a month.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to know how long it took you. I asked you. You said it was habit.”

“It is.”

“I know.” She came and stood beside him. At the bottom of the board the row for the first of May was empty.

“Today?”

“I didn’t time you,” she said. “You didn’t get up.”

He was quiet.

“Big Wu told me about a man he shared a cell with,” she said, carefully, “who touched every wall in the morning because he needed to know they were still there.” She took his hand. “I’m not saying that’s you. And I’m not asking you to stop checking the doors. You can check the doors for the rest of your life if you want. I just wanted you to know you don’t have to do it before you’re allowed to come back to bed.”

He looked at the board. Four twelve. Two forty-one. A month of ordinary mornings measured by somebody who had been watching him without once asking him to explain himself.

“You kept them all.”

“Yes.”

“Even the bad ones.”

“Especially the bad ones.”

“Why?”

“Because they were yours,” she said.

He didn’t say anything for a while. Then he took the marker off the ledge, and uncapped it, and wrote in the empty row in his small square capitals:

1 MAY — NO CHECK.

He capped the marker.

“You could have told me.”

“I wanted you to find out by yourself that you could forget.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night they went up early. The garage was locked. He knew it was locked. He’d checked it at ten, as he always did, and would again.

But in the morning, when he woke before her at six oh eight, he didn’t get up. He turned over. She was already awake, watching him in the grey light.

“Morning,” she whispered.

“Morning.”

He kissed her. Slowly, in no hurry at all, while the first train of the day went over.

“Are you checking anything today?” she said against his mouth.

“No.”

“Not even the shutter?”

“It’s locked.”

“The side door?”

“Bolted.”

“The roof?”

“Shut.”

“You remember.”

“Yes,” he said. “I just don’t need to go and look.”

She pulled him down. And for once the first thing Qin Haozhen did in the morning wasn’t to make sure the world was safe.

It was to kiss his wife.

chapters.title: The Military Academy at Sixteen
chapters.desc: September 2010. A slow train south from a mining town, a dormitory of forty boys under a roof that leaks onto bed eleven, a firing range in the snow, and a boy who laughs with his whole face and gives away the window seat. Two years later, a woman with red wool on her needles asks a question about a map. The boy they chose because he never hesitated.
chapters.epigraph: “You can’t spend your whole life waiting for somebody to tell you where to go.”
chapters.content:
The train left the mining town at twenty to seven on Wednesday the first of September 2010.

He was sixteen. He had one canvas bag, a letter from the county education office saying that his marks in the provincial test had earned him a place at a state academy in the south, and enough money for the journey and not much more. His mother had packed two boiled eggs, a steamed bun, a twist of salted vegetables, and a blue jumper he didn’t need.

“It’s cold there,” she said.

“It’s September.”

“It will become cold.”

On the platform she straightened his collar three times. The third time she left her hands on his shoulders.

“Eat properly. Write when you get there. And don’t give your things away.”

“I don’t.”

“You gave the boy downstairs your winter gloves.”

“They were too small for me.”

“You gave your cousin your new shoes.”

“His had holes.”

“You gave the widow’s grandson your schoolbag.”

“He didn’t have one.”

Liang Shufen sighed. “Keep something for yourself, Haozhen. Just once.”

He nodded, and got on the train, and didn’t know how to say goodbye to her, so he stood at the window and watched her get smaller on the platform until the cutting took her.

The journey was eleven hours. He counted telegraph poles and read the academy’s list of rules four times. Somewhere after noon an old man across the aisle asked if he was going to school.

“Yes.”

“Far?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” said the old man. “Young people should see somewhere else.”

He looked out at the rice and the rivers going by and didn’t know whether the old man was right. But he was going somewhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dormitory had forty beds and a roof that leaked.

He’d been given bed twelve, by the window, which was dry. At seventeen minutes past ten on the first night the rain came, and the leak came with it, through a stain in the ceiling directly above bed eleven, onto the pillow of the boy in it, who sat up with water on his face and laughed. Loudly. Not quietly to himself: a big, unrestrained laugh that made two boys at the far end turn over and swear.

“Bad luck,” the boy said, to the ceiling.

Haozhen looked at him. He looked at the drip. He got up, took his own blanket off bed twelve, and put it on the wet mattress of bed eleven.

“Move.”

The boy stared at him. “What?”

“Take mine. It’s dry.”

“Why?”

Haozhen thought about it. He didn’t have an answer that would have made sense to anyone but his mother. “You’re the one who’s wet.”

The boy looked at him in the light from the corridor. Then he picked up his pillow and moved to bed twelve, and lay down, and said, “Mo Tianyi.”

“Qin Haozhen.”

“You’re mad, Qin Haozhen,” said Tianyi, comfortably, and went to sleep.

Haozhen lay down in the wet bed and put his bag under his head and listened to the drip land on the floor beside him, one, two, one, two, all night. It was the first night in his life he’d slept anywhere but in his mother’s flat. In the morning there was a boiled egg on his pillow. His mother’s egg, from his own bag. Tianyi was already half dressed.

“You’ve got too much food,” Tianyi said. “And you’ll give it all away anyway. I’m saving you the trouble.”

That Sunday, and every Sunday after it for two years, when the academy bus took them into the town, Tianyi got on first and sat in the window seat and then stood up again when Haozhen got on, and moved to the aisle, and never once said why. Haozhen never asked. He knew why. Tianyi had noticed on the first day that the new boy couldn’t sit with his back to anything, and liked to watch the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

They became friends because neither of them had much choice. They shared a locker. They took turns with the washing. Tianyi talked enough for both of them, with his whole body, his hands going, standing up halfway through a story and nearly knocking the desk over. Haozhen listened, and remembered everything: which instructor hated late arrivals, which stairwell door stuck in the damp, which woman in the canteen gave you more rice if you said please.

“You’re a walking noticeboard,” Tianyi told him.

“You’re noisy.”

When Tianyi failed a written test on law and procedure, Haozhen sat up with him for three nights until he passed the retake. When Haozhen came top of the section in the spring, Tianyi celebrated as if he’d done it himself.

“You’re buying dinner.”

“I didn’t win anything.”

“You won the test.”

“You failed.”

“Exactly. We need to celebrate you before I bring the average down again.”

Haozhen laughed. It came out of him before he could stop it, his whole face changing, and Tianyi pointed at him across the canteen table and shouted “There!” so loudly that an instructor looked up.

“What?”

“You can laugh.”

“Unfortunately,” said Haozhen, still laughing, and Tianyi spent the rest of the week trying to make him do it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The range was outside the walls, a strip of concrete in a field. In winter the snow banked up at the edges and the steel targets froze so cold they burned your fingers.

In January 2012, sixteen months in, they had the practical. Five rounds. He checked the weapon, listened to the brief, took the line, and put all five through the paper in a group you could have covered with a coin.

The instructor walked down and looked at it, and walked back.

“Do you know what you’ve done?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

He looked at the target. “Sorry, sir.”

The instructor stared at him. “Don’t apologise for being good, cadet.”

Behind the observation glass, a woman in a grey coat whom nobody had introduced was standing still with her hands in her pockets and a ball of wool in a cloth bag over her arm. She had come that morning in a black car with no number on the front, and she watched every one of the forty of them shoot, and wrote nothing down. When he looked up at the glass she was looking straight at him.

Tianyi came off the line two places down with his group the size of a fist.

“It’s irritating,” he said.

“What is?”

“You.” He leaned in. “Do you ever get nervous?”

“Before every test.”

“You don’t look it.”

“I don’t need to look it.”

“Next time I’m beating you.”

“Good luck.”

“Don’t say it like you’ve already seen the results,” said Tianyi, and threw a snowball at his back.

✦ ✦ ✦

In June the letters came. Three of them, out of forty. One was his. Tianyi’s wasn’t.

They were on the bus into town the following Sunday, the last Sunday, Haozhen at the window, when Tianyi said, “Capital?”

“Yes.”

“What for?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you want to go?”

Haozhen looked out at the road. “It’s an assignment.”

“That isn’t what I asked.” Tianyi was quiet for a while. “When we’re out of here, I’m going somewhere with a sea. I’ve looked at walls long enough.”

“Good.”

“And you?”

He thought about the town. The headframe. The wheel. His mother at the machine. “I don’t know.”

“You should decide,” said Tianyi. “You can’t spend your whole life waiting for somebody to tell you where to go.”

He didn’t answer. On the last day, in the dormitory, with their bags on the bare mattresses, Tianyi put out his hand, and then pulled him into a hug, badly, because neither of them knew how.

“Don’t turn into someone I don’t recognise,” Tianyi said.

“I won’t,” he said. He meant it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The office in the capital was on the seventh floor of a building with no name.

The woman from behind the glass sat at a desk with a map spread across it and a half-finished piece of knitting, something plain and grey, beside her elbow. She was in her forties then, with neat hair and reading glasses, and she didn’t ask him to sit.

“Tell me what you see.”

A grid of streets. Three buildings marked in pencil. A railway line. A narrow lane behind the largest building.

“Which way would you take him out?” she said.

He was answering before she’d finished. “The lane. The main road’s visible from the front entrance. The level crossing holds you if the traffic backs up. The lane has two ways out and a covered loading bay.”

She put the knitting down.

“Most of them ask for more,” she said. “Who he is. What he’s done. Whether he’ll come quietly. You didn’t ask me anything.”

“You asked which way.”

“Will you want to know what happens to the people you move?”

He looked at the map. He had been praised for two years for never hesitating.

“No,” he said.

“Good,” said Duan Qiuyan, and picked up the needles. “There’s a teacher.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The postcard came on Thursday the eleventh of March 2027. A railway station in winter. He knew the hand before he’d turned it over.

I resigned too. They made a fuss. I let them.

The window seat is better than I remembered.

He laughed.

Not the dry exhale he gave people who told him jokes. A real one. His head went down over the bench and his shoulders shook and he laughed the way he had once laughed across a canteen table at sixteen, and Serafina, coming down the stairs, stopped on the bottom step with her hand on the rail.

“What?”

He gave her the card. She read it twice.

“The window seat.”

“He gave it to me. Every Sunday. On the bus. For two years.”

“Why?”

“Because I gave him my bed. The first night. The roof leaked on his.” He took the card back and looked at it. “He remembered.”

“So did you,” she said, and came and took his face in both hands, and he kissed her at the bench with the card in his fingers and the train going over.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night in the loft she asked him to tell her about it, and he did. The egg on the pillow. The drip. The snowball. The woman behind the glass. The map, and the lane, and the word he’d said.

“You were eighteen,” she said when he’d finished.

“I thought I was ready.”

“Were you ever happy there?”

“Sometimes. Tianyi. The snow. My mother coming at the end in her good coat with a bag of oranges.” He turned his head on the pillow. “Small things.”

“You were a boy,” she said, and kissed him.

He reached for her. It was slow, and it was different: not the care of a man trying to control every movement but something softer, as if having said all of it out loud he had put something down that he’d been carrying since he was sixteen without noticing its weight. She undressed him. He let her. She kissed the scar above his elbow and the old white line on his forearm and his mouth, and when he rolled her under him she held his face and said, “You don’t have to answer before anyone finishes asking. Not with me,” and he said, “I know,” and went into her slowly, watching her, until she arched and caught her breath, and he stayed there and made it last, her hands in his hair and her heels at the backs of his thighs, the train going over, the lamp still on, nothing in the world waiting for an answer. She came holding his face. He came with her name against her throat and his eyes open.

In the morning she bought a postcard of the railway bridge at the corner shop and wrote on the back of it in big letters:

HE LAUGHED. Properly. Not a polite smile. You were right about the window seat. — Serafina.

“You’re reporting on me,” he said, reading it over her shoulder.

“It’s important information.”

“You don’t have to tell him everything.”

“I’m not,” she said, and sealed it. “Just the important part. Post it?”

He took it. When he went out under the shutter he wasn’t carrying an order from somebody who’d chosen him because he never asked. He was carrying a postcard from his wife to the boy from the next bed.

chapters.title: Forty-Three Songs for the Car
chapters.desc: Nonna’s tape deck has been broken since 2017 and Serafina plays everything off her phone, in the same order, every time: forty-three songs, and she always skips the seventeenth. He doesn’t own a single piece of music. Over a summer he learns all forty-three, by heart, in order. Then he fixes the tape deck.
chapters.epigraph: “Because you always come home.”
chapters.content:
She had forty-three songs in the car. Not forty-two, not forty-four.

He learned this in the third week of March 2023, the week she started taking him round the loop at night in Nonna instead of his grey estate, with her phone wired into a small speaker she had zip-tied under the dashboard. Below the radio sat Nonna’s original cassette deck, its buttons gone yellow, a crack across the smoked plastic door, and a small daisy sticker beside the eject button that somebody had put there in about 1994.

“It’s broken,” she said. “Since 2017.”

“You haven’t fixed it.”

“I’ve been meaning to.”

“Why not just replace it?”

She looked at him as if he’d suggested replacing her grandmother. “Because it’s Nonna’s.”

“Right,” he said.

He didn’t own music. He’d never seen the point of collecting it. He knew songs from radios in restaurants and lifts and other people’s phones, and the phone in his own pocket had a calculator, a map and nineteen contacts in it. She had looked at it once and asked if he was eighty. He’d said eighty-year-olds probably had more music. She had laughed for a full minute.

“Forty-three,” she said now. “You have to listen properly. I made it.”

“Is that a reason?”

“It’s the best reason there is.”

By the fourth song he had learned that she sang when she was happy and tapped the wheel when she was thinking. By the eighth, that she hated remixes and knew exactly when to change lanes without breaking a chorus. By the sixteenth, that she always sang the last line of a song a little louder than the rest.

Then the seventeenth began, and a woman’s voice filled the car, high and huge, and Serafina reached out and skipped it before the second bar.

He glanced at the screen as the eighteenth came in. Puccini.

“What was that?”

“Nothing.”

“You skipped it.”

“I don’t like it.”

He didn’t ask again. At the end of the forty-third, as they came back past the harbour wall with the sky going grey, she said, “That’s all of them.”

“Good.”

“Good?”

“It’s a good playlist.” He looked out at the water. Then, after a while: “Can we hear it again?”

Her face lit up in the dashboard light. “Of course.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By April he knew the order. By May he knew the songs. By June he knew which ones she’d sing and which she’d only hum and which made her go quiet: the first for early mornings, the sixth for rain, the thirty-first for nights when she was too tired to talk. He knew the forty-third was her favourite, and that she’d never once admit it.

One night on the coast road, with her shoulders down round her ears after a bad day on Gilded’s gearbox, he reached out and turned the twenty-third down two notches.

“What are you doing?”

“You’re tired.”

She looked at him. “You know them now.”

“Yes.”

“In order?”

“Yes.”

“What’s twenty-six?”

He told her. She stared at the road.

“And before it? And after?”

He told her both.

“You’ve memorised my playlist.”

“It repeats.”

“That isn’t an explanation.”

“You play it every time,” he said. “Because you like it.”

She didn’t know what to say to that, so she took her hand off the gearstick and held his.

✦ ✦ ✦

The seventeenth was always skipped. Sometimes before the first note. Sometimes when the title came up. Once, on a night in May when she was talking, she let the opening run four seconds by accident, and her hand went to the screen so fast it was like a reflex.

He didn’t say anything. But he remembered the title, and the opening, and the shape of her hand.

In June, parked under the bridge with the engine off and neither of them wanting to get out, he said, “Was that your mother’s?”

Her hand went still on the gearstick.

“The seventeenth,” he said.

She didn’t answer.

“She played it on Sunday afternoons,” she said at last. “On the big stereo in the drawing room at the Peak, with the doors open onto the garden. And sang along. Badly. She got the high bit wrong every single time and said the soprano was the one who’d got it wrong.” Something like a smile. “I used to lie under the piano and listen. I was six.”

He waited.

“After I left, I couldn’t listen to it. I tried. I can’t get past the first line.”

He didn’t ask why she kept it on the list. He didn’t ask if she missed her mother. He said, “You don’t have to play it.”

“I know. I just haven’t deleted it.”

He touched her knuckles once with his thumb. The next time the playlist reached seventeen, he didn’t reach for anything. He let her skip it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In July he went to the electronics market under the flyover on the old ring road.

He’d spent a week looking at the deck in Nonna whenever she wasn’t in the garage. He knew nothing about car audio. But he’d been around machines long enough to know that most things stop for a reason.

A man at a stall at the back, thin, with a jeweller’s loupe on a string round his neck, looked at the photographs on his phone.

“Old car?”

“1992.”

“Why not just put a new one in?”

“It’s hers,” said Haozhen.

The man nodded as if that settled everything. They spent an hour over a cardboard box of parts. The drive belt had perished. The capstan motor was filthy. The contacts were green. The eject was sticking because somebody, at some point, had tried to post a coin into it.

He bought a belt and a motor and a bottle of contact cleaner, and came back the next afternoon with the deck itself in a cloth bag, and the afternoon after that. By the fourth day the stall owner had stopped asking why he was there and just pushed a stool towards him.

“You’re learning.”

“Yes.”

“For her?”

“She likes it,” he said.

“Good enough,” said the man.

✦ ✦ ✦

He made two tapes on a borrowed recorder at the bench at three in the morning, in the weeks she was away testing in the north.

On the first he put all forty-three songs, in order, checked against her list on his own phone. At seventeen he let the tape run for four seconds with nothing on it. Just the hiss. Then eighteen.

The second he made the same. But at the end, after the forty-third, he checked the counter and saw that there was tape left. He sat at the bench with his thumb on the record button.

Then he pressed it.

For a while there was only the hiss. Then, because it was eleven minutes since the last one, a train came over the bridge, and the whole garage hummed, and the recorder caught it, the long low rumble going over and dying away. He waited until it had gone.

“Come home,” he said, into the dark.

He stopped the tape. He listened to it once and didn’t recognise his own voice. He almost wiped it. He didn’t.

He labelled the first in small square capitals: NONNA — 43.

The second: NONNA — 43 + 1.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Saturday in September he finished putting the deck back into the dashboard, and came and found her under Gilded arguing with Big Wu about a bracket.

“Come here a minute.”

“Why?”

“Something’s ready.”

She slid out on the creeper and came over, wiping her hands. He held up a cassette.

She looked at it. Then at the dashboard. Then at him.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“You fixed it?”

He pushed the tape in. The old mechanism took it with a soft clunk, a sound she hadn’t heard since she was twenty, and the hiss came up through the original speakers, and then the first song.

Her playlist. Not songs he thought she might like. Her forty-three, in order.

“All of them?”

“All of them.”

“Even seventeen?”

“There are four seconds of nothing,” he said. “Where it goes.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed, unsteadily, and took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went out before sunrise, in Nonna, with the tape playing through speakers that had been silent for six years. She drove with her knees angled and her head back. At the seventeenth, the hiss ran four seconds. She didn’t reach for anything. She listened to the silence. Then the eighteenth came in and she looked out of her window, and her eyes were bright, and she was smiling.

The forty-third ended as she pulled into the lay-by above the harbour. She switched the engine off. The tape kept turning on the battery.

Hiss. Then, out of the speakers, a train going over a bridge.

She frowned at the deck. “Wait.”

The train faded. A breath of silence.

Come home.

She stopped breathing. She turned. He wasn’t looking at the deck. He was looking at her.

“That’s forty-four,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“You put yourself on as a hidden track.”

“I didn’t know what else to put.”

“You could have put anything.”

“I know.”

“Why that?”

“Because you always come home,” he said. “I wanted you to know I’d be there when you did.”

She leaned across the gearstick and kissed him, one hand on his cheek, and he met her halfway, and then she laughed against his mouth and he smiled, and she kissed him again, harder, while the sky went pink over the harbour and the old deck hummed and the tape hissed on into nothing.

“You could just have told me,” she said into his jaw, “that you wanted me to come home.”

“I know.”

“Instead you rebuilt a thirty-one-year-old tape deck.”

“Thirty-one isn’t particularly old.”

“Of course that’s your answer.” She looked at the deck. Then at him. “Play it again.”

He pressed rewind. The tape went backwards with the small busy whirr she’d forgotten, and she settled into her seat and held his hand. Forty-three songs. Four seconds of silence. And one more reason to come home.

chapters.title: Wedding Planning With a Spreadsheet
chapters.desc: February 2026. Two hundred guests, nine round tables, one garage, and a laptop open on the long table on the forty-fourth floor. He has colour-coded everyone. There is a column for who must face the door. There is a column called “Score-neutral”. Aurelia reads it for an hour without speaking, and then says the nicest thing she has ever said to anyone who wasn’t her husband.
chapters.epigraph: “I want you to be able to find me.”
chapters.content:
Qin Haozhen had nineteen columns for the wedding.

Serafina found this out at sixteen minutes past two on Sunday the fifteenth of February, coming out of the kitchen at the back of the garage with two cups of tea, to find her fiancé at the long bench with his laptop open and the expression of a man coordinating an evacuation.

Nine long trestle tables. Two hundred guests. One garage under a railway bridge. One caterer named Mr. Kwok. And, apparently, a threat assessment.

She put his tea down by his elbow. “What are you doing?”

“Seating.”

She leaned over his shoulder. WEDDING — GUEST ALLOCATION — REVISION 8.

“Eight?”

“People changed their availability.”

“Of course they did.”

Name. Party. Table. Seat. Dietary. Relationship to couple. Mobility. Arrival. Departure. And then, in column K: PREFERRED ORIENTATION.

She clicked it. “What’s this?”

“Which way they face.”

“Why does it say door next to half of them?”

“Some guests prefer to face an entrance.”

She looked at him. “Some guests.”

He didn’t answer. She read down the column.

Chen Si — door (shutter), left field.

Zhao Zhendong — door (side), right field.

Elowen Lin — neutral.

Vittoria Song — door (shutter), primary.

She turned her head slowly. “My mother?”

“Yes.”

“Why does my mother need to face the door?”

“She likes to see people coming.”

“She likes to see people coming so she can decide what she thinks of them before they get to her.”

He considered this. “That’s also a reason.”

Serafina pressed her lips together. It didn’t help.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia arrived twenty minutes later to go over the drinks, expecting a seating plan, and found her sister bent double over the bench and Haozhen explaining in a level voice why Chen Si and Zhao had been put back to back.

“Wait,” said Aurelia. “Why are my husband and his brother sitting back to back?”

“They cover each other’s doors.”

There was a silence. Serafina drank some tea.

“Does he know it’s a wedding?” Aurelia asked her.

“Yes.”

“Does he know it isn’t a summit?”

“I know,” said Haozhen.

“Then why is there a column for sightlines?”

“Because the tables run north–south and the shutter faces east.”

Aurelia shut her eyes.

Then she pulled out a stool. “Show me all of it.”

She went through it for an hour, hardly speaking. He explained when she asked. He’d put the guests in groups by family and work and friendship. He’d kept the Songs well away from anyone likely to provoke Vittoria, and anyone Vittoria was likely to provoke. He’d put Granny Shum in the middle of the first table, where she could see the whole room and was as far from the speakers as the garage allowed, because loud music hurt her ears and she wouldn’t say so. Mr. Kwok by the kitchen door, because he’d be up and down all afternoon whatever anyone said. Big Wu next to him to carry. His mother next to Granny Shum, so they could disapprove of things together. Mouse at the end of table six, next to the only socket on that wall, because she would bring her laptop to her own funeral.

And one name with a seat but a note: Mo Tianyi — invited. Table four, seat nine, facing the food. Will not come. Keep it anyway.

Serafina looked at that one for a while and didn’t say anything.

Then Aurelia reached column N. SCORE-NEUTRAL.

“What’s this?”

“People who shouldn’t sit next to each other for professional reasons. Old disputes. People who’ll compare results.”

Aurelia read the two names in it. Her own, and Elowen Lin’s.

“Why am I score-neutral?”

“Both of you have spent years taking apart other people’s accounts for fun. If you sit together you’ll talk about money all afternoon. If you sit opposite each other, you’ll talk about everything else.”

Elowen, who had just come in under the shutter with a box of sample ribbons, stopped behind Aurelia’s stool and read it over her shoulder.

“Oh,” she said. “That’s actually rather lovely.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything. She was looking at the spreadsheet. There was something deeply absurd about a man who had spent twelve years arranging the movement of people out of rooms applying exactly the same precision to a banquet. There was also something else. He’d remembered that Granny Shum hated loud music. That Mr. Kwok would want the kitchen. That Mouse needed a socket. That her mother liked to see the door. That she and Elowen deserved one afternoon off.

“You’re wasted on security,” Aurelia said.

“Donatella says the same.”

“You should be running weddings.”

Serafina laughed out loud, and even he smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

The trouble was that the spreadsheet wasn’t finished. Aurelia, scrolling right, noticed that the columns went from R to T.

“Where’s S?”

His hand moved toward the trackpad a fraction of a second too late.

Serafina saw it. “What?”

“Nothing.”

Aurelia unhid the column. S — FINAL POSITION.

There was one entry in it.

SONG, Serafina. Table: top. Seat: 01. Orientation: window. Facing: me.

Nobody said anything at all.

Serafina turned and looked at him. He was looking steadily at the laptop. His face was composed. His ears had gone red.

“You’ve got a column for me.”

“Yes.”

“Facing: me?”

He looked up at last. “You should be able to see me.”

“You’ll be sitting next to me.”

“I know.”

“So why does it matter?”

He paused. Then, very quietly: “I want you to be able to find me. Wherever you look up from.”

Aurelia turned and looked out of the window. Elowen became deeply interested in a sample of ivory grosgrain.

For all the ridiculous columns, the sightlines and the orientations and the doors, it was the only line in the whole thing Serafina wanted to keep. She closed the laptop.

“That’s enough.”

“It isn’t final.”

“It is now.”

“Four people haven’t replied.”

“They can sit where they like.”

He frowned. “That would unbalance table seven.”

She took his hand. “Upstairs.”

“Serafina—”

“Your bride,” she said, “is requesting your attention.”

He stood up. Aurelia watched them go up the iron stairs. When the loft door shut Elowen leaned over.

“That’s very sweet.”

“It’s ridiculous.” Aurelia looked at the closed laptop. “It’s also very sweet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the loft she pushed him back against the door.

“What’s the matter?”

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

She came up on her toes and kissed him. He caught her waist. The kiss was short, and then it wasn’t, when she put her arms round his neck and he lifted her off her feet against him.

“You put me in seat one,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Facing you.”

“Yes.”

“Not facing the door.”

“No.”

“Not covering anybody.”

“No.”

“Not score-neutral.”

“You’re not neutral,” he said, and she laughed into his mouth.

“You’re the reason there’s a plan at all,” he said. “You should have the best seat.”

“I’ve already got the best seat.”

“Which?”

“Next to you,” she said. “And underneath you, in about a minute.”

He carried her to the bed. She pulled his jumper over his head and he pulled hers, and she lay back on the quilt with the mountain road on it and reached for his belt, and he caught her hands.

“Slowly.”

“You’ve been doing spreadsheets for three hours. I’ve waited long enough.”

“Slowly,” he said again, and kissed the inside of her wrist, and the plate under her collarbone, gently, and then lower, not gently at all, until she stopped arguing.

He didn’t count anything. Not the trains going over, not the minutes, not the four guests who hadn’t replied. He undressed her as if he had all afternoon, and took her with his mouth until she was gripping the quilt with both hands and saying his name to the ceiling, and only then came up over her and into her, slowly, with her ankles crossed behind his back and her eyes on his. She held his face in both hands. He moved in her in long deep strokes, unhurried, and she let him set it for once, and the light from the little window went gold across them both, and when she came it was with her mouth against his shoulder and her whole body shaking under him, and he followed her a moment later, his forehead pressed to hers, his eyes open, finding her exactly where he’d planned she’d be.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven forty-three that night he came down to shut the laptop.

He checked the final allocation once. Two hundred guests. Nine tables. Nineteen columns. Then he noticed something.

Seat one, top table, was still marked Orientation: window.

He changed it to Orientation: facing Haozhen, and saved the file, and shut the lid.

Upstairs his bride was asleep on his side of the bed with one hand on his pillow. The wedding was ten weeks away. There were flowers to choose and words to write and a hundred things he hadn’t thought of yet.

They could wait. He got in beside her and let her pull him close. He didn’t count the exits. For one night there was only one place he wanted to be, and he was in it.

chapters.title: The Youngest Sister Hacks the Bodyguard
chapters.desc: March 2025. Zhao is in Rotterdam and the youngest Lin sister is giving a talk about a bank that would rather she didn’t. Elowen asks for a favour. He has no identity card, no job and a brand-new phone. She has his phone open in four minutes. He is very impressed. She is very annoyed that he is impressed.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t make it weird.”
chapters.content:
At seventeen minutes past eight on Sunday the twenty-third of March, Elowen Lin rang him.

He was in the garage holding a door panel against Nonna while Serafina wrestled the last clip home. He answered on speaker.

“I need a favour,” said Elowen.

She sounded tired. In his experience that meant something had already happened.

“Zhendong’s in Rotterdam. His flight’s been cancelled; he won’t be back till tomorrow night. Eliana’s giving a lecture at the university at ten tomorrow morning. About a bank.” A pause. “A bank that has recently become very interested in where Eliana goes. Somebody’s been ringing the department asking for her timetable. And on Friday a man followed her from the library to the bus stop.”

Serafina put the trim tool down.

“I don’t want to make a fuss,” said Elowen. “I also don’t want her going on her own. Would you take her? Just until Zhendong lands.”

He looked at Serafina. She nodded.

“Yes,” he said.

“Thank you. I’ll send the address.” Another pause. “One thing. She’ll be difficult.”

“How difficult?” said Serafina.

“She’s my youngest sister,” said Elowen, and rang off.

✦ ✦ ✦

Eliana Lin opened the door of the Lin house in the Walled City at twenty-five to eight on Monday morning, twenty-two years old, in an enormous grey university hoodie and black trousers and one sock. The other sock was in her hand. Her hair was up in a claw clip and her round glasses were on top of her head.

She looked at him. Then past him at the empty street.

“Where’s Zhendong’s replacement?”

“I’m taking you.”

She looked him up and down. Dark jacket, plain trousers, clean resoled shoes. No earpiece. No badge. No card on a lanyard.

“Name?”

“Qin Haozhen.”

“Occupation?”

“Today? This.”

“That’s not an occupation. Identification?”

“I haven’t got any,” he said. “At the moment, officially, I’ve never existed. There’s a letter.”

She stared at him.

“Come in,” she said at last. “I need to check you’re not terrible.”

Serafina, who had driven him there, leaned on the door frame. “Good luck.”

Eliana looked at her. “You’re the one with the car.”

“I’m the one with several cars.”

“Is he always like this?”

“Only when he’s being polite.”

“Interesting,” said Eliana, and held out her hand to him, palm up. “Phone.”

“Why?”

“Security assessment.”

He gave it to her.

“Hao,” said Serafina. “You’re handing a stranger your phone.”

“She’s Elowen’s sister.”

“That is not a security credential.”

Eliana was already walking away with it. “Three minutes,” she called.

It took her three minutes and fifty seconds. He knew because he timed her, standing in the kitchen while she sat at the table with his phone on a cable to her laptop, typing fast.

“Stop watching my hands.”

“You’ve got my phone.”

“Exactly. I’m concentrating.”

He stopped watching her hands and watched her screen. She sighed loudly.

At three fifty she unplugged it and held it out. “Done.”

His lock screen had gone. In its place was a photograph of a matte black car with a white seven, coming over the last crest at Baizhang with two wheels nearly off the road and the summit flag behind it. When he touched the screen to check the time, the phone made the noise of an engine at full throttle on the limiter.

“What have you done?”

“Improved it.”

He went into the settings. She had taken off two old apps, updated a system he’d been ignoring for a year, and put on a security tool he’d heard of and approved of. She’d turned off three notifications that leaked his location. She had made a new contact group called PEOPLE WHO WILL ACTUALLY ANSWER.

“Why is Serafina first?”

“Because she’s your emergency contact.”

“She isn’t.”

“Your phone says she is now.”

He looked up. “That’s efficient. Three minutes fifty.”

“You timed me?”

“Yes. It was very impressive.”

Eliana looked genuinely offended. “Don’t patronise me.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re using the voice people use when they’re patronising someone.”

“It’s the only voice I’ve got,” he said.

“Is he always like this?” Eliana asked Serafina again.

“Unfortunately,” said Serafina, laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lecture theatre was half full by ten to ten. She went down to the front with her laptop bag, and he took a seat at the back, by the door, where he could see the room and the two exits and nobody would think about him.

She noticed. “You’re not going to stand next to the lectern?”

“No.”

“Good. I don’t want people thinking I’m important.”

“You are important.”

He said it so plainly that she didn’t know what to do with it. She turned round. “Don’t make it weird.”

Her lecture was called Open Doors. It was about a bank whose systems had been built to keep strangers out and had never once been designed to stop the people already inside. She showed, step by step and without a single live password on the screen, how permissions had been handed down from one job to the next for nine years without anybody taking them away; how a contractor’s access token from 2016 had never been switched off; how a “restricted” system could be reached through a forgotten administrative door that anyone with a staff login could walk through. She used the bank’s own published documents, and records passed to her by somebody inside who had asked to remain unnamed, and a demonstration on a dummy network of her own. She didn’t touch anything real.

Her point was simple. A locked front door means nothing if you’ve left the staff entrance open.

He listened. He understood enough to recognise the shape of it: a bank relying on a perimeter that wasn’t there.

At the questions a man in the third row stood up. “You’re saying the bank’s negligent?”

“I’m saying its controls are inadequate.”

“Can you prove it?”

“To the regulator. On Thursday.”

He sat down. She took six more. She was sharp and quick and obviously enjoying herself.

He wasn’t watching her. He was watching a man by the door at the side, in a grey coat, who had come in twenty minutes late and hadn’t once looked at the slides.

When the applause started the man left before it ended.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting at the side entrance when they came out, a man in his forties with a phone held low at his hip, lens out.

“Miss Lin.”

Eliana stopped. “Do I know you?”

“No. But I think we should have a word. Privately.”

Haozhen stepped half a pace forward. “No.”

“I’m not talking to you.”

“I know.”

“You’ve made some allegations,” the man told Eliana. “People are worried about where they lead. You’re young. You don’t understand how these things are done.”

Eliana’s chin came up. “I understand enough.”

The man took a step toward her.

Haozhen moved once. Not fast. He changed where he was standing, so that the man could no longer get to her without going through him. Then he held out his hand.

“Phone.”

“What?”

“You’ve been recording her for six minutes. Give me the phone.”

The man laughed. Haozhen didn’t. He just went on holding out his hand, and looking at the man, and after four seconds the man stopped laughing.

He gave him the phone.

Haozhen didn’t look at the video. He went to the call log, and read out loud, pleasantly, the name and the extension of the last number the man had rung, at ten past nine that morning: a switchboard at the bank, and a department, and a first name.

“That’s who sent you,” he said. “I’ll ring him myself this afternoon, and tell him he’s employing a man who stands outside lecture theatres filming girls of twenty-two on a phone registered in his own name. Then I’ll ring the regulator, who Miss Lin is seeing on Thursday, and tell them the same thing.” He deleted the video, and the copy in the cloud, and held the phone out. “Or you can walk away now and he’ll never know you were careless.”

The man looked at him. Two campus security officers in yellow jackets were coming round the corner of the building.

He took his phone and went.

Eliana watched him go. Then she looked at Haozhen.

“You didn’t touch him.”

“No.”

“You didn’t even raise your voice.”

“No.”

“That was the most frightening thing I’ve ever seen.”

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.” She was quiet. “I think I see why Elowen rang you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They stopped at a café. She had something iced and sweet. He had tea. She put her laptop on the table and turned it round.

“I want to show you something.”

On the screen was a live map, a small blue dot moving slowly round an oval.

“What’s that?”

“Serafina.”

He looked at it properly. The circuit in the north. The dot was taking the Needle.

“She asked me to set up location sharing for the team,” said Eliana. “In case anyone breaks down on the motorway. I made it a bit more useful. It reads her phone’s GPS in her suit pocket. Every two seconds.” She tapped the screen. “That’s lap nine. She’s a tenth up on lap eight.”

“Did she agree to that?”

“She agreed to location sharing.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I know,” said Eliana serenely.

His phone went off on the table with the sound of an engine on the rev limiter. Half the café turned round. Eliana nearly spilt her drink.

“Hello?”

“Why does your phone sound like that?” said Serafina, from the pit lane.

“Ask your new friend.”

“She’s done something to you, hasn’t she?”

“Yes.”

“Good. You needed updating. Are you coming?”

“After four.”

“Bring egg sandwiches.”

“I know.”

“Love you.”

“Love you,” he said, and rang off, and found Eliana looking at him over her glasses with enormous satisfaction.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty past five a young man in a black leather jacket was waiting on the kerb outside the Lin house with two coffees, looking at his watch. Wang Yu Chen, from the Wang house on the other side of the wall, who had been waiting for her on one kerb or another since she was nine.

“You’re late,” he said.

“I was giving a lecture.”

“You said four.”

“It finished at four.”

“It’s twenty past five.”

“Then you’ve been waiting an hour and twenty minutes,” said Eliana. “Good arithmetic.”

Yu Chen looked past her at Haozhen. “Who’s he?”

“My bodyguard.”

“I’m not her bodyguard,” said Haozhen.

“Same thing,” said Eliana.

Yu Chen looked at him a moment longer. “Thanks for bringing her back.”

“Look after her.”

“I can hear you both,” said Eliana. She took one of the coffees out of Yu Chen’s hand. “Go home, Qin Haozhen. Zhendong lands at seven.”

“Ring if anything happens.”

“Yes, Dad.” Then, as he turned: “Your wallpaper. Don’t change it.”

“I wasn’t going to,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he got back to the garage Serafina was flat on the creeper under Gilded with only her boots showing.

“Don’t move,” she said. “Pass me the ten.”

He handed it down. She took it without looking. A minute later she rolled out, grease across one cheek and her hair falling down.

“Why are you smiling?”

“She hacked my phone in three minutes fifty.”

“I know.”

“She’s put a tracker on you that reads your suit every two seconds.”

“I know.” Serafina grinned up at him. “I asked her for location sharing. I didn’t know she’d make your phone sound like a grid.”

His phone lit up in his hand. Her car, at the top of the mountain.

“It’s cute,” she said.

“Cute.”

“Very.”

She was still lying on the creeper, her head on the padded end, looking up at him. He crouched down by her head, and then lower, and put one hand flat on the concrete beside her ear, and leaned down over her, and kissed her upside down.

She laughed into his mouth and reached up and caught his collar. “Hello.”

“Hello.”

“Long day?”

“Yes.”

“Did you miss me?”

“Yes,” he said, and kissed her again, and this time she pulled him down so that his hair brushed Gilded’s sill, and he didn’t care.

“You’re getting grease on your good jacket.”

“I know.”

He slid one arm under her knees and the other behind her back and lifted her off the creeper.

“Hao! I’m not done!”

“You’ve been under there for an hour.”

“I’ve got a job.”

“So have I.”

“What job?”

“Taking you upstairs,” he said, already on the iron steps with her in his arms and the ten-millimetre spanner still in her hand.

Behind them Gilded ticked as she cooled. In his pocket the phone lit up once more on its own, her car on top of the mountain, and he decided he could live with that, and with the engine too.

chapters.title: The Fake Name He Liked Best
chapters.desc: May 2027, a ferry on Lake Como, on the way to see an old man with eleven cars and a parrot and a red rally car with a forged chassis plate. He has had nineteen names. On the ferry, he tells her about the one he liked best: a deckhand called Ah Sang, on an island boat in a southern sea, whom nobody ever wanted anything from. She calls him by it once.
chapters.epigraph: “I want you to use mine.”
chapters.content:
The ferry was late, and Serafina took it personally.

She stood at the rail on Saturday the fifteenth of May 2027 with a paper cup of coffee and watched the lake go by underneath: green and then blue and then green again, the mountains stacked up behind in layers of grey, villas and cypresses scattered down the lower slopes like dropped dice. Behind her Haozhen was reading Signor Bassi’s email for the fourth time.

“Eleven cars,” he said.

“You’ve read it.”

“And a parrot.”

“I believe in the parrot. Nobody invents a parrot when they’ve already got eleven cars.”

“You’d be surprised what people invent,” he said, and folded the printout.

Bassi was eighty-six. He had bought Lot 9 after all, in the end, the red 1974 rally car from the Autumn Reception, for a third of its estimate at a dealer’s in Turin in the spring of 2023, forged chassis plate and all, because he’d decided that a beautiful car with one lie in it was still a beautiful car. He wanted her to see it again, and drive it. And he’d added a line at the bottom of the email that Serafina had shown Haozhen without comment.

Bring your husband. I believe I have seen him before. Some faces are easier to remember than others.

“You’ve had nineteen names,” she said, watching the water. It wasn’t quite a question.

“Officially, nineteen.”

“Officially?”

“Some only lasted a few days. Some were only on one piece of paper.”

“Did you like any of them?”

He thought about it. “Most of them were useful.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

The ferry went into a patch of sun. He leaned on the rail next to her.

“Ah Sang,” he said.

She turned her head.

“A deckhand. On an island boat in the southern sea. I was twenty-three. Seven months.” He looked at the water. “He carried bags. Coiled the ropes. Helped old women off at the landing and knew which passengers would be sick and which wanted to sit by the engine because it was warm. He lived in a room over a shop that sold fishing line, and bought noodles from a woman at the harbour every night, and played cards with the other deckhands on Sundays and lost.”

“Did they know his real name?”

“No. He knew all of theirs.”

“And nobody wanted anything from him?”

“Nothing that mattered. Carry this. Fix that. Take an extra crossing.” A small smile. “One old woman wanted cigarettes from across the border. He bought the wrong ones. She complained for three days.”

“Terrible service.”

“He went back and bought the right ones.”

“Ah Sang sounds nice.”

“He was,” said Haozhen. “For seven months nobody needed me to know anything. Nobody asked me to find anyone. I wasn’t responsible for what happened to anybody after the boat left the quay. I was a man who could tie a knot.”

She slipped her hand into his. “Ah Sang,” she said, trying it.

His fingers closed round hers. “Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Call me that.” He looked at her. “I want you to use mine.”

“Haozhen,” she said.

“Yes.”

She lifted his hand and kissed the knuckles. He turned to look at the lake. But she saw his face change, and she understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

Signor Bassi lived above the water at the end of a gravel drive between lemon trees, with eleven cars in two long garages and a grey parrot on a stand in the hall.

“Bastardo!” the parrot told Haozhen, before he was through the door.

“Good morning,” said Haozhen.

“Bastardo!”

“Ah! You’ve met Lorenzo,” said Bassi, coming down the hall on a stick, silver-haired and delighted. “He says it only to people he respects.”

“Then I’m honoured,” said Serafina, and Bassi kissed her on both cheeks and said she looked more like her grandmother every year and less like her mother, and that both were compliments.

Then he looked at Haozhen, the way he’d look at a car he was being asked to buy.

“Qin Haozhen.”

“Signor Bassi.”

“I wondered if you’d come.” He turned and led them into his study. Rally photographs on every wall. Models on every shelf. A newspaper page in a frame by the window, yellowing: page nine of the business section, from a Sunday in October 2022, a photograph of a terrace on Battery Hill with four hundred people on it and a red car in a glass pavilion.

Bassi tapped the glass with the end of his stick, at the very edge of the picture, by a service door.

A man in a dark suit. Ordinary shoes. A face nobody would remember.

“I bought that paper for my car,” said Bassi, pouring coffee. “And then in January I read in the Brussels paper that a Belgian man called Marchal had vanished from that same terrace on that same night, and his wife was begging anybody who had seen anything. So I looked at my picture again.” He set a cup down by Haozhen. “Sixty years I’ve spent watching rally mechanics who don’t want to be noticed. You were not very good at being invisible to an old man with a magnifying glass.”

Serafina looked at Haozhen. Haozhen looked at the photograph.

“No,” he said.

“He’s home now? The Belgian?”

“He’s home. The year before last.”

“Good,” said Bassi. He looked at Haozhen longer. “Then I won’t ask you anything else. Now. The car.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lot 9 was alone in the second garage under a single light.

Even before the door went up Serafina could smell it: old leather, old fuel, the faint warm metal of a car that was kept carefully and not driven enough. Then the red came up under the light, short as a sneeze and low as a cat, and she stopped in the doorway.

“Oh.”

Not pristine, not a museum piece. Small chips in the paint, old repairs at the edges of the arches, the leather on the driver’s bolster worn shiny. But it stood the way it had stood in a glass pavilion five years ago, like a thing built for one purpose only.

She crouched by the front of the cockpit. The plate was different. Clean, original, the right rivets.

“You found the real one.”

“In a scrapyard outside Bologna. Four years it took.” Bassi lifted something wrapped in a cloth off the bench. “So this is no longer needed.”

He unfolded it. The forged plate. Right shape, right number, wrong rivets. Still stained brown round the edges with somebody’s cold tea.

“I bought the car,” said Bassi. “Not the lie. But I kept the lie, because it was the only dishonest thing about an honest car.” He put it into her hands. “And because you saw it, in your sister’s dress, on your back on a marble floor. Take it.”

“Signor Bassi, it’s part of the car’s history—”

“Exactly. And you understand what that means.” He pressed the keys into her other hand. “Now drive it.”

“On the road?”

“Unless you’d prefer my garden.”

Haozhen took one step forward. “Is it insured?”

Bassi stared at him. Then he laughed so hard that Lorenzo began shouting from the hall.

“Madonna! The woman asks about the car. The man asks about the insurance.”

“That’s why he’s coming,” said Serafina.

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was louder than she’d remembered: a hard, high, mechanical voice that filled the narrow road between the villa walls and came back off the lake. She drove carefully at first. The clutch. The steering, which was alive in her hands. The brakes, which were firm and old.

“Tyres?” he said.

“Not ideal.”

“Then don’t push.”

“I’m not going to race it.”

“You sound disappointed.”

“I’m relieved,” he said, with one hand resting easily on his knee.

The road curved under a long line of cypresses and opened onto the water, wide and blue with the sun moving across it. She changed down. The engine answered. There was nothing in the world but the road and the sound and him beside her.

She pulled into a lay-by under the cypresses and switched off. The silence came back slowly, the engine ticking.

He looked at her. “What?”

She leaned across the gap between the seats.

“Ah Sang,” she said.

His eyes changed. Then he reached up and put his hand on her cheek.

“I asked you not to.”

“I know. I wanted to see if you’d answer to it.”

“Did I?”

“No,” she said. “You answered to me. Haozhen.”

He kissed her. Slow and warm and in no hurry, with his thumb under her eye, in a car older than either of them on the edge of a lake. When they came apart she rested her forehead against his and said it again, his real name, and he kissed her again, and this time she felt him smile against her mouth.

✦ ✦ ✦

A year later they found Auntie Choi.

She lived on the second floor over a bakery in a harbour town in the south, where the sea air had turned the balcony railings white and the stairwell smelled of warm bread. He knew the building before they reached the first landing. He stopped on it.

“All right?”

He nodded. Then shook his head. “I’m not sure.”

“Do you want to go?”

“No,” he said. “I want to see her.”

She was small and white-haired and bent, with bright eyes, and when she opened the door she looked at him without saying anything. Then she reached up and put her dry old palm against his face.

“Ah Sang.”

He shut his eyes.

“You took your time,” said Auntie Choi.

“Yes.”

“You bought me the wrong cigarettes.”

“I bought you the right ones.”

“Three days later.” She looked past him at Serafina. “And this?”

“My wife,” he said.

“Good. You look better with somebody next to you. You always did look like a man who’d been left on the quay.” She stood back. “Come in. Both of you.”

The flat was full of ordinary things. A kettle. A sewing basket. A television under a crocheted cover. A small carved wooden boat on the windowsill. Then Auntie Choi opened a cupboard and took out a dented tin locker box, the kind the boat company had given its crews, and set it on the table.

“You left this. When you went. In a hurry, without your wages. I kept it.”

Inside: a faded work shirt. A cheap watch that had stopped. A pocket notebook, blank. And a photograph of the crew on the quay, eleven men squinting into the sun.

He was in the back row. Twenty-three. Thinner. Longer hair. And smiling: a real, broad, unguarded smile that changed his whole face. Serafina could count on one hand the times she had seen that smile.

“You were happy,” she said.

“I was.”

Auntie Choi made tea. Then she sat down and folded her hands and looked at him.

“Sing.”

He looked up. “What?”

“You sang while you swabbed the deck. Every morning. The same song. You had the worst voice on the southern sea.” She turned to Serafina. “Terrible. The gulls left.”

Serafina looked at him. She knew perfectly well what his voice could do. She’d heard it get ninety-eight in a room above a bar.

“Please,” she said. “Just one.”

“No.”

“Sing, Ah Sang,” said Auntie Choi.

He sighed. Then sitting at her kitchen table, he began.

It was terrible. Not slightly off, not charmingly rough. Terrible: flat from the first note, losing the tune in the middle, the words falling apart in the second verse. Auntie Choi put her head back and laughed until she cried. And Serafina, laughing with her, saw his breathing stay perfectly even under every wrong note, and his timing land exactly where he meant it not to, and understood that he was lifting again. On purpose. For an old woman in a flat over a bakery who had loved a deckhand who couldn’t sing.

This time she didn’t catch his sleeve. She let him.

“You haven’t improved,” said Auntie Choi, wiping her eyes.

“I wasn’t trying.”

“Good. It would be a shame to lose a gift like that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the harbour was bright. A boat was going out, its engine thudding. He watched it all the way to the mouth of the harbour.

“You were happy there,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Do you miss it?”

“I miss how simple it was,” he said. “Not the name.”

“Good.”

He turned to her. “I’m glad you know that version of me. He was real.”

“I’m glad he existed,” she said. “I’m gladder he’s you.”

He bent and kissed her on the harbour wall with the boat going out behind them.

“Hello, Haozhen,” she said.

“Hello, Sera.”

And when somebody called his name now, he didn’t have to remember which one he was supposed to answer to.
